quote: The AUROC, sensitivity, and specificity of the AI were 0.648 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.630-0.665), 35.3% (CI, 24.7-47.8), and 94.2% (CI, 93.3-95.0), respectively.

title: Effect of a Machine Learning Recommender System and Viral Peer Marketing Intervention on Smoking Cessation
outcome: 6-month self-reported 7-day point prevalence smoking cessation, ML recommender vs standard messaging
effect: No significant difference: 35.4% (146/412) ML recommender vs 40.1% (156/389) standard; adjusted OR 0.81 (95% CI 0.61-1.08).
quote: There was no significant difference in 6-month smoking cessation between ML recommender (146 of 412 participants [35.4%] with outcome data) and standard messaging (156 of 389 participants [40.1%] with outcome data) groups (adjusted odds ratio, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.61-1.08).

title: Long-term Effect of Machine Learning-Triggered Behavioral Nudges on Serious Illness Conversations and End-of-Life Outcomes Among Patients With Cancer: A Randomized Clinical Trial
outcome: Intervention effect on SIC rates across sociodemographic subgroups
effect: Effect significant across all subgroups; greater impact among Medicaid beneficiaries (5.2% vs 0.9%; aOR 2.19, P = .03 for interaction); no other significant interactions.
quote: The intervention effect was significant across all subgroups (eTable 2 in Supplement 2 ); interaction models revealed a greater impact on SIC rates among Medicaid beneficiaries (5.2% of encounters in the intervention group vs 0.9% in the control group; aOR, 2.19 [95% CI, 1.10-4.37]; P = .03 for interaction).

title: Long-term Effect of Machine Learning-Triggered Behavioral Nudges on Serious Illness Conversations and End-of-Life Outcomes Among Patients With Cancer: A Randomized Clinical Trial
outcome: End-of-life systemic therapy and other end-of-life outcomes versus usual care
effect: End-of-life systemic therapy: 7.5% [72 of 957 patients] vs 10.4% [24 of 231 patients]; aOR, 0.25 [95% CI, 0.11-0.57]; P = .001. Other end-of-life outcomes did not differ.
quote: Intervention patients were less likely than control patients to receive systemic therapy at the end of life (all decedents: 7.5% [72 of 957 patients] vs 10.4% [24 of 231 patients]; aOR, 0.25 [95% CI, 0.11-0.57]; P = .001; high-risk decedents: 7.2% [50 of 696 patients] vs 8.3% [15 of 181 patients]; aOR, 0.37 [95% CI, 0.13-1.04]; P = .06) ( Table ).

title: Long-term Effect of Machine Learning-Triggered Behavioral Nudges on Serious Illness Conversations and End-of-Life Outcomes Among Patients With Cancer: A Randomized Clinical Trial
outcome: SIC rates and end-of-life outcomes versus usual care in stepped-wedge RCT
effect: SICs increased (aOR 2.09, 95% CI 1.53-2.87); end-of-life systemic therapy decreased (7.5% vs 10.4%; aOR 0.25); no effect on hospice enrollment or length of stay, inpatient death, or end-of-life ICU use.
quote: In adjusted analyses, the intervention was associated with increased SICs for all patients (adjusted odds ratio, 2.09 [95% CI, 1.53-2.87]; P < .001) and decreased end-of-life systemic therapy (7.5% [72 of 957 patients] vs 10.4% [24 of 231 patients]; adjusted odds ratio, 0.25 [95% CI, 0.11-0.57]; P = .001) relative to controls, but there was no effect on hospice enrollment or length of stay, inpatient death, or end-of-life ICU use.

title: Long-term Effect of Machine Learning-Triggered Behavioral Nudges on Serious Illness Conversations and End-of-Life Outcomes Among Patients With Cancer: A Randomized Clinical Trial
outcome: Serious illness conversations following risk-triggered clinician prompts specifying the intended action
effect: With the bundled intervention, high-risk encounter SIC rates increased from 3.4% (59 of 1754 encounters) to 13.5% (510 of 3765 encounters); aOR, 2.62 [95% CI, 1.84-3.72]; P < .001.
quote: Among encounters with high-risk patients, the unadjusted SIC rate was 3.4% (59 of 1754 encounters) and 13.5% (510 of 3765 encounters) in the control and intervention periods, respectively.

title: Long-term Effect of Machine Learning-Triggered Behavioral Nudges on Serious Illness Conversations and End-of-Life Outcomes Among Patients With Cancer: A Randomized Clinical Trial
outcome: outcomes by sociodemographic subgroup
effect: The intervention significantly increased serious illness conversation rates across all subgroups, with a significantly greater impact among Medicaid beneficiaries (aOR 2.19).
quote: The intervention effect was significant across all subgroups (eTable 2 in Supplement 2 ); interaction models revealed a greater impact on SIC rates among Medicaid beneficiaries (5.2% of encounters in the intervention group vs 0.9% in the control group; aOR, 2.19 [95% CI, 1.10-4.37]; P = .03 for interaction).

title: A hybrid machine learning framework to improve prediction of all-cause rehospitalization among elderly patients in Hong Kong
outcome: Prospective validation of the model's rehospitalisation predictions after a pilot implementation at the hospital
effect: tZIP prediction of rehospitalisation from 28 to 365 days achieved above 80% discrimination accuracy retrospectively and prospectively in two out-of-sample cohorts, outperforming Cox and linear models.
quote: The tZIP prediction of rehospitalisation from 28 days to 365 days was achieved at above 80% discrimination accuracy retrospectively and prospectively in two out-of-sample cohorts.

title: User-centred design of a clinical decision support system for palliative care: Insights from healthcare professionals
outcome: Whether usability testing with potential users identified workflow implementation issues
effect: Think-aloud and UX assessment identified most workflow implementation issues; SUS 62.7±14.1 and 65±26.2 in two rounds; UEQ-S 1.42 and 1.5.
quote: The think-aloud method and including the UX dimension helped us to identify most of the workflow implementation issues.

title: A recalibrated prediction model can identify level-1 trauma patients at risk of nosocomial pneumonia
venue: Archives of orthopaedic and trauma surgery
outcome: Calibration and discrimination after local intercept and full recalibration of imported model
effect: Intercept moved from -3.08 to 0.80, giving better calibration; full recalibration AUC 0.84 and Brier 0.089 to 0.087; adding age raised AUC to 0.87.
quote: After intercept recalibration, the model’s intercept increased from -3.08 in the Croce model to 0.80 in our cohort, showing better calibration (Fig. 2 B).

title: A recalibrated prediction model can identify level-1 trauma patients at risk of nosocomial pneumonia
venue: Archives of orthopaedic and trauma surgery
outcome: Differences between development and local cohorts and resulting miscalibration
effect: Croce cohort had more penetrating trauma (23% vs 3%), younger patients (median 35 vs 51), more laparotomy (14% vs 3%); pneumonia incidence 5.6% vs 10.6%; calibration slope 0.63.
quote: However, in Croce’s cohort, the incidence of penetrating trauma was higher (23% vs. 3%), patients were younger (median 35 vs. 51 years), and relatively more patients underwent an emergent laparotomy (14% vs. 3%) compared to the Dutch cohort [ 6 ].

title: A recalibrated prediction model can identify level-1 trauma patients at risk of nosocomial pneumonia
venue: Archives of orthopaedic and trauma surgery
outcome: Model performance at a new external site relative to development
effect: AUC fell from 0.97 at internal validation to 0.83 externally; predicted risk too low (6.4% vs 10.6%); calibration slope 0.63.
quote: The original model showed good discriminatory capacity (AUC 0.83, 95% CI 0.79 – 0.87) but was overfitted for use in the Dutch population (calibration slope 0.63; mean predicted risk 6.4% vs. 10.6% observed risk).

title: A recalibrated prediction model can identify level-1 trauma patients at risk of nosocomial pneumonia
venue: Archives of orthopaedic and trauma surgery
outcome: Local validation performance
effect: On local Dutch historical data, AUC was 0.83 (95% CI 0.79 – 0.87), calibration slope 0.63, and predicted risk 6.4% vs. 10.6% observed.
quote: The original model showed good discriminatory capacity (AUC 0.83, 95% CI 0.79 – 0.87) but was overfitted for use in the Dutch population (calibration slope 0.63; mean predicted risk 6.4% vs. 10.6% observed risk).

title: A recalibrated prediction model can identify level-1 trauma patients at risk of nosocomial pneumonia
venue: Archives of orthopaedic and trauma surgery
outcome: Discrimination and calibration of externally developed model on local historical data before and after recalibration
effect: Original AUC 0.83, mean predicted risk 6.4% vs observed 10.6%, calibration slope 0.63; after full recalibration AUC 0.84, Brier 0.087, calibration improved.
quote: After full model recalibration, discrimination (AUC 0.84, 95% CI 0.80-0.88) and calibration improved.

title: A recalibrated prediction model can identify level-1 trauma patients at risk of nosocomial pneumonia
venue: Archives of orthopaedic and trauma surgery
outcome: Generalization of predictive model to a new population and outcome definition
effect: Model developed for VAP in a US center underpredicted nosocomial pneumonia in a Dutch cohort; calibration slope 0.63.
quote: The calibration slope was 0.63, suggesting some overfitting in the original study compared to our population.

title: A recalibrated prediction model can identify level-1 trauma patients at risk of nosocomial pneumonia
venue: Archives of orthopaedic and trauma surgery
outcome: Discrimination-calibration mismatch
effect: Despite AUC 0.83 (95% CI 0.79 – 0.87), calibration was poor: slope 0.63 and mean predicted risk 6.4% vs. 10.6% observed.
quote: The original model showed good discriminatory capacity (AUC 0.83, 95% CI 0.79 – 0.87) but was overfitted for use in the Dutch population (calibration slope 0.63; mean predicted risk 6.4% vs. 10.6% observed risk).

title: Is the generalizability of a developed artificial intelligence algorithm for COVID-19 on chest CT sufficient for clinical use? Results from the International Consortium for COVID-19 Imaging AI (ICOVAI)
outcome: Performance on internal test versus independent external multicenter validation (CO-RADS kappa, lung opacity DSC)
effect: CO-RADS linear weighted kappa fell from 0.78 internal to 0.62 external (p<0.0001); opacity segmentation fell from DSC 0.76 to mDSC 0.59 (p<0.0001); lung contour unchanged (0.97).
quote: External validation can highlight the shortcomings of a predictive model, which were not apparent during internal testing on CT scans sampled out of the same cohort.

title: Is the generalizability of a developed artificial intelligence algorithm for COVID-19 on chest CT sufficient for clinical use? Results from the International Consortium for COVID-19 Imaging AI (ICOVAI)
outcome: Performance drop when applied to data from other institutions than development
effect: Significant reduction in lung opacity segmentation (DSC 0.76 to 0.59) and CO-RADS agreement (kappa 0.78 to 0.62) on external multicenter data.
quote: Our work shows that published results of COVID-19 segmentation on internal test sets may not generalize well to patient data from other institutions.

title: Is the generalizability of a developed artificial intelligence algorithm for COVID-19 on chest CT sufficient for clinical use? Results from the International Consortium for COVID-19 Imaging AI (ICOVAI)
outcome: Independent external validation versus internal testing by developers
effect: Independent validation revealed significantly lower performance (kappa 0.62 vs 0.78; opacity DSC 0.59 vs 0.76), showing that internal results overstated performance.
quote: The study demonstrates the importance of independent external validation of AI models.

title: Is the generalizability of a developed artificial intelligence algorithm for COVID-19 on chest CT sufficient for clinical use? Results from the International Consortium for COVID-19 Imaging AI (ICOVAI)
outcome: Performance across sites in external multicenter validation
effect: External multicenter validation (five hospitals) showed reduced performance versus internal test; annotation platform differences and site variation may contribute. Site-specific results not reported.
quote: We observed a significant reduction in performance on the external test as compared to the internal test for lung opacity segmentation and CO-RADS prediction, but not for lung contour segmentation.

title: Is the generalizability of a developed artificial intelligence algorithm for COVID-19 on chest CT sufficient for clinical use? Results from the International Consortium for COVID-19 Imaging AI (ICOVAI)
outcome: COVID-19 opacity segmentation accuracy
effect: Lung opacities DSC was 0.59 on external validation versus 0.76 internally (p < 0.0001).
quote: Lung opacities segmentation performance was adequate internally (DSC = 0.76), but significantly worse on external validation (DSC = 0.59, p < 0.0001).

title: Is the generalizability of a developed artificial intelligence algorithm for COVID-19 on chest CT sufficient for clinical use? Results from the International Consortium for COVID-19 Imaging AI (ICOVAI)
outcome: external vs internal segmentation and CO-RADS classification performance
effect: Internal vs external: lung opacity DSC was 0.76 vs 0.59 (p < 0.0001); CO-RADS linear kappa was 0.78 vs 0.62 (p < 0.0001); lung contour DSC was 0.97 in both (p = 0.97).
quote: Lung opacities segmentation performance was adequate internally (DSC = 0.76), but significantly worse on external validation (DSC = 0.59, p < 0.0001).

title: Prospective Real-Time Validation of a Lung Ultrasound Deep Learning Model in the ICU
outcome: Translation of previously validated classification performance to real-time bedside use
effect: Bedside performance was reported as equally good as prior validation: accuracy of 95%, sensitivity of 93%, and specificity of 96% against expert annotation.
quote: A previously validated DL classification model performs equally well in real-time at the bedside when platformed on a portable device.

title: Prospective Real-Time Validation of a Lung Ultrasound Deep Learning Model in the ICU
outcome: Prospective real-time bedside accuracy versus blinded expert annotation
effect: Real-time inference accuracy 95%, sensitivity 93%, specificity 96% for B line pattern; previously validated model performed equally well in real time at bedside.
quote: When compared with gold standard expert annotation, the real-time inference yielded an accuracy of 95%, sensitivity of 93%, and specificity of 96% for identification of the B line pattern.

title: DeepFundus: A flow-cytometry-like image quality classifier for boosting the whole life cycle of medical artificial intelligence
outcome: Diagnostic AI sensitivity/accuracy for drusen in good vs poor quality images after DeepFundus filtering
effect: Overall quality filter: drusen sensitivity 0.853 (GQ) vs 0.494 (PQ), difference 0.360, p<0.001; accuracy 0.938 vs 0.914, p=0.002. Similar results in other 6 filters.
quote: the GQ group demonstrated significantly higher sensitivity and accuracy values.

title: DeepFundus: A flow-cytometry-like image quality classifier for boosting the whole life cycle of medical artificial intelligence
outcome: Diagnostic performance under poor image quality
effect: Drusen sensitivity/accuracy: GQ 0.853/0.938 vs PQ 0.494/0.914; differences 0.360 and 0.024, p<0.001 and p=0.002.
quote: In a community-based cohort for AMD screening, AI achieved sensitivities of 0.853 (95% CI: 0.830–0.874) and 0.494 (0.430–0.557); specificities of 0.975 (0.968–0.981) and 0.981 (0.972–0.987); and accuracies of 0.938 (0.929–0.946) and 0.914 (0.900–0.926) in detecting drusen in the overall GQ and PQ groups, respectively; the GQ group demonstrated significantly higher sensitivity and accuracy values.

title: Automatic mammographic breast density classification in Chinese women: clinical validation of a deep learning model
outcome: Radiologist inter-reader consistency (kappa, ICC) before versus after DL model assistance; overreliance not assessed
effect: Two-category K/ICC rose to 0.81, 0.81, 0.80 from 0.73, 0.75, 0.76; four-category rose to 0.81, 0.82, 0.82 from 0.73, 0.79, 0.78. Overreliance was not assessed.
quote: The consistency within the junior group, the senior group, and among all radiologists improved with the help of the DL model.

title: Non-task expert physicians benefit from correct explainable AI advice when reviewing X-rays
outcome: Physician diagnostic accuracy with vs without visual annotation on X-ray advice
effect: Annotated advice raised accuracy overall (OR 2.30, p=0.002); IM/EM physicians improved by 5.66% (p=0.042); radiologists 3.41% (p=0.120, non-significant).
quote: When looking at the results separated by task expertise (defined by discipline), we found that providing annotated advice improved the mean performance of the IM/EM physicians in our experiment by 5.66% ( p = 0.042, see Fig. 2 a).

title: Non-task expert physicians benefit from correct explainable AI advice when reviewing X-rays
outcome: Effect of visual explanation of AI advice on diagnostic accuracy and advice quality rating
effect: Annotated (explainable) advice increased accuracy (OR 2.30, p=0.002) and quality ratings (+0.25, p=0.001); benefit significant for non-task experts, not for radiologists.
quote: The results indicate that having an explanation (i.e., annotation on the X-ray indicating the area that determined the prediction) as part of the advice positively affected physicians' diagnostic accuracy and their quality rating.

title: Fairness in the prediction of acute postoperative pain using machine learning models
outcome: Model fairness metrics across age, race, ADI, insurance, sex, language, and health literacy subgroups
effect: AUC 0.71 overall, but bias detected for age, race, ADI and insurance type; no bias for sex, language, health literacy. Older adults TPR ratio 0.52, predictive equality 0.29.
quote: The bias we detected in the developed models clearly shows that despite the promising overall performance of the model (AUC, 0.71; balanced accuracy, 0.64), the performance suffers significantly for some of the subcohorts.

title: Fairness in the prediction of acute postoperative pain using machine learning models
outcome: Effect of reweighing on subgroup bias in model performance
effect: Reweighing reduced bias for ADI but introduced bias for language (equal opportunity ratio 0.91 to 1.35, predictive equality 0.84 to 0.29) and worsened race bias when reweighing on ADI.
quote: Reweighing the prediction models based on each protected attribute helped reduce the bias for some cases (e.g., ADI), but it introduced bias in some other cases where there was no bias (language).

title: Fairness in the prediction of acute postoperative pain using machine learning models
outcome: Model performance and fairness across patient subgroups on local data
effect: Model biased for age, race (FPR 1.36-1.39 times higher for non-White), ADI (three of five metrics) and insurance type (three of five metrics).
quote: The model was biased against the patients with other (non-White) races in terms of FPR.

title: Examining clinician choice to follow-up (or not) on automated notifications of medication non-adherence by clinical decision support systems
venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
outcome: Proportion of CDSS non-adherence flags clinicians followed up versus not followed up
effect: 260 (78%) of flags were Not Followed-up; 71 (22%) were Followed-up. Anti-depressant flags were less likely to be followed up than Anti-Psychotic and Anxiolytic flags (p < 0.001).
quote: The majority of clients were Not Followed-up (n = 260; 78%; Followed-up: n = 71; 22%).

title: Rationing scarce healthcare capacity: A study of the ventilator allocation guidelines during the COVID-19 pandemic
outcome: Racial disparity in access to the ventilator priority queue under three prioritization schemes
effect: ISP-LU yields a Pareto-improvement over SOFA-P and ISP in saved lives while limiting racial disparity in access to the priority queue; no numeric values are given in the abstract.
quote: We also show that ISP-LU is a robust priority scheme whose implementation yields a Pareto-improvement over both SOFA-P and ISP in terms of maximizing saved lives after mechanical ventilation while limiting racial disparity in access to the priority queue.

title: Vickybot, a Chatbot for Anxiety-Depressive Symptoms and Work-Related Burnout in Primary Care and Health Care Professionals: Development, Feasibility, and Potential Effectiveness Studies
outcome: Suicide alert detection and research team response to acute suicide risk in chatbot users
effect: Suicidal alerts were received correctly in simulation; 9% (3/34) of patients activated the suicide alert and the research team intervened promptly with successful outcomes.
quote: Furthermore, 9% (3/34) of patients activated the suicide alert, and the research team promptly intervened with successful outcomes.
sample_unit: patients (primary care patients and health care workers) completing first self-assessment

title: Assessment of the Role of Artificial Intelligence in the Association Between Time of Day and Colonoscopy Quality
outcome: Adenoma detection rate by session time with versus without AI assistance
effect: Unassisted ADR early vs late sessions 13.73% vs 5.70% (P=.005); with AI 22.95% vs 22.06% (P=.78). AI assistance OR 3.81 in late vs 1.60 in early sessions.
quote: After the intervention of the AI system, as expected, no statistically significant difference was found (22.95% vs 22.06%, P = .78; OR, 0.96; 95% CI; 0.71-1.29).

title: Assessment of the Role of Artificial Intelligence in the Association Between Time of Day and Colonoscopy Quality
outcome: ADR improvement with AI-assisted versus unassisted colonoscopy in randomized trials
effect: AI-assisted colonoscopy raised ADR and eliminated early-late session gap; AI OR 3.81 (2.10-6.91) in late sessions and 1.60 (1.10-2.34) in early sessions.
quote: Furthermore, the AI systems showed better assistance ability on ADR in late sessions compared with early sessions (odds ratio, 3.81; 95% CI, 2.10-6.91 vs 1.60; 95% CI, 1.10-2.34).

title: Validation in Indonesia of two published scores for mortality prediction after cardiac surgery
outcome: Calibration and discrimination after local recalibration of EuroSCORE II
effect: After recalibration, calibration good (HL P=0.79) and predicted mortality 3.2% vs observed 3.8%; AUC 0.777 not significantly different from original (P=0.92)
quote: The total mortality rate was slightly underestimated by the recalibrated EuroSCORE II model (3.2% vs. observed mortality 3.8%). However, calibration was still good (HL test P = 0.79, [ Figure 2 ]).

title: Validation in Indonesia of two published scores for mortality prediction after cardiac surgery
outcome: Differences between development and local populations and resulting miscalibration
effect: Local patients younger (53 vs 65 years), more critical preoperative state (9.8% vs 4.1%), more elective surgery (94% vs 77%); scores underestimated mortality in all risk groups
quote: The patients were younger (53 vs. 65 years), had lower creatinine clearance (74.97 mL/min vs. 83.6 mL/min), were more often in critical preoperative state (9.8% vs. 4.1%), and a higher proportion had elective surgery (94% vs. 77%) than in the EuroSCORE II population.

title: Validation in Indonesia of two published scores for mortality prediction after cardiac surgery
outcome: local in-hospital mortality calibration
effect: Observed mortality 3.8%; predicted 2.1% by EuroSCORE II and 2.4% by ACEF; both poorly calibrated, HL P < 0.001.
quote: In-hospital mortality occurred in 3.8% of the patients and was considerably underestimated both by the EuroSCORE II (2.1%) and ACEF score (2.4%).

title: Validation in Indonesia of two published scores for mortality prediction after cardiac surgery
outcome: Local validation of published mortality scores on local historical data against observed in-hospital mortality
effect: Observed mortality 3.8% vs predicted 2.1% (EuroSCORE II) and 2.4% (ACEF); both poorly calibrated (HL P<0.001); EuroSCORE II AUC 0.774, ACEF AUC 0.638
quote: In-hospital mortality occurred in 3.8% of the patients and was considerably underestimated both by the EuroSCORE II (2.1%) and ACEF score (2.4%).

title: Validation in Indonesia of two published scores for mortality prediction after cardiac surgery
outcome: Generalization of predictive model to a new population
effect: EuroSCORE II and ACEF underestimated mortality in all risk groups and were poorly calibrated (HL P<0.001) in the Indonesian population
quote: The EuroSCORE II and ACEF score underestimated mortality in all risk groups, and both scores were poorly calibrated.

title: Validation in Indonesia of two published scores for mortality prediction after cardiac surgery
outcome: model discrimination comparison
effect: EuroSCORE II AUC 0.774 (0.714–0.834) versus ACEF AUC 0.638 (0.561–0.718); AUC difference P = 0.007.
quote: The EuroSCORE II had good discrimination with AUC 0.774 (0.714–0.834), whereas the ACEF score had poor discrimination with AUC 0.638 (0.561–0.718).

title: Validation in Indonesia of two published scores for mortality prediction after cardiac surgery
outcome: poor calibration despite discrimination
effect: EuroSCORE II AUC 0.774 (0.714–0.834), but HL P < 0.001 and mortality underestimated 2.1% predicted versus 3.8% observed.
quote: The EuroSCORE II, despite good discrimination, showed poor calibration.

title: The Effects of a Health Care Chatbot's Complexity and Persona on User Trust, Perceived Usability, and Effectiveness: Mixed Methods Study
outcome: Knowledge test improvement (high effectiveness group) by technical vs nontechnical reading level of chatbot responses
effect: Technical language (grade 12+) responses more likely in high-effectiveness group than nontechnical (grade 8 or below): OR 2.73, 95% CI 1.05-7.41; P=.04; participants were college students with high literacy.
quote: A binary logistic regression predicting effectiveness ( Table 4 ) revealed that participants who received technical language responses were significantly more likely to be in the high effectiveness group (OR 2.73, 95% CI 1.05-7.41; P =.04) when compared to participants who received nontechnical language responses.

title: The Effects of a Health Care Chatbot's Complexity and Persona on User Trust, Perceived Usability, and Effectiveness: Mixed Methods Study
outcome: Knowledge-test improvement after chatbot use
effect: Technical language outperformed nontechnical: OR 2.73 (95% CI 1.05-7.41; P=.04) for high effectiveness.
quote: Analysis of 71 participants found that participants who received technical language responses were significantly more likely to be in the high effectiveness group, which had higher improvements in test scores (odds ratio [OR] 2.73, 95% CI 1.05-7.41; P=.04).

title: OB HUB: Remote Electronic Fetal Monitoring Surveillance
venue: MCN. The American journal of maternal child nursing
outcome: Neonatal outcomes and perceived safety with remote nurse AI-assisted fetal surveillance
effect: Cooling 6 (0.25%) pre vs 2 (0.08%) during trial, p = .10; no significant differences in neonatal outcomes; 78.8% of responding nurses said OB HUB improved safety.
quote: There were no significant differences between groups for neonatal outcomes.

title: OB HUB: Remote Electronic Fetal Monitoring Surveillance
venue: MCN. The American journal of maternal child nursing
outcome: neonatal outcomes
effect: Cooling occurred in 0.25% of pre-implementation births and 0.08% of trial births, which was not statistically significant.
quote: Six births (0.25%) resulted in cooling prior to implementation and 2 (0.08%) cooling events occurred during the trial; these differences were not significant (p = .10).

title: Code-free machine learning for classification of central nervous system histopathology images
venue: Journal of neuropathology and experimental neurology

quote: External validation of the predicted accuracy and negative control experiments were found to be crucial for verification of the accuracy predicted by the algorithms.

title: The Deterioration Risk Index: Developing and Piloting a Machine Learning Algorithm to Reduce Pediatric Inpatient Deterioration

outcome: Sensitivity and alarms per detected event of new ML model versus existing situational awareness program

quote: The Deterioration Risk Index (DRI) was 2.4 times as sensitive as our existing situational awareness program (sensitivities of 53% and 22%, respectively; p < 0.001) and required 2.3 times fewer alarms per detected event (121 DRI alarms per detected event vs 276 for existing program).

title: Clinical Implementation of a Combined Artificial Intelligence and Natural Language Processing Quality Assurance Program for Pulmonary Nodule Detection in the Emergency Department Setting
venue: Journal of the American College of Radiology : JACR

quote: This was achieved without disrupting in-shift radiologist workflow or causing significant delays in patient follow for the diagnosed pulmonary nodule.

title: Identification of Active Pulmonary Tuberculosis Among Patients With Positive Interferon-Gamma Release Assay Results: Value of a Deep Learning-based Computer-aided Detection System in Different Scenarios of Implementation
outcome: Radiologist sensitivity and specificity with versus without CAD assistance

quote: The CAD-assisted interpretation exhibited a higher sensitivity (81.8% vs. 72.7%; P =0.046) but lower specificity than the radiologists' interpretation (84.1% vs. 85.7%; P <0.001).

title: Identification of Active Pulmonary Tuberculosis Among Patients With Positive Interferon-Gamma Release Assay Results: Value of a Deep Learning-based Computer-aided Detection System in Different Scenarios of Implementation
outcome: CAD sensitivity versus radiologists on the same data in reader test
effect: CAD sensitivity 72.7% vs. radiologists 59.5% (P=0.005) at the same specificity of 88.0%.
quote: In the reader test, the CAD exhibited a higher sensitivity than radiologists (72.7% vs. 59.5%; P =0.005) at the same specificity (88.0%), and CAD-assisted interpretation significantly improved the sensitivity of radiologists' interpretation (72.3%; P <0.001).

title: Identification of Active Pulmonary Tuberculosis Among Patients With Positive Interferon-Gamma Release Assay Results: Value of a Deep Learning-based Computer-aided Detection System in Different Scenarios of Implementation
outcome: Prescreening versus radiologist interpretation of all cases
effect: Specificity 88.8% vs. 85.7% (P <0.001) at same sensitivity; workload reduced 85.2% (1780 to 263).
quote: The CAD-based prescreening exhibited a higher specificity than the radiologists' interpretation (88.8% vs. 85.7%; P <0.001) at the same sensitivity, with a workload reduction of 85.2% (1780 to 263).

title: Artificial intelligence in radiology: trainees want more
outcome: Trainee demand for AI education versus availability of AI teaching in training programmes
effect: 98.7% felt AI should be taught in training; only one respondent reported their programme had implemented AI teaching; 71.4% had no experience working with AI.
quote: Almost all (98.7%) felt that AI should be taught during their training, yet only one respondent stated that their training programme had implemented AI teaching.

title: Multicenter Evaluation of AI-generated DIR and PSIR for Cortical and Juxtacortical Multiple Sclerosis Lesion Detection
outcome: Between-center reliability (ICC) of lesion detection on AI-generated DIR and PSIR images
effect: Reliability was good across centers: ICC 0.81 for AI-generated DIR and 0.75 for AI-generated PSIR, in a seven-center sample.
quote: Reliability was good for both DIR (ICC, 0.81) and PSIR (ICC, 0.75) across centers.
sample_unit: patients with multiple sclerosis (MRI scans from seven centers)

title: AI Improves Nodule Detection on Chest Radiographs in a Health Screening Population: A Randomized Controlled Trial
outcome: Detection rate of actionable lung nodules on chest radiographs, AI vs non-AI arm, randomized
effect: Detection rate 0.59% (31/5238) in AI group vs 0.25% (13/5238) in non-AI group; OR 2.4; 95% CI 1.3, 4.7; P = .008. Malignant nodule detection 0.15% vs 0.0%.
quote: The trial met the predefined primary outcome, demonstrating an improved detection rate of actionable nodules in the AI group compared with the non-AI group (0.59% [31 of 5238 participants] vs 0.25% [13 of 5238 participants], respectively; odds ratio, 2.4; 95% CI: 1.3, 4.7; P = .008).

title: AI Improves Nodule Detection on Chest Radiographs in a Health Screening Population: A Randomized Controlled Trial
outcome: Radiologist performance with versus without AI assistance in the intended deployment mode
effect: Radiologists referring to AI results detected more actionable nodules (0.59% vs 0.25%) with similar false-referral rates (45.9% vs 56.0%, P = .14) and positive-report rates (2.3% vs 1.9%, P = .14).
quote: The AI and non-AI groups showed similar false-referral rates (45.9% [56 of 122 participants] vs 56.0% [56 of 100 participants], respectively; P = .14) and positive-report rates (2.3% [122 of 5238 participants] vs 1.9% [100 of 5238 participants]; P = .14).

title: Healthcare provider evaluation of machine learning-directed care: reactions to deployment on a randomised controlled study
outcome: Staff-reported workflow disruption after ML-directed evaluations in randomised study
effect: 81% of 59 respondents (of 71 surveyed, 83% response) disagreed/strongly disagreed that their workflow was disrupted.
quote: 81% disagreed/strongly disagreed their workflow was disrupted.

title: Optimizing the Implementation of Clinical Predictive Models to Minimize National Costs: Sepsis Case Study
outcome: Excess sepsis cost savings from cost-optimized thresholds versus fixed 80% sensitivity threshold
effect: Optimized uniform threshold saved US $4.3B vs US $3.9B for uniform 80% sensitivity; heterogeneous optimized thresholds saved US $4.6B, almost US $700M more than the 80% standard.
quote: At the pair where the highest savings are achieved, heterogeneous thresholds can save over US $300 million relative to uniform thresholds (US $4.3 billion cost savings with uniform and US $4.6 billion with heterogeneous) and almost US $700 million compared to the 80% standard.

title: Optimizing the Implementation of Clinical Predictive Models to Minimize National Costs: Sepsis Case Study
outcome: Cost savings and DOR when alert cutoffs are chosen accounting for false alarm tolerance and department incidence
effect: Department-specific optimized thresholds raised DOR by up to 50 versus uniform recommended threshold (DOR up to 116) and increased savings; simulated only, no clinician input tested.
quote: Figure 5 D shows that DOR can increase by as much as 50 when switching from a uniform recommended threshold to heterogeneous thresholds, even though DOR is not directly maximized.

title: Optimizing the Implementation of Clinical Predictive Models to Minimize National Costs: Sepsis Case Study
outcome: Cost savings from tuning classification thresholds by diagnostic category for out-of-the-box models
effect: Heterogeneous thresholds gave gains highest for lower-accuracy models: US $3.7B vs US $3B with uniform at AUC 0.82; overall savings up to 12.3% from customized thresholds.
quote: Figure 4 C shows that the gains from choosing heterogenous thresholds by MDCs are the highest for lower-accuracy models.

title: Conventional Versus Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Interpretation of Chest Radiographs in Patients With Acute Respiratory Symptoms in Emergency Department: A Pragmatic Randomized Clinical Trial
outcome: Sensitivity and false-positive rate of chest radiograph interpretation with vs without AI-CAD in a randomized trial
effect: Sensitivity 67.2% (317/472) vs 66.0% (324/491), OR 1.02 (0.70-1.49), P=0.917; false-positive rate 19.3% vs 18.5%, OR 1.00 (0.79-1.26), P=0.985; no improvement with AI-CAD.
quote: AI-CAD did not improve the sensitivity and false-positive rate of CR interpretation for diagnosing acute thoracic disease in patients with acute respiratory symptoms who presented to the ED.

title: Conventional Versus Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Interpretation of Chest Radiographs in Patients With Acute Respiratory Symptoms in Emergency Department: A Pragmatic Randomized Clinical Trial
outcome: Human-plus-AI vs human-only radiologist performance in the intended deployment mode
effect: Radiologists with AI-CAD had sensitivity 67.2% vs 66.0% without and false-positive rate 19.3% vs 18.5%; no significant differences (P=0.917, P=0.985).
quote: The sensitivity (67.2% [317/472] in the intervention group vs. 66.0% [324/491] in the control group; odds ratio, 1.02 [95% confidence interval, 0.70-1.49]; P = 0.917) and false-positive rate (19.3% [249/1289] vs. 18.5% [245/1324]; odds ratio, 1.00 [95% confidence interval, 0.79-1.26]; P = 0.985) of CR interpretation by duty radiologists were not associated with the use of AI-CAD.

title: Healthcare Professionals' Expectations of Medical Artificial Intelligence and Strategies for its Clinical Implementation: A Qualitative Study
outcome: Clinician concerns about deskilling from medical AI use, from interviews
effect: Participants mentioned deskilling as a concern about medical AI, alongside workflow distortion, alert fatigue, and unsophisticated algorithms. No frequency was reported in the abstract.
quote: While the participants expressed expectations that medical AI could enhance their patients' outcomes, increase work efficiency, and reduce hospital operating costs, they also mentioned concerns regarding distortions in the workflow, deskilling, alert fatigue, and unsophisticated algorithms.

title: Healthcare Professionals' Expectations of Medical Artificial Intelligence and Strategies for its Clinical Implementation: A Qualitative Study
outcome: Clinician concerns about alert fatigue from medical AI in ER/ICU settings
effect: Participants raised alert fatigue as a concern about medical AI. The authors highlighted alert fatigue management as important. No frequency was reported in the abstract.
quote: They also highlighted the importance of alert fatigue management and the integration of AI systems into the workflow.

title: Generalisability of fetal ultrasound deep learning models to low-resource imaging settings in five African countries
outcome: AUC of model fine-tuned on small local African samples versus trained from scratch
effect: Fine-tuning raised AUC to 99.2%, 98.8%, 99.8% (Malawi, Egypt, Algeria) versus 93.3%, 90.8%, 90.3% from scratch; maximum AUC reached with about 4-6 local patients.
quote: For example, in the case of Malawi, Egypt and Algeria, the maximum average AUC when training from scratch is 93.3%, 90.8% and 90.3%, respectively, while transfer learning increases the average performance to 99.2%, 98.8% and 99.8%.
country: Spain, Denmark, Egypt, Algeria, Uganda, Ghana, Malawi

title: Generalisability of fetal ultrasound deep learning models to low-resource imaging settings in five African countries
outcome: Performance of Spanish-trained model on African low-resource centres versus Danish high-resource centre
effect: Danish AUC >95% with n>500; African centres showed inconsistent and lower performance, especially with scarce training samples; single-centre model did not reach desired performance.
quote: Although the Spanish model has a good generalisation ability in another European dataset, the African clinical centres with low-resource settings manifest an inconsistent pattern and lower performance, especially when the number of training samples is scarce.
country: Spain, Denmark, Egypt, Algeria, Uganda, Ghana, Malawi

title: Generalisability of fetal ultrasound deep learning models to low-resource imaging settings in five African countries
outcome: Performance variation across sites and scanner devices
effect: Performance varied across five African centres with different scanners; Algeria with similar protocol reached AUC 97.9 ± 1.9% with over 1000 training samples, others lower and inconsistent.
quote: In the case where the images are acquired using a similar protocol to that of the European datasets, such as Algeria (Table 1 ), the model shows a competitive performance (average AUC of 97.9 ± 1.9 %) when more than 1000 samples are used for training.
country: Spain, Denmark, Egypt, Algeria, Uganda, Ghana, Malawi

title: Generalisability of fetal ultrasound deep learning models to low-resource imaging settings in five African countries
outcome: Generalisation of model to new population/context (low-resource African centres)
effect: Single-centre model trained in Spain did not reach desired performance in Malawi, Egypt, Algeria, Uganda or Ghana.
quote: Our results showed that a model trained using a single-centre approach did not reach the desired performance when applied to a new centre in low-resource settings acquired in Malawi, Egypt, Algeria, Uganda or Ghana.
country: Spain, Denmark, Egypt, Algeria, Uganda, Ghana, Malawi

title: Generalisability of fetal ultrasound deep learning models to low-resource imaging settings in five African countries
outcome: External generalisation AUC
effect: Denmark average AUC >95% when n>500; African low-resource centres had inconsistent/lower performance; Algeria 97.9 ± 1.9% when protocol was similar.
quote: Although the Spanish model has a good generalisation ability in another European dataset, the African clinical centres with low-resource settings manifest an inconsistent pattern and lower performance, especially when the number of training samples is scarce.
country: Spain, Denmark, Egypt, Algeria, Uganda, Ghana, Malawi

title: Generalisability of fetal ultrasound deep learning models to low-resource imaging settings in five African countries
outcome: Local low-resource performance
effect: Single-centre Spanish model did not reach desired performance in Malawi, Egypt, Algeria, Uganda or Ghana; Denmark AUC was >95% when n>500.
quote: Our results showed that a model trained using a single-centre approach did not reach the desired performance when applied to a new centre in low-resource settings acquired in Malawi, Egypt, Algeria, Uganda or Ghana.
country: Spain, Denmark, Egypt, Algeria, Uganda, Ghana, Malawi

title: Stress-testing pelvic autosegmentation algorithms using anatomical edge cases
venue: Physics and imaging in radiation oncology
outcome: Autosegmentation accuracy (Dice, surface distance, Hausdorff) on anatomic edge cases versus normal cohort
effect: Edge case performance was lower than the normal cohort, with a 0.12 mean DSC reduction; deep learning outperformed atlas-based and model-based methods.
quote: However, edge case performance was lower versus the normal cohort (0.12 mean DSC reduction).
sample_unit: prostate cancer patients with anatomic variations (edge cases)

title: Performance and attitudes toward real-time computer-aided polyp detection during colonoscopy in a large tertiary referral center in the United States
outcome: Adenomas per colonoscopy and ADR with CADe versus historical controls in routine practice
effect: No significant difference in adenomas per colonoscopy (1.08 vs 1.04, P = .65), or (1.27 vs 1.17, P = .45) after exclusions. No significant difference in ADR, median procedure or withdrawal times.
quote: CADe did not improve adenoma detection in daily practice among endoscopists with high baseline ADRs.

title: Performance and attitudes toward real-time computer-aided polyp detection during colonoscopy in a large tertiary referral center in the United States
outcome: Staff and endoscopist concerns about false positives, distraction and procedure time after CADe deployment
effect: Main concerns were false-positive signals (82.4%), high level of distraction (58.8%), and impression it prolonged procedure time (47.1%).
quote: Survey results demonstrated mixed attitudes toward AI-assisted colonoscopy, of which main concerns were high number of false-positive signals (82.4%), high level of distraction (58.8%), and impression it prolonged procedure time (47.1%).

title: Assessing the net benefit of machine learning models in the presence of resource constraints
outcome: optimal strategy and realized net benefit
effect: Accounting for resource constraints changed optimal ICU bed allocation strategy in 4 case studies.
quote: Accounting for the constraint changes the optimal strategy for ICU bed allocation.

title: Assessing the net benefit of machine learning models in the presence of resource constraints
outcome: realized net benefit under resource constraints
effect: An absolute constraint of 3 available ICU beds diminishes the realized net benefit across 4 case studies.
quote: Using 4 case studies, we demonstrate the degree to which an absolute constraint (eg, only 3 available intensive care unit [ICU] beds) diminishes the RNB of a hypothetical ICU admission model.

title: The impact of inconsistent human annotations on AI driven clinical decision making
outcome: Agreement between models trained on different experts' labels on external validation
effect: Internal Fleiss' κ = 0.383 (fair); external pairwise average Cohen's κ = 0.255 (minimal); discharge κ = 0.174 vs mortality κ = 0.267; majority vote consensus consistently suboptimal.
quote: Further, broad external validation (on both static and time series datasets) of these 11 classifiers was carried out on a HiRID external dataset, where the models' classifications were found to have low pairwise agreements (average Cohen's κ = 0.255 i.e., minimal agreement).
sample_unit: ICU consultant annotators (each yielding a model)

title: Evaluation of Feature Selection Methods for Preserving Machine Learning Performance in the Presence of Temporal Dataset Shift in Clinical Medicine
outcome: Baseline model out-of-distribution versus in-distribution performance under temporal shift
effect: Baseline model showed significantly worse OOD (2017-2019) performance than ID (2008-2010) on long LOS and sepsis tasks.
quote: The baseline model showed significantly worse OOD performance with the long LOS and sepsis tasks when compared with the ID performance.

title: Evaluation of Feature Selection Methods for Preserving Machine Learning Performance in the Presence of Temporal Dataset Shift in Clinical Medicine
outcome: OOD versus ID model performance
effect: Baseline model had significantly worse OOD performance for long LOS and sepsis than ID performance.
quote: The baseline model showed significantly worse OOD performance with the long LOS and sepsis tasks when compared with the ID performance.

title: Evaluation of Feature Selection Methods for Preserving Machine Learning Performance in the Presence of Temporal Dataset Shift in Clinical Medicine
outcome: Retrained parsimonious model performance
effect: Retraining on 2017-2019 data with 2008-2010-selected features generally reached parity with oracle models trained on 2017-2019 data using all features.
quote: The retraining of these models on 2017-2019 data using features selected from training on 2008-2010 data generally reached parity with oracle models trained directly on 2017-2019 data using all available features.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Community-Based Diabetic Retinopathy Telemedicine Screening in Urban China: Cost-effectiveness and Cost-Utility Analyses With Real-world Data
outcome: Cost-effectiveness of AI grading versus manual grading in DR telemedicine screening
effect: AI model ICER US $2553.39 per year without blindness; ICUR US $15,216.96 per QALY; AI not cost-effective versus manual grading (costs $3182.50 vs $3265.40).
quote: The ICER for the AI-assisted model was US $2553.39 per year without blindness, and the ICUR was US $15,216.96 per QALY, which indicated that AI-assisted model was not cost-effective.

title: Monitoring Methodology for an AI Tool for Breast Cancer Screening Deployed in Clinical Centers
outcome: Output score distribution drift monitoring vs. pre-deployment reference, detection of mismatched configurations
effect: Matched-reference PCCs 0.975–0.998 with no significant chi-squared differences (p 0.346–0.853); unmatched references gave PCCs 0.364–0.825, showing the method flags deviations.
quote: The low PCC value found when an unmatched manufacturer is used for the reference shows that finding a difference could be the source of an alert, which would facilitate the detection of software malfunctions or deviations (such as an unsupported manufacturer or a version of the tool that is not suitable for the analyzed mammogram).

title: Effect of an Artificial Intelligence Decision Support Tool on Palliative Care Referral in Hospitalized Patients: A Randomized Clinical Trial
venue: Journal of pain and symptom management
outcome: Palliative care consultation rate and readmissions with AI tool versus usual care in stepped-wedge trial
effect: Intervention had higher palliative care consultation incidence (IRR 1.44, 95% CI 1.11-1.92). Exploratory 60-day and 90-day readmissions were lower (OR 0.75 and 0.72).
quote: Patients randomized to the intervention had a statistically significant higher incidence rate of palliative care consultation compared to the control group (IRR, 1.44 [95% CI, 1.11-1.92]).

title: Computed tomography and radiation dose images-based deep-learning model for predicting radiation pneumonitis in lung cancer patients after radiation therapy
venue: Radiotherapy and oncology : journal of the European Society for Therapeutic Radiology and Oncology
outcome: AUC on external cohorts before and after adjusting model weights with local subset
effect: Baseline AUC 0.55 (test-set-2) and 0.63 (test-set-3); after adjusting weights with 40 local patients, AUC improved to 0.65 and 0.70.
quote: After adjusting CT and RD weights of the model using a subset of the RTOG-0617 subjects, the discriminatory power of test-set-2 and 3 improved to AUC 0.65 and AUC 0.70, respectively.

title: Computed tomography and radiation dose images-based deep-learning model for predicting radiation pneumonitis in lung cancer patients after radiation therapy
venue: Radiotherapy and oncology : journal of the European Society for Therapeutic Radiology and Oncology
outcome: Discrimination of baseline model on external validation cohorts versus internal prospective test set
effect: Baseline AUC 0.83 for test-set-1, but 0.55 for test-set-2 and 0.63 for test-set-3 in external RTOG 0617 cohorts.
quote: The discriminative ability of a baseline trained model had an AUC of 0.83 for test-set-1, 0.55 for test-set-2, and 0.63 for test-set-3.

title: Computed tomography and radiation dose images-based deep-learning model for predicting radiation pneumonitis in lung cancer patients after radiation therapy
venue: Radiotherapy and oncology : journal of the European Society for Therapeutic Radiology and Oncology
outcome: Performance on cohorts with different settings
effect: Baseline AUC dropped from 0.83 in test-set-1 to 0.55 and 0.63 in RTOG-0617 cohorts.
quote: The discriminative ability of a baseline trained model had an AUC of 0.83 for test-set-1, 0.55 for test-set-2, and 0.63 for test-set-3.

title: Decision-making support systems on extended hospital length of stay: Validation and recalibration of a model for patients with AMI
outcome: Performance after local recalibration versus unadjusted model
effect: Recalibrating on local data improved AUC from 0.702 (VM) to 0.745 (RM) and recall from 58% to 69%; Hosmer-Lemeshow p=0.692; specificity fell from 73% to 68%.
quote: Regarding the performance measures for the population of patients with AMI who were discharged alive, the results obtained in the RM were worse compared to the validation by Magalhães et al. ( 13 ) and improved compared to the VM (expected result, since the model was adjusted to the population).

title: Decision-making support systems on extended hospital length of stay: Validation and recalibration of a model for patients with AMI
outcome: Generalizability of model developed at small hospital to larger hospital population
effect: Model developed on a ~400-bed hospital did not generalize to a ~1,000-bed hospital in a different period; AUC dropped 0.828 to 0.702 and predictor ORs and CIs differed.
quote: Therefore, it highlights the need to recalibrate the models to new populations, as the models cannot be generalized to different populations without losing their predictive capacity.

title: Decision-making support systems on extended hospital length of stay: Validation and recalibration of a model for patients with AMI
outcome: local validation performance drop
effect: Recall 72% to 58%; specificity 75% to 73%; AUC 0.828 to 0.702.
quote: According to the data presented in Table 3 , there is a decrease in the predictive capacity of the VM compared to the results obtained in the model by Magalhães et al. ( 13 ).

title: Decision-making support systems on extended hospital length of stay: Validation and recalibration of a model for patients with AMI
outcome: Discrimination of previously developed model on new hospital's historical data against reference outcome
effect: On new-hospital data the model's AUC fell from 0.828 to 0.702 and recall from 72% to 58%; specificity 75% to 73%, showing worse local performance than original evidence.
quote: According to the data presented in Table 3 , there is a decrease in the predictive capacity of the VM compared to the results obtained in the model by Magalhães et al. ( 13 ).

title: Decision-making support systems on extended hospital length of stay: Validation and recalibration of a model for patients with AMI
outcome: Model performance when applied to a new population/context
effect: Prior model applied to a new population lost predictive capacity (AUC 0.828 to 0.702; recall 72% to 58%), requiring recalibration.
quote: As a result, the model required recalibration in the population under study.

title: SCORE2 cardiovascular risk prediction models in an ethnic and socioeconomic diverse population in the Netherlands: an external validation study
outcome: Calibration (observed/expected ratio) of SCORE2 by socioeconomic and ethnic subgroups
effect: Low-risk model underpredicted CVD overall (OE 1.30 men, 1.22 women), most in lowest SES (1.54 men, 1.64 women) and Surinamese subgroups (1.92 men, 1.86 women); lowest-SES Surinamese men OE 2.53.
quote: Underprediction in the Surinamese subgroup was largest (OE-ratio 1.9, in men and women), particularly in the low socioeconomic Surinamese subgroups (OE-ratio 2.5 and 2.1 in men and women).

title: SCORE2 cardiovascular risk prediction models in an ethnic and socioeconomic diverse population in the Netherlands: an external validation study
outcome: Local performance of SCORE2 low-risk model in Dutch routine care population versus development
effect: 6966 CVD events observed versus 5495 predicted by the low-risk model intended for the Netherlands; OE-ratio 1.30 men and 1.22 women; C-statistics 0.70 and 0.72.
quote: At external validation of the SCORE2 low-risk model (intended for use in the Netherlands), we found that for the total population the SCORE2 low-risk model predicted 5495 CVD events in the population included in this study, whereas 6966 CVD events were observed.

title: SCORE2 cardiovascular risk prediction models in an ethnic and socioeconomic diverse population in the Netherlands: an external validation study
outcome: Subgroup calibration and discrimination of SCORE2 by SES and ethnicity
effect: Underprediction was larger in low SES (OE 1.5 men, 1.6 women) and Surinamese subgroups (OE up to 2.5); discrimination moderate, C-statistics 0.63 to 0.76 across subgroups.
quote: Underprediction was larger in low socioeconomic subgroups of the overall study population (OE-ratio 1.5 and 1.6 in men and women, respectively), and comparable in Dutch and the combined "other ethnicities" low socioeconomic subgroups.

title: SCORE2 cardiovascular risk prediction models in an ethnic and socioeconomic diverse population in the Netherlands: an external validation study
outcome: Whether switching to higher-risk SCORE2 recalibrated models improved calibration in underpredicted subgroups
effect: In subgroups with underprediction, moderate/high-risk models improved OE-ratios (e.g., moderate-risk OE 1.02 overall; high-risk OE 1.05 in other-ethnicity men), though Surinamese men remained at 1.45.
quote: In the subgroups with underprediction in the low-risk model, the intermediate or high-risk SCORE2 models showed improved OE-ratios.

title: An artificially intelligent, natural language processing chatbot designed to promote COVID-19 vaccination: A proof-of-concept pilot study
outcome: Chatbot accuracy in matching responses to user intents as COVID-19 information evolved
effect: Accuracy ranged from 54% to 91.1%; it lagged when new information emerged (e.g., Delta variant) and increased after new content was added.
quote: Accuracy lagged when new information related to COVID emerged, such as that related to the Delta variant.

title: Implementation of deep learning artificial intelligence in vision-threatening disease screenings for an underserved community during COVID-19
outcome: AI referral accuracy and ungradable rate in real-world community non-mydriatic screenings versus gold standard
effect: 38.9% of eyes ungradable by AI versus 2.6% by humans; sensitivity 63.2%, specificity 94.5%, PPV 32.0%, NPV 98.4%; all 4 eyes with multiple diseases referred.
quote: Deep learning artificial intelligence had 63.2% sensitivity, 94.5% specificity, 32.0% positive predictive value, and 98.4% negative predictive value in vision-threatening disease referrals.

title: Reducing Avoidable Emergency Visits and Hospitalizations With Patient Risk-Based Prescriptive Analytics: A Quality Improvement Project at an Oncology Care Model Practice
outcome: Change in ED visits and admissions after risk-prediction-driven nurse outreach
effect: Monthly ED visits per 100 OCM patients fell from 13.7 to 11.5 (18%); quarterly admissions fell from 19.5 to 17.1 (13%). This was a pre-post comparison with no control group.
quote: Per 100 unique OCM patients, monthly ED visits dropped from 13.7 to 11.5 (18%), a sustained month-over-month improvement.

title: Improving bowel preparation for colonoscopy with a smartphone application driven by artificial intelligence
outcome: Adequate bowel preparation rate and BBPS score, AI app vs control, in randomized trial
effect: Adequate preparation 88.54% vs 65.59% (P<0.001); mean BBPS 6.74±1.25 vs 5.97±1.81 (P<0.001); higher compliance with dietary and purgative instructions.
quote: In the full analysis set (n = 500), adequate preparation is significantly higher in the AI-driven app group (88.54 vs. 65.59%; P < 0.001).

title: The exciting potential for ChatGPT in obstetrics and gynecology
venue: American journal of obstetrics and gynecology
outcome: Currency of ChatGPT's training data and clinical knowledge in obstetrics and gynecology answers
effect: Training data were not readily updated; the model did not reliably (if at all) source data from after 2021, so answers can be outdated.
quote: The specific model that was assessed here, seems to not reliably (if at all) source data from after 2021.

title: The exciting potential for ChatGPT in obstetrics and gynecology
venue: American journal of obstetrics and gynecology
outcome: Ability of ChatGPT to cite sources for generated answers
effect: ChatGPT could not cite sources, so users cannot trace or verify its claims, which the authors say gives it the capability to mislead.
quote: An inability to cite sources or to truly understand what the user is asking suggests that it has the capability to mislead.

title: Clinical assistant decision-making model of tuberculosis based on electronic health records
outcome: Prospective performance of the tuberculosis model in live clinical use after retrospective validation
effect: Real clinic deployment for 4 months, 692,949 patients monitored, 484 confirmed TB; model predicted 440 cases; positive recognition rate 90.91%, false-negative rate 3.83%.
quote: The MSI-PTDM prediction model was installed at a doctor workstation and operated in a real clinic environment for 4 months.

title: External Validation and Comparison of a General Ward Deterioration Index Between Diversely Different Health Systems
outcome: Model discrimination (AUROC, AUPRC) on local retrospective data from a second hospital
effect: External hospital AUROC 0.875 (0.851-0.902), AUPRC 0.339 (0.281-0.398) vs 0.870 and 0.298 at the development hospital; performance consistent despite differences.
quote: PICTURE was able to identify general ward patients at risk of deterioration at both hospitals with consistent performance (AUROC and AUPRC) and compared favorably to existing metrics.

title: External Validation and Comparison of a General Ward Deterioration Index Between Diversely Different Health Systems
outcome: Comparison of PICTURE against Epic Deterioration Index and NEWS on the same data
effect: PICTURE outperformed both the Epic Deterioration Index and the National Early Warning Score at both institutions.
quote: PICTURE also outperformed both the Epic Deterioration Index and the National Early Warning Score at both institutions.

title: External Validation and Comparison of a General Ward Deterioration Index Between Diversely Different Health Systems
outcome: Comparison of development vs local populations, data and missingness, and effect on model performance
effect: Hospitals differed in missingness (>5% difference in 9/52 features), deterioration rate (4.5% vs 2.5%), and racial makeup (20% vs 49% non-White); performance remained consistent.
quote: The hospitals were found to have significant differences in missingness rates (> 5% difference in 9/52 features), deterioration rate (4.5% vs 2.5%), and racial makeup (20% non-White vs 49% non-White).

title: Recalibration of a Deep Learning Model for Low-Dose Computed Tomographic Images to Inform Lung Cancer Screening Intervals
outcome: AUC for predicting 1-year lung cancer risk, deep learning vs statistical model vs Lung-RADS on same data
effect: Recalibrated LCP-CNN AUC 0.87 vs LCRAT + CT 0.79 and Lung-RADS 0.69 (P < .001); lower 1-year delay risk at 66% biennial assignment (0.28% vs 0.60% vs 0.97%).
quote: The recalibrated LCP-CNN had substantially higher area under the curve (0.87) than LCRAT + CT (0.79) or Lung-RADS (0.69) to predict 1-year lung cancer risk (P < .001).
