quote: Major transparency gaps included missing documentation on training data, ethical considerations, and limitations for deployment.

title: A trustworthy AI reality-check: the lack of transparency of artificial intelligence products in healthcare
outcome: Public documentation of limitations and deployment caveats for different demographics and settings
effect: Deployment caveats for different demographics and medical settings were scarce; limitations for deployment often missing.
quote: Furthermore, deployment caveats for different demographics and medical settings were scarce.

title: Bridging the literacy gap for surgical consents: an AI-human expert collaborative approach
outcome: Reading level of existing surgical consent forms versus average American reading level
effect: Original consent forms had median Flesch-Kincaid Reading Level 13.9 and Reading Ease 35.3 (college level), versus 8th grade average American reading level.
quote: Prior to LLM processing, surgical consent forms had a median Flesch-Kincaid Reading Level of 13.9 (IQR = 12.8–14.2; Fig. 1B ) and Flesch Reading Ease score of 35.3 (IQR = 33.0–39.9; Fig. 1C ), both denoting a college education level of readability difficulty.
sample_unit: consent forms from academic medical centers

title: Bridging the literacy gap for surgical consents: an AI-human expert collaborative approach
outcome: Readability of consent forms before vs after GPT-4 plain-language simplification
effect: Reading level fell from 13.9 to 8.9 (P = 0.004); Reading Ease rose from 35.3 to 63.8 (P < 0.001); passive voice fell from 38.4% to 20.0%; word rarity fell.
quote: After simplification, there was a significant decrease in the Reading Level (before = 13.9 vs. after = 8.9, P = 0.004) and improvement in Reading Ease (before = 35.3 vs. after = 63.8 P < 0.001) from the reading level of a college freshman to that of an 8th grade student.
sample_unit: consent forms from academic medical centers

title: Bridging the literacy gap for surgical consents: an AI-human expert collaborative approach
outcome: Flesch-Kincaid reading level
effect: Median grade level decreased from 13.9 to 8.9 (P = 0.004).
quote: After simplification, there was a significant decrease in the Reading Level (before = 13.9 vs. after = 8.9, P = 0.004) and improvement in Reading Ease (before = 35.3 vs. after = 63.8 P < 0.001) from the reading level of a college freshman to that of an 8th grade student.
sample_unit: consent forms from academic medical centers

title: Generative Pre-trained Transformer 4 makes cardiovascular magnetic resonance reports easy to understand
venue: Journal of cardiovascular magnetic resonance : official journal of the Society for Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance
outcome: Readability (ARI) and layperson understandability of GPT-4 simplified reports vs original reports
effect: ARI 10 [9-12] original vs 5 [4-6] GPT-4 (p<0.001); 2/60 (3%) GPT-4 reports vs 18/20 (90%) originals at 8th grade level or higher; laypersons rated GPT-4 easier to understand (1 vs 4, p<0.001).
quote: Eighteen out of 20 (90%) standard CMR reports and 2/60 (3%) GPT-generated reports had an ARI score corresponding to the 8th grade level or higher.
sample_unit: GPT-4 generated simplified CMR reports (from 20 original reports)

title: Generative Pre-trained Transformer 4 makes cardiovascular magnetic resonance reports easy to understand
venue: Journal of cardiovascular magnetic resonance : official journal of the Society for Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance
outcome: Factual correctness, completeness, and lack of harm of GPT-4 report explanations rated by radiologists
effect: Ratings median 5 for correctness, completeness, and lack of harm; strong agreement for factual correctness in 94% (113/120) and completeness in 81% (97/120) of ratings. Not tested specifically in low-literacy users.
quote: Radiologists' ratings of the GPT-4 reports reached high levels for correctness (5 [4, 5]), completeness (5 [5]), and lack of potential harm (5 [5]); with "strong agreement" for factual correctness in 94% (113/120) and completeness of relevant findings in 81% (97/120) of reports.
sample_unit: GPT-4 generated simplified CMR reports (from 20 original reports)

title: Generative Pre-trained Transformer 4 makes cardiovascular magnetic resonance reports easy to understand
venue: Journal of cardiovascular magnetic resonance : official journal of the Society for Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance
outcome: Reproducibility of layperson understandability across three GPT-4 outputs from same report
effect: Test-retest agreement for layperson understandability ratings across three simplified reports was substantial (ICC 0.62; p<0.001).
quote: Test-retest agreement for layperson understandability ratings between the three simplified reports generated from the same original report was substantial (ICC: 0.62; p < 0.001).
sample_unit: GPT-4 generated simplified CMR reports (from 20 original reports)

title: Nordic radiographers' and students' perspectives on artificial intelligence - A cross-sectional online survey
outcome: Proportion of radiographers who received AI training in clinical practice
effect: 43% (n = 254) had not received any AI training in clinical practice; 13% (n = 76) received AI content in undergraduate training; 77.9% (n = 412) interested in AI education.
quote: A total of 43% (n = 254) of the respondents had not received any AI training in clinical practice.
country: Nordic countries (Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Iceland, Greenland, Faroe Islands)

title: Nordic radiographers' and students' perspectives on artificial intelligence - A cross-sectional online survey
outcome: Radiographers' AI awareness versus AI educational level
effect: AI awareness high (82.8% aware of potential use) but educational level low; 77.9% interested in pursuing AI education.
quote: In general, awareness of AI applications is high, but the educational level is low for Nordic radiographers.
country: Nordic countries (Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Iceland, Greenland, Faroe Islands)

title: Clinical Decision Support for Hypertension Management in Chronic Kidney Disease: A Randomized Clinical Trial
outcome: Change in mean systolic blood pressure at 180 days, CDS vs usual care (silent mode)
effect: Mean SBP change -14.6 vs -11.7 mm Hg (P = .005). BP control did not differ (50.4% vs 47.1%). Aligned actions 49.9% vs 34.6% (P < .001).
quote: From the linear mixed model, there was a statistically significant difference in mean SBP change in the intervention group compared with the usual care group (change, -14.6 [95% CI, -13.1 to -16.0] mm Hg vs -11.7 [-10.2 to -13.1] mm Hg; P = .005).

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence to Transform Inpatient Discharge Summaries to Patient-Friendly Language and Format
outcome: Readability (Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level) of original discharge summaries versus LLM patient-friendly versions
effect: Mean FK grade level 11.0 (SD 1.5) for original summaries vs 6.2 (SD 0.5) for LLM patient-friendly versions (P < .001); PEMAT understandability 13% vs 81%.
quote: Mean (SD) Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level was significantly lower in the patient-friendly discharge summaries (6.2 [0.5] vs 11.0 [1.5]; P < .001).

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence to Transform Inpatient Discharge Summaries to Patient-Friendly Language and Format
outcome: Accuracy, completeness, and safety concerns in LLM-generated patient-friendly discharge summaries
effect: 54% of 100 reviews gave the best accuracy rating of 6; 56% rated entirely complete; 18 reviews noted safety concerns, mostly omissions plus some hallucinations.
quote: Eighteen reviews noted safety concerns, mostly involving omissions, but also several inaccurate statements (termed hallucinations).

title: Characterising user engagement with mHealth for chronic disease self-management and impact on machine learning performance
outcome: ML exacerbation prediction performance by user engagement level (data sparsity)
effect: Performance was better for the most engaged users; the decrease for less frequent users was mostly offset when they engaged more near exacerbation. 60.3% engage frequently; 18.4% show transitional engagement.
quote: Machine learning performed better for users who engaged the most, however, this performance decrease can be mostly offset for less frequent users who engage more near exacerbation.

title: Large language models and bariatric surgery patient education: a comparative readability analysis of GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Bard, and online institutional resources
outcome: Reading level of patient education materials versus 6th grade AMA recommendation
effect: Institutional PEMs and initial LLM responses exceeded the 6th grade level; institutional grade range 10th grade to college sophomore; simplified GPT-4 met the recommendation on only 2 of 6 instruments.
quote: Our analysis shows that institutional websites’ PEMs remain too complex for the public, falling short of the AMA recommendation that PEMs be written at a 6th grade level or below [ 13 ].

title: Large language models and bariatric surgery patient education: a comparative readability analysis of GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Bard, and online institutional resources
outcome: Readability change after prompting LLM to explain in simpler terms
effect: Simplified responses had significantly higher FRE and lower grade levels than initial for all LLMs (p<0.05); GPT-4 FRE 42.7 to 74.0, reading levels 6th to 9th grade.
quote: Simplified responses from GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and Bard received higher FRE scores, as well as lower grade levels across all instruments, compared to those of initial responses from GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and Bard, respectively ( p < 0.05) (Table 3 , Supplementary Table 7).

title: Large language models and bariatric surgery patient education: a comparative readability analysis of GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Bard, and online institutional resources
outcome: Reading grade level of institutional and initial LLM bariatric surgery patient education responses
effect: Institutional and initial LLM responses had poor readability, average reading levels 9th grade to college graduate; institutional FRE 48.1, GPT-3.5 initial 31.4, GPT-4 initial 42.7, Bard initial 56.3.
quote: All institutional and initial LLM responses had poor readability, with average reading levels ranging from 9th grade to college graduate.

title: Large language models and bariatric surgery patient education: a comparative readability analysis of GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Bard, and online institutional resources
outcome: Accuracy and comprehensiveness of simplified versus initial LLM responses for lower-literacy readers
effect: Accuracy similar between initial and simplified; comprehensiveness maintained for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 (92.4% equal) but 34.8% of Bard simplified responses were less comprehensive.
quote: However, 34.8% of simplified Bard responses were rated as less comprehensive than initial responses (Supplementary Table 8).

title: Evaluating the Robustness of a Deep Learning Bone Age Algorithm to Clinical Image Variation Using Computational Stress Testing
outcome: Change in bone age prediction error under image transformations (rotation, flip, brightness, contrast, inversion, resolution)
effect: Significant MAD differences for all transformation groups except RSNA laterality marker (P=.86); clinically significant error proportions differed for 19 of 33 (57%) DHA transformations.
quote: There were significant differences in proportion of CSEs for 57% of the image transformations (19 of 33) performed on the DHA dataset.
sample_unit: pediatric hand radiographs (1425 RSNA internal test, 1202 DHA external test)

title: Evaluating the Robustness of a Deep Learning Bone Age Algorithm to Clinical Image Variation Using Computational Stress Testing
outcome: Generalization of model performance from internal to external test set at baseline
effect: No evidence of MAD difference between baseline test sets (RSNA 6.8 months, DHA 6.9 months; P=.05), indicating good generalization to curated external images.
quote: There was no evidence of a difference in MAD of the model on the two baseline test sets (RSNA = 6.8 months, DHA = 6.9 months; P = .05), indicating good model generalization to external data.
sample_unit: pediatric hand radiographs (1425 RSNA internal test, 1202 DHA external test)

title: Assistive AI in Lung Cancer Screening: A Retrospective Multinational Study in the United States and Japan
outcome: Reader AUC, specificity and sensitivity with versus without AI assistance in two multireader studies
effect: US AUC 0.70 to 0.72 (P=.02); Japan 0.93 to 0.96 (P=.18). Specificity rose 5.5% (US) and 6.7% (Japan); sensitivity unchanged. Standalone AI AUC 0.75 (US), 0.88 (Japan).
quote: With AI assistance, the radiologists’ AUC increased by 0.023 (0.70 to 0.72, P = .02) for the US study and by 0.023 (0.93 to 0.96, P = .18) for the Japan study.
sample_unit: low-dose chest CT cases (each read twice, 7,524 interpretations)

title: Clinical decision support for bipolar depression using large language models
venue: Neuropsychopharmacology : official publication of the American College of Neuropsychopharmacology
outcome: Rate of selecting expert-defined optimal treatment with vs without guideline grounding in prompt
effect: Augmented model chose optimal treatment for 50.8% vs 23.4% for un-augmented model (McNemar's p<0.001); kappa 0.31 vs 0.09.
quote: For 234 (23.4%) of vignettes, the model identified the optimal treatment, a result significantly poorer than for the augmented model (McNemar’s p < 0.001)
sample_unit: clinical vignettes (each run 20 times, 1000 model outputs per condition)

title: Clinical decision support for bipolar depression using large language models
venue: Neuropsychopharmacology : official publication of the American College of Neuropsychopharmacology
outcome: Augmented LLM versus community clinicians and base model on expert-defined optimal choice
effect: Augmented model 50.8% optimal vs community clinicians 23.1% (McNemar p<0.001) and base model 23.4%.
quote: A sample of community clinicians scoring the same vignettes identified the optimal choice for 23.1% (95% CI 15.7-30.5%) of vignettes, on average; McNemar's p < 0.001 versus augmented model.
sample_unit: clinical vignettes (each run 20 times, 1000 model outputs per condition)

title: Clinical decision support for bipolar depression using large language models
venue: Neuropsychopharmacology : official publication of the American College of Neuropsychopharmacology
outcome: race and gender counterfactual performance differences
effect: Omnibus subgroup differences p = 0.02; Black women performed significantly poorer than white men, Bonferroni-corrected p = 0.03.
quote: In post-hoc pairwise contrasts using McNemar’s test, model performance in Black women was significantly poorer than white men (Bonferroni-corrected p = 0.03).
sample_unit: clinical vignettes (each run 20 times, 1000 model outputs per condition)

title: Clinical decision support for bipolar depression using large language models
venue: Neuropsychopharmacology : official publication of the American College of Neuropsychopharmacology
outcome: Change in model treatment selection when vignette gender and race were permuted
effect: Augmented model performance differed modestly across gender-race pairs (p=0.02); Black women significantly poorer than white men (Bonferroni p=0.03); base model showed no significant differences (p=0.17).
quote: In post-hoc pairwise contrasts using McNemar’s test, model performance in Black women was significantly poorer than white men (Bonferroni-corrected p = 0.03).
sample_unit: clinical vignettes (each run 20 times, 1000 model outputs per condition)

title: Clinical decision support for bipolar depression using large language models
venue: Neuropsychopharmacology : official publication of the American College of Neuropsychopharmacology
outcome: Model performance across gender-race subgroups
effect: Omnibus test showed modest but statistically significant differences across 4 gender-race groups (p=0.02); optimal choice 48.4% in Black women vs 53.2% in white men.
quote: In subgroup analyses of the 4 gender-race pairs, model performance exhibited differences of modest magnitude (Table 1 ; Supplementary Table 1 ) that were statistically significant ( p = 0.02).
sample_unit: clinical vignettes (each run 20 times, 1000 model outputs per condition)

title: Clinical decision support for bipolar depression using large language models
venue: Neuropsychopharmacology : official publication of the American College of Neuropsychopharmacology
outcome: Frequency of LLM selecting poor or contraindicated medications among top choices
effect: Augmented model selected at least one poor/contraindicated medication in 12.0% of vignettes; base model 10.8%; community clinicians 22-24%.
quote: Conversely, for 120 (12.0%) of vignettes, the model selected a medication considered by the experts to be a poor choice, or contraindicated.
sample_unit: clinical vignettes (each run 20 times, 1000 model outputs per condition)

title: Automated HEART score determination via ChatGPT: Honing a framework for iterative prompt development
venue: Journal of the American College of Emergency Physicians open
outcome: LLM HEART subscore accuracy against physician gold-standard reference
effect: GPT-4 final prompts predicted correct risk group in 100% (96.3%–100%) of calculations versus 81.5% (71.7%–88.4%) for GPT-3.5, judged against blinded physician gold standards.
quote: Given the final overall HEART score risk stratification buckets (0‐3, 4–6, or 7–10 points when summing all 5 HEART subscores), 81.5% (71.7%–88.4%) of GPT‐3.5 and 100% (96.3%–100%) of GPT‐4 numerical final HEART score calculations predicted the correct risk group.
sample_unit: synthetic clinical notes (four simulated patients; 1200 queries per model)

title: Automated HEART score determination via ChatGPT: Honing a framework for iterative prompt development
venue: Journal of the American College of Emergency Physicians open
outcome: Effect of iterative prompt refinement on LLM output validity and accuracy
effect: Across three iterations, GPT-4 mean error decreased from 0.16 to 0.10 and non-numerical responses fell for both models; GPT-3.5 mean error stayed at 0.42.
quote: For GPT‐4, this same average error decreased from 0.16 (0.11–0.22) to 0.10 (0.07–0.14) points.
sample_unit: synthetic clinical notes (four simulated patients; 1200 queries per model)

title: Automated HEART score determination via ChatGPT: Honing a framework for iterative prompt development
venue: Journal of the American College of Emergency Physicians open
outcome: response variability across repeated runs
effect: Final-prompt numerical subscore SD was 0.52 for GPT-3.5 versus 0.33 for GPT-4.
quote: GPT‐3.5 had higher variability in its responses, with the mean numerical subscore for the final prompts having a standard deviation of 0.52 for GPT‐3.5 compared to 0.33 for GPT‐4.
sample_unit: synthetic clinical notes (four simulated patients; 1200 queries per model)

title: Assisting the infection preventionist: Use of artificial intelligence for health care-associated infection surveillance
outcome: LLM accuracy identifying CLABSI/CAUTI under ambiguous or varied prompt formats, repeated runs
effect: Both models accurately identified CLABSI and CAUTI in all scenarios with clear prompts; ambiguous prompts with Arabic numeral dates, abbreviations, and special characters caused occasional inaccuracies in repeated tests.
quote: Challenges appeared with ambiguous prompts including Arabic numeral dates, abbreviations, and special characters, causing occasional inaccuracies in repeated tests.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Radiotherapy Contouring and Planning to Improve Global Access to Cancer Care
outcome: Clinician-rated acceptability of AI contours and plans on 5-point Likert scale
effect: Head/neck CTVs acceptable as-is in 40% (93% with minor edits); postmastectomy breast plans usable as-is in 44% (91% with minor edits); cervical VMAT plans acceptable as-is in 99%.
quote: The clinical target volumes (CTVs) were acceptable as-is in 40% (with minor edits 93%).
sample_unit: cases (RPA contours and plans reviewed by at least three physicians each)
country: Multinational (31 radiation oncologists at 16 institutions in six countries on five continents)

title: Application of generative language models to orthopaedic practice
outcome: Accuracy of LLM-generated clinical letters rated by three orthopaedic clinicians
effect: ChatGPT letters 8.7/10 (SD 0.60) vs GPT-3 7.3/10 (SD 1.41), p=0.024; both sometimes omitted key information or added guidance that was at worst inaccurate.
quote: However, both LLMs sometimes omitted key information or added additional guidance which was at worst inaccurate.

title: From technical to understandable: Artificial Intelligence Large Language Models improve the readability of knee radiology reports
venue: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
outcome: Flesch-Kincaid reading level and reading ease of original vs AI-LLM patient-language reports
effect: Mean FKRL fell from 12.7 to 7.2 (X-ray), 13.4 to 7.5 (CT), 13.5 to 7.5 (MRI); FRE rose from 39.5 to 76.8, 27.3 to 73.1, 26.8 to 73.4; all statistically significant.
quote: Statistically significant improvements in mean FKRL scores in the AI-LLM generated X-ray report (12.7 ± 1.0-7.2 ± 0.6), CT report (13.4 ± 1.0-7.5 ± 0.5) and MRI report (13.5 ± 0.9-7.5 ± 0.6) were observed.

title: From technical to understandable: Artificial Intelligence Large Language Models improve the readability of knee radiology reports
venue: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
outcome: Reading grade level of AI-simplified reports versus original radiology reports
effect: Reading level dropped from about 13 (college level) to about 7.5 across modalities; FRE rose to 73-77.
quote: Statistically significant improvements in mean FRE scores in the AI-LLM generated X-ray report (39.5 ± 7.5-76.8 ± 5.1), CT report (27.3 ± 5.9-73.1 ± 5.6) and MRI report (26.8 ± 6.4-73.4 ± 5.0) were observed.

title: From technical to understandable: Artificial Intelligence Large Language Models improve the readability of knee radiology reports
venue: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
outcome: Hallucination or inaccurate text rate in AI-LLM-generated patient-language reports
effect: Hallucination rates were 2% (X-ray), 5% (CT) and 5% (MRI) of AI-generated reports.
quote: The hallucination rates in the AI-LLM generated X-ray report, CT report and MRI report were 2%, 5% and 5%, respectively.

title: Assessment of ChatGPT's adherence to ETA-thyroid nodule management guideline over two different time intervals 14 days apart: in binary and multiple-choice queries
outcome: Reproducibility of ChatGPT answers to same guideline questions across repeated runs 14 days apart
effect: Binary queries: 8 of 11 non-compliant responses unchanged, 3 rectified, 6 initially compliant became non-compliant. Multiple-choice: 43 (86%) stayed correct, 4 stayed incorrect, 3 correct became non-compliant.
quote: Conversely, 6 initially compliant answers transitioned to non-compliance after 14 days.

title: Use and Application of Large Language Models for Patient Questions Following Total Knee Arthroplasty
outcome: Surgeon-graded appropriateness of ChatGPT-4 answers to common post-TKA patient questions
effect: 44/60 (73.3%) ChatGPT answers appropriate, same as nurses; 5 graded inappropriate, 0 unreliable (nurses: 4 inappropriate, 1 unreliable).
quote: For the ChatGPT response, there were 5 responses graded "inappropriate" and no responses graded "unreliable."

title: An artificial intelligence language model improves readability of burns first aid information
venue: Burns : journal of the International Society for Burn Injuries
outcome: Proportion of patient education materials meeting target reading level
effect: In original form, only 4% of PEMs met the target readability level across all tools; median grade 6.9 (SD=1.1), not significantly below target (p = .31).
quote: In their original form, only 4% of the patient education materials (PEMs) met the target readability level across all tools.

title: An artificial intelligence language model improves readability of burns first aid information
venue: Burns : journal of the International Society for Burn Injuries
outcome: Readability of burns first aid materials before and after AI rewriting to an 11-year-old literacy level
effect: Original: 4% met target on all tools, median grade 6.9. After AI: 18% met target, median grade 6 (p<.001); all readability scores improved significantly (p<.001).
quote: Once rewritten using AI, paired t-test demonstrated that all readability scores improved significantly (p < .001).

title: An artificial intelligence language model improves readability of burns first aid information
venue: Burns : journal of the International Society for Burn Injuries
outcome: Readability of burns first aid materials
effect: Original: 4% met target; AI-modified: 18% met target, median grade 6 (SD=0.9), all scores improved p < .001.
quote: Once rewritten using AI, paired t-test demonstrated that all readability scores improved significantly (p < .001).

title: An artificial intelligence language model improves readability of burns first aid information
venue: Burns : journal of the International Society for Burn Injuries
outcome: Readability of AI-modified patient education materials
effect: Only 18% of AI-modified PEMs reached target readability level across all tools, though median grade was 6 (SD=0.9, p < .001)
quote: After AI-modification, 18% of PEMs reached the target level using all tools, with a median grade of 6 (SD=0.9), which was significantly below the target level (p < .001).

title: Application of MALDI-TOF MS and machine learning for the detection of SARS-CoV-2 and non-SARS-CoV-2 respiratory infections
outcome: Detection accuracy/AUC on Kazakhstan samples before vs after retraining on local data
effect: Applying original pipeline gave AUC 0.67 (RF) and 0.60 (SVM-R) for Kazakhstan; retraining on combined SA-Kaz data raised AUC to 0.93 (RF) and 0.98 (SVM-R). NCARI accuracy rose from 48% to 95%.
quote: Re-training the ML models to incorporate MALDI peak information from a diverse pool of Kazakhstan samples, including SARS-CoV-2+, NCARI subjects, and asymptomatic controls, led to a substantial improvement in detection accuracy.

title: Application of MALDI-TOF MS and machine learning for the detection of SARS-CoV-2 and non-SARS-CoV-2 respiratory infections
outcome: Performance of model trained on South American data when applied to Kazakhstan samples
effect: Original pipeline trained on South American samples showed reduced efficiency on Kazakhstan samples; 2021 SARS-CoV-2 accuracy <60% for all models, similar to NCARI identification.
quote: Our initial application of the original MALDI-TOF MS/ML pipeline, trained on South American samples ( 4 ), demonstrated reduced efficiency in identifying samples from Kazakhstan.

title: Application of MALDI-TOF MS and machine learning for the detection of SARS-CoV-2 and non-SARS-CoV-2 respiratory infections
outcome: Local diagnostic accuracy
effect: Established pipeline: SARS-CoV-2+ detection 91.0%, but NCARI accuracy 48.0% and AC 67.0% by top random forest model.
quote: Applying the established MALDI-TOF MS pipeline "as is" resulted in a high detection rate for SARS-CoV-2+ samples (91.0%), but low accuracy for NCARIs (48.0%) and ACs (67.0%) by the top-performing random forest model.

title: Development and Validation of an Interpretable Conformal Predictor to Predict Sepsis Mortality Risk: Retrospective Cohort Study
outcome: Dataset shift between development (MIMIC-IV) and external (eICU-CRD) populations and effect on performance
effect: 93 of 103 features differed significantly between databases; AUC dropped from 0.858 to 0.800, and flagged uncertain predictions rose from 29.4% to 38.6%.
quote: Multimedia Appendix 1 shows that 93 out of 103 features were statistically different ( P ≤.05) between MIMIC-IV and eICU-CRD.

title: Development and Validation of an Interpretable Conformal Predictor to Predict Sepsis Mortality Risk: Retrospective Cohort Study
outcome: External validation discrimination
effect: All models deteriorated externally; CPMORS AUC decreased from 0.858 internally to 0.800 externally.
quote: Consistent with these studies, the prediction results in this study reported that all AI models deteriorated when externally validated on eICU-CRD, with the AUC of CPMORS decreasing from 0.858 to 0.800.

title: Development and Validation of an Interpretable Conformal Predictor to Predict Sepsis Mortality Risk: Retrospective Cohort Study
outcome: Complex cases flagged for clinician review
effect: Flagged survivors had more AKI (22.4% vs 20.2%; 24% vs 20.4%) and longer ICU stays (89 vs 55; 78 vs 55 hours).
quote: In addition, for those patients who survived, the analysis showed that patients identified for clinician review (those with uncertain predictions) were more likely to develop new acute kidney injury after the first day of ICU admission (n=227, 22.4% vs n=428, 20.2% for MIMIC-IV; n=799, 24% vs n=875, 20.4% for eICU-CRD) and had longer ICU stays with a median of 89 (IQR 54-173) hours versus 55 (IQR 37-99) hours for MIMIC-IV, and 78 (IQR 48-141) hours versus 55 (IQR 40-91) hours for eICU-CRD, compared to the patients who were not flagged for review.

title: Development and Validation of an Interpretable Conformal Predictor to Predict Sepsis Mortality Risk: Retrospective Cohort Study
outcome: Error rate with conformal uncertainty
effect: At 90% confidence, errors were 438/4187 (10.5%) internal and 1221/10,362 (11.8%) external versus 1449 (34.6%) and 4540 (43.8%) point-prediction errors.
quote: In this case, the conformal predictor still produced significantly lower error rates compared to the point predictions by AI (n=1221, 11.8% vs n=4540, 43.8%).

title: Development and Validation of an Interpretable Conformal Predictor to Predict Sepsis Mortality Risk: Retrospective Cohort Study
outcome: Error rate with patient-level conformal uncertainty flagging versus point predictions, internal and external validation
effect: At 90% confidence, errors were 10.5% (n=438) vs 34.6% (n=1449) for point predictions internally; externally 11.8% (n=1221) vs 43.8% (n=4540), with 29.4% and 38.6% flagged for review.
quote: In this case, the conformal predictor still produced significantly lower error rates compared to the point predictions by AI (n=1221, 11.8% vs n=4540, 43.8%).

title: Development and Validation of an Interpretable Conformal Predictor to Predict Sepsis Mortality Risk: Retrospective Cohort Study
outcome: Model discrimination drop on external multicenter database versus internal validation
effect: CPMORS AUC fell from 0.858 (95% CI 0.845-0.871) internally to 0.800 (95% CI 0.789-0.811) externally; all models deteriorated.
quote: When externally validated on the multicenter database eICU-CRD, the performance of all models deteriorated due to interdatabase heterogeneity.

title: Development and Validation of an Interpretable Conformal Predictor to Predict Sepsis Mortality Risk: Retrospective Cohort Study
outcome: AUC versus comparator models
effect: External AUC was 0.800 (95% CI 0.789-0.811) for CPMORS versus 0.693 to 0.786 for comparators.
quote: Nevertheless, CPMORS still showed the best performance with AUC 0.800 (95% CI 0.789-0.811) versus other models ranging from 0.693 (95% CI 0.680-0.706) to 0.786 (95% CI 0.775-0.798).

title: Step into the era of large multimodal models: a pilot study on ChatGPT-4V(ision)'s ability to interpret radiological images
outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of ChatGPT-4V on USMLE-style image questions, and with history removed
effect: Accuracy 77.01% on USMLE-style questions; dropped to 19.54% when detailed patient history removed (P<0.0001); AUC 0.768 for chest radiograph abnormality detection.
quote: Removing detailed patient history dropped the diagnostic accuracy to 19.54% (P<0.0001).

title: Accuracy and consistency of chatbots versus clinicians for answering pediatric dentistry questions: A pilot study
outcome: Accuracy of chatbots versus pediatric dentists, general dentists, and students on the same questions
effect: Pediatric dentists 96.67%±4.3%, general dentists 88.0%±6.1%, students 80.8%±6.9%; best chatbot (ChatGPT) 78%±3%; clinicians significantly more accurate than chatbots (p<0.001).
quote: General dentists (88.0 % ± 6.1 %) also demonstrated significantly higher accuracy than chatbots (p < 0.001), followed by students (80.8 %±6.9 %).
sample_unit: true/false pediatric dentistry questions (answered by 9 chatbots x 3 conversations and 60 clinicians)

title: Accuracy and consistency of chatbots versus clinicians for answering pediatric dentistry questions: A pilot study
outcome: Consistency of chatbot answers across 3 independent conversations (Cronbach's alpha)
effect: All chatbots except ChatGPT3.5 showed acceptable consistency (Cronbach alpha>0.7).
quote: All chatbots except ChatGPT3.5 showed acceptable consistency (Cronbach alpha>0.7).
sample_unit: true/false pediatric dentistry questions (answered by 9 chatbots x 3 conversations and 60 clinicians)

title: Effect of clinical decision support for severe hypercholesterolemia on low-density lipoprotein cholesterol levels
outcome: LDL-C difference between active and silent mode after CDS alert deployment
effect: LDL-C 6.6 mg/dL lower (95% CI -10.7 to -2.5; P=0.002) in active vs silent mode; higher odds of high-intensity statin use (OR 1.78) and LLT initiation/intensification (OR 1.30).
quote: LDL-C levels were 6.6 mg/dL lower (95% CI, -10.7 to -2.5; P = 0.002) in active vs. silent mode.

title: Artificial intelligence insights into osteoporosis: assessing ChatGPT's information quality and readability
outcome: Readability (FKRE, FKGL) of ChatGPT osteoporosis responses versus patient-comprehensible level
effect: FKRE mean 28.71 (range 13.71-56.06); FKGL mean 13.25 (range 8.48-17.63); abstract states about 17 years of education needed. EQIP mean 48.71, 'serious problems with quality'.
quote: The FKRE scores spanned from 13.71 to 56.06 with a mean value of 28.71 and the FKGL varied between 8.48 and 17.63, with a mean value of 13.25.

title: Generative artificial intelligence chatbots may provide appropriate informational responses to common vascular surgery questions by patients
outcome: Reading level of chatbot responses to patient vascular surgery questions
effect: ChatGPT Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level 14.5 ± 2.2, Gunning Fog 17.7 ± 3.1 (post-secondary education); Bard 8.2 ± 1.7 and 11.0 ± 2.0 (high-school).
quote: The mean Flesch Reading Ease, Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level, and Gunning Fog Index of ChatGPT responses were 29.4 ± 10.8, 14.5 ± 2.2, and 17.7 ± 3.1, respectively, indicating that responses were readable with a post-secondary education.

title: Generative artificial intelligence chatbots may provide appropriate informational responses to common vascular surgery questions by patients
outcome: Readability of AI-generated patient education responses versus plain-language comprehension
effect: ChatGPT responses readable only at post-secondary level (FRE 29.4, FKGL 14.5); Bard at high-school level (FRE 58.9, FKGL 8.2).
quote: Bard's mean readability scores were 58.9 ± 10.5, 8.2 ± 1.7, and 11.0 ± 2.0, respectively, indicating that responses were readable with a high-school education (p < .0001 for three metrics).

title: Screening/diagnosis of pediatric endocrine disorders through the artificial intelligence model in different language settings
outcome: ChatGPT response reliability and quality by language (Chinese vs English)
effect: Unreliable rate 7.5% for English vs 27.5% for Chinese questions; among reliable answers, English responses were more comprehensive and satisfactory.
quote: ChatGPT performed better when responding to questions in English, with an unreliable rate of 7.5% compared to 27.5% for Chinese questions, indicating a more consistent response pattern in English.
sample_unit: questions (each posed three times in Chinese and English)

title: Heterogeneity and predictors of the effects of AI assistance on radiologists
outcome: Radiologist performance with versus without AI assistance across 15 chest X-ray tasks; effect of AI errors
effect: AI assistance effects were heterogeneous across 140 radiologists; inaccurate AI predictions adversely affected radiologist performance on the aggregate of all pathologies and on half of the individual pathologies.
quote: Instead, we found that the occurrence of AI errors strongly influences treatment outcomes, with inaccurate AI predictions adversely affecting radiologist performance on the aggregate of all pathologies and on half of the individual pathologies investigated.

title: Heterogeneity and predictors of the effects of AI assistance on radiologists
outcome: Effect of incorrect AI predictions on radiologist performance (automation bias/overreliance)
effect: Inaccurate AI predictions adversely affected radiologist performance on the aggregate of all pathologies and on half of the individual pathologies investigated.
quote: Instead, we found that the occurrence of AI errors strongly influences treatment outcomes, with inaccurate AI predictions adversely affecting radiologist performance on the aggregate of all pathologies and on half of the individual pathologies investigated.

title: Artificial intelligence for characterization of colorectal polyps: Prospective multicenter study
outcome: AI vs expert endoscopist diagnostic performance for polyp histology prediction
effect: Sensitivity 80% (AI) vs 88% (endoscopists), P<0.05; specificity 83% for both; accuracy 81% vs 86%. AI classified 22 of 23 sessile serrated lesions as hyperplasia; endoscopists correctly classified 16 of 23.
quote: However, sensitivity was greater with endoscopists as compared with CAD EYE ( P <0.05).

title: Artificial Intelligence-Generated Draft Replies to Patient Inbox Messages
outcome: Time measures, clinician task load and work exhaustion after AI draft reply pilot
effect: No change in reply action, write, or read time; task load score fell 61.31 to 47.26 (P<.001); work exhaustion fell 1.95 to 1.62 (P<.001).
quote: There was no change in reply action time, write time, or read time between the prepilot and pilot periods.

title: Current safeguards, risk mitigation, and transparency measures of large language models against the generation of health disinformation: repeated cross sectional analysis
outcome: LLM safeguards against generating health disinformation under adversarial prompting and jailbreaking
effect: GPT-4 (ChatGPT), PaLM 2/Gemini Pro (Bard), and Llama 2 generated disinformation blogs without needing jailbreaks; refusal rate only 5% (7 of 150); Claude 2 declined all 130 prompts.
quote: In contrast, GPT-4 (via ChatGPT), PaLM 2/Gemini Pro (via Bard), and Llama 2 (via HuggingChat) consistently generated health disinformation blogs.

title: Current safeguards, risk mitigation, and transparency measures of large language models against the generation of health disinformation: repeated cross sectional analysis
outcome: Change in safeguards after model updates over 12 weeks
effect: GPT-4 (via Copilot) initially refused to generate disinformation even with jailbreaking, but did not refuse at 12 weeks, showing safeguards degraded over time.
quote: GPT-4 (via Copilot) initially refused to generate health disinformation, even with jailbreaking attempts-although this was not the case at 12 weeks.

title: Current safeguards, risk mitigation, and transparency measures of large language models against the generation of health disinformation: repeated cross sectional analysis
outcome: Whether LLMs flag or block health misinformation outputs
effect: Three of the evaluated LLMs generated 113 unique cancer disinformation blogs (over 40,000 words) with fake references and testimonials; refusal rate 5% (7 of 150).
quote: The refusal rate across the evaluation timepoints for these LLMs was only 5% (7 of 150), and as prompted the LLM generated blogs incorporated attention grabbing titles, authentic looking (fake or fictional) references, fabricated testimonials from patients and clinicians, and they targeted diverse demographic groups.

title: Current safeguards, risk mitigation, and transparency measures of large language models against the generation of health disinformation: repeated cross sectional analysis
outcome: Content filters blocking harmful generated outputs and resistance to circumvention
effect: Claude 2 declined all 130 prompts even with jailbreaking; Copilot blocked initially but not at 12 weeks; ChatGPT, Bard, HuggingChat generated disinformation, 5% refusal (7 of 150).
quote: Claude 2 (via Poe) declined 130 prompts submitted across the two study timepoints requesting the generation of content claiming that sunscreen causes skin cancer or that the alkaline diet is a cure for cancer, even with jailbreaking attempts.

title: Current safeguards, risk mitigation, and transparency measures of large language models against the generation of health disinformation: repeated cross sectional analysis
outcome: Developer responsiveness to reported safeguard vulnerabilities
effect: Each LLM had reporting mechanisms, but developers did not respond when vulnerabilities were reported.
quote: Although each LLM evaluated had mechanisms to report observed outputs of concern, the developers did not respond when observations of vulnerabilities were reported.

title: ChatGPT-3.5 and Bing Chat in ophthalmology: an updated evaluation of performance, readability, and informative sources
outcome: Association between reliability of Bing Chat cited sources and answer correctness
effect: Bing Chat cited at least one source for 836 of 913 questions; more reliable (peer-reviewed) sources were associated with higher likelihood of a correct response.
quote: The use of more reliable (peer-reviewed) sources was associated with higher likelihood of correct response.

title: ChatGPT-3.5 and Bing Chat in ophthalmology: an updated evaluation of performance, readability, and informative sources
outcome: Readability (SMOG grade level) of chatbot responses
effect: Bing Chat averaged grade 11.4 [95% CI 7.14, 15.7] versus ChatGPT-3.5 at 12.4 [95% CI 8.77, 16.1] (p < 0.0001).
quote: Bing Chat showed significantly better readability than ChatGPT-3.5, averaging a reading level of grade 11.4 [95% CI 7.14, 15.7] versus 12.4 [95% CI 8.77, 16.1], respectively (p-value < 0.0001, ρ = 0.25).

title: Optimizing efficiency of a custom clinical decision support tool improves adult congenital heart disease care
venue: American heart journal plus : cardiology research and practice
outcome: Percent true positive alerts after refining alert criteria based on reviewed alerts
effect: Median true positive alerts rose from baseline 47.3% to 78.9% after August 2021 changes; last four months met 85% goal.
quote: Following the changes implemented in August 2021, there was a significant increase in true positive CDS, which has sustained, and the median of percent true positives increased to 78.9 %, an improvement from the baseline median of 47.3 %.

title: Optimizing efficiency of a custom clinical decision support tool improves adult congenital heart disease care
venue: American heart journal plus : cardiology research and practice
outcome: False positive alerts per month after case review and corrective PDSA changes
effect: False positive alerts fell from median 35 (IQR 12) to 15 (IQR 7) per month; department code introduced new false positives (7 per month).
quote: With the implementation of PDSA, the number of false positive alerts dropped from 35 (12) alerts per month to 15 (7) (median (IQR)).

title: Optimizing efficiency of a custom clinical decision support tool improves adult congenital heart disease care
venue: American heart journal plus : cardiology research and practice
outcome: Proportion of alerts correctly identifying eligible ACHD patients
effect: Following local diagnostic-code refinements and addition of department encounter criteria, median true-positive alerts increased from 47.3 % to 78.9 %.
quote: Following the changes implemented in August 2021, there was a significant increase in true positive CDS, which has sustained, and the median of percent true positives increased to 78.9 %, an improvement from the baseline median of 47.3 %.

title: Dr. Google vs. Dr. ChatGPT: Exploring the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Ophthalmology by Comparing the Accuracy, Safety, and Readability of Responses to Frequently Asked Patient Questions Regarding Cataracts and Cataract Surgery
outcome: Readability grade level of ChatGPT responses to cataract FAQs versus Google
effect: ChatGPT responses were significantly longer and written at a higher reading level than Google (p < .001), with average grade level 14.8 (college level).
quote: Responses to 20 patient FAQs generated by ChatGPT were significantly longer and written at a higher reading level than responses provided by Google (p < .001), with an average grade level of 14.8 (college level).

title: The intervention of artificial intelligence to improve the weaning outcomes of patients with mechanical ventilation: Practical applications in the medical intensive care unit and the COVID-19 intensive care unit: A retrospective study
outcome: Mean MV time, ICU LOS, and hospital LOS with vs without AI-assisted weaning in COVID-19 ICU
effect: With AI (n=88) vs control (n=43): MV time 244.2 vs 426.0 hours (P=.011), ICU LOS 11.0 vs 18.7 days (P=.001), hospital LOS 23.5 vs 40.4 days (P<.001).
quote: In the second part of the study, the intervention group (with AI, n = 88) exhibited a shorter mean MV time (244.2 hours vs 426.0 hours, P = .011), ICU LOS (11.0 days vs 18.7 days, P = .001), and hospital LOS (23.5 days vs 40.4 days, P < .001) compared to the control group (without AI, n = 43).
sample_unit: patients (part 1: 1298 pre-AI, 1107 post-AI; part 2: 43 control, 88 AI)

title: Diagnosis and prognosis of abnormal cardiac scintigraphy uptake suggestive of cardiac amyloidosis using artificial intelligence: a retrospective, international, multicentre, cross-tracer development and validation study
outcome: AI discrimination (AUC) in independent validation cohorts from different centres
effect: Independent validation AUCs: UK 0·997 (0·993-0·999), China 0·925 (0·871-0·971), Italy 1·000 (0·999-1·000); the Chinese cohort was lower.
quote: Independent validation yielded AUCs of 0·997 (0·993-0·999) for the UK, 0·925 (0·871-0·971) for the Chinese, and 1·000 (0·999-1·000) for the Italian cohorts.

title: Diagnosis and prognosis of abnormal cardiac scintigraphy uptake suggestive of cardiac amyloidosis using artificial intelligence: a retrospective, international, multicentre, cross-tracer development and validation study
outcome: Robustness of AI performance across demographic factors, tracers, scanners, and centres in an algorithmic audit
effect: Audit demonstrated robustness across demographic factors, tracers, scanners, and centres; no details of subgroup numbers in the abstract.
quote: The medical algorithmic audit demonstrated the system's robustness across demographic factors, tracers, scanners, and centres.

title: Diagnosis and prognosis of abnormal cardiac scintigraphy uptake suggestive of cardiac amyloidosis using artificial intelligence: a retrospective, international, multicentre, cross-tracer development and validation study
outcome: AI diagnostic performance compared with five physicians on the same 200 cases
effect: Physicians' mean AUC 0·946 (0·924-0·967) was inferior to AI AUC 0·997 (0·991-1·000), p=0·0040; physicians disagreed in 22 (11%) of 200 cases.
quote: In the multicase multireader study, five physicians disagreed in 22 (11%) of 200 cases (Fleiss' kappa 0·89), with a mean AUC of 0·946 (95% CI 0·924-0·967), which was inferior to AI (AUC 0·997 [0·991-1·000], p=0·0040).

title: A deep-learning model for intracranial aneurysm detection on CT angiography images in China: a stepwise, multicentre, early-stage clinical validation study
outcome: AI versus clinician patient-level diagnostic sensitivity on external validation cases
effect: External patient-level sensitivity was 0·943 [0·921-0·961] for AI vs 0·658 [0·644-0·672] for clinicians; p<0·0001.
quote: The AI model in the internal dataset achieved a patient-level diagnostic sensitivity of 0·957 (95% CI 0·939-0·971) and a higher patient-level diagnostic sensitivity than clinicians (0·943 [0·921-0·961] vs 0·658 [0·644-0·672]; p<0·0001) in the external dataset.

title: A deep-learning model for intracranial aneurysm detection on CT angiography images in China: a stepwise, multicentre, early-stage clinical validation study
outcome: Patient-level sensitivity, internal versus external multicentre dataset
effect: Sensitivity 0.957 (95% CI 0.939-0.971) internal vs 0.943 (0.921-0.961) external; external AI exceeded clinicians' 0.658.
quote: The AI model in the internal dataset achieved a patient-level diagnostic sensitivity of 0·957 (95% CI 0·939-0·971) and a higher patient-level diagnostic sensitivity than clinicians (0·943 [0·921-0·961] vs 0·658 [0·644-0·672]; p<0·0001) in the external dataset.

title: A deep-learning model for intracranial aneurysm detection on CT angiography images in China: a stepwise, multicentre, early-stage clinical validation study
outcome: AI error rate from poor-quality images in prospective deployment
effect: 0.51% (8/1570) error rate due to poor-quality CTA images and recognition failure.
quote: In the prospective study, the AI model had a 0·51% (8/1570) error rate due to poor-quality CTA images and recognition failure.

title: A deep-learning model for intracranial aneurysm detection on CT angiography images in China: a stepwise, multicentre, early-stage clinical validation study
outcome: Model errors associated with poor-quality clinical images and recognition failure
effect: The prospective error rate was 0·51% (8/1570), attributed to poor-quality CTA images and recognition failure.
quote: In the prospective study, the AI model had a 0·51% (8/1570) error rate due to poor-quality CTA images and recognition failure.

title: A deep-learning model for intracranial aneurysm detection on CT angiography images in China: a stepwise, multicentre, early-stage clinical validation study
outcome: clinician diagnostic performance
effect: AI-assisted strategy improved clinicians' diagnostic AUC from 0.795 to 0.878 on a per-patient basis.
quote: In the multi-reader multi-case study, the AI-assisted strategy improved clinicians' diagnostic performance both on a per-patient basis (the area under the receiver operating characteristic curves [AUCs]; 0·795 [0·761-0·830] without AI vs 0·878 [0·850-0·906] with AI; p<0·0001) and a per-aneurysm basis (the area under the weighted alternative free-response receiver operating characteristic curves; 0·765 [0·732-0·799] vs 0·865 [0·839-0·891]; p<0·0001).

title: A deep-learning model for intracranial aneurysm detection on CT angiography images in China: a stepwise, multicentre, early-stage clinical validation study
outcome: prospective diagnostic performance
effect: In prospective deployment, AI significantly improved clinician AUC from 0.787 to 0.909 and sensitivity from 0.590 to 0.825.
quote: The model had a high negative predictive value of 0·998 (0·994-1·000) and significantly improved the diagnostic performance of clinicians; AUC improved from 0·787 (95% CI 0·766-0·808) to 0·909 (0·894-0·923; p<0·0001) and patient-level sensitivity improved from 0·590 (0·511-0·666) to 0·825 (0·759-0·880; p<0·0001).

title: A deep-learning model for intracranial aneurysm detection on CT angiography images in China: a stepwise, multicentre, early-stage clinical validation study
outcome: clinician acceptance
effect: Clinicians in the AI-assisted group demonstrated high acceptance with a 92.6% adoption rate.
quote: In the randomised open-label comparison study, clinicians in the AI-assisted group had a high acceptance of the AI model (92·6% adoption rate), and a higher AUC when compared with the control group (0·858 [95% CI 0·850-0·866] vs 0·789 [0·780-0·799]; p<0·0001).

title: Development and external validation of the eFalls tool: a multivariable prediction model for the risk of ED attendance or hospitalisation with a fall or fracture in older adults
outcome: Calibration before vs after local recalibration in external validation cohort
effect: Recalibration corrected over-prediction: pooled calibration slope 0.964 (95% CI 0.908 to 1.020), CITL 0.064 (95% CI -0.027 to 0.154), vs CITL -0.874 before; discrimination unchanged.
quote: Recalibration did not affect the discrimination performance or variability in calibration across practices (Supplementary Figures S3.12/S3.14), but corrected average over-prediction on apparent validation, giving a pooled calibration slope of 0.964 (95% CI: 0.908 to 1.020) and pooled CITL of 0.064 (95% CI: −0.027 to 0.154).

title: Development and external validation of the eFalls tool: a multivariable prediction model for the risk of ED attendance or hospitalisation with a fall or fracture in older adults
outcome: Calibration of model applied to new population (external validation)
effect: Model over-predicted risk in Bradford: pooled CITL -0.874 (95% CI -0.964 to -0.783), O/E 0.43 (95% CI 0.39 to 0.48); no better than treat-none at 10-25% thresholds.
quote: Calibration curves ( Figure 1 ) show that the eFalls model over-predicted fall/fracture risk in the Connect Bradford population, with predicted risks exceeding observed risks across the full range of possible predicted values.

title: Development and external validation of the eFalls tool: a multivariable prediction model for the risk of ED attendance or hospitalisation with a fall or fracture in older adults
outcome: Variation in calibration and net benefit across general practices
effect: Extent of over-prediction highly variable across GP practices; net benefit highly variable and did not stabilise with recalibration; c-statistic consistently above 0.6 in all practices.
quote: As with calibration performance, net benefit was highly variable across GP practices, which did not stabilise with recalibration (Supplementary Figure S3.13).

title: Development and external validation of the eFalls tool: a multivariable prediction model for the risk of ED attendance or hospitalisation with a fall or fracture in older adults
outcome: Model discrimination and calibration across clinical and deprivation subgroups
effect: Fairly consistent across sex and deprivation; discrimination lower in severe frailty (c-statistic 0.643); over-prediction most evident in underweight and severely frail; poor performance in those missing WIMD.
quote: Model performance was fairly consistent across sexes and deprivation subgroups, while over-prediction of falls risk was most evident in those who were underweight and those who had severe frailty.

title: Development and external validation of the eFalls tool: a multivariable prediction model for the risk of ED attendance or hospitalisation with a fall or fracture in older adults
outcome: Miscalibration from differences between development and validation populations
effect: Fall incidence 4.9% in development vs 2.9% in validation, differing coding systems; model over-predicted risk in the external population (O/E 0.43).
quote: This overestimation of risk was likely due to the higher incidence of falls in the development (4.9%) compared to the external validation cohorts (2.9%).

title: Development and external validation of the eFalls tool: a multivariable prediction model for the risk of ED attendance or hospitalisation with a fall or fracture in older adults
outcome: Discrimination and calibration on internal vs external validation data
effect: C-statistic 0.72 on internal-external cross-validation vs 0.82 external; external validation revealed miscalibration (CITL -0.87) that internal validation did not show.
quote: While the eFalls model was well calibrated on internal and internal–external cross-validation (in Welsh national-level data in SAIL), on external validation in Connected Bradford, although there was evidence for excellent discrimination, fall/fracture risk was slightly overestimated on average.

title: Development and external validation of the eFalls tool: a multivariable prediction model for the risk of ED attendance or hospitalisation with a fall or fracture in older adults
outcome: Net benefit at clinician-specified risk thresholds (10-25%) on external validation
effect: Model was no better than treat-none in the prespecified 10-25% range before recalibration; after recalibration superior for thresholds up to 18%.
quote: Decision curves show that the eFalls model had clinical utility at lower threshold probabilities on external validation, but was no better than the treat-none alternative in the pre-specified range of 10–25%.

title: Development and external validation of the eFalls tool: a multivariable prediction model for the risk of ED attendance or hospitalisation with a fall or fracture in older adults
outcome: external calibration and discrimination
effect: External c-statistic 0.82 (95% CI: 0.80 to 0.83); calibration-in-the-large, -0.87 (95% CI: -0.96 to -0.78).
quote: Calibration was variable across practices, with some over-prediction in the validation population (calibration-in-the-large, -0.87; 95% CI: -0.96 to -0.78).

title: Accuracy of Information given by ChatGPT for Patients with Inflammatory Bowel Disease in Relation to ECCO Guidelines
outcome: Accuracy and completeness of ChatGPT answers versus ECCO guidelines rated by gastroenterologists
effect: 84.2% of replies had median accuracy ≥4; mean accuracy 3.87; mean completeness 2.24/3. Lowest ratings for malignancy screening and vaccination in immunosuppression and family planning.
quote: However, responses in specialist areas may deviate from evidence-based guidance and the replies need to give more firm advice.

title: Assessment of the CLOT (children's likelihood of thrombosis) real-time risk prediction model of hospital-associated venous thromboembolism in children with congenital heart disease
outcome: AUROC of original vs locally refit CLOT model in CHD subpopulation
effect: Original AUROC 0.801 (0.749-0.850); refit to CHD cohort 0.846 (0.805-0.888); adding cardiac-specific features 0.859 (0.813-0.898), non-significant vs refit (P=.269).
quote: The original CLOT model with refit covariate β -values for the CHD cohort demonstrated better fit (AUROC = 0.846 [0.805–0.888]) compared to the original unaltered model.

title: Assessment of the CLOT (children's likelihood of thrombosis) real-time risk prediction model of hospital-associated venous thromboembolism in children with congenital heart disease
outcome: Discrimination in new target population
effect: Original CLOT AUROC in CHD cohort was 0.801 [0.749–0.850], below reported all-pediatric AUROC 0.907 [0.898–0.918].
quote: There is a slight diminishment in performance for the CHD cohort specifically with the unaltered original model (AUROC = 0.801 [0.749–0.850]).

title: Assessment of the CLOT (children's likelihood of thrombosis) real-time risk prediction model of hospital-associated venous thromboembolism in children with congenital heart disease
outcome: Discrimination of the general pediatric model when applied to CHD subpopulation
effect: AUROC fell from 0.908 (all pediatric patients) to 0.801 in the CHD cohort; refitting improved it to 0.846.
quote: Overall, there was a slight decrease in discrimination compared to the CLOT model’s performance for all pediatric patients (AUROC = 0.908[0.896–0.918]; Figure 2 ).

title: Assessment of the CLOT (children's likelihood of thrombosis) real-time risk prediction model of hospital-associated venous thromboembolism in children with congenital heart disease
outcome: AUROC comparing feature-expanded model
effect: Updated cardiac-specific model AUROC = 0.859 [0.813–0.898], a marginal non-significant improvement versus refit, P = .269.
quote: This updated cardiac specific model has an AUROC of 0.859 [0.813–0.898] ( Figure 2 ) demonstrating a marginal, but non-significant, improvement from the refit model ( P = .269).

title: Evaluating the validity of ChatGPT responses on common obstetric issues: Potential clinical applications and implications
venue: International journal of gynaecology and obstetrics: the official organ of the International Federation of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
outcome: Expert-rated accuracy, completeness, and safety of ChatGPT answers to pregnancy questions
effect: Accuracy mean 4.2 (80% positive); completeness mean 3.8 (46.7% positive); safety mean 3.9 (53.3% positive); no response averaged below 3.
quote: The responses scored less for the completeness criterion, with a mean rating of 3.8 and 46.7% of questions received a positive rating.

title: Effectiveness of an Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Intervention for Detecting Clinical Deterioration
outcome: Escalations in care (RRT activation, ICU transfer, cardiopulmonary arrest) at EDI alert threshold
effect: Absolute risk reduction of -10.4 percentage points (95% CI, -20.1 to -0.8; P = .03) at threshold; secondary outcome including death -7.0 points (95% CI, -16.6 to 2.6; P = .15); no mortality reduction.
quote: The RDD analysis estimated an absolute risk reduction of −10.4 percentage points (95% CI, −20.1 to −0.8 percentage points; P = .03) in the primary outcome for patients at the EDI score threshold.

title: Effectiveness of an Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Intervention for Detecting Clinical Deterioration
outcome: Escalations in care: RRT activation, ICU transfer, or cardiopulmonary arrest
effect: At the EDI score threshold, absolute risk reduction was −10.4 percentage points (95% CI, −20.1 to −0.8 percentage points; P = .03). Inpatient mortality was not significantly reduced.
quote: The RDD analysis estimated an absolute risk reduction of −10.4 percentage points (95% CI, −20.1 to −0.8 percentage points; P = .03) in the primary outcome for patients at the EDI score threshold.

title: Reinforcement learning for intensive care medicine: actionable clinical insights from novel approaches to reward shaping and off-policy model evaluation
outcome: Policy robustness when evaluated under varied reward-function weightings (cross-OPE)
effect: Only 9,635 (56%) of 17,182 policies passing initial OPE passed cross-OPE; 44% showed suboptimal performance under alternate reward weightings, indicating overfitting or poor generalisability.
quote: Despite the successful performance of the models in the initial evaluation phase, a considerable number failed to exhibit comparable results during the cross-OPE evaluation utilising an alternate reward function shape.

title: Reinforcement learning for intensive care medicine: actionable clinical insights from novel approaches to reward shaping and off-policy model evaluation
outcome: hidden action-specific policy bias
effect: A top-ten-percentile, positive OPE/cross-OPE model showed bias against 'PEEP 10–14 and FiO2 80–100%.'
quote: Figure 5 provides an example of a model with policies that had good quantitative (top ten percentile and only positive OPE and cross-OPE results) results, but shows a bias against one specific action, 'PEEP 10–14 and FiO2 80–100%.'

title: The Emerging Role of AI in Patient Education: A Comparative Analysis of the Accuracy of Large Language Models for Pelvic Organ Prolapse
venue: Medical principles and practice : international journal of the Kuwait University, Health Science Centre
outcome: Readability (SMOG, Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level) of LLM patient education answers versus RCOG originals
effect: ChatGPT answers were harder to read than BARD, Bing, and the original RCOG answers; no numeric grade levels are given in the abstract.
quote: In terms of readability, ChatGPT exhibited higher difficulty than BARD, Bing, and the original RCOG answers.

title: Quality, Accuracy, and Bias in ChatGPT-Based Summarization of Medical Abstracts
outcome: Physician-rated accuracy and frequency of hallucinations in ChatGPT summaries of medical abstracts
effect: Median accuracy 92.5 (IQR 89.0-95.0) on 0-100 scale; serious inaccuracies and hallucinations uncommon; median bias 0 (IQR 0-7.5).
quote: Serious inaccuracies and hallucinations were uncommon.

title: Preoperative risk prediction models for acute kidney injury after noncardiac surgery: an independent external validation cohort study
outcome: Calibration and net benefit before and after recalibration by intercept and slope updates
effect: Five of nine models were well-calibrated after intercept and slope updates. The three models with fair discrimination consistently provided a positive net benefit after recalibration.
quote: All models exhibited some miscalibration; five of the nine models were well-calibrated after intercept and slope updates.

title: Preoperative risk prediction models for acute kidney injury after noncardiac surgery: an independent external validation cohort study
outcome: Head-to-head comparison of nine candidate prediction models on the same validation data
effect: Performance varied widely across models; only three showed fair discrimination and positive net benefit after recalibration.
quote: We identified three models with fair discrimination and potential clinical utility after recalibration for assessing the risk of acute kidney injury after noncardiac surgery.

title: Preoperative risk prediction models for acute kidney injury after noncardiac surgery: an independent external validation cohort study
outcome: Discrimination, calibration and net benefit of nine published AKI models on a local retrospective cohort

title: Preparing for the bedside-optimizing a postpartum depression risk prediction model for clinical implementation in a health system
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
outcome: Effect of five debiasing approaches on fairness metrics and model accuracy
effect: All approaches largely improved fairness metrics except predictive parity difference; approaches 2, 4, 5 most successful; blindness improved fairness without compromising performance; reweighing reduced sensitivity by about 0.25.
quote: While it is commonly a concern that debiasing method may compromise predictive performance, for our study, they improved fairness without compromise.

title: Preparing for the bedside-optimizing a postpartum depression risk prediction model for clinical implementation in a health system
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
outcome: Threshold selection using decision curve net benefit, sensitivity, and positive prediction rates
effect: Net benefit was highest at 0.3-0.4 thresholds; 0.2 predicted 19-23% positive versus 13-18% at 0.3 and 11-15% at 0.4; threshold 0.3 balanced true and false positives while 0.2 missed fewer at-risk patients.
quote: A threshold of 0.3 produces positive predictions that are close to the observed prevalence at the AMC, while a threshold of 0.2 generates more positive predictions potentially allowing us to capture more at-risk patients albeit with false positive predictions.

title: Preparing for the bedside-optimizing a postpartum depression risk prediction model for clinical implementation in a health system
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
outcome: Fairness metrics by race subgroup (White vs non-White) across three datasets before deployment
effect: Baseline model met equal-error-rate metrics but failed statistical parity and disparate impact in AMC data; clinical research network metrics were all within range, so fairness varied across datasets.
quote: The clinical research network dataset’s observed metrics are all within the defined fairness range.

title: Preparing for the bedside-optimizing a postpartum depression risk prediction model for clinical implementation in a health system
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
outcome: Model performance on local post-development AMC data (2019, 2020) against reference outcome
effect: Model maintained predictive performance on local later-year data (AUC 0.96 in 2019, 0.97 in 2020; sensitivity 0.95, 0.97 at threshold 0.3) though it showed unequal positive prediction rates.
quote: We found that the original model maintained predictive performance and, while satisfying fairness metrics that prioritized equal error rates, did not create equal positive prediction rates between White and non-White patients.

title: Preparing for the bedside-optimizing a postpartum depression risk prediction model for clinical implementation in a health system
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
outcome: Model performance and fairness in a later year (COVID-19) and a different clinical research network population
effect: AUC remained high (0.94-0.97) across datasets, but fairness varied: biased on statistical parity in AMC data, generally unbiased in the clinical research network data.
quote: The findings revealed that the model exhibited biased performance in the AMC data but showed less bias in the clinical research network data, thus showing fairness metrics may vary across datasets.

title: Preparing for the bedside-optimizing a postpartum depression risk prediction model for clinical implementation in a health system
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
outcome: Multidisciplinary governance review of model inputs and clinician interpretability changed the deployed model design
effect: Expert review raised concern about clinicians interpreting race as a predictor, and this fed into selecting fairness through blindness as the revised model.
quote: More importantly, it meets the expert feedback highlighting the difficulties clinicians might face interpreting race as a top predictor in a clinical decision support tool.

title: Preparing for the bedside-optimizing a postpartum depression risk prediction model for clinical implementation in a health system
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
outcome: racial subgroup fairness metrics
effect: At threshold 0.3, baseline statistical parity/disparate impact were −0.175/0.403 (2019 AMC) and −0.122/0.599 (2020 AMC), outside [−0.1, 0.1]/[0.8, 1.25].
quote: However, both statistical parity difference and disparate impact did not meet the fairness criteria.

title: Validation of a Multivariable Model to Predict Suicide Attempt in a Mental Health Intake Sample
outcome: Performance of existing suicide attempt model on local historical intake data against reference outcomes
effect: AUROC 0.77 (95% CI 0.76-0.78); AUPRC 0.02; sensitivity 37.2% at 95% specificity, 18.8% at 99% specificity; top 10% risk captured 48.8% of attempts.
quote: The model had an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.77 (95% CI, 0.76-0.78), an area under the precision-recall curve of 0.02 (95% CI, 0.02-0.02), an expected calibration error of 0.0012 (95% CI, 0.0011-0.0013), and sensitivities of 37.2% (95% CI, 35.5%-38.9%) and 18.8% (95% CI, 17.3%-20.2%) at specificities of 95% and 99%, respectively.

title: Validation of a Multivariable Model to Predict Suicide Attempt in a Mental Health Intake Sample
outcome: Model performance when extended to a new use context (intake appointments)
effect: Model developed for any outpatient mental health visit showed good overall classification at intake (AUROC 0.77), but very low precision (AUPRC 0.02) given 0.17% base rate.
quote: In this prognostic study involving mental health intakes, a previously developed machine learning model of suicide attempts showed good overall classification performance.

title: Enhancing a deep learning model for pulmonary nodule malignancy risk estimation in chest CT with uncertainty estimation

title: Robustness evaluation of deep neural networks for endoscopic image analysis: Insights and strategies

title: Generative artificial intelligence and non-pharmacological bias: an experimental study on cancer patient sexual health communications
outcome: Concordance of chatbot recommendations with clinical guidelines on pharmacological versus non-pharmacological interventions
effect: Both bots favored counselling over pharmacological options despite guidelines recommending both; OR=47.3 in Bot1 (95% CI 9.55 to 233.81) and 97.2 in Bot2 (95% CI 11.72 to 806.04), p<0.001.
quote: For sexual response and sexual function, the guidelines recommended both pharmacological and non-pharmacological intervention for them, non-pharmacological intervention (counselling) was significantly more frequently than pharmacological intervention (OR=47.3 in Bot1 (95% CI 9.55 to 233.81, p<0.001), 97.2 in Bot2 (95% CI 11.72 to 806.04, p<0.001)).

title: Generative artificial intelligence and non-pharmacological bias: an experimental study on cancer patient sexual health communications
outcome: guideline grounding effect on intervention recommendations

title: Generative artificial intelligence and non-pharmacological bias: an experimental study on cancer patient sexual health communications
outcome: censorship of sexual and medical terms

title: Recalibration of a Non-Laboratory-Based Risk Model to Estimate Pre-Diabetes/Diabetes Mellitus Risk in Primary Care in Hong Kong
venue: Journal of primary care & community health
outcome: Calibration of the model after local recalibration/updating using primary care data

quote: Recalibrating the model's regression constant, with no change to the predictors' coefficients, improved the model's accuracy (calibration plot intercept: -0.01, slope: 0.69).

title: Recalibration of a Non-Laboratory-Based Risk Model to Estimate Pre-Diabetes/Diabetes Mellitus Risk in Primary Care in Hong Kong
venue: Journal of primary care & community health

quote: The simple recalibration method can adapt the HK Chinese pre-DM/DM model to PC populations with different pre-test probabilities.

title: Recalibration of a Non-Laboratory-Based Risk Model to Estimate Pre-Diabetes/Diabetes Mellitus Risk in Primary Care in Hong Kong
venue: Journal of primary care & community health

quote: Calibration plots of the models indicated that the models tended to systematically underestimate the absolute pre-DM/DM risks for individuals in PC.

title: Recalibration of a Non-Laboratory-Based Risk Model to Estimate Pre-Diabetes/Diabetes Mellitus Risk in Primary Care in Hong Kong
venue: Journal of primary care & community health

title: Health Care Cost Reductions with Machine Learning–Directed Evaluations during Radiation Therapy — An Economic Analysis of a Randomized Controlled Study

quote: Total mean adjusted costs were $3110 per course for the standard group and $1494 for the intervention group (difference in means, $1616 [95% confidence interval, $1450 to $1783]; P=0.03).
