outcome: Readability (Flesch-Kincaid) and word length of ChatGPT patient education articles versus ACOG articles
effect: AI articles had lower Flesch-Kincaid score (mean 46 vs. 59; p<0.0001) and greater average word length (5.3 vs. 4.8), so were harder to read than ACOG materials.
quote: Characteristics of the 25 AI-generated articles included fewer overall characters than original articles (mean 3,066 vs. 7,426; p < 0.0001), a greater average word length (mean 5.3 vs. 4.8; p < 0.0001), and a lower Flesch-Kincaid score (mean 46 vs. 59; p < 0.0001).

title: Identifying ChatGPT-Written Patient Education Materials Using Text Analysis and Readability
outcome: Readability of AI-generated patient education articles
effect: AI-generated articles had lower Flesch-Kincaid scores than original articles: mean 46 vs. 59; p<0.0001.
quote: Characteristics of the 25 AI-generated articles included fewer overall characters than original articles (mean 3,066 vs. 7,426; p < 0.0001), a greater average word length (mean 5.3 vs. 4.8; p < 0.0001), and a lower Flesch-Kincaid score (mean 46 vs. 59; p < 0.0001).

title: ChatGPT-4 generates orthopedic discharge documents faster than humans maintaining comparable quality: a pilot study of 6 cases
outcome: Hallucination events in AI-generated discharge documents versus physician-written
effect: 4 hallucination events found in ChatGPT-4-generated content, compared with 6 events in physician-produced notes; quality comparable overall.
quote: 4 events of hallucinations were found in the ChatGPT-4-generated content, compared with 6 events in the human/physician produced notes.
sample_unit: fictional orthopedic cases (discharge documents rated by 15 expert panelists)

title: Interventional cardiologists' perspectives and knowledge towards artificial intelligence
outcome: Clinician self-reported AI knowledge and perceived need for training
effect: 73.5% believed physicians know too little about AI to use it on patients; 46.1% agreed training will be necessary; 84.7% could explain or somewhat knew what AI is.
quote: However, 73.5% believed that physicians know too little about AI to use it on patients and most (46.1%) agreed that training will be necessary.

title: Generative models improve fairness of medical classifiers under distribution shifts
outcome: Subgroup diagnostic accuracy and robustness with vs without synthetic augmentation, in and out of distribution
effect: Adding diffusion-generated synthetic samples improved robustness in all three tasks and improved accuracy within underrepresented groups, especially out of distribution. Numbers not given in the text.
quote: Complementing real samples with synthetic ones improved the robustness of models in all three medical tasks and increased fairness by improving the accuracy of clinical diagnosis within underrepresented groups, especially out of distribution.

title: Doctor's Orders-Why Radiologists Should Consider Adjusting Commercial Machine Learning Applications in Chest Radiography to Fit Their Specific Needs
outcome: Accuracy of combined comprehensive reading of seven abnormalities without human supervision
effect: Combined reading: sensitivity 31.37%, specificity 14.55%; 364 (76.31%) patients with false positives and 35 (7.34%) with missed findings; not suitable for unsupervised use.
quote: Therefore and as of today, DL applications appear not to be suitable for completely unsupervised application in the clinical setting.

title: Doctor's Orders-Why Radiologists Should Consider Adjusting Commercial Machine Learning Applications in Chest Radiography to Fit Their Specific Needs
outcome: subgroup effects on DL results
effect: Gold-standard negatives: multimorbidity β = 0.151, age β = 0.089, and sex β = −0.038 were significant.
quote: Significant effects were found for the parameters of multimorbidity ( β = 0.151, p < 0.001), age ( β = 0.089, p < 0.001), and sex ( β = −0.038, p = 0.031; sex was dummy coded using “0” for male and “1” for female).

title: Doctor's Orders-Why Radiologists Should Consider Adjusting Commercial Machine Learning Applications in Chest Radiography to Fit Their Specific Needs
outcome: Effect of locally adjusted DL thresholds on workload reduction and NPV in chest radiograph screening
effect: Threshold adjustment to 95% sensitivity ruled out about 40% of cases for single-disease screening with NPV around 99%; default Youden thresholds gave sensitivity 85.33%, specificity 75.1%.
quote: It might enable a significant workload reduction of about 40% in ruling out specific diseases, thereby maintaining sensitivities above 95% and NPVs around 99% when reasonable optimized cutoff values for DL results are applied.

title: Doctor's Orders-Why Radiologists Should Consider Adjusting Commercial Machine Learning Applications in Chest Radiography to Fit Their Specific Needs
outcome: Influence of sex, age, multimorbidity on DL-radiologist agreement
effect: In gold-standard negatives, multimorbidity (β=0.151), age (β=0.089) and sex (β=-0.038) significantly influenced DL results; in positives, female sex (β=0.153, p=0.026) linked to lower DL results.
quote: Significant effects were found for the parameters of multimorbidity ( β = 0.151, p < 0.001), age ( β = 0.089, p < 0.001), and sex ( β = −0.038, p = 0.031; sex was dummy coded using “0” for male and “1” for female).

title: Doctor's Orders-Why Radiologists Should Consider Adjusting Commercial Machine Learning Applications in Chest Radiography to Fit Their Specific Needs
outcome: threshold effects on single-disease screening
effect: At ≥95% sensitivity cutoffs: 31 (6.5%) true positive, 197 (41.3%) true negative, 248 (51.99%) false positive, 1 (0.21%) false negative.
quote: When scanning for only one kind of abnormal finding using these cutoff values, on average around 31 (6.5%) of all cases were classfied true positive, 197 (41.3%) true negative, 248 (51.99%) false positive, and 1 (0.21%) case false negative.

title: Doctor's Orders-Why Radiologists Should Consider Adjusting Commercial Machine Learning Applications in Chest Radiography to Fit Their Specific Needs
outcome: missed findings when autonomously ruling out cases
effect: Autonomous triage using Youden-optimized cutoffs achieved 13% workload reduction but missed positive findings in 35 patients (7.34%).
quote: The findings for these cutoff values would allow for some workload reduction of about 13% but at the cost of missing findings in around 7.34% of patients, which is not acceptable, as the minimum goal of applying DL tools in the clinical setting should be noninferiority to the current gold standard to avert potential danger for patients.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Medical Imaging: Analyzing the Performance of ChatGPT and Microsoft Bing in Scoliosis Detection and Cobb Angle Assessment
outcome: General-purpose LLM accuracy on intended-use imaging tasks (scoliosis detection, Cobb angle) versus expert assessment
effect: ChatGPT detected scoliosis in 100% of images but Bing detected none; ChatGPT accurate for Cobb angle in only 43.5%, with limited accuracy for curve direction, type, and vertebral rotation.
quote: However, ChatGPT had limited effectiveness (43.5%) in assessing Cobb angles, showing significant inaccuracy and discrepancy compared to human assessments.
sample_unit: posturographic X-ray images of severe single-curve scoliosis

title: Using Large Language Models to Generate Educational Materials on Childhood Glaucoma
outcome: Whether LLM rewrites of existing online materials achieved 6th-grade reading level
effect: Prompt C rewrites consistently reduced mean SMOG and FKGL, but only ChatGPT-4 achieved the 6th-grade level (SMOG 4.8 ± 0.8, FKGL 3.7 ± 1.9).
quote: Although Prompt C responses showed consistent reduction of mean SMOG and FKGL scores, only ChatGPT-4 achieved the specified 6th-grade reading level (4.8 ± 0.8 and 3.7 ± 1.9, respectively).
sample_unit: LLM-generated patient education materials (3 LLMs, 3 prompts; 20 existing online resources rewritten)

title: Using Large Language Models to Generate Educational Materials on Childhood Glaucoma
outcome: Readability (SMOG, FKGL) of LLM patient education materials with explicit 6th-grade prompt versus general understandability prompt
effect: Prompt B (6th-grade SMOG) responses were more readable than Prompt A for all 3 LLMs (P ≤ .001); ChatGPT-4 most readable.
quote: Prompt B responses were more readable than Prompt A responses for all 3 LLM (P ≤ .001).
sample_unit: LLM-generated patient education materials (3 LLMs, 3 prompts; 20 existing online resources rewritten)

title: Using Large Language Models to Generate Educational Materials on Childhood Glaucoma
outcome: reading level of rewritten patient education materials
effect: ChatGPT-4 achieved 6th-grade level (SMOG 4.8 ± 0.8, FKGL 3.7 ± 1.9), while ChatGPT-3.5 and Bard did not
quote: Although Prompt C responses showed consistent reduction of mean SMOG and FKGL scores, only ChatGPT-4 achieved the specified 6th-grade reading level (4.8 ± 0.8 and 3.7 ± 1.9, respectively).
sample_unit: LLM-generated patient education materials (3 LLMs, 3 prompts; 20 existing online resources rewritten)

title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of a Generative Pretrained Transformer-Based Dietary Recommendation System in Managing Potassium Intake for Hemodialysis Patients
venue: Journal of renal nutrition : the official journal of the Council on Renal Nutrition of the National Kidney Foundation
outcome: Predialysis serum potassium and hyperkalemia proportion after GPT-based versus conventional dietary education
effect: Serum potassium 4.57 ± 0.76 vs 4.84 ± 0.94 mmol/L (P = .004); hyperkalemia fell from 39.8% to 25% (P = .036). Sequential before-after design, not randomized.
quote: Importantly, compared to traditional dietary education, dietary education based on the GPTs tool reduced the proportion of hyperkalemia in HD patients from 39.8% to 25% (P = .036).

title: An artificial intelligence model for detecting pathological lymph node metastasis in prostate cancer using whole slide images: a retrospective, multicentre, diagnostic study
outcome: AUROC of model trained at one centre and externally validated at four other centres
effect: AUROC ranged from 0.975 (0.953-0.998) to 0.992 (0.982-1.000) in training and validation datasets, sensitivities >0.955 and specificities >0.921; cross-cancer AUROC 0.979.
quote: The AUROC of ProCaLNMD ranged from 0.975 (95% confidence interval 0.953-0.998) to 0.992 (0.982-1.000) in the training and validation datasets, with sensitivities > 0.955 and specificities > 0.921.
sample_unit: patients with prostate cancer (8158 slides, 18,761 lymph nodes)

title: An artificial intelligence model for detecting pathological lymph node metastasis in prostate cancer using whole slide images: a retrospective, multicentre, diagnostic study
outcome: AI sensitivity compared with junior and senior pathologists on the same data
effect: AI sensitivity 0.983 exceeded two junior pathologists (0.862, P=0.023; 0.879, P=0.041) by 10-12% and matched two senior pathologists (both 0.983).
quote: In the human-AI comparison and collaboration study, the sensitivity of ProCaLNMD (0.983 [0.908-1.000]) surpassed that of two junior pathologists (0.862 [0.746-0.939], P = 0.023; 0.879 [0.767-0.950], P = 0.041) by 10-12% and showed no difference to that of two senior pathologists (both 0.983 [0.908-1.000], both P > 0.99).
sample_unit: patients with prostate cancer (8158 slides, 18,761 lymph nodes)

title: Prediction of cardiovascular risk factors from retinal fundus photographs: Validation of a deep learning algorithm in a prospective non-interventional study in Kenya
outcome: Differences between development (UK Biobank) and Kenyan deployment population characteristics
effect: Kenyan participants were younger, likely Black/African, with higher BMI and higher prevalence of DM and hypertension than UK Biobank development population.
quote: Compared with the UK Biobank population used for algorithm development, participants from Kenya were younger and would probably report Black/African ethnicity, with a higher body mass index and prevalence of DM and hypertension.

title: Prediction of cardiovascular risk factors from retinal fundus photographs: Validation of a deep learning algorithm in a prospective non-interventional study in Kenya
outcome: Model performance on local Kenyan data versus development data
effect: MAE comparable or slightly greater; DM AUROC 0.762 (0.818 in UK Biobank); hypertension AUROC 0.765 (0.738 in UK Biobank).
quote: The model trained to identify DM had an area under the receiver operating curve of 0.762 (0.818 in the UK Biobank) and the hypertension model had an area under the receiver operating curve of 0.765 (0.738 in the UK Biobank).

title: AI-Generated Draft Replies Integrated Into Health Records and Physicians' Electronic Communication
outcome: Physician time reading and replying to messages and reply length with vs without GenAI drafts
effect: GenAI associated with 21.8% increase in read time (95% CI 5.2% to 41.0%; P=.008), -5.9% reply time (P=.33), 17.9% increase in reply length (P<.001).
quote: The estimated association of GenAI was a 21.8% increase in read time (95% CI, 5.2% to 41.0%; P = .008), a -5.9% change in reply time (95% CI, -16.6% to 6.2%; P = .33), and a 17.9% increase in reply length (95% CI, 10.1% to 26.2%; P < .001).

title: Identifying social determinants of health from clinical narratives: A study of performance, documentation ratio, and potential bias
outcome: NLP SDoH extraction performance across race and gender subgroups
effect: Small performance gap (~4%) between males and females, but a large performance gap (>16%) among race groups.
quote: There is a small performance gap (∼4%) between Males and Females, but a large performance gap (>16 %) among race groups.
sample_unit: clinical notes (cancer corpus; plus 200 opioid-use notes for cross-disease validation)

title: Identifying social determinants of health from clinical narratives: A study of performance, documentation ratio, and potential bias
outcome: Performance of cancer SDoH model on opioid cohort before and after local fine-tuning
effect: Performance dropped when the cancer SDoH model was applied to the opioid cohort; fine-tuning using a smaller opioid SDoH corpus improved performance.
quote: The performance dropped when we applied the cancer SDoH model to the opioid cohort; fine-tuning using a smaller opioid SDoH corpus improved the performance.
sample_unit: clinical notes (cancer corpus; plus 200 opioid-use notes for cross-disease validation)

title: Data Extraction from Free-Text Reports on Mechanical Thrombectomy in Acute Ischemic Stroke Using ChatGPT: A Retrospective Analysis
outcome: Correct data extraction by GPT-4 versus GPT-3.5 on the same reports against manual reference standard
effect: GPT-4 extracted 2631 of 2800 entries correctly (94.0%) vs GPT-3.5 1788 of 2800 (63.9%), P<.001; external reports 90.5% vs 64.2%, P<.001.
quote: With 1788 of 2800 correct data entries, GPT-3.5 produced fewer correct data entries than did GPT-4 (63.9% [95% CI: 62.0, 65.6]; range per category, 14%-99%; P < .001).

title: Data Extraction from Free-Text Reports on Mechanical Thrombectomy in Acute Ischemic Stroke Using ChatGPT: A Retrospective Analysis
outcome: GPT-4 extraction accuracy on external institution reports versus internal reports
effect: GPT-4 extracted 760 of 840 (90.5%) correct entries on external reports vs 94.0% internally; GPT-3.5 539 of 840 (64.2%).
quote: For the external reports, GPT-4 extracted 760 of 840 (90.5% [95% CI: 88.3, 92.4]) correct data entries, while GPT-3.5 extracted 539 of 840 (64.2% [95% CI: 60.8, 67.4]; P < .001).

title: Potential of GPT-4 for Detecting Errors in Radiology Reports: Implications for Reporting Accuracy
outcome: GPT-4 error detection rate versus radiologists on the same reports
effect: GPT-4 detected 82.7% (124/150) of errors, matching average radiologist performance (80.0% to 89.3%; P range .522-.99); one senior radiologist outperformed GPT-4 (94.7%, P=.006).
quote: GPT-4 (detection rate, 82.7%;124 of 150; 95% CI: 75.8, 87.9) matched the average detection performance of radiologists independent of their experience (senior radiologists, 89.3% [134 of 150; 95% CI: 83.4, 93.3]; attending physicians, 80.0% [120 of 150; 95% CI: 72.9, 85.6]; residents, 80.0% [120 of 150; 95% CI: 72.9, 85.6]; P value range, .522-.99).

title: Integrating Explainable Machine Learning in Clinical Decision Support Systems: Study Involving a Modified Design Thinking Approach
outcome: Clinician trust and acceptance of prototype designed with continuous end-user engagement
effect: Physicians found the prototype design elegant and domain appropriate, and appreciated the explainability overlay and multi-image comparison. No comparator was used, so this is qualitative support only.
quote: Our work shows the importance and value of engaging end users prior to tool development.

title: Biomedical text readability after hypernym substitution with fine-tuned large language models
outcome: Readability and sentence complexity of biomedical text before vs after LLM hypernym substitution
effect: All three fine-tuned LLM approaches improved readability and sentence complexity; scores moved from collegiate to US high-school level; GPT-J-6b best on sentence complexity.
quote: Readability scores were translated from a pre-processed collegiate reading level to a post-processed US high-school level.

title: ChatGPT provides inconsistent risk-stratification of patients with atraumatic chest pain
outcome: Consistency of ChatGPT-4 risk scores across five repeated runs on identical simulated chest pain cases
effect: Different risk given 45-48% of the time for a fixed TIMI or HEART score; on the 44-variable model, majority agreement on diagnosis category only 56%, risk score correlation r = 0.605.
quote: ChatGPT-4 gave a different risk 45-48% of the time for a fixed TIMI or HEART score.

title: The virtual reference radiologist: comprehensive AI assistance for clinical image reading and interpretation
outcome: Radiologist diagnostic accuracy and confidence with vs without GPT-4 assistance
effect: Top-3 diagnostic accuracy improved from 181/240 (75.4%) unassisted to 188/240 (78.3%) AI-assisted; diagnostic confidence significantly higher with AI assistance.
quote: When assessing if the correct diagnosis was among the top-3 differential diagnoses, diagnostic accuracy improved slightly from 181/240 (75.4%, unassisted) to 188/240 (78.3%, AI-assisted).
sample_unit: readings (6 radiologists x 40 imaging studies per session)

title: The virtual reference radiologist: comprehensive AI assistance for clinical image reading and interpretation
outcome: Rate of hallucinations and misinterpretations in GPT-4 responses
effect: 23 responses (7.4%) classified as hallucinations and 2 (0.6%) as misinterpretations among 309 prompts.
quote: Twenty-three responses (7.4%) were classified as hallucinations, while two (0.6%) were misinterpretations.
sample_unit: readings (6 radiologists x 40 imaging studies per session)

title: Validation of GPT-4 for clinical event classification: A comparative analysis with ICD codes and human reviewers
outcome: GPT-4 accuracy versus ICD codes and human reviewers for GI bleeding classification on same data
effect: GPT-4 accuracy 94.4% vs ICD codes 63.5% (P<0.001); vs Reviewer 1 98.5% (P<0.001); vs Reviewer 2 90.8% (P=0.170).
quote: GPT-4 exhibited an accuracy of 94.4% in identifying GI bleeding occurrences, outperforming ICD codes (accuracy 63.5%, P < 0.001).

title: Quality of Answers of Generative Large Language Models Versus Peer Users for Interpreting Laboratory Test Results for Lay Patients: Evaluation Study
outcome: LLM answer quality (relevance, correctness, helpfulness, safety) on patient lab-result questions versus peers and other LLMs
effect: GPT-4 scored better than all other LLMs and human answers on all 4 aspects, but some GPT-4 responses were inaccurate or not individualized.
quote: The results of the win rate and medical expert evaluation both showed that GPT-4's responses achieved better scores than all the other LLM responses and human responses on all 4 aspects (relevance, correctness, helpfulness, and safety).

title: ROAD2H: Development and evaluation of an open-source explainable artificial intelligence approach for managing co-morbidity and clinical guidelines
outcome: Pulmonologists' agreement with CDSS assessments and reception of explainable argumentation
effect: Pulmonologists agreed 97% with symptom severity assessment and 98% with one of the proposed care plans; comments favourable on explainable argumentation, with suggestion to customise explanation level by expertise.
quote: Comments were favourable on the principles of explainable argumentation; inclusion of additional co-morbidities was suggested in the future along with customisation of the level of explanation with expertise.

title: Academic Detailing as a Health Information Technology Implementation Method: Supporting the Design and Implementation of an Emergency Department-Based Clinical Decision Support Tool to Prevent Future Falls
outcome: Whether structured clinician interviews during early implementation identify workflow-fit and use factors for a CDS tool
effect: 10-minute academic detailing interviews (n=16) identified five categories of factors affecting CDS use (design, understanding, busy ED, patient perception, opaque referral process) and allowed concurrent correction of misconceptions.
quote: Thus, academic detailing can inform both real-time adjustments of a tool's implementation, for example, refinement of the language used to introduce the tool, and larger scale redesign of the CDS tool to better fit the dynamic work environment of clinicians.
sample_unit: clinicians (resident emergency medicine physicians and advanced practice providers)

title: Evaluating ChatGPT's efficacy in assessing the safety of non-prescription medications and supplements in patients with kidney disease
outcome: Concordance of ChatGPT drug safety classification with Micromedex for kidney disease patients
effect: Agreement with Micromedex was 64.5% for ChatGPT-3.5 and 81.4% for ChatGPT-4. ChatGPT-3.5 flagged 11 (8.9%) as potentially harmful versus Micromedex 35 (28.2%).
quote: The overall agreement between Micromedex and ChatGPT-3.5 was 64.5% and ChatGPT-4 demonstrated a higher agreement at 81.4%.

title: Evaluating ChatGPT's efficacy in assessing the safety of non-prescription medications and supplements in patients with kidney disease
outcome: Accuracy of LLM safety assessments against reference standard (Micromedex)
effect: ChatGPT-3.5 agreement 64.5%, ChatGPT-4 81.4%; ChatGPT-3.5 lower concordance for supplements at 60.3%. Neither model recommended as a reliable drug information source.
quote: Neither ChatGPT-3.5 nor ChatGPT-4 can be currently recommended as reliable drug information sources for this demographic.

title: A Multidisciplinary Assessment of ChatGPT's Knowledge of Amyloidosis: Observational Study
outcome: Readability grade level of ChatGPT-4 responses versus recommended fifth- to sixth-grade level
effect: ChatGPT-4 readability ranged from 10th to beyond graduate US grade levels, average 15.5 (SD 1.9), exceeding AMA's recommended fifth- to sixth-grade level.
quote: The readability of ChatGPT-4's responses ranged from 10th to beyond graduate US grade levels with an average of 15.5 (SD 1.9).

title: A Multidisciplinary Assessment of ChatGPT's Knowledge of Amyloidosis: Observational Study
outcome: Plain-language comprehensibility of AI-generated patient education responses
effect: ChatGPT-4 responses averaged grade 15.5 (SD 1.9), well above the AMA-recommended fifth- to sixth-grade reading level.
quote: However, ChatGPT's responses exceeded the American Medical Association's recommended fifth- to sixth-grade reading level.

title: A Multidisciplinary Assessment of ChatGPT's Knowledge of Amyloidosis: Observational Study
outcome: Reproducibility of responses when each question input twice
effect: 96 of 98 (98%) ChatGPT-4 responses and 73 of 83 (88%) ChatGPT-3.5 responses were reproducible.
quote: Overall, 96 of 98 (98%) responses for ChatGPT-4 and 73 of 83 (88%) for ChatGPT-3.5 were reproducible.

title: Comparison of ChatGPT knowledge against 2020 consensus statement on ankyloglossia in children
outcome: Alignment of ChatGPT responses with expert consensus mean scores on ankyloglossia statements
effect: 67% of ChatGPT responses closely aligned with expert consensus; 17% (11/63) differed from the consensus mean by 2.0 or greater.
quote: However, 17 % (11/63) were statements in which the ChatGPT mean response was different from the CCS mean by 2.0 or greater, raising concerns about ChatGPT's potential influence in disseminating uncertain or debated medical information.

title: Harnessing artificial intelligence in bariatric surgery: comparative analysis of ChatGPT-4, Bing, and Bard in generating clinician-level bariatric surgery recommendations
venue: Surgery for obesity and related diseases : official journal of the American Society for Bariatric Surgery
outcome: Surgeon-rated appropriateness of LLM answers to guideline-based bariatric surgery questions
effect: Appropriate answers: ChatGPT-4 85.7%, Bard 74.3%, Bing 25.7% (P < .001); mean Likert 4.46, 3.89, 3.11.
quote: There was a significant difference between the 3 LLMs in the proportion of appropriate answers, with ChatGPT-4 at 85.7%, Bard at 74.3%, and Bing at 25.7% (P < .001).

title: ChatGPT's adherence to otolaryngology clinical practice guidelines
venue: European archives of oto-rhino-laryngology : official journal of the European Federation of Oto-Rhino-Laryngological Societies (EUFOS) : affiliated with the German Society for Oto-Rhino-Laryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
outcome: ChatGPT accuracy versus AAO-HNS clinical practice guidelines across otolaryngology subspecialties
effect: 59.7% (43/72) highly accurate; 2.8% (2/72) directly contradicted guidelines; accuracy 100% Head and Neck, 66% Rhinology and Otology, 50% Laryngology, 8% Pediatrics.
quote: The model showed 100% accuracy in Head and Neck, but lower accuracy in Rhinology and Otology/Neurotology (66%), Laryngology (50%), and Pediatrics (8%).

title: ChatGPT's adherence to otolaryngology clinical practice guidelines
venue: European archives of oto-rhino-laryngology : official journal of the European Federation of Oto-Rhino-Laryngological Societies (EUFOS) : affiliated with the German Society for Oto-Rhino-Laryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
outcome: Consistency of ChatGPT responses across three repeated runs of the same questions
effect: Responses consistent in 17/24 (70.8%) of questions; Cronbach's alpha 0.87.
quote: The model's responses were consistent in 17/24 (70.8%), with a Cronbach's alpha value of 0.87, indicating a reasonable consistency across tests.

title: ChatGPT's Performance in Cardiac Arrest and Bradycardia Simulations Using the American Heart Association's Advanced Cardiovascular Life Support Guidelines: Exploratory Study
outcome: Reproducibility of ChatGPT outputs across repeated identical simulation runs
effect: ChatGPT's outputs varied despite consistent input across 20 repeated runs; same actions persistently missed.
quote: We found that ChatGPT's outputs varied despite consistent input, the same actions were persistently missed, repetitive overemphasis hindered guidance, and erroneous medication information was presented.

title: ChatGPT's Performance in Cardiac Arrest and Bradycardia Simulations Using the American Heart Association's Advanced Cardiovascular Life Support Guidelines: Exploratory Study
outcome: Accuracy of ChatGPT adherence to 2020 AHA ACLS guidelines steps
effect: Median step accuracy 85% (IQR 40%-100%) cardiac arrest, 30% (IQR 13%-81%) bradycardia; per-attempt median 69% and 42%.
quote: ChatGPT's median accuracy over 20 simulation attempts for cardiac arrest was 69% (IQR 67%-74%) and for bradycardia was 42% (IQR 33%-50%).

title: ChatGPT's Performance in Cardiac Arrest and Bradycardia Simulations Using the American Heart Association's Advanced Cardiovascular Life Support Guidelines: Exploratory Study
outcome: Erroneous medication information in ChatGPT ACLS outputs
effect: Erroneous medication information was presented in ChatGPT's responses during simulations.
quote: We found that ChatGPT's outputs varied despite consistent input, the same actions were persistently missed, repetitive overemphasis hindered guidance, and erroneous medication information was presented.

title: Using ChatGPT-4 to Create Structured Medical Notes From Audio Recordings of Physician-Patient Encounters: Comparative Study
outcome: Errors in AI-generated SOAP notes: omissions, additions, incorrect facts versus gold standard
effect: 23.6 errors per clinical case on average; omissions 86%, additions 10.5%, incorrect facts 3.2%.
quote: Although ChatGPT-4 consistently generated SOAP-style notes, there were, on average, 23.6 errors per clinical case, with errors of omission (86%) being the most common, followed by addition errors (10.5%) and inclusion of incorrect facts (3.2%).

title: Using ChatGPT-4 to Create Structured Medical Notes From Audio Recordings of Physician-Patient Encounters: Comparative Study
outcome: Reproducibility of note content across repeated runs of the same case
effect: Significant variance between replicates; only 52.9% of data elements reported correctly across all 3 replicates.
quote: There was significant variance between replicates of the same case, with only 52.9% of data elements reported correctly across all 3 replicates.

title: Performance of Artificial Intelligence Chatbots on Glaucoma Questions Adapted From Patient Brochures
outcome: Flesch-Kincaid reading grade level of chatbot glaucoma responses versus AAO brochures
effect: Readability levels for AAO, ChatGPT, Bing, and Bard were 8.11, 13.01, 11.73, and 7.90; ChatGPT and Bing were above AAO (p<0.0001).
quote: AAO information and Bard responses were at the most accessible readability levels (AAO versus ChatGPT, AAO versus Bing, Bard versus ChatGPT, Bard versus Bing, all p<0.0001), with readability levels for AAO, ChatGPT, Bing, and Bard at 8.11, 13.01, 11.73, and 7.90, respectively.

title: Performance of Artificial Intelligence Chatbots on Glaucoma Questions Adapted From Patient Brochures
outcome: Readability of chatbot patient-education responses relative to patient comprehension levels
effect: ChatGPT and Bing responses were at FKGL 13.01 and 11.73, above AAO brochures at 8.11; Bard was 7.90.
quote: With accuracy scores and comprehensiveness below that of AAO brochures and elevated readability levels, AI chatbots require improvements to be a more useful supplementary source of glaucoma information for patients.

title: To trust or not to trust: evaluating the reliability and safety of AI responses to laryngeal cancer queries
venue: European archives of oto-rhino-laryngology : official journal of the European Federation of Oto-Rhino-Laryngological Societies (EUFOS) : affiliated with the German Society for Oto-Rhino-Laryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
outcome: Safety and quality scores of LLM laryngeal cancer answers rated by blinded reviewers
effect: ChatGPT 3.5 scored highest in safety (mean 2.70) and GQS (3.95); ChatGPT 4.0 2.56 and 3.65; Bard 2.42 and 3.38. About 4.2% of responses fell into the lowest safety category.
quote: Analysis revealed that ChatGPT 3.5 scored highest in both safety (mean: 2.70) and GQS (mean: 3.95).

title: Optimization of hepatological clinical guidelines interpretation by large language models: a retrieval augmented generation-based framework
outcome: LLM answer accuracy on hepatitis C guideline questions with vs without guideline context (RAG)
effect: Accuracy rose from 43% to 99% (p < 0.001) when guidelines were provided as context in a coherent text corpus with non-text sources converted to text.
quote: The results showed a significant improvement in accuracy from 43 to 99% (p < 0.001), when guidelines were provided as context in a coherent corpus of text and non-text sources were converted into text.

title: A Comparative Study of Responses to Retina Questions from Either Experts, Expert-Edited Large Language Models, or Expert-Edited Large Language Models Alone
outcome: Safety metrics of expert-edited LLM drafts versus expert-written and unedited LLM responses
effect: Expert-edited drafts (Expert + AI) had higher quality and empathy than Expert alone, but were worse than Expert on most safety metrics; e.g. incorrect content low risk 0.801 vs 0.832, with 2% high-risk vs 0%.

title: A Comparative Study of Responses to Retina Questions from Either Experts, Expert-Edited Large Language Models, or Expert-Edited Large Language Models Alone

title: A Comparative Study of Responses to Retina Questions from Either Experts, Expert-Edited Large Language Models, or Expert-Edited Large Language Models Alone
