title: Comparison of different Lunit INSIGHT CXR software versions when reading chest radiographs for tuberculosis
outcome: Effect of recalibrating decision threshold after model update on specificity and testing volume
effect: Without recalibration new version specificity fell to 23.1% (+36.4% testing); after recalibration to 0.480, specificity 43.2% and +4.1% testing, not significantly different from old version.
quote: When using an cut-off threshold optimized for the older software version, the newer software was significantly less accurate than its predecessors.

title: Comparison of different Lunit INSIGHT CXR software versions when reading chest radiographs for tuberculosis
outcome: Sensitivity, specificity and added testing after software version update, with and without threshold recalibration
effect: At the old cut-off 0.217, new version had sensitivity 96.4% but specificity 23.1% (p<0.001), +36.4% Ultra testing; recalibrated to 0.480, specificity 43.2%, +4.1% testing, p=0.148.
quote: When a second cut-off threshold is selected for the newer v3.9.0.1 software so that it achieves a 90% sensitivity (0.480), there is no statistical difference with the newer software’s specificity (43.2%) or the additional Ultra tests indicated (+4.1%) compared with the v3.1.0.0 software version (p = 0.148) at its original threshold.

title: Comparison of different Lunit INSIGHT CXR software versions when reading chest radiographs for tuberculosis
outcome: Sensitivity/specificity of new software at original versus re-calibrated cut-off threshold
effect: Original threshold: specificity 23.1% vs 45.8% for old version; re-calibrated threshold 0.480 gave 90.4% sensitivity and 43.2% specificity, no significant difference (p=0.148).
quote: However, when the cut-off threshold was re-calibrated, there were no significant differences in sensitivity and specificity between the software versions.

title: Comparison of different Lunit INSIGHT CXR software versions when reading chest radiographs for tuberculosis
outcome: Performance of updated software version at previously validated threshold
effect: New version at old threshold: specificity 23.1% vs 45.8%, +36.4% diagnostic testing; performance matched predecessor only after recalibration.
quote: Between successive Lunit CAD software versions, there was a significant increase in the median abnormality score which translates to significantly decreased specificity and thus significantly increased diagnostic testing indication if the abnormality score cut-off threshold is not re-calibrated for the new software version.

title: Comparison of different Lunit INSIGHT CXR software versions when reading chest radiographs for tuberculosis
outcome: Retesting after software update to confirm performance and thresholds remain valid
effect: Update raised AUC 0.76 to 0.78 (p=0.029) but shifted abnormality scores, cutting specificity at old threshold from 45.8% to 23.1%.
quote: As new CAD software versions are rolled out, cut-off thresholds must be re-calibrated to ensure the continued accuracy of CXR interpretation.

title: Comparison of different Lunit INSIGHT CXR software versions when reading chest radiographs for tuberculosis
outcome: Performance after software update at unchanged cutoff
effect: At cutoff 0.217, v3.9.0.1 had sensitivity 96.4%, specificity 23.1%, and +36.4% Ultra testing versus v3.1.0.0 specificity 45.8%.
quote: Using this same cut-off threshold, the newer v3.9.0.1 software achieves a significantly higher sensitivity of 96.4%, but a significantly lower specificity of 23.1% (p < 0.001).

title: Comparison of different Lunit INSIGHT CXR software versions when reading chest radiographs for tuberculosis
outcome: AUC differences across demographic and clinical subgroups
effect: Newer software improved AUC in past TB 0.67 vs 0.73 (p=0.003), older individuals 0.75 vs 0.77 (p=0.040), and males 0.73 vs 0.76 (p=0.008).
quote: Similarly, there were no significant differences AUCs between the CAD software versions in younger individuals (0.78 vs 0.80, p = 0.425) and females (0.80 vs 0.79, p = 0.875), but the newer v3.9.0.1 software’s AUCs were significantly higher among older individuals (0.75 vs 0.77, p = 0.040) and males (0.73 vs 0.76, p = 0.008).

title: Comparison of ChatGPT's Diagnostic and Management Accuracy of Foot and Ankle Bone-Related Pathologies to Orthopaedic Surgeons
venue: The Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
outcome: Fabrication (hallucination) of treatment options in ChatGPT-4 responses to foot and ankle cases
effect: ChatGPT did not fabricate treatment options; the no-fabrication criterion received the second-highest overall average score. Overall average case score was 22.7 of 25.
quote: Importantly, ChatGPT did not fabricate treatment options (ie, hallucination phenomenon), which has been previously well-documented in the literature, notably receiving its second-highest overall average score in this criterion.

title: Comparison of ChatGPT's Diagnostic and Management Accuracy of Foot and Ankle Bone-Related Pathologies to Orthopaedic Surgeons
venue: The Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
outcome: Completeness of ChatGPT-4 clinical knowledge and treatment options for foot and ankle bone pathologies
effect: Average score 4.53/5 per criterion and 22.7/25 per case; lowest for hallux rigidus (21.3). Comprehensive information beyond standard treatment options was limited.
quote: ChatGPT struggled to provide comprehensive information beyond standard treatment options.

title: ChatGPT-4 for addressing patient-centred frequently asked questions in age-related macular degeneration clinical practice
outcome: Expert-rated factuality and comprehensiveness of ChatGPT-4 AMD answers; outdated technologies noted
effect: 23 (62%) of 37 questions had mean comprehensiveness below 4 and 21 (57%) had factuality below 4; comments flagged superseded or older technologies and techniques not routinely used in practice.
quote: Free-text comments highlighted issues related to superseded or older technologies, and techniques that are not routinely used in clinical practice, such as genetic testing.

title: Unraveling relevant cross-waves pattern drifts in patient-hospital risk factors among hospitalized COVID-19 patients using explainable machine learning methods
outcome: Temporal drift in predictive model performance across pandemic waves for ICU, IMV, and death
effect: Recall for the positive class fell from wave 1 to wave 3: ICU 0.4211 to 0.1951; IMV 0.2089 to 0.0438; death 0.2711 to 0.1175.
quote: Temporal drifts were observed due to a decrease in various metrics, such as the recall for the positive class [ICU: 0.4211 (wave 1) to 0.1951 (wave 3); IMV: 0.2089 (wave 1) to 0.0438 (wave 3); death: 0.2711 (wave 1) to 0.1175 (wave 3)].

title: Performance of artificial intelligence chatbots in responding to the frequently asked questions of patients regarding dental prostheses
outcome: Readability (FKGL, FRE) of chatbot responses to dental prosthesis patient FAQs
effect: ChatGPT FKGL 10.45 ± 1.26 vs Gemini 7.82 ± 1.19 and Copilot 8.38 ± 1.59 (P<.001); ChatGPT FRE 53.05 ± 7.16 (fairly difficult), Gemini 64.94 ± 7.29 (plain English).
quote: Readability analysis showed ChatGPT (10.45 ± 1.26) produced significantly more complex responses compared to Gemini (7.82 ± 1.19) and Copilot (8.38 ± 1.59) (P <.001).

title: Performance of artificial intelligence chatbots in responding to the frequently asked questions of patients regarding dental prostheses
outcome: Reading grade level of chatbot patient-education responses
effect: ChatGPT responses averaged FKGL 10.45 and were rated fairly difficult (FRE 53.05); Gemini FKGL 7.82, Copilot 8.38.
quote: FRE scores indicated that ChatGPT's responses were categorized as fairly difficult (53.05 ± 7.16), while Gemini's responses were in plain English (64.94 ± 7.29), with a significant difference between them (P <.001).

title: Comparison of Deep Learning and Clinician Performance for Detecting Referable Glaucoma from Fundus Photographs in a Safety Net Population
outcome: DL algorithm AUROC/sensitivity/specificity versus 13 clinician graders on same test set
effect: Algorithm matched or exceeded all independent clinician graders (AUROC 0.92 with optometrist labels, 0.93 with expert panel labels); clinician sensitivity ranged 0.33-0.99, specificity 0.68-0.98.
quote: Algorithm performance matched or exceeded that of all independent clinician graders in detecting patient-level referable glaucoma based on LAC DHS optometrist (AUROC = 0.92) or expert panel (AUROC = 0.93) reference labels.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Low-Dose CT Lung Cancer Screening: Comparison of Utilization Scenarios
outcome: clinician review of all cases
effect: Prescreener: per-nodule sensitivity 62.9% vs 64.2% (p = .16); specificity 90.3% vs 88.8% (p = .04); time 143 vs 164 seconds.
quote: An approach whereby radiologists only interpret LDCT examinations with a positive AI result can reduce radiologists' workload while preserving sensitivity.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Low-Dose CT Lung Cancer Screening: Comparison of Utilization Scenarios
outcome: Recall rate, specificity, sensitivity and time for radiologists with vs without AI assistance
effect: AI assistant: recall 30.3% vs 22.1% (p<.001), specificity 81.1% vs 88.8%, sensitivity 64.8% vs 64.2% (p=.86), time 161 vs 164 s (p=.48).
quote: Compared with interpretation without AI (recall rate, 22.1%; per-nodule sensitivity, 64.2%; per-examination specificity, 88.8%; mean interpretation time, 164 seconds), AI as an assistant showed higher recall rate (30.3%; p < .001), lower per-examination specificity (81.1%), and no significant change in per-nodule sensitivity (64.8%; p = .86) or mean interpretation time (161 seconds; p = .48)

title: Artificial Intelligence for Low-Dose CT Lung Cancer Screening: Comparison of Utilization Scenarios
outcome: Reader performance with AI assistance in workflow versus without AI
effect: AI assistance raised recall rate to 30.3% from 22.1% and lowered specificity to 81.1% from 88.8%, with no sensitivity gain (64.8% vs 64.2%).
quote: Compared with interpretation without AI (recall rate, 22.1%; per-nodule sensitivity, 64.2%; per-examination specificity, 88.8%; mean interpretation time, 164 seconds), AI as an assistant showed higher recall rate (30.3%; p < .001), lower per-examination specificity (81.1%), and no significant change in per-nodule sensitivity (64.8%; p = .86) or mean interpretation time (161 seconds; p = .48)

title: Artificial Intelligence for Low-Dose CT Lung Cancer Screening: Comparison of Utilization Scenarios
outcome: performance versus no AI
effect: Only prescreener had higher net benefit than no AI; assistant had least net benefit. Prescreener sensitivity 62.9% vs 64.2%, time 143 vs 164 seconds.
quote: Among scenarios, only AI as a prescreener demonstrated higher net benefit than interpretation without AI; AI as an assistant had the least net benefit.

title: Multimodal Large Language Model With Knowledge Retrieval Using Flowchart Embedding for Forming Follow-Up Recommendations for Pancreatic Cystic Lesions
outcome: follow-up recommendation accuracy
effect: flowchart embedding 89.9–91.9% vs default 39.9–42.4% and plain-text RAG 23.7–25.3%; p < .001
quote: The accuracy of the LLM follow-up recommendations based on default knowledge, plain-text RAG, and flowchart embedding for radiologist 1 was 42.4%, 23.7%, and 89.9% (p < .001), respectively; radiologist 2 was 39.9%, 24.2%, and 91.9% (p < .001); and radiologist 3 was 40.9%, 25.3%, and 91.9% (p < .001).

title: Assessing the Quality and Reliability of ChatGPT's Responses to Radiotherapy-Related Patient Queries: Comparative Study With GPT-3.5 and GPT-4
outcome: Readability (Flesch Reading Ease, Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level) of ChatGPT radiotherapy responses
effect: Both versions were college level: GPT-4 FRES 34.61 and FKGL 12.32; GPT-3.5 FRES 32.98 and FKGL 13.32. Responses were challenging for the general public.
quote: Readability scores for both versions were considered college level, with GPT-4 scoring slightly better in the Flesch Reading Ease Score (34.61) and Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level (12.32) compared to GPT-3.5 (32.98 and 13.32, respectively).

title: Assessing the Quality and Reliability of ChatGPT's Responses to Radiotherapy-Related Patient Queries: Comparative Study With GPT-3.5 and GPT-4
outcome: Comprehensibility of AI-generated patient information for the general public
effect: Readability of both GPT versions was college level (FKGL 12.32 for GPT-4, 13.32 for GPT-3.5), deemed challenging for the general public.
quote: Responses by both versions were deemed challenging for the general public.

title: Evaluating Large Language Models in Cardiovascular Antithrombotic Care: Performance, Accuracy, and Implications for Clinical Practice
outcome: LLM accuracy on validated cardiovascular antithrombotic care scenarios
effect: Claude 3 Opus answered 85% correctly; GPT-4o 55%, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 44%, GPT-3.5 10%. Some free-tier models gave inappropriate medical advice to clinicians.
quote: The performance of LLMs in cardiovascular clinical scenarios varied widely, with some models outperforming clinicians, and some free-tier models providing inappropriate medical advice to clinicians.

title: Clinical implementation of an AI-enabled ECG for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy detection
outcome: Alert percentage and enrolment rate after optimised operating point deployment
effect: Alert percentage fell from 4.4% (2097/47868) to 2.3% (2251/97980), p<0.0001, with no difference in enrolment rate by alerts reviewed
quote: During the study, deployment of an optimised algorithm operating point helped reduce the alert percentage of algorithm-screened patients from 4.4% (2097/47868) to 2.3% (2251/97980), p<0.0001, with no difference in the enrolment rate by alerts reviewed.

title: Clinical implementation of an AI-enabled ECG for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy detection
outcome: Alert percentage and enrolment rate after algorithm operating-point optimisation
effect: Alert percentage decreased from 4.4% (2097/47868) to 2.3% (2251/97980), p<0.0001, with no difference in the enrolment rate by alerts reviewed.
quote: During the study, deployment of an optimised algorithm operating point helped reduce the alert percentage of algorithm-screened patients from 4.4% (2097/47868) to 2.3% (2251/97980), p<0.0001, with no difference in the enrolment rate by alerts reviewed.

title: Improving Accessibility to Facial Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery Patient Resources Using Artificial Intelligence: A Pilot Study in Patient Education Materials
outcome: Readability of original AAFPRS patient education materials versus 6th-grade standard
effect: Original PEMs had mean FKGL 10.7, GFI 13.48, and FKRE 50.8, exceeding the recommended level; AI-translated versions improved to FKGL 8.41, GFI 10.62, FKRE 64.43 (p<0.001), still above 6th grade.
quote: Original PEMs had a mean FKGL, GFI, and FKRE of 10.7, 13.48, and 50.8 respectively, which exceed the recommended level.

title: External Validation of SCORE2-Diabetes Risk Prediction Model in Chinese Patients with Diabetes
outcome: Calibration of original versus recalibrated SCORE2-Diabetes in Chinese patients
effect: Original underestimated risk by 30% in men and 50% in women; recalibrated with high-risk region scaling factor overestimated by 4% in men and underestimated by 7% in women.
quote: The original SCORE2-Diabetes underestimated risk by 30% in men and 50% in women, whereas the recalibrated SCORE2-Diabetes using high-risk region scaling factor had the best calibration, overestimating risk by only 4% in men and underestimating by 7% in women.

title: External Validation of SCORE2-Diabetes Risk Prediction Model in Chinese Patients with Diabetes
outcome: Discrimination and calibration of original model in a new Chinese population
effect: C-statistic 0.702 (95%CI 0.691-0.713) in men and 0.726 (0.716-0.736) in women; original model underestimated risk by 30% in men and 50% in women.
quote: The original SCORE2-Diabetes underestimated risk by 30% in men and 50% in women, whereas the recalibrated SCORE2-Diabetes using high-risk region scaling factor had the best calibration, overestimating risk by only 4% in men and underestimating by 7% in women.

title: External Validation of SCORE2-Diabetes Risk Prediction Model in Chinese Patients with Diabetes
outcome: sex-specific calibration
effect: Original SCORE2-Diabetes underestimated risk by 30% in men and 50% in women.
quote: The original SCORE2-Diabetes underestimated risk by 30% in men and 50% in women, whereas the recalibrated SCORE2-Diabetes using high-risk region scaling factor had the best calibration, overestimating risk by only 4% in men and underestimating by 7% in women.

title: External Validation of SCORE2-Diabetes Risk Prediction Model in Chinese Patients with Diabetes
outcome: generalization to Chinese patients
effect: Original SCORE2-Diabetes underestimated risk by 30% in men and 50% in women before recalibration.
quote: The original SCORE2-Diabetes underestimated risk by 30% in men and 50% in women, whereas the recalibrated SCORE2-Diabetes using high-risk region scaling factor had the best calibration, overestimating risk by only 4% in men and underestimating by 7% in women.

title: Enhancing Physician-Patient Communication in Oncology Using GPT-4 Through Simplified Radiology Reports: Multicenter Quantitative Study
outcome: Lay comprehension, reading time, and consultation time for original vs GPT-4 simplified radiology reports
effect: Comprehension scores rose from 5.51 to 7.83 (P<.001); consultation time fell from 1116.11 to 745.30 seconds (P<.001); reading rate rose from 72.15 to 104.70 words per minute.
quote: Physician-patient communication time significantly decreased, from 1116.11 seconds to 745.30 seconds (P<.001), and patient comprehension scores improved from 5.51 to 7.83 (P<.001).

title: Evaluating the Performance and Safety of Large Language Models in Generating Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Management Plans: A Comparative Study With Physicians Using Real Patient Records
outcome: Safety issues in GPT-4-generated diabetes management plans
effect: Safety issues were noted in 16% of GPT-4-generated plans, indicating that unverified AI plans could carry risk.
quote: Safety issues were noted in 16% of the plans generated by GPT-4, highlighting potential risks associated with AI-generated management plans.

title: Evaluating the Performance and Safety of Large Language Models in Generating Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Management Plans: A Comparative Study With Physicians Using Real Patient Records
outcome: Completeness and necessity of medications in GPT-4 plans versus guideline-based reference plan
effect: Physicians' plans had fewer missing medications than GPT-4 (p=0.008). GPT-4 plans included fewer unnecessary medications (p=0.003). Dosage accuracy (p=0.975) and overall error scores (p=0.301) did not differ.
quote: Results indicated that physicians' management plans had fewer missing medications compared to those generated by GPT-4 (p=0.008).

title: Comparative Analysis of ChatGPT and Google Gemini in Generating Patient Educational Resources on Cardiac Health: A Focus on Exercise-Induced Arrhythmia, Sleep Habits, and Dietary Habits
outcome: Readability (ease score, grade level) of AI-generated cardiac patient education guides
effect: No significant difference in ease score (p = 0.7244) between models; ChatGPT tended to produce more complex content on some topics; Gemini generally easier to read.
quote: ChatGPT tended to produce more complex content for certain topics, whereas Google Gemini's responses were generally easier to read.
sample_unit: AI-generated patient education guides (3 topics x 2 models)

title: Effectiveness of generative AI-large language models' recognition of veteran suicide risk: a comparison with human mental health providers using a risk stratification model
outcome: LLM recognition of acute suicide risk in vignettes versus mental health providers
effect: GAI-LLMs rated the most acute case as less acute than MHCPs and the least acute case as more acute; ChatGPT-3.5 gave lower acute risk ratings than ChatGPT-4o and Gemini.
quote: GAI-LLMs' assessments showed discrepancies with MHCPs, particularly rating the most acute case as less acute and the least acute case as more acute.

title: Evaluation of error detection and treatment recommendations in nucleic acid test reports using ChatGPT models
outcome: Reproducibility of GPT error identification across three repeated runs
effect: Pairwise comparisons of the same GPT model's outputs across three repeated runs showed almost perfect agreement (kappa 0.912 to 0.996).
quote: The pairwise comparisons of the same GPT model's outputs across three repeated runs showed almost perfect agreement (kappa [min, max]: 0.912, 0.996).
sample_unit: nucleic acid test reports (with 285 introduced errors)

title: Evaluation of error detection and treatment recommendations in nucleic acid test reports using ChatGPT models
outcome: GPT error detection agreement and speed compared with senior scientists and interns
effect: GPT models agreed substantially to almost perfectly with SMLS (kappa 0.778-0.837), moderately lower with MLI (0.632-0.696), and read reports faster than both (p<0.001).
quote: GPT models exhibited substantial to almost perfect agreement with SMLS in detecting total errors (kappa [min, max]: 0.778, 0.837).
sample_unit: nucleic acid test reports (with 285 introduced errors)

title: AtlasGPT: a language model grounded in neurosurgery with domain-specific data and document retrieval
outcome: Accuracy, robustness to misinformation, and hallucination for grounded (fine-tuned plus retrieval) LLM versus general LLMs
effect: AtlasGPT was fooled 14% of the time in adversarial misinformation testing versus 44% for GPT-4 and 68% for Gemini Advanced. Accuracy was 96% versus 88% and 93%. No hallucination was found.
quote: In adversarial testing, under which AtlasGPT was tasked with identifying medical misinformation, it was fooled 14% of the time, compared with 44% for GPT-4 and 68% for Gemini Advanced.

title: Large language model-generated clinical practice guideline for appendicitis
outcome: LLM performance on guideline development tasks versus SAGES guideline (AGREE-S)
effect: LLMs could not independently perform systematic literature search or reliably perform screening, data extraction, or risk of bias assessment. AGREE-S total 119 for LLM-derived guideline vs 156 for SAGES.
quote: These LLMs were unable to independently perform a systematic literature search or reliably perform screening, data extraction, or risk of bias assessment at the time of testing.
sample_unit: guidelines (LLM-derived guideline appraised with AGREE-S vs SAGES guideline)

title: AI for fracture diagnosis in clinical practice: Four approaches to systematic AI-implementation and their impact on AI-effectiveness
outcome: False negatives and false positives of radiologist alone versus radiologist plus AI under four implementation modes
effect: Radiologist 2.7% FN (40/1508); AI-safety net 0.07% FN (1/1508), FP 7.6%; AI-problem-solving 3.2% FN; AI-triage 2.1% FN; all changes p<0.001.
quote: Implementation methods have a large impact on AI-effectiveness.

title: AI for fracture diagnosis in clinical practice: Four approaches to systematic AI-implementation and their impact on AI-effectiveness
outcome: Missed fractures when AI triages cases versus radiologist reviewing all cases
effect: AI-triage (radiologist findings consulted only when AI in doubt) increased FN to 2.1% (32/1508) vs radiologist 2.7% overall, but increased FN in all subgroups except radiologists-in-training.
quote: Subgroups show similar trends, except AI-triage increased FN for all subgroups except radiologists-in-training.

title: AI for fracture diagnosis in clinical practice: Four approaches to systematic AI-implementation and their impact on AI-effectiveness
outcome: false negatives and false positives across workflows
effect: Radiologist 2.7% FN/1.2% FP; standalone 1.5%/6.8%; problem-solving 3.2%/0.6%; triage 2.1%/1.7%; safety-net 0.07%/7.6%.
quote: All AI-implementation methods changed overall FN and FP with statistical significance (p < 0.001): AI-standalone 1.5 % FN (23/1508; 11 consequences), 6.8 % FP (103/1508); AI-problem-solving 3.2 % FN (48/1508; 31 consequences), 0.6 % FP (9/1508); AI-triage 2.1 % FN (32/1508; 18 consequences), 1.7 % FP (26/1508); AI-safety net 0.07 % FN (1/1508; 1 consequence), 7.6 % FP (115/1508).

title: AI for fracture diagnosis in clinical practice: Four approaches to systematic AI-implementation and their impact on AI-effectiveness
outcome: standalone versus adjunct fracture diagnosis errors
effect: Safety-net had 0.07% FN (1/1508; 1 consequence) versus standalone 1.5% FN (23/1508; 11 consequences), but FP was 7.6% versus 6.8%.
quote: Best results were obtained implementing AI as safety net, which eliminates missed fractures with serious clinical consequences; even though false positives are increased, unnecessary treatments are limited.

title: AI for fracture diagnosis in clinical practice: Four approaches to systematic AI-implementation and their impact on AI-effectiveness
outcome: fracture detection error rates by AI deployment mode
effect: Standalone AI (1.5% FN, 6.8% FP) differed significantly (p < 0.001) from problem-solving (3.2% FN, 0.6% FP), triage (2.1% FN, 1.7% FP), and safety net (0.07% FN, 7.6% FP).
quote: All AI-implementation methods changed overall FN and FP with statistical significance (p < 0.001): AI-standalone 1.5 % FN (23/1508; 11 consequences), 6.8 % FP (103/1508); AI-problem-solving 3.2 % FN (48/1508; 31 consequences), 0.6 % FP (9/1508); AI-triage 2.1 % FN (32/1508; 18 consequences), 1.7 % FP (26/1508); AI-safety net 0.07 % FN (1/1508; 1 consequence), 7.6 % FP (115/1508).

title: AI for fracture diagnosis in clinical practice: Four approaches to systematic AI-implementation and their impact on AI-effectiveness
outcome: subgroup false negative rates with AI triage
effect: AI-triage resulted in 2.1% FN (32/1508; 18 consequences) and increased FN for all reader subgroups except radiologists-in-training compared to radiologist baseline (2.7%).
quote: Subgroups show similar trends, except AI-triage increased FN for all subgroups except radiologists-in-training.

title: CORAL: Expert-Curated Oncology Reports to Advance Language Model Inference
outcome: LLM extraction errors from oncology notes: missing information and hallucinations
effect: GPT-4 average accuracy 68% on expert manual evaluation of a subset; common errors included partial responses with missing information and hallucinations with note-specific information.
quote: Common errors included partial responses with missing information and hallucinations with note-specific information.
sample_unit: deidentified breast and pancreatic cancer progress notes

title: Deep Learning-Driven Glaucoma Medication Bottle Recognition: A Multilingual Clinical Validation Study in Patients with Impaired Vision
outcome: Medication identification accuracy and time with versus without the AI app, in the same patients
effect: Accuracy rose from 27.6% without the app to 99.2% with it (OR 319.353, P<0.001), with no significant change in identification time.
quote: Identification accuracy significantly improved from 27.6% without the app to 99.2% with the app across all participants, with no significant change in identification time.

title: Deep Learning-Driven Glaucoma Medication Bottle Recognition: A Multilingual Clinical Validation Study in Patients with Impaired Vision
outcome: Identification accuracy improvement with the app in non-English versus English-speaking patients
effect: Improvement was similar in non-English speakers (71.6%) and English speakers (71.4%). Ease-of-use ratings differed: 81% of English speakers versus 30% of non-English speakers found the app very easy.
quote: This observed improvement in accuracy was similar among non-English-speaking (71.6%) and English-speaking (71.4%) participants.

title: Large Language Models: Pioneering New Educational Frontiers in Childhood Myopia
outcome: Readability (FKGL, SMOG) of LLM patient materials with vs without sixth-grade reading level instruction
effect: Prompt B lowered FKGL: ChatGPT-3.5 7.7 to 6.2, ChatGPT-4o 7.5 to 6.0, Gemini 8.5 to 7.0 (all p<0.001); Gemini did not reach sixth grade.
quote: Our readability analysis revealed that prompt B produced more readable PEMs compared to prompt A, as reflected by lower SMOG and FKGL scores for both ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4o (o1 Preview) ( p < 0.001).

title: Large Language Models: Pioneering New Educational Frontiers in Childhood Myopia
outcome: Readability of existing online patient education materials after LLM plain-language rewriting
effect: Original online PEMs FKGL 9.7 and SMOG 10.3; after rewriting ChatGPT-4o FKGL 5.8, ChatGPT-3.5 7.7, Gemini 7.5 (p<0.001).
quote: Using prompt C, the three LLMs significantly improved the readability of existing online educational resources, as evidenced by a marked enhancement in average readability scores ( p ≤ 0.001) (Fig. 2 ).

title: Large Language Models: Pioneering New Educational Frontiers in Childhood Myopia
outcome: Misinformation in LLM-generated patient education materials on Likert scale
effect: All 120 responses scored 1 (no misinformation) across the three LLMs.
quote: All 120 responses received a score of 1 on the Likert misinformation scale, indicating that these three LLMs did not produce any misinformation across the 120 newly generated PEMs.

title: Large Language Models: Pioneering New Educational Frontiers in Childhood Myopia
outcome: reading level of generated patient education materials
effect: Under prompt B, ChatGPT-4o and ChatGPT-3.5 achieved sixth-grade reading level (FKGL 6 ± 0.6 and 6.2 ± 0.3), while Google Gemini did not (FKGL 7 ± 0.6).
quote: Among these LLMs, both ChatGPT-4o (o1 Preview) and ChatGPT-3.5 could generate educational materials at or below the sixth-grade reading level in response to prompt B, respectively (FGKL scores 6 ± 0.6; FGKL scores 6.2 ± 0.3), while Google Gemini could not produce material at this grade level (FGKL scores; 7 ± 0.6).

title: An artificial intelligence perspective on geriatric syndromes: assessing the information accuracy and readability of ChatGPT
outcome: Readability of ChatGPT responses (Flesch-Kincaid Reading Ease and Grade Level)
effect: Mean FKRE score 25.2 and mean FKGL score 14.5; text very difficult to read, best understood by college graduates.
quote: The mean FKRE score of the texts was 25.2, while the mean FKGL score was 14.5.
sample_unit: ChatGPT responses to FAQs about geriatric syndromes

title: An artificial intelligence perspective on geriatric syndromes: assessing the information accuracy and readability of ChatGPT
outcome: Reading level of ChatGPT-generated patient information versus appropriate level
effect: Mean FKGL 14.5 and FKRE 25.2; text very difficult to read and best understood by college graduates.
quote: Moreover, the text generated by ChatGPT was very difficult to read and best understood by college graduates.
sample_unit: ChatGPT responses to FAQs about geriatric syndromes

title: An artificial intelligence perspective on geriatric syndromes: assessing the information accuracy and readability of ChatGPT
outcome: Geriatrician-rated accuracy of ChatGPT answers against current guidelines (0-4 scale)
effect: Overall mean accuracy 88% (3.52/4); lowest for sarcopenia diagnosis (2.0) and depression treatment (2.5).
quote: Responses generated for sarcopenia diagnosis and depression treatment in older adults had the lowest accuracy scores (2.0 and 2.5, respectively).
sample_unit: ChatGPT responses to FAQs about geriatric syndromes

title: Clinical Trial Notifications Triggered by Artificial Intelligence–Detected Cancer Progression
outcome: Clinical trial enrollment after AI-triggered oncologist notifications versus no notifications
effect: Enrollment 2.20% intervention vs 2.03% control; difference 0.18 percentage points (95% CI -0.25 to 0.58; P = .41). No significant benefit.
quote: The intervention had no significant impact on the trial enrollment rate (intervention, 2.20% [95% CI, 1.97%-2.46%]; control, 2.03% [95% CI, 1.72%-2.39%]; difference, 0.18 [95% CI, -0.25 to 0.58] percentage points; P = .41).

title: Prostate Cancer Risk Stratification and Scan Tailoring Using Deep Learning on Abbreviated Prostate MRI
venue: Journal of magnetic resonance imaging : JMRI
outcome: Prospective performance of DL model on live bpMRI data
effect: In the prospective cohort, AUC 0.83 (95% CI: 0.77-0.89) for PI-RADS ≥ 3, with 93% sensitivity and 54% specificity.
quote: In the prospective cohort, the model achieved an AUC of 0.83 (95% CI: 0.77-0.89) for PI-RADS ≥ 3 classification, with 93% sensitivity and 54% specificity.

title: Assessment of ChatGPT's adherence to EULAR diagnostic criteria and therapeutic protocols for rheumatoid arthritis at two distinct time points, 14 days apart, utilizing binary and multiple-choice inquiries
outcome: Consistency of ChatGPT answers to identical RA questions repeated 14 days apart
effect: Multiple-choice: 43 (86%) correct at baseline vs 42 (84%) on day 14. Three of seven initially erroneous answers stayed unchanged, four were corrected, and one new error appeared. Binary questions were more consistent than multiple-choice questions.
quote: Three of the seven initially erroneous responses remained unaltered.

title: Assessment of ChatGPT's adherence to EULAR diagnostic criteria and therapeutic protocols for rheumatoid arthritis at two distinct time points, 14 days apart, utilizing binary and multiple-choice inquiries
outcome: Accuracy of ChatGPT clinical knowledge against EULAR RA guideline-based questions
effect: 86% (43/50 multiple-choice items) correct at baseline and 84% (42/50) on day 14. Some errors persisted, so knowledge was largely but not fully guideline-concordant.
quote: At baseline, 43 (86%) of the multiple-choice items were answered correctly.

title: Semantic Clinical Artificial Intelligence vs Native Large Language Model Performance on the USMLE
outcome: USMLE question accuracy of Llama models with vs without semantic clinical knowledge RAG
effect: SCAI RAG significantly improved 13B on Steps 1 and 3, 70B on Step 2, 405B on Step 3; 13B with RAG passed Step 3 (60.2%). 70B and 405B passed all steps with or without RAG.
quote: Significant improvements associated with SCAI RAG were found for the 13B model on Steps 1 and 3, the 70B model on Step 2, and the 405B parameter model on Step 3.

title: Comparative analysis of the effectiveness of microsoft copilot artificial intelligence chatbot and google search in answering patient inquiries about infertility: evaluating readability, understandability, and actionability
outcome: Readability grade level of Copilot and Google Search infertility answers versus 8th-grade level
effect: Both GS and MC outputs had readability scores above the 8th-grade level; GS had higher ARI and FKGL than MC (p = 0.044); no differences on FRE, Gunning Fog, SMOG, Coleman-Liau.
quote: Both GS and MC outputs had readability scores above the 8th-grade level, indicating advanced reading levels.

title: Artificial intelligence-generated responses to frequently asked questions on coccydynia: Evaluating the accuracy and consistency of GPT-4o's performance
outcome: Reproducibility of GPT-4o responses across repeated queries at different times and accounts
effect: 75% of responses differed between the two rounds; 34.9% of initially incomplete answers improved in the second round.
quote: The interreviewer agreement was substantial (kappa=0.67), but 75% of the responses differed between the two rounds.

title: Assessing bias in AI-driven psychiatric recommendations: A comparative cross-sectional study of chatbot-classified and CANMAT 2023 guideline for adjunctive therapy in difficult-to-treat depression
outcome: Agreement of chatbot adjunctive-therapy classifications with CANMAT 2023 guidelines (Cohen's kappa)
effect: Gemini 2.0 Flash kappa 0.82 (SE 0.052); OpenAI o1 kappa 0.746 (SE 0.057). Overestimated quetiapine and lithium; underestimated modafinil and ketamine.
quote: Results reveal substantial agreement for high-performing models, such as Google AI's Gemini 2.0 Flash, which achieved the highest Cohen's kappa value of 0.82 (SE = 0.052).

title: Decoding wisdom: Evaluating ChatGPT's accuracy and reproducibility in analyzing orthopantomographic images for third molar assessment
outcome: Reproducibility of ChatGPT-4o responses across 30 repeated runs per radiograph
effect: Percentage agreement among repeated responses was 82.7%, but Gwet's coefficient of agreement was 60.4%, suggesting only moderate repeatability.
quote: The percentage agreement among repeated responses was 82.7 %, indicating high consistency, though Gwet's coefficient of agreement (60.4 %) suggested only moderate repeatability.
sample_unit: ChatGPT-4o responses (30 per each of 30 orthopantomograms)

title: Decoding wisdom: Evaluating ChatGPT's accuracy and reproducibility in analyzing orthopantomographic images for third molar assessment
outcome: Accuracy of ChatGPT-4o interpretation of orthopantomograms for third molar assessment
effect: Accuracy was 38.44% (95% CI 35.27%-41.62%); responses frequently incomplete or fabricated, insufficient for unsupervised clinical use.
quote: ChatGPT-4o achieved an accuracy rate of 38.44 % (95 % CI: 35.27 %-41.62 %).
sample_unit: ChatGPT-4o responses (30 per each of 30 orthopantomograms)

title: Deep learning-based automatic segmentation of brain structures on MRI: A test-retest reproducibility analysis
outcome: Test-retest consistency of deep learning brain segmentation volumes across scanner types and field strengths
effect: High consistency on the same scanner type (1.5 T to 1.5 T or 3 T to 3 T), slightly better at 1.5 T than 3 T. Cross-scanner (1.5 T vs 3 T) consistency was slightly lower. No numbers reported in the abstract.
quote: However, cross-comparisons between different scanner types (1.5 T vs. 3 T) demonstrated slightly less consistency, highlighting the influence of magnetic field strength on segmentation accuracy.

title: Precision Oncology in Non-small Cell Lung Cancer: A Comparative Study of Contextualized ChatGPT Models
outcome: Agreement with NCCN guideline-preferred therapies, with vs without guideline PDF grounding
effect: PDF+Prompt agreement 23/24 vs 17/24 for GPT-4 (P=0.040) and 18/24 for GPT-4o (P=0.089); prompting alone did not significantly improve agreement.
quote: The PDF+Prompt contextualized model demonstrated elevated agreement scores of 23/24 versus 17/24 for GPT-4 (P = 0.040) and 18/24 for GPT-4o (P = 0.089).

title: Precision Oncology in Non-small Cell Lung Cancer: A Comparative Study of Contextualized ChatGPT Models
outcome: Recommendation of guideline non-concordant therapies by base GPT models
effect: Base GPT-4 gave non-concordant therapies in 4/12 responses and GPT-4o in 5/12; PDF+Prompt model had none.
quote: No PDF+Prompt model responses contained guideline non-concordant therapies in contrast to 4/12 responses for GPT4 (P = 0.093) and 5/12 responses for GPT4o (P = 0.037).

title: Unveiling Public Stigma for Borderline Personality Disorder: A Comparative Study of Artificial Intelligence and Mental Health Care Providers
outcome: Differences in GAI stigma, empathy and chronicity ratings between woman and man BPD vignette characters
effect: Gender biases across GAI; Gemini showed less empathy, more negative reactions and greater stigma, especially for the woman with BPD; all GAI rated the woman's problems as more chronic than the man's.
quote: Across GAI, gender biases were found with Google Gemini showing less empathy, more negative reactions, and greater public stigma, particularly for a woman with BPD, than either ChatGPT-3.5 or ChatGPT-4.
sample_unit: mental health care practitioners in the comparison sample (number of GAI responses not reported)

title: Unveiling Public Stigma for Borderline Personality Disorder: A Comparative Study of Artificial Intelligence and Mental Health Care Providers
outcome: Stereotyped and stigmatizing content in GAI responses about people with BPD
effect: GAI rated characters as less trustworthy, more likely to have difficulty forming close relationships, and more chronic and unchangeable than MHCPs did; gender bias and stereotyped beliefs reflected.
quote: Overall, these results suggest that GAI may express empathy but reflects gender bias and stereotyped beliefs for people with BPD.
sample_unit: mental health care practitioners in the comparison sample (number of GAI responses not reported)

title: Patient and Clinician Perceptions of a "People-Like-Me" Tool for Personalized Rehabilitation After Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Qualitative Interview Study
outcome: Patient comprehension of the tool's outputs (percentiles, line graphs, jargon)
effect: Most patients understood the tool's take-home message, but some patients and clinicians felt percentiles, line graphs, and medical jargon decreased clarity and comprehension.
quote: some patients and clinicians felt the use of percentiles, line graphs, and medical jargon decreased patients' clarity and comprehension of the tool

title: Comprehensive DVT risk assessment model for meningioma surgery: development, validation and clinical implementation
outcome: Model discrimination in derivation versus bootstrap-validation cohort
effect: Derivation AUC 0.83 (95% CI 0.78-0.89); bootstrap validation AUC 0.81 (95% CI 0.75-0.87). Internal validation only, single center.
quote: The model achieved superior discrimination (derivation cohort: AUC = 0.83, 95% CI: 0.78-0.89; validation cohort: AUC = 0.81, 95% CI: 0.75-0.87) compared to existing risk assessment tools.

title: Opportunities and risks of artificial intelligence in patient portal messaging in primary care
outcome: Whether physician review of AI-drafted patient messages caught and corrected embedded errors
effect: Each erroneous draft was missed by 13-15 of 20 PCPs; 35-45% submitted unedited; only one participant addressed all four errors; mean 2.67 of 4 missed.
quote: Each erroneous AI draft was “missed” by at least 13 participants (65%) and was submitted entirely unedited by at least seven participants (35%).

title: Opportunities and risks of artificial intelligence in patient portal messaging in primary care
outcome: Whether physicians detected incorrect AI outputs (automation bias/overreliance)
effect: Physicians missed 65-75% of erroneous drafts (13-15 of 20); 90% agreed they trusted the AI tool and 75% believed drafts were safe to use.
quote: Participants missed an average of 2.67 out of four (66.6%) erroneous AI drafts.

title: Opportunities and risks of artificial intelligence in patient portal messaging in primary care
outcome: Harmful errors or delayed escalation in AI-drafted replies to symptom-related messages
effect: Two of four erroneous drafts were potentially harmful omissions (blood clot, DKA), which physicians missed in 65% and 75% of cases.
quote: These erroneous messages were then categorized via team consensus: two were identified as objective inaccuracies, and two were identified as potentially harmful omission (Table 3 ).

title: Opportunities and risks of artificial intelligence in patient portal messaging in primary care
outcome: Outdated clinical knowledge and omission of serious diagnoses in AI drafts
effect: AI drafts contained outdated COVID vaccine timing advice and omitted DKA and blood clot urgency; 4 of 18 drafts (22%) erroneous.
quote: Four (22%) of these PPMs were identified as erroneous.

title: Opportunities and risks of artificial intelligence in patient portal messaging in primary care
outcome: Automation complacency letting erroneous AI-drafted messages reach patients after physician review
effect: All but one physician sent at least one erroneous response; likelihood of a missed error significantly greater than zero (p<0.001) for each erroneous draft; 90% trusted the tool.
quote: In this simulated environment, all but one physician ‘sent’ at least one fictitious response to a patient that contained an error.

title: Opportunities and risks of artificial intelligence in patient portal messaging in primary care
outcome: Passive acceptance of flawed AI drafts in a standard editable draft interface
effect: With a standard editable draft interface, 35-45% of erroneous drafts were submitted entirely unedited and 65-75% were insufficiently corrected.
quote: Each erroneous AI draft was “missed” by at least 13 participants (65%) and was submitted entirely unedited by at least seven participants (35%).

title: Opportunities and risks of artificial intelligence in patient portal messaging in primary care
outcome: AI drafts failing to escalate urgent conditions (blood clot, DKA) in patient messages
effect: AI drafts for blood clot risk and DKA risk omitted urgent escalation; these were missed by 13 (65%) and 15 (75%) physicians respectively.
quote: The AI draft does not address the risk of diabetic ketoacidosis which requires urgent intervention.

title: Opportunities and risks of artificial intelligence in patient portal messaging in primary care
outcome: unedited erroneous drafts
effect: 35-45% of erroneous drafts were submitted entirely unedited.
quote: Each error was insufficiently addressed by 13-15 participants, and 35-45% of erroneous drafts were submitted entirely unedited.

title: Opportunities and risks of artificial intelligence in patient portal messaging in primary care
outcome: emergency care instructions
effect: Blood-clot-risk draft did not urgently advise urgent/emergency care evaluation.
quote: While the AI draft does mention the risk of blood clot and to make an appointment as soon as possible, it does not urgently inform the patient to seek an evaluation at urgent or emergency care to address the risk of a blood clot.

title: A cross-sectional study on ChatGPT's alignment with clinical practice guidelines in musculoskeletal rehabilitation
outcome: Rater-scored alignment of ChatGPT answers with musculoskeletal rehabilitation clinical practice guidelines
effect: Mean Likert scores: clarity 4.85, accuracy 4.62, relevance 4.50, completeness 4.20, consistency 3.85; lower agreement and performance in rehabilitation than disease information.
quote: ChatGPT's responses received the highest average score for clarity (4.85), followed by accuracy (4.62), relevance (4.50), and completeness (4.20).

title: Myo-Guide: A Machine Learning-Based Web Application for Neuromuscular Disease Diagnosis With MRI
venue: Journal of cachexia, sarcopenia and muscle
outcome: Top-3 diagnostic accuracy of model versus four expert clinicians on 14 unseen MRI scans
effect: Model obtained the highest top-3 accuracy (75.0% ± 4.8%) compared to four expert clinicians.
quote: Compared to four expert clinicians, the model obtained the highest top-3 accuracy (75.0% ± 4.8%).

title: ChatGPT-4o-Generated Exercise Plans for Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus-Assessment of Their Safety and Other Quality Criteria by Coaching Experts
outcome: Safety of AI exercise plans vs ADA/ACSM guidelines, including contraindications and medical check-up advice
effect: Most common safety gap was missing advice for medical check-up (rated low in 8 of 9 plans); high-intensity training recommended for a patient with proliferative retinopathy; safety instructions incomplete.
quote: High-intensity training was recommended for Patient 3 with proliferative retinopathy.

title: ChatGPT-4o-Generated Exercise Plans for Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus-Assessment of Their Safety and Other Quality Criteria by Coaching Experts
outcome: Effect of prompt detail on plan quality and safety ratings across three prompts
effect: Safety ratings by prompt: Prompt 1 4L/3M/2S, Prompt 2 2L/2M/5S, Prompt 3 3L/2M/4S; more detailed prompts gave minimal safety improvement, and quality improved in some training criteria.
quote: Using more detailed prompts (Prompts 2 and 3) generally resulted in minimal quality improvement ( Figure 1 , Prompt 1: 4× L, 3× M, 2× S, Prompt 2: 2× L, 2× M, 5× S, Prompt 3: 3× L, 2× M, 4× S)

title: ChatGPT-4o-Generated Exercise Plans for Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus-Assessment of Their Safety and Other Quality Criteria by Coaching Experts
outcome: safety under prompt variation
effect: Safety ratings varied by prompt: Prompt 1 4×L/3×M/2×S; Prompt 2 2×L/2×M/5×S; Prompt 3 3×L/2×M/4×S.
quote: Using more detailed prompts (Prompts 2 and 3) generally resulted in minimal quality improvement ( Figure 1 , Prompt 1: 4× L, 3× M, 2× S, Prompt 2: 2× L, 2× M, 5× S, Prompt 3: 3× L, 2× M, 4× S), primarily in terms of tailoring the plans for individuals with secondary complications by avoiding conflicts between training and potential contraindications and providing additional safety instructions.

title: ChatGPT-4o-Generated Exercise Plans for Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus-Assessment of Their Safety and Other Quality Criteria by Coaching Experts
outcome: consumer chatbot exercise advice safety
effect: Across nine plans for three T2DM profiles, authors concluded the plans were not fully safe, especially for secondary diseases/complications.
quote: Our results imply that ChatGPT-4o-generated exercise plans are not (yet) fully safe for patients with T2DM, especially not for those with secondary diseases/complications.

title: Expert and Interdisciplinary Analysis of AI-Driven Chatbots for Mental Health Support: Mixed Methods Study
outcome: Mental health professionals' perceptions of chatbot harm, dependence, and manipulation risk
effect: Professionals had emphatic initial impressions of responses likely to produce harm and a generic mode of care, and saw risk of user dependence and manipulation. Trust scores were medium to low, with no difference between chatbots (t6=-0.76; P=.48).
quote: Qualitative analysis revealed emphatic initial impressions among mental health professionals of chatbot responses likely to produce harm, exhibiting a generic mode of care, and risking user dependence and manipulation given the central role of trust in the therapeutic relationship.

title: Assessing artificial intelligence-generated patient discharge information for the emergency department: a pilot study
outcome: Readability indices (Flesch, FKGL, SMOG, Coleman-Liau) of AI-generated Dutch discharge brochures
effect: Brochures required high school- to college-level comprehension, though the authors consider this likely an overestimate due to context-specific reasons and features of the Dutch language.
quote: Readability analysis indicated that brochures require high school- to college-level comprehension, but this is likely an overestimation due to context-specific reasons as well as features inherent to the Dutch language.

title: PRECISE framework: Enhanced radiology reporting with GPT for improved readability, reliability, and patient-centered care
outcome: Readability scores of original vs GPT-4 sixth-grade-level summaries of radiology reports
effect: Flesch Reading Ease rose from 38.28 to 80.82; Gunning Fog fell from 13.04 to 6.99; ARI improved from 13.33 to 5.86 (all p<0.001).
quote: Readability scores significantly improved, with the mean Flesch Reading Ease score increasing from 38.28 to 80.82 (p-value < 0.001), the Gunning Fog Index decreasing from 13.04 to 6.99 (p-value < 0.001), and the ARI score improving from 13.33 to 5.86 (p-value < 0.001).

title: PRECISE framework: Enhanced radiology reporting with GPT for improved readability, reliability, and patient-centered care
outcome: Understandability of plain-language AI-generated radiology summaries rated by non-medical volunteers and reliability by clinicians
effect: Non-medical volunteers rated 97% of PRECISE summaries fully understandable; clinicians found 95% reliable.
quote: Clinical volunteer assessments found 95 % of the summaries reliable, and non-medical volunteers rated 97 % of the PRECISE-generated summaries as fully understandable.

title: Can ChatGPT provide parent education for oral immunotherapy?
venue: Annals of allergy, asthma & immunology : official publication of the American College of Allergy, Asthma, & Immunology
outcome: Readability of ChatGPT responses to parent OIT questions (Flesch scores)
effect: ChatGPT responses exhibited low readability scores corresponding with a high-grade reading level; understandability 73% to 84%, reduced by response complexity.
quote: ChatGPT responses exhibited low readability scores, corresponding with a high-grade reading level.

title: Can ChatGPT provide parent education for oral immunotherapy?
venue: Annals of allergy, asthma & immunology : official publication of the American College of Allergy, Asthma, & Immunology
outcome: Reading grade level of AI-generated patient education content
effect: Responses had low Flesch Reading Ease scores, corresponding with a high-grade reading level, above what is suitable for parents.
quote: ChatGPT responses exhibited low readability scores, corresponding with a high-grade reading level.

title: Underestimation of Cardiovascular Risk by the SCORE2 Model in Primary Care: A Call for Recalibration
outcome: SCORE2 observed-to-expected risk ratio in Dutch primary care patients
effect: Mean observed 10-year risk 10.1% vs model-predicted 6.2%; O/E ratio 1.54 in females and 1.68 in men; ~35% of patients potentially missed preventive treatment.
quote: Results indicated a mean observed 10-year risk of 10.1%, notably higher than the model-predicted risk of 6.2%.

title: Comparison of CT referral justification using clinical decision support and large language models in a large European cohort
outcome: CT referral test justification accuracy of LLMs vs independent experts vs ESR iGuide reference
effect: Independent experts achieved highest accuracy (92.4%) for medical test justification, surpassing GPT-4 (88.8%) and Claude-3 Haiku (85.2%).
quote: Independent experts achieved the highest accuracy (92.4%) for medical test justification, surpassing GPT-4 (88.8%) and Claude-3 Haiku (85.2%).

title: Readability, accuracy and appropriateness and quality of AI chatbot responses as a patient information source on root canal retreatment: A comparative assessment
outcome: Readability of chatbot responses versus recommended sixth-grade reading level
effect: All chatbots exceeded the recommended readability level, suitable for readers at or above 10th-grade level; Gemini significantly more readable (p<0.05); none met standards.
quote: All chatbots generated responses exceeding the recommended readability level, making them suitable for readers at or above the 10th-grade level.

title: Readability, accuracy and appropriateness and quality of AI chatbot responses as a patient information source on root canal retreatment: A comparative assessment
outcome: Reading grade level of chatbot patient-education responses versus sixth-grade recommendation
effect: All three chatbots exceeded the sixth-grade target, requiring 10th-grade level or above; none met recommended readability standards for patient education materials.
quote: None of the chatbots met the recommended readability standards for patient education materials.

title: Artificial Intelligence Large Language Models Improve Patient Comprehension of Radiologist Magnetic Resonance Imaging Reports
venue: Arthroscopy : the journal of arthroscopic & related surgery : official publication of the Arthroscopy Association of North America and the International Arthroscopy Association
outcome: Patient comprehension quiz score for AI plain-language MRI report versus standard radiologist report
effect: AI group scored 20% higher than standard MRI group on comprehension quiz (74.7% vs 54.7%, P < .001); 87.5% preferred AI translation; clarity 4.5 vs 2.2 of 5.
quote: Patients in the AI group scored 20% higher than those in the standard MRI group on the comprehension quiz (74.7% vs 54.7%, P < .001).

title: Evaluation of Six Large Language Models for Clinical Decision Support: Application in Transfusion Decision-making for RhD Blood-type Patients
outcome: Reproducibility of LLM answers when the same question was repeated
effect: All LLM models changed their responses or did not respond when the same question was repeated.
quote: All LLM models changed their responses or did not respond when the same question was repeated.

title: Testing a Program to Help Patients Prepare for Kidney Failure Treatment – The PREPARE NOW Study
outcome: Effect of risk-prediction-based care-management enrollment bundle on patient-reported, hospitalization, referral, and documentation outcomes
effect: Risk-flagged high-risk patients were screened for care management (71%). No improvement in empowerment, self-efficacy, or self-care choice; hospitalization RR 0.70 (0.51-0.96); referral OR 0.67 (0.33-1.33); preference documentation IRR 1.34 (1.06-1.69).
quote: In intervention clinics, uptake of the Patient-Centered Kidney Transitions Care intervention's education and self-management programs was low; however, the kidney transitions specialists screened most (n = 318 [71%]) of those classified as high risk and receiving care in intervention clinics for enrollment into care management.
sample_unit: patients in the Kidney Transitions Registry (EHR outcomes); 1473 surveyed, 836 chart-reviewed

title: AI in Home Care-Evaluation of Large Language Models for Future Training of Informal Caregivers: Observational Comparative Case Study
outcome: Rate of incorrect information and omissions in LLM home care instructions versus professional gold standard
effect: Copilot incorrect information 20% (2/10), GPT-4o 10% (1/10), GPT-3.5 0%; details omitted in 60% (6/10) of cases for GPT-4o and Copilot and 80% (8/10) for GPT-3.5; error frequency did not differ across models (P=.65).
quote: Furthermore, error frequency did not differ significantly across models (P=.65), though Copilot had the highest rate of incorrect information (20%, 2/10 vs 10%, 1/10 for GPT-4o and 0%, 0/0 for GPT-3.5).

title: Microsoft Copilot Provides More Accurate and Reliable Information About Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury and Repair Than ChatGPT and Google Gemini; However, No Resource Was Overall the Best
outcome: Readability of LLM answers about ACL injury (Flesch-Kincaid Reading Ease and Grade Level)
effect: Reading Ease <30 for all sources except Copilot Fact (31.9); all Grade Level scores >13, i.e., college level or above.
quote: Similarly, all Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level scores were >13, indicating a minimum readability level of college level or college graduate.

title: Microsoft Copilot Provides More Accurate and Reliable Information About Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury and Repair Than ChatGPT and Google Gemini; However, No Resource Was Overall the Best
outcome: Reading level of AI-generated patient information versus appropriate reading level
effect: All three LLMs produced answers at college reading level or above (Grade Level >13; Reading Ease <30 except Copilot Fact at 31.9).
quote: Similarly, all Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level scores were >13, indicating a minimum readability level of college level or college graduate.

title: Assessing the quality and readability of ChatGPT responses to frequently asked questions about trigger finger release
venue: Journal of plastic, reconstructive & aesthetic surgery : JPRAS
outcome: Reading grade level of ChatGPT responses versus recommended patient material level
effect: Average reading level of responses was 12th grade, exceeding the recommended 7th-8th-grade level for patient materials.
quote: The average reading level of responses was at a 12th-grade level, which exceeds the recommended 7th-8th-grade level for patient materials.

title: Assessing the quality and readability of ChatGPT responses to frequently asked questions about trigger finger release
venue: Journal of plastic, reconstructive & aesthetic surgery : JPRAS
outcome: Comprehensibility of AI-generated patient education responses via Flesch-Kincaid reading level
effect: Responses averaged a 12th-grade reading level, above the recommended 7th-8th-grade level for patient materials.
quote: The average reading level of responses was at a 12th-grade level, which exceeds the recommended 7th-8th-grade level for patient materials.

title: Assessing the quality and readability of ChatGPT responses to frequently asked questions about trigger finger release
venue: Journal of plastic, reconstructive & aesthetic surgery : JPRAS
outcome: Accuracy of ChatGPT clinical answers about trigger finger release on four-point scale
effect: Average accuracy score 1.9 (between excellent and satisfactory); one incorrect response and occasional factual inaccuracies, particularly treatment recommendations.
quote: Although the chatbot provided largely accurate information, it produced an incorrect response in one case and displayed occasional factual inaccuracies, particularly regarding treatment recommendations.

title: Generalizability of FDA-Approved AI-Enabled Medical Devices for Clinical Use
outcome: Public reporting of sex- and age-specific data in clinical studies of FDA-approved AI devices
effect: Among clinical studies, 145 (28.7%) provided sex-specific data and 117 (23.2%) addressed age-related subgroups.
quote: Among clinical studies, less than one-third provided sex-specific data (145 studies [28.7%]), and only 117 studies (23.2%) addressed age-related subgroups.

title: Generalizability of FDA-Approved AI-Enabled Medical Devices for Clinical Use
outcome: Reporting of discriminatory performance metrics in public summaries
effect: Reported in 200 summaries; sensitivity 183 devices (36.2%), specificity 176 (34.9%), AUC 82 (16.2%).
quote: Discriminatory performance metrics were reported in 200 of the available summaries (sensitivity: 183 devices [36.2%]; specificity: 176 devices [34.9%]; area under the curve: 82 devices [16.2%]).

title: Generalizability of FDA-Approved AI-Enabled Medical Devices for Clinical Use
outcome: Study designs of clinical performance studies for approved AI devices
effect: Retrospective 193 (38.2%); prospective 41 (8.1%); randomized 12 (2.4%). 218 devices (24.1%) reported no performance studies.
quote: Retrospective study designs were most common (193 studies [38.2%]), with only 41 studies (8.1%) being prospective and 12 studies (2.4%) randomized.

title: Generalizability of FDA-Approved AI-Enabled Medical Devices for Clinical Use
outcome: Availability of development details in publicly provided device summaries
effect: Detailed descriptions of development were absent from most publicly provided summaries.
quote: Detailed descriptions of development were absent from most publicly provided summaries.

title: Automated extraction of functional biomarkers of verbal and ambulatory ability from multi-institutional clinical notes using large language models
outcome: LLM extraction accuracy of verbal and ambulatory ability across two institutional cohorts
effect: Ambulatory weighted-F1 >.90 in both cohorts; verbal ability predictions were more accurate in the BGR cohort than in the CP clinic cohort.
quote: However, verbal ability predictions were more accurate in the BGR cohort, likely due to higher adherence between the prompt and ground-truth assessment questions.
sample_unit: clinical notes (3,245 from 125 individuals in BGR; 5,462 from 260 individuals in CP clinic)

title: Patient-facing chatbots: Enhancing healthcare accessibility while navigating digital literacy challenges and isolation risks-a mixed-methods study
outcome: Patient-reported ability to understand chatbot responses and feeling understood by chatbot
effect: 213/609 (35.0%) felt they could not understand the chatbot completely; 376/614 (61.2%) felt the chatbot did not completely understand them.
quote: In surveys, 213/609 (35.0%) felt they could not understand the chatbot completely, and 376/614 (61.2%) felt the chatbot did not completely understand them.

title: Specialized Large Language Model Outperforms Neurologists at Complex Diagnosis in Blinded Case-Based Evaluation
outcome: Relevance and verifiability of AI-provided references, including hallucinated content
effect: All AI-provided references were classified as relevant with no hallucinatory content detected.
quote: All AI-provided references were classified as relevant with no hallucinatory content detected.
sample_unit: neurologists (plus the AI system) evaluated on 5 clinical scenarios

title: Specialized Large Language Model Outperforms Neurologists at Complex Diagnosis in Blinded Case-Based Evaluation
outcome: Normalized diagnostic score of AI versus neurologists on same cases
effect: AI achieved a significantly higher normalized score (86.17%) compared to neurologists (55.11%, p < 0.001). Differential diagnosis: 85% vs 46.15%; final diagnosis: 88.24% vs 70.93%.
quote: AI achieved a significantly higher normalized score (86.17%) compared to neurologists (55.11%, p < 0.001).
sample_unit: neurologists (plus the AI system) evaluated on 5 clinical scenarios

title: AI-Driven Information for Relatives of Patients with Malignant Middle Cerebral Artery Infarction: A Preliminary Validation Study Using GPT-4o
outcome: Readability of GPT-4o answers for relatives (FRE, FKG, Gunning Fog)

quote: The readability assessment revealed an FRE score of 7.23, an FKG score of 15.87 and a GF index of 18.15.

title: AI-Driven Information for Relatives of Patients with Malignant Middle Cerebral Artery Infarction: A Preliminary Validation Study Using GPT-4o
outcome: Whether GPT-4o responses supplied sources for its claims
effect: GPT-4o did not systematically provide references; sourcing was among the poorest-scoring QAMAI categories, so users cannot trace claims.
quote: GPT-4o did not systematically provide references for their responses.

title: Non-invasive biopsy diagnosis of diabetic kidney disease via deep learning applied to retinal images: a population-based study
outcome: DKD detection AUC on internal validation versus ten external multi-ethnic validation datasets
effect: AUC 0·842 (95% CI 0·838-0·846) on internal validation and 0·791-0·826 across external validation datasets from China, Singapore, Malaysia, Australia, and the UK.
quote: For detecting DKD, DeepDKD achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0·842 (95% CI 0·838-0·846) on the internal validation dataset and AUCs of 0·791-0·826 across external validation datasets.

title: Non-invasive biopsy diagnosis of diabetic kidney disease via deep learning applied to retinal images: a population-based study
outcome: Sensitivity for detecting DKD, DeepDKD versus a metadata-only model, in a prospective study
effect: DeepDKD detected DKD with higher sensitivity than the metadata model (89·8% vs 66·3%, p<0·0001).
quote: In the prospective study, compared with the metadata model, DeepDKD could detect DKD with higher sensitivity (89·8% vs 66·3%, p<0·0001).

title: Evaluation of an Ambient Artificial Intelligence Documentation Platform for Clinicians
outcome: Local ambient scribe assessment of usability, clinician well-being, time in notes, and workload before and after implementation
effect: Time in notes per appointment fell from 6.2 to 5.3 minutes (P<.001); NASA-TLX mental demand 12.2 to 6.3; burnout 42.1% to 35.1% (P=.12); benefit varied by sex and specialty.
quote: Mean (SD) time in notes per appointment significantly decreased from 6.2 (4.0) to 5.3 (3.5) minutes (P < .001), with a bigger decrease for female vs male clinicians (8.1 [3.9] to 6.7 [3.6] minutes vs 4.7 [3.5] to 4.2 [3.1] minutes; P = .001).

title: Application of Generative Artificial Intelligence for Physician and Patient Oncology Letters-AI-OncLetters
outcome: Readability and understandability of AI-generated patient letters
effect: Mean Flesch Reading Ease 73.3 (seventh-grade reading level); PEMAT-P understandability score above 80%.
quote: Patient-directed letters achieved a mean Flesch Reading Ease score of 73.3 (seventh-grade reading level) and a PEMAT-P score above 80%, indicating high understandability.
sample_unit: synthetic oncology case notes (physician and patient letters generated)

title: Expert of Experts Verification and Alignment (EVAL) Framework for Large Language Models Safety in Gastroenterology
outcome: Reward model alignment with human grading and accuracy gain from rejection sampling
effect: Reward model replicated human grading in 87.9% of cases across temperature settings and improved accuracy through rejection sampling by 8.36% overall.
quote: The reward model replicated human grading with 87.9% of cases across temperature settings and significantly improved accuracy through rejection sampling by 8.36% overall.

title: Mitigating the risk of health inequity exacerbated by large language models
outcome: LLM output changes when non-decisive socio-demographic factors are added to inputs; EquityGuard detection and mitigation
effect: Adding non-decisive socio-demographic factors (race, sex, income, LGBT+ status, homelessness, illiteracy, disability, unemployment) led to incorrect and harmful outputs. EquityGuard was reported effective in promoting equitable outcomes; no numbers given in the abstract.
quote: However, our study shows that incorporating non-decisive socio-demographic factors, such as race, sex, income level, LGBT+ status, homelessness, illiteracy, disability, and unemployment, into the input of LLMs can lead to incorrect and harmful outputs.

title: The FAIIR conversational AI agent assistant for youth mental health service provision
outcome: Performance drop from retrospective evaluation to silent testing on live data
effect: During silent testing, performance remained robust with less than a 2% drop in all metrics.
quote: During the silent testing phase, its performance remained robust, with less than a 2% drop in all metrics.

title: Synthetic medical education in dermatology leveraging generative artificial intelligence
outcome: Expert-rated demographic bias and demographic diversity in GPT-4-generated dermatology vignettes
effect: Experts rated demographic bias low (1.52/5), but vignettes lacked significant demographic diversity.
quote: Vignettes did not incorporate significant demographic diversity.

title: Nephrologist's Perceptions of Risk of Severe Chronic Kidney Disease and Outpatient Follow-up After Hospitalization With AKI: Multinational Randomized Survey Study
venue: Canadian journal of kidney health and disease
outcome: Clinician follow-up decisions with versus without AI risk prediction in randomized vignettes
effect: Randomized comparison showed risk reporting changed decisions: <10% risk mean difference -0.71; ≥50% risk mean difference 0.49; OR 0.35 and 2.21 for score ≥5.
quote: When the predicted risk of severe CKD is reported, nephrologists are less likely to recommend follow-up for lower risk patients with AKI and more likely to recommend follow-up for higher risk patients, leading to better alignment of recommendations for outpatient follow-up with patient risk of severe CKD.

title: Nephrologist's Perceptions of Risk of Severe Chronic Kidney Disease and Outpatient Follow-up After Hospitalization With AKI: Multinational Randomized Survey Study
venue: Canadian journal of kidney health and disease
outcome: Nephrologist follow-up recommendations by CKD risk
effect: Reported risk changed Likert scores: <10% mean difference = -0.71 [95% CI = -1.19, -0.23]; ≥50% mean difference = 0.49 [95% CI = 0.04, 0.93].
quote: Nephrologists were significantly less likely to recommend outpatient nephrology follow-up for patients with a <10% predicted risk of severe CKD when the risk was reported (mean difference = -0.71 [95% CI = -1.19, -0.23]), and significantly more likely to recommend follow-up for patients with a ≥50% predicted risk when the risk of severe CKD was reported (mean difference = 0.49 [95% CI = 0.04, 0.93]).

title: Performance of Large Language Models (ChatGPT and Gemini Advanced) in Gastrointestinal Pathology and Clinical Review of Applications in Gastroenterology
outcome: Rate of fabricated (nonexistent) references cited by LLMs in gastrointestinal pathology scenarios
effect: 25-50% of model responses cited references that do not exist (hallucinations); none of the models gave accurate TNM staging.
quote: None of the models could provide the accurate TNM staging for these clinical scenarios, with 25-50% citing references that do not exist (hallucinations).

title: Physician- and Large Language Model-Generated Hospital Discharge Summaries
outcome: Errors (inaccuracies, omissions, hallucinations) in LLM-generated discharge summary narratives vs physician-written
effect: LLM narratives averaged 2.91 errors per summary vs 1.82 for physicians; LLM narratives were less comprehensive (3.72 vs 4.13, P < .001).
quote: LLM-generated narratives contained more unique errors (mean [SD] errors per summary, 2.91 [2.54]) than physician-generated narratives (mean [SD] errors per summary, 1.82 [1.94]).

title: Physician- and Large Language Model-Generated Hospital Discharge Summaries
outcome: Potential harmfulness of errors in unreviewed LLM-drafted discharge summaries
effect: Narrative-level harm was low but higher for LLM (0.84 vs 0.36, P < .001); 1 LLM narrative scored 4 or greater vs 0 for physicians; 6 vs 5 individual errors scored 4+.
quote: Both LLM- and physician-generated narratives had low overall potential for harm (scores <1 on a scale ranging from 0-7), with LLM-generated narratives scoring higher than physician narratives (mean [SD] score of 0.84 [0.98] vs 0.36 [0.70]; P < .001) and only 1 LLM-generated narrative (compared with 0 physician-generated narratives) scoring 4 or greater.

title: The Effectiveness of a Custom AI Chatbot for Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Health Literacy: Development and Evaluation Study
outcome: Appropriateness of RAG chatbot responses grounded in reference documents versus general knowledge
effect: 32 of 44 responses cited reference documents; 30 of 32 (94%) fully appropriate, 2 partly appropriate. Of 12 general knowledge responses, 1 (8%) was inappropriate. All 16 simulated consultation responses were appropriate and sourced.
quote: Among the 32 sourced responses, 30 (94%) were deemed fully appropriate, with the remaining 2 (6%) being deemed partly appropriate.

title: The Effectiveness of a Custom AI Chatbot for Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Health Literacy: Development and Evaluation Study
outcome: Source attribution of chatbot answers and flagging of general-knowledge answers
effect: 32 of 44 (73%) responses cited reference documents and 12 (27%) were attributed to general knowledge; all 16 simulated consultation responses were sourced from the reference documents.
quote: Of the 44 evaluated questions, 32 (73%) responses cited reference documents, and 12 (27%) were attributed to general knowledge.

title: Behavior recognition technology based on deep learning used in pediatric behavioral audiometry
outcome: AI vs manual behavioral audiometry sensitivity, specificity, AUC by age group
effect: Ages 2.5-4: AI sensitivity 0.929 vs manual 0.900, but manual specificity 0.824 and AUC 0.901 higher. Ages 4-6: manual sensitivity 0.943, specificity 0.947, AUC 0.924 all higher than AI.
quote: For children aged 4-6 years, the sensitivity (0.943), specificity (0.947), and AUC (0.924) of artificial behavioral audiometry were higher than those of AI behavioral audiometry.

title: AI-Enhanced Speech Recognition in Triage
