sample_unit: prompts (drug orders requiring renal dose adjustment)

title: Dosage adjustments in renal impairment among medical ward patients: ChatGPT® and DeepSeek® models' effectiveness in assessing those adjustments
venue: Exploratory research in clinical and social pharmacy
outcome: AI clinical knowledge on renal dosing compared with current guideline (UpToDate)
effect: Accuracy 61.7% for ChatGPT 5.0 and 67.5% for DeepThink against UpToDate; modest improvement across ChatGPT versions.
quote: With advances in the ChatGPT® model, there was a modest improvement in prediction capacity, with the latest ChatGPT® 5.0 achieving balanced performance (64.3 % sensitivity, 54.8 % specificity, 61.7 % accuracy).
sample_unit: prompts (drug orders requiring renal dose adjustment)

title: Retrospective modeling study of ChatGPT (GPT 4) warfarin dose adjustment in patients with INRs outside the therapeutic range
outcome: GPT-4 warfarin dose recommendations compared with physician dosing and modeled INR normalization
effect: Doses within ±1 mg/week of physician in 74% and ±2 mg/week in 84%; mean 27.5 vs 28.0 mg/week (p=.12); modeled therapeutic INR 69% vs 72% (p=.15).
quote: Seventy-two percent of patients achieved therapeutic INR under physician-managed dosing, while the model suggested a 69% success rate for ChatGPT-guided dosing (p = .15).

title: Identifying Volar Locking Plates on Plain Radiographs: Can Artificial Intelligence Models 'Beat' Clinicians?
outcome: Manufacturer identification accuracy of ChatGPT 5 versus five hand consultants on the same radiographs
effect: ChatGPT 5 correctly identified 3 of 52 (5.8%); consultants 13.5-46.2% (mean 30.8%); humans had 7.26 times higher odds of correct identification (OR 7.26, 95% CI 2.27-23.18, p<0.001).
quote: In a standard logistic regression with clustered standard errors, the human cohort had 7.26 times higher odds of correct identification compared with the AI (OR 7.26, 95% CI 2.27-23.18, p < 0.001).

title: Large Language Model-Enabled Editing of Patient Audio Interviews From "This Is My Story" Conversations: Comparative Study
outcome: Blinded expert ratings of AI-edited vs expert- and novice-edited audio summaries
effect: Expert audio 4.84/content 4.83; novice 3.84/3.63; AI 3.49/3.20. AI and novice rated significantly lower than expert (P<.001) but not significantly different from each other.
quote: Novice and AI edits were rated significantly lower than the expert edits (P<.001), but not significantly different from each other.

title: Increasing Use of a Postpartum and Newborn Chatbot among Birthing Individuals and Caregivers: Development and Implementation Study
outcome: Chatbot reach (opening) by race, insurance, prenatal care location
effect: Lower postpartum reach for Black (OR 0.73) vs White, public insurance (OR 0.72) vs private; newborn reach lower for Black (OR 0.61), public insurance (OR 0.63), FQHC prenatal care (OR 0.50)
quote: The odds of opening the postpartum chatbot were significantly lower for individuals identified in the EHR as Black (odds ratio [OR] 0.73, 95% CI 0.61- 0.88) compared to White individuals.
sample_unit: chatbot recipients (6505 birthing individuals and 7489 newborn caregivers)

title: Increasing Use of a Postpartum and Newborn Chatbot among Birthing Individuals and Caregivers: Development and Implementation Study
outcome: Chatbot reach before vs after feedback-based content and outreach revision
effect: No change after revision: postpartum 64.1% to 62.8% (OR 0.95, 0.85-1.05); newborn 65.9% to 65.2% (OR 0.97, 0.88-1.07); Spanish version improved newborn reach 58% to 66.2% (OR 1.42)
quote: No significant changes in reach were found after launching the updated version of the newborn and postpartum outreach and chatbot content, nor after including the chatbot information in patients’ discharge paperwork ( Table 5 ); thus, we focused on results in the combined analyses for the full time period.
sample_unit: chatbot recipients (6505 birthing individuals and 7489 newborn caregivers)

title: Increasing Use of a Postpartum and Newborn Chatbot among Birthing Individuals and Caregivers: Development and Implementation Study
outcome: Chatbot reach after adding chatbot information to discharge paperwork
effect: Postpartum reach changed from 63.6% to 63.9% (OR 1.02, 95% CI 0.90-1.15); newborn reach changed from 66.2% to 64.6% (OR 0.93, 95% CI 0.83-1.05). Neither change was significant.
quote: No significant changes in reach were found after launching the updated version of the newborn and postpartum outreach and chatbot content, nor after including the chatbot information in patients’ discharge paperwork ( Table 5 ); thus, we focused on results in the combined analyses for the full time period.
sample_unit: chatbot recipients (6505 birthing individuals and 7489 newborn caregivers)

title: Clinical Trial Patient Matching: A Real-Time, Common Data Model and Artificial Intelligence-Driven System for Semiautomated Patient Prescreening in Cancer Clinical Trials
outcome: Tool accuracy and sensitivity versus gold standard chart review, retrospective and prospective
effect: 94% retrospective and 88% prospective accuracy, 100% sensitivity versus gold standard chart review in a single CRC trial
quote: For the single CRC trial, CTPM achieved 94% retrospective and 88% prospective accuracy, matching gold standard clinical chart review with 100% sensitivity.

title: Clinical Trial Patient Matching: A Real-Time, Common Data Model and Artificial Intelligence-Driven System for Semiautomated Patient Prescreening in Cancer Clinical Trials
outcome: Chart review workload and screening time compared with manual chart review
effect: Chart review workload reduced 10-fold; screening time reduced 41% (3.1 to 1.8 minutes per chart) for reviewed patients
quote: Implementation reduced chart review workload 10-fold and screening time by 41% (3.1 to 1.8 minutes per chart) for those patients who did undergo review.

title: Out of the Laboratory and Into the Clinic: Out-of-Domain Validation of Machine Learning Models for Velopharyngeal Dysfunction Detection
outcome: Model performance under real-world recording variation versus standardized test set
effect: Whisper/SVM reached 100% accuracy in-domain; out-of-domain deep learning models failed to generalize; MFCC/SVM best at 64.1% accuracy, macro F1 0.61.
quote: Cross-domain generalization testing on the out-of-domain dataset demonstrated severe performance degradation.

title: Out of the Laboratory and Into the Clinic: Out-of-Domain Validation of Machine Learning Models for Velopharyngeal Dysfunction Detection
outcome: Overestimated performance on standardized test data versus external out-of-domain data
effect: Near-perfect in-domain performance (100% accuracy, 1.0 macro F1) fell to 64.1% accuracy and 0.61 macro F1 for the best model out-of-domain.
quote: State-of-the-art deep learning models failed to generalize.

title: Real world deployment of a pancreatic cancer risk model: impact of refitting, imputation, and computational burden
outcome: Effect of recalibrating/refitting on calibration under population and temporal change
effect: Refitting improved alignment between predicted and observed risks; residual miscalibration remained in the 95–100th percentile (GND p < 0.001 all methods).
quote: Refitting improved alignment between predicted and observed risks across most groups, with residual miscalibration primarily confined to the 95–100th percentile (GND p < 0.001 across all methods), as shown in Fig. 2 .

title: Real world deployment of a pancreatic cancer risk model: impact of refitting, imputation, and computational burden
outcome: Model discrimination and calibration by racial/ethnic subgroup
effect: C-index ranged 0.78 to 0.89 across groups; calibration poorest for Black patients, with risk underestimation.
quote: Calibration is poorest for Black patients, but SMI was the best among all three imputation strategies ( Fig. 3 ).

title: Real world deployment of a pancreatic cancer risk model: impact of refitting, imputation, and computational burden
outcome: C-index and calibration of original versus refit model on 2020 cohort
effect: Without refitting C-index ranged 0.69 to 0.84; with refitting 0.79 to 0.85 (abstract: 0.79 to 0.83); calibration improved markedly.
quote: Refitting the RSF model using the 2018–2019 cohort led to consistent improvements in predictive performance across all modelling configurations when evaluated on the 2020 evaluation cohort ( Table 2 ).

title: Real world deployment of a pancreatic cancer risk model: impact of refitting, imputation, and computational burden
outcome: Discrimination and calibration before versus after refitting model on recent local data
effect: Refitting improved C-index across all scenarios (e.g., non-imputed 0.69 to 0.81) and improved alignment of predicted and observed risk.
quote: After refitting, the C-index improved across all scenarios, ranging from 0.79 to 0.85, with the most notable gain in the non-imputed condition (from 0.69 to 0.81).

title: Real world deployment of a pancreatic cancer risk model: impact of refitting, imputation, and computational burden
outcome: Runtime and feasibility of deployment pipeline across imputation methods in simulated weekly batches
effect: Mean imputation and execution time per batch: SME 0.71 min, IFCE 19.54 min, SMI 383.77 min; data extraction 13.30 hours.
quote: In contrast, SMI was not only less effective in prediction but also computationally intensive, requiring an average of over 6 h per batch (383.77 min), which may limit scalability.

title: Real world deployment of a pancreatic cancer risk model: impact of refitting, imputation, and computational burden
outcome: Runtime in simulated deployment
effect: Simulation identified scalability differences: SMI 383.77 min/batch; IFCE 19.54 min/batch while capturing 22.91% of top-2.5% cases.
quote: In contrast, SMI was not only less effective in prediction but also computationally intensive, requiring an average of over 6 h per batch (383.77 min), which may limit scalability.

title: Comparative analysis of five AI platforms for mandibular canal segmentation on CBCT images
outcome: Segmentation accuracy compared across five competing AI platforms against expert reference on same scans
effect: Significant differences among platforms (p < 0.001); Relu Creator and 3D Slicer most accurate (≈0.5 mm, no >2.0 mm deviations); Atomica and BlueSkyPlan more variable with more deviations >2.0 mm.
quote: Significant performance differences were observed among platforms (p < 0.001).

title: Comparative analysis of five AI platforms for mandibular canal segmentation on CBCT images
outcome: Performance variation by scanner and canal side
effect: Scanner- and side-related effects were statistically significant but clinically negligible.
quote: Scanner- and side-related effects were statistically significant but clinically negligible.

title: Evaluating Medical Text Summaries Using Automatic Evaluation Metrics and LLM-as-a-Judge Approach: A Pilot Study
outcome: Ability of automatic metrics and LLM judges to detect hallucinations in LLM summaries
effect: Both LLM judges identified only two of nine hallucinations detected by experts; metric correlations with expert hallucination scores were 0.10-0.23 (Spearman).
quote: However, both LLMs identified only two of the nine hallucinations detected by the experts.
sample_unit: LLM-generated summaries (30 EHR documents x 6 LLMs)

title: Evaluating Medical Text Summaries Using Automatic Evaluation Metrics and LLM-as-a-Judge Approach: A Pilot Study
outcome: Automatic metric detection of hallucinations
effect: Hallucinations Spearman coefficients were ROUGE-1 0.17, ROUGE-2 0.10, ROUGE-L 0.19, BLEU 0.11, METEOR 0.14, BERTScore 0.23.
quote: The expectedly low correlation between the automatic evaluation metrics and the expert scores provides evidence of their infeasibility as reliable independent evaluators.
sample_unit: LLM-generated summaries (30 EHR documents x 6 LLMs)

title: Evaluating Medical Text Summaries Using Automatic Evaluation Metrics and LLM-as-a-Judge Approach: A Pilot Study
outcome: factual inaccuracies and hallucinations in LLM-generated summaries
effect: Experts detected 9 hallucinations across 180 summaries from 6 LLMs, including fabricated history, contradictory statements, and numerical analysis errors (reporting 39.0 °C instead of 36.6 °C).
quote: The analysis revealed several factual inaccuracies in LLM-generated summaries.
sample_unit: LLM-generated summaries (30 EHR documents x 6 LLMs)

title: Enhancing Patient Understanding of Perianal Fistula MRI Findings Using ChatGPT: A Randomized, Single Centre Study
outcome: Patient-rated readability, comprehension, usefulness, and Flesch-Kincaid score of AI plain-language summaries versus original MRI reports
effect: AI summaries scored significantly higher for readability, comprehension, and usefulness than original reports (all p<0.001), with equivalent trust; mean Flesch-Kincaid 66 vs 26 (p<0.001).
quote: AI summaries scored significantly higher for readability, comprehension, and usefulness than original reports (all p < 0.001), with equivalent trust ratings.

title: Enhancing Patient Understanding of Perianal Fistula MRI Findings Using ChatGPT: A Randomized, Single Centre Study
outcome: Hallucination rate and unverified recommendations in GPT-4o MRI fistula report summaries
effect: Hallucinations occurred in 11% of 250 outputs, with unverified recommendations also identified.
quote: In Phase II, hallucinations occurred in 11% of outputs, with unverified recommendations also identified.

title: Publicly Available Large Language Models for Trichoscopy: A Head-to-Head Comparison with Dermatologists
outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of public LLMs versus dermatologists on the same trichoscopic images
effect: LLM accuracy 18.2% for suspected diagnosis and 44.4% for SD + DD, versus dermatologists 58.1% and 68.3%; all human-AI differences p < 0.001. Best model Gemini 2.5 Flash reached 62.5% for SD + DD.
quote: In trichology, publicly available LLMs currently underperform compared to human experts, especially in providing a single correct diagnosis.
sample_unit: dermatologists (5 residents, 4 board-certified, 6 trichology experts) compared with 4 LLMs on trichoscopic images

title: AI Decision-Making Performance in Maternal-Fetal Medicine: Comparison of ChatGPT-4, Gemini, and Human Specialists in a Cross-Sectional Case-Based Study
outcome: LLM vs MFM specialist accuracy ratings on same hypothetical cases, blinded evaluation
effect: No significant difference between ChatGPT-4 and clinicians in median accuracy (Wilcoxon p = 0.18); Gemini significantly lower accuracy (p < 0.01).
quote: No significant difference was found between ChatGPT-4 and clinicians in median accuracy scores (Wilcoxon p = 0.18), while Gemini showed significantly lower accuracy (p < 0.01).

title: KT-LLM: an evidence-grounded and sequence text framework for auditable kidney transplant modeling
outcome: Evidence attribution and predictive calibration versus baselines when outputs are grounded in retrieved authoritative sources
effect: KT-LLM, with retrieval-augmented grounding in Banff, OPTN and SRTR documents, outperformed strong baselines in evidence attribution and predictive calibration; no numbers reported in the abstract.
quote: On de-identified OPTN and UNOS cohorts, KT-LLM outperformed strong baselines in evidence attribution and predictive calibration.
sample_unit: kidney transplant recipient records (de-identified OPTN/UNOS cohorts)

title: A Heart Rate Variability-Derived Decision Support Tool for Prognostication in Emergency Department Patients With Suspected Infection
outcome: Clinician and nurse usability feedback during pilot and its use to revise the tool
effect: Interviews with nurses and physicians identified barriers (interpreting results, time constraints, changing routines, buy-in); feedback informed four improved versions of the tool.
quote: User-centered feedback informed four improved versions of the tool.

title: Evaluation and improvement of algorithmic fairness for COVID-19 severity classification using Explainable Artificial Intelligence-based bias mitigation
outcome: Sex-based accuracy parity difference of baseline COVID-19 severity model
effect: Baseline model achieved 90.68% accuracy but exhibited a 10.11% Subset Accuracy Parity Difference between sexes, indicating a relatively large bias.
quote: The baseline (unmitigated) classification model achieved 90.68% accuracy but exhibited a 10.11% Subset Accuracy Parity Difference between sexes, indicating a relatively large bias.

title: Evaluation and improvement of algorithmic fairness for COVID-19 severity classification using Explainable Artificial Intelligence-based bias mitigation
outcome: Fairness (SAPD, LEOD) and accuracy after bias mitigation methods versus baseline
effect: XAI-based mitigation reduced sex-based disparities without significant accuracy loss, with a better fairness-accuracy trade-off than three traditional mitigation methods that compromised accuracy more.
quote: The XAI-driven bias mitigation intervention effectively reduces sex-based disparities in COVID-19 severity prediction without the significant accuracy loss observed in traditional methods.

title: Key Information Influencing Patient Decision-Making About AI in Health Care: Survey Experiment Study
outcome: Effect of AI label information elements on patient trust and acceptance
effect: Regulatory approval, high performance, HCP oversight, and added value raised trust by 14.1%-19.3% and acceptance by 13.3%-17.9% (AME); safety management info not significant.
quote: The discrete choice experiment showed that information about regulatory approval, high device performance, provider oversight, and AI's value added to usual care significantly increased the likelihood of patient trust by 14.1%-19.3% and acceptance by 13.3%-17.9%.

title: Key Information Influencing Patient Decision-Making About AI in Health Care: Survey Experiment Study
outcome: User reactions (credibility, effectiveness, trust, intention to use) to AI disclosure label content
effect: Provider oversight, regulatory approval, performance, added value improved credibility/effectiveness (OR 1.35-2.05), reduced doubts (OR 0.61-0.77), increased trust/intention to use (OR 1.47-1.73).
quote: The single profile factorial experiment showed that patients reported good label comprehension, and that information about provider oversight, regulatory approval, device performance, and AI's added value improved perceived credibility and effectiveness of the AI label (odds ratio [OR] range: 1.35-2.05), reduced doubts in the AI device (OR range: 0.61-0.77), and increased trust and intention to use the AI device (OR range: 1.47-1.73).

title: Key Information Influencing Patient Decision-Making About AI in Health Care: Survey Experiment Study
outcome: Patient comprehension of AI label prototypes and information elements' effect on understanding
effect: 86.7% found labels easy to read, 84.2% easy to understand; information elements had no significant effect on legibility, comprehensibility, or overload.
quote: Most participants reported that the AI labels were easy to read (perceived legibility; 86.7%) and understand (comprehensibility; 84.2%).

title: Key Information Influencing Patient Decision-Making About AI in Health Care: Survey Experiment Study
outcome: Self-reported label legibility and comprehension
effect: 86.7% reported labels easy to read; 84.2% reported easy to understand.
quote: Most participants reported that the AI labels were easy to read (perceived legibility; 86.7%) and understand (comprehensibility; 84.2%).

title: Key Information Influencing Patient Decision-Making About AI in Health Care: Survey Experiment Study
outcome: Information overload from AI labels
effect: 63.9% reported reading labels was not too mentally demanding.
quote: They also reported that reading the labels was not too mentally demanding (no information overload; 63.9%).

title: Auditor models to suppress poor artificial intelligence predictions can improve human-artificial intelligence collaborative performance
outcome: human-AI collaborative performance and fairness
effect: When ML outperformed humans, suppression outperformed human alone (P < 8.2 × 10-6) and did not degrade fairness; when humans outperformed ML, humans were fairer than suppression (P < 8.2 × 10-4) or no different.
quote: When the ML outperforms humans, suppression outperforms the human alone (P < 8.2 × 10-6) and at least does not degrade fairness.
sample_unit: patient records (VUMC n=58,817; MIMIC-IV-ED n=363,145) with simulated clinician acceptance

title: Assessing the informatics utility of artificial intelligence chatbots for patient and clinician support: the case of adrenal incidentaloma
outcome: Hallucination tendency of chatbot responses to adrenal incidentaloma questions, rated on a Likert scale
effect: Perplexity hallucinated more than the other models (p < 0.001). DeepSeek had the lowest tendency to hallucinate and the highest accuracy.
quote: Perplexity exhibited a higher tendency to hallucinate compared to the other models (p < 0.001).

title: Evaluating the clinical utility of large language models for hepatocellular carcinoma treatment recommendations: A nationwide retrospective registry study
outcome: Concordance of LLM treatment recommendations with real-world physician decisions in HCC registry
effect: Concordance rates were 31.1% (ChatGPT 4o), 32.7% (Gemini 2.0), and 26.8% (Claude 3.5); concordance in BCLC-C associated with worse survival (ChatGPT 4o HR 1.650).
quote: Concordance rates between LLM recommendations and physician decisions were 31.1% (ChatGPT 4o), 32.7% (Gemini 2.0), and 26.8% (Claude 3.5).

title: Evaluating the clinical utility of large language models for hepatocellular carcinoma treatment recommendations: A nationwide retrospective registry study
outcome: Survival of patients whose treatment matched LLM recommendations versus mismatched, by BCLC stage
effect: BCLC-A concordance improved survival (ChatGPT 4o HR 0.743); BCLC-C concordance worse survival (HR 1.650, Gemini 1.586, Claude 1.483); BCLC-B modest or nonsignificant.
quote: In BCLC-A patients, treatment concordance with LLM recommendations was associated with significantly improved survival (ChatGPT 4o HR: 0.743, 95% CI [0.665, 0.831], P < 0.001).

title: Diffusion of responsibility: Patient moral judgments of generative AI-informed clinical decisions
outcome: Patient moral blame of physician after adverse outcome, by adherence to GAI advice
effect: Physicians who adhered to GAI advice incurred significantly less moral blame than those who did not (p < 0.001). The effect was stronger for personalized regimens (p < 0.001) than for standard-of-care (p < 0.05).
quote: The analysis shows a significant diffusion of responsibility i.e., when an adverse outcome occurs, physicians who adhere to GAI advice incur significantly less moral blame than those who do not (p < 0.001).

title: Diffusion of responsibility: Patient moral judgments of generative AI-informed clinical decisions
outcome: Diffusion of accountability from physician to GAI in patient blame judgments
effect: Adherence to GAI advice significantly reduced moral blame directed at the physician (p < 0.001), most strongly for personalized treatment. This is consistent with diffusion of accountability.
quote: The analysis shows a significant diffusion of responsibility i.e., when an adverse outcome occurs, physicians who adhere to GAI advice incur significantly less moral blame than those who do not (p < 0.001).

title: Bridging the analog divide: a comparison of printed X-ray films and digital images when using computer-aided detection software for tuberculosis screening
outcome: Genki specificity versus 10 human readers at matched sensitivity for TB screening
effect: At matched sensitivity (79.0%), Genki specificity was 95.2% (DICOM) and 92.1% (JPEG) versus 84.8% for human readers, p < 0.001.
quote: The corresponding specificity for the Genki software is significantly higher than the human readers, whether using the DICOM (84.8% vs 95.2%, p < 0.001) or JPEG files (84.8% vs 92.1%, p < 0.001).

title: Bridging the analog divide: a comparison of printed X-ray films and digital images when using computer-aided detection software for tuberculosis screening
outcome: AUC and specificity when input format changes from DICOM to photographed film JPEG
effect: AUC did not differ significantly (0.94 vs 0.92, p = 0.190), but specificity was significantly lower with JPEG (e.g., 95.2% vs 92.1%, p < 0.001) and abnormality scores were higher.
quote: There is no significant difference in the AUC for the Genki CAD software when processing either DICOM or JPEG files (0.94 vs 0.92, p = 0.190).

title: Bridging the analog divide: a comparison of printed X-ray films and digital images when using computer-aided detection software for tuberculosis screening
outcome: Performance variation by acquisition format (DICOM vs photographed film); no site-specific analysis
effect: AUC was similar across file types, but specificity was significantly lower with JPEG at matched thresholds (81.1% vs 89.3% at 91.4% sensitivity, p < 0.001).
quote: Although the Genki CAD software met the TPP criteria when using photographs of printed X-ray films, its specificity was significantly lower compared to processing DICOM files.

title: Bridging the analog divide: a comparison of printed X-ray films and digital images when using computer-aided detection software for tuberculosis screening
outcome: Specificity after choosing tuned abnormality score thresholds to reach target sensitivity
effect: Calibrating thresholds to 90% sensitivity gave specificity of 89.3% (DICOM) and 81.1% (JPEG), meeting the TPP criteria.
quote: When the software's abnormality score thresholds were calibrated to achieve 90% sensitivity, Genki maintained high specificity with both DICOM (89.3%) and JPEG (81.1%) file types, meeting the minimum Target Product Profile (TPP) criteria for a high-sensitivity, high-specificity screening test.

title: Bridging the analog divide: a comparison of printed X-ray films and digital images when using computer-aided detection software for tuberculosis screening
outcome: specificity under JPEG versus DICOM inputs
effect: At matched 87.9% sensitivity, specificity was 90.9% for DICOM vs 81.6% for JPEG, p<0.001.
quote: Again, the software’s specificity with JPEG files is significantly lower than with DICOM files (90.9% vs 81.6%, p < 0.001).

title: Bridging the analog divide: a comparison of printed X-ray films and digital images when using computer-aided detection software for tuberculosis screening
outcome: power for subgroup performance analyses
effect: Test library had only 58 TB cases; some key subgroups had fewer than 10 TB cases, insufficient for reliable subgroup analyses.
quote: However, this evaluation’s test library includes only 58 individuals with TB and is therefore insufficiently powered to support reliable subgroup analyses, particularly when some key subgroups comprise fewer than 10 people with TB.

title: Bridging the analog divide: a comparison of printed X-ray films and digital images when using computer-aided detection software for tuberculosis screening
outcome: Genki specificity compared with human readers at matched sensitivity
effect: Genki specificity was significantly higher than human readers (84.8%) using DICOM (95.2%, p < 0.001) or JPEG (92.1%, p < 0.001) at matched sensitivity (79.0%).
quote: The corresponding specificity for the Genki software is significantly higher than the human readers, whether using the DICOM (84.8% vs 95.2%, p < 0.001) or JPEG files (84.8% vs 92.1%, p < 0.001).

title: AI in the Shadows: Unveiling the Strengths and Blind Spots of Medios AI Retinal Screening in Cancer Care
outcome: AI performance when applied to oncology patients outside its intended DR/ARMD/glaucoma screening population
effect: Eight patients with leukemic retinopathy were incorrectly flagged as having DR; optic atrophy was not detected; AI correct for glaucoma (3), DR (2), ARMD (2).
quote: However, eight patients with leukemic retinopathy were incorrectly flagged as having DR, revealing a lack of specificity in distinguishing vascular retinal pathologies.

title: Assessing the Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence-Generated Clinical Summaries From Ambulatory Glaucoma Subspecialty Clinical Encounters
outcome: Accuracy of LLM-generated patient-friendly summaries of glaucoma clinic notes rated by ophthalmologists
effect: LLaMA 2 correctly summarized 97 notes (66%) in paragraph and 103 (70%) in bullet format; 44 (30%) and 41 (28%) partially correct. ChatGPT-4 46% correct paragraph, 50% bullet.
quote: LLaMA 2 correctly summarized 97 notes (66%) in paragraph and 103 (70%) in bullet format.

title: ChatGPT-guided translation of pediatric emergency department discharge instructions
outcome: Bilingual raters' accuracy, safety, understandability of translated discharge instructions, by language
effect: ChatGPT-4 more accurate than Google Translate in Arabic (4.1 vs 3.7, p=0.003) and Chinese (4.4 vs 4.2, p=0.010); no significant safety or understandability differences in either language.
quote: There were no significant differences in safety or understandability between ChatGPT-4 and Google Translate in either language.
sample_unit: discharge instruction documents translated (rated by 8 bilingual medical professionals)

title: Quantifying the impact of a computer-aided diagnostic score on the clinical diagnosis of functional seizures
outcome: Reader diagnostic accuracy with versus without FSLS; overreliance assessed via change analysis
effect: Groups containing 66% of readers improved accuracy by 12%-15% with FSLS (p<.05); other groups had no net change (p>.75); no reader adopted FSLS errors uncritically.
quote: Machine learning‐assisted identification with the FSLS improved the performance of groups containing 66% of readers by 12%–15%, but other readers could not effectively identify when to change their diagnosis based on the FSLS.

title: Quantifying the impact of a computer-aided diagnostic score on the clinical diagnosis of functional seizures
outcome: clinicians misled by incorrect FSLS
effect: Group 5 accuracy improved 21% from persuasion and decreased 4% from being misled.
quote: The accuracy of the reference group (Group 5) improved by 21% due to persuasion by the FSLS and reduced by 4% due to being misled.

title: Quantifying the impact of a computer-aided diagnostic score on the clinical diagnosis of functional seizures
outcome: Clinician performance with the AI score in the intended workflow versus history alone
effect: Reference group accuracy rose from 41% to 60% (+19%) and near-highest group from 67% to 82% (+15%) with FSLS; other groups no net change.
quote: The group of average readers (Group 5) was able to understand the FSLS enough to improve their accuracy from 44% to 60%.

title: Quantifying the impact of a computer-aided diagnostic score on the clinical diagnosis of functional seizures
outcome: Whether users detect incorrect AI outputs; rates of being persuaded or misled by FSLS
effect: Group 2 was never misled; Group 5 improved 21% from persuasion and lost 4% from being misled; readers persuaded in only 30%-45% of cases when FSLS was correct.
quote: The accuracy of the near highest performance group (Group 2) improved because they were persuaded by the FSLS, but they were never misled (Figures 4 and S4–S6).

title: Exploration of Mental Health and Stress Among Nursing Interns Through a Chatbot: A Single-Group Pilot Study
outcome: Keyword-triggered chatbot alerts detecting high-risk distress expressions among nursing interns
effect: Chatbot flagged 16 high-risk expressions per 100 messages; suicidal ideation declined (10-4) pre/post, with no comparator and no evaluation of alert accuracy or response.
quote: The chatbot flagged 16 high-risk expressions per 100 messages, notably so tired and under pressure; 60.6% reported internship distress.

title: An old disease, a new linguistic challenge for large language models: patient education on psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis in an underrepresented medical language
outcome: Readability (Ateşman) and DISCERN reliability of Turkish LLM patient education brochures
effect: Readability scores ranged from 61.6 to 80.2 (mean 71.3 ± 6.9); DISCERN reliability scores ranged from 38.5 to 60.5, with only Claude 3.7 Sonnet and Gemini 2.0 Flash consistently patient-centered.
quote: Readability scores ranged from 61.6 to 80.2 (mean = 71.3 ± 6.9), with ChatGPT-4o and Qwen 2.5 generating the most accessible texts.
sample_unit: LLM-generated Turkish patient education brochures (one per model)

title: Readability, reliability, and quality of kyphosis-related information provided by artificial intelligence chatbots: A cross-sectional study
outcome: Readability of chatbot kyphosis answers versus AMA-recommended sixth-grade reading level
effect: All six chatbots wrote above the sixth-grade level, and no significant readability differences were found among them (FKGL, FKRS, SMOG, ARI, GFOG). Outputs were hard for average patients to understand.
quote: All chatbots presented content at a readability level higher than the AMA-recommended sixth-grade level.

title: Assessing the safety of patient-centred discharge medication instructions generated by an AI model
outcome: Proportion of cases with at least one potential safety issue, compared across age, complexity, insurance
effect: Safety issues differed across age groups (p = 0.031), patient complexity (p < 0.001) and insurance types (p = 0.047); medication correctness and UMS format did not differ by group.
quote: There was evidence of a difference in the proportion of cases with at least one potential safety issue across age groups (p = 0.031), patient complexity (p < 0.001) and insurance types (p = 0.047).

title: Assessing the safety of patient-centred discharge medication instructions generated by an AI model
outcome: Presence of potential safety issues in AI-generated medication instructions rated by clinical experts
effect: Potential safety issues in 69.3% (97/140) of cases, despite most medications being included (95% had all medications included).
quote: Despite most medications being included, potential safety issues were identified in 69.3 % (97/140).

title: Increasing engagement with cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) using generative AI: a randomized controlled trial (RCT)
outcome: Engagement and symptom change (GAD-7, PHQ-9) for genAI CBT app versus digital workbook, plus adverse events
effect: genAI raised engagement frequency 2.4x and duration 3.8x versus workbooks. Anxiety and depression outcomes were comparable, with no differences in adverse events. No overall symptom benefit.
quote: Over six weeks, the genAI solution (n = 322) increases engagement frequency (2.4×) and duration (3.8×) compared to digital workbooks (n = 209), with moderate to large effect sizes.
sample_unit: participants analyzed (322 genAI app, 209 digital workbook control)

title: Performance of ChatGPT-5 in Diagnosing Fractures on Proximal Humerus and Intertrochanteric Femur X-Rays
outcome: Fracture detection specificity of ChatGPT-5 on hip radiographs (false positives) as standalone diagnostic
effect: IT femur: 100% sensitivity but only 16.7% specificity (κ = 0.24); hallucinated fractures in normal hip X-rays; proximal humerus 87.5% sensitivity, 100% specificity (κ = 0.74).
quote: However, limitations in specificity and fine-detail recognition restrict its autonomous clinical use.

title: Performance of ChatGPT-5 in Diagnosing Fractures on Proximal Humerus and Intertrochanteric Femur X-Rays
outcome: False-positive fracture detection by AI on normal hip radiographs
effect: ChatGPT-5 had 16.7% specificity in IT femur fractures and frequently hallucinated fractures in normal hip X-rays.
quote: While it identified major fracture patterns and comminution reliably, it frequently hallucinated fractures in normal hip X-rays and missed fine details such as lesser tuberosity fragments and dislocations.

title: Reliability of AI Tools in Generating Patient Education Brochures for Bariatric Surgery: An Observational Study
outcome: Readability of AI-generated bariatric surgery patient brochures (Flesch-Kincaid)
effect: Both ChatGPT and Gemini produced content at approximately college-level readability, higher than ideal for the average patient, with limited accessibility for lower-literacy individuals.
quote: Despite these structural differences, both tools produced content with similar readability levels - approximately college-level - and comparable reliability scores.
sample_unit: brochures (6 bariatric procedures x 2 AI tools)

title: Reliability of AI Tools in Generating Patient Education Brochures for Bariatric Surgery: An Observational Study
outcome: Reading level of AI-generated patient brochures relative to appropriate patient reading level
effect: Both tools generated patient information at approximately college reading level, with limited accessibility for individuals with lower literacy.
quote: Overall, both tools generated patient information of good reliability but with limited accessibility for individuals with lower literacy.
sample_unit: brochures (6 bariatric procedures x 2 AI tools)

title: Comparative Evaluation of Popular Gen-AI Chatbots in Generating Patient Education Material on Pulmonary Artery Catheter Insertion
outcome: Readability (Flesch Reading Ease, Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level) of chatbot-generated patient education materials
effect: Gemini FRE 65 vs ChatGPT 54; FKGL 7.58 vs 8.64. Both are above a 6th-grade level, and ChatGPT was harder to read.
quote: ChatGPT scored significantly higher on accuracy [9.00 vs. 8.00; P = 0.021] and perceived trustworthiness, while Gemini outperformed in readability (Flesch Reading Ease score: 65 vs. 54; Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level: 7.58 vs. 8.64) and clarity.

title: A context-augmented large language model for accurate precision oncology medicine recommendations
outcome: Accuracy of biomarker-driven treatment recommendations, RAG-LLM using MOAlmanac versus LLM-only
effect: RAG-LLM reached up to 95% accuracy on synthetic queries and 93% on real-world oncologist queries; it was benchmarked against an LLM-only approach, but no LLM-only figures are given in the text.
quote: Our RAG-LLM achieved up to 95% accuracy on synthetic queries and 93% on real-world queries collected from practicing oncologists.

title: [Study of the performances of conversational agents in interpreting textual description of lesions in pathology]
outcome: Diagnostic accuracy and serious diagnostic errors (hallucinations) of chatbots on pathology descriptions
effect: Correct diagnoses on first attempt up to 82% (ChatGPT), 91% after follow-up prompt; serious diagnostic errors up to 9% (Gemini).
quote: Serious diagnostic errors ("hallucinations") occurred in as many as 9% of cases (Gemini).

title: [Study of the performances of conversational agents in interpreting textual description of lesions in pathology]
outcome: Domain-specific clinical competency of general-purpose LLM chatbots in pathology
effect: Response quality varied among the four chatbots; up to 82% correct diagnoses first attempt; quality correlated with online documentation volume per pathology.
quote: Out of 200 texts submitted, response quality varied among the four CAs, with up to 82% (ChatGPT) of correct diagnoses on the first attempt (91% after a follow-up prompt).

title: Foundation models enable wearable signal screening for cardiovascular disease among people living with HIV
outcome: CVD detection AUROC with vs without locally trained classifier on foundation model embeddings
effect: Zero-shot NormWear PPG AUROC 0.560 (AP 0.226); NormWear with local classifier 0.667; frozen PaPaGei plus locally trained calibrated classifier AUROC 0.769 (AP 0.489). Small sample (13 cases), confounded by model differences.
quote: Our zero-shot baseline (NormWear, AUROC 0.560) represents truly label-free deployment but yields insufficient discrimination, highlighting that some local labels substantially improve utility.

title: Foundation models enable wearable signal screening for cardiovascular disease among people living with HIV
outcome: Discordance between AUROC and operating-threshold sensitivity
effect: With ECG embeddings, LightGBM achieved AUROC 0.756 ± 0.10 but recall 0.000 ± 0.00 and Balanced Accuracy 0.500 ± 0.00; XGBoost showed a similar pattern.
quote: In contrast, tree ensembles frequently exhibited a small- n failure mode: LightGBM attained a high AUROC (0.756 ± 0.10) but defaulted to no positive calls (recall 0.000 ± 0.00; Balanced Accuracy 0.500 ± 0.00), with a similar pattern for XGBoost.

title: Foundation models enable wearable signal screening for cardiovascular disease among people living with HIV
outcome: CVD detection AUROC and average precision
effect: The AI approach achieved AUROC 0.769 and average precision 0.489, outperforming simpler PCA features (0.651; 0.208) and supervised clinical models (0.744; 0.433).
quote: Here we show that the PaPaGei-embedding approach achieves area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.769 (95% confidence interval: 0.70, 0.84) and average precision 0.489 (0.37, 0.61) in this pilot cohort, numerically higher than zero-shot NormWear (0.610; 0.226), principal component analysis features (0.651; 0.208), and supervised clinical models (0.744; 0.433).

title: Impact of labelling inaccuracy and image noise on tooth segmentation in panoramic radiographs using federated, centralized, and local learning
outcome: Whether per-client loss trajectory monitoring detects corrupted data from a faulty site
effect: Loss curve monitoring reliably flagged the corrupted site in label and image-noise corruption scenarios.
quote: Loss curve monitoring reliably flagged the corrupted site.

title: Reference Accuracy in Large Language Model Chatbots: A Metric for Inherent Misinformation?
venue: Medical science monitor : international medical journal of experimental and clinical research
outcome: Accuracy of bibliographic references (authors, details, DOI) generated by chatbots, verified against databases
effect: 1947 references checked; best accuracy 51% (ChatGPT-4.1 with web search), Gemini 2.5 Pro 41%; common errors were wrong author names and erroneous DOIs.
quote: Across the 6 chatbots, ChatGPT-4.1 (with web search enabled) achieved the best accuracy, with a score of 51%, with Gemini 2.5 Pro being second at 41%.

title: Reference Accuracy in Large Language Model Chatbots: A Metric for Inherent Misinformation?
venue: Medical science monitor : international medical journal of experimental and clinical research
outcome: Reference accuracy with versus without web search retrieval
effect: The 2 chatbot versions with web search performed better than the 4 without, though best accuracy was still only 51%.
quote: The 2 versions with a web search facility performed better than the 4 versions without.

title: Understanding psychiatrist readiness for AI: a study of access, self-efficacy, trust, and design expectations
outcome: Source of psychiatrists' AI knowledge (structured versus informal)
effect: Psychiatrists reported broad exposure to AI, but knowledge was largely acquired through informal rather than structured sources; limited access to formal training was noted.
quote: Psychiatrists reported broad exposure to AI, though knowledge was largely acquired through informal rather than structured sources.

title: Evaluation of large language models in nutrition risk screening: a comparative analysis across 8 LLMs based on real-world EHR datasets
venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
outcome: Reproducibility of LLM assessments across two repeated runs (consistent assessment rate, Cohen's kappa)
effect: Larger models showed high repeatability (Cohen's κ up to 0.99); smaller models like Qwen3-8B declined (κ = 0.69). Domain consistency was lower for disease burden.
quote: Larger parameter scales LLMs demonstrated higher accuracy and repeatability, with Cohen’s κ up to 0.99, whereas smaller LLMs like Qwen3-8B showed marked declines (κ = 0.69).

title: A randomized controlled trial of a WeChat-based artificial intelligence agent for postoperative care in orthopedic patients
outcome: Patient functional outcomes and satisfaction, AI agent vs doctor-led care in RCT
effect: AI group had significantly better knee function (IKDC), physical health (PCS), and satisfaction at 1 and 3 months (all p<0.05); differences not significant at 6 months (p>0.05).
quote: At 1 and 3 months, the AI group achieved significantly better outcomes in knee function (IKDC), physical health (PCS), and overall satisfaction (all p < 0.05).

title: A randomized controlled trial of a WeChat-based artificial intelligence agent for postoperative care in orthopedic patients
outcome: AI agent response speed, quality and accuracy compared with physician communication
effect: AI responded faster (0.5±0.6 vs 358±47.5 min, p<0.05) with higher perceived quality but slightly lower accuracy (93.9% vs 98.1%, p<0.05).
quote: The AI system responded far more rapidly (0.5 ± 0.6 vs. 358 ± 47.5 min, p < 0.05) and provided feedback of higher perceived quality, though with slightly reduced accuracy (93.9% vs. 98.1%, p < 0.05).

title: Prospective validation and real-time implementation of an automated machine learning postoperative mortality prediction model
outcome: Prospective performance of the implemented model on live EHR data versus retrospective 58-feature model
effect: Prospective 32-feature model AUROC 0.874 (95% CI 0.860-0.887) versus 0.925 (95% CI 0.900-0.947) for the 58-feature model; AUCPR 0.111.
quote: The AUROC for the prospectively implemented model was 0.874 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.860-0.887), and the AUCPR was 0.111.

title: Prospective validation and real-time implementation of an automated machine learning postoperative mortality prediction model
outcome: Comparison of the ML model against ASA physical status baseline
effect: ML model AUROC 0.874 vs ASA physical status AUROC 0.814 (95% CI 0.802-0.827); AUCPR 0.111 vs 0.103.
quote: By comparison, the AUROC for the 58-feature model was 0.925 (95% CI 0.900-0.947), and for ASA physical status the AUROC was 0.814 (95% CI 0.802-0.827) and the AUCPR was 0.103.

title: Assessing the communication gap between AI models and healthcare professionals: Explainability, utility and trust in AI-driven clinical decision-making
outcome: HCP concordance with correct decisions when the model intentionally recommended wrong discharge
effect: In Daniel's case 65% (15/23) followed the wrong discharge recommendation; in Christine's 48% (11/23). Only 35% (CS) and 52% (CS+Exp) overrode the model.
quote: The results strongly suggest that for both types of output (CS and CS+Ex) HCPs over-relied in the recommendation provided by the model.

title: Assessing the communication gap between AI models and healthcare professionals: Explainability, utility and trust in AI-driven clinical decision-making
outcome: Effect of SHAP feature-contribution explanations on HCP understanding, trust, satisfaction, and critical understanding
effect: No significant change in satisfaction, trust, or understanding (CS vs CS+Exp); explanation did not change understanding of wrong recommendations for 57% and lowered it for 17%.
quote: The explanation did not improve satisfaction (RQ2, Fig. 7 question A), trust (RQ3, Fig. 7 questions B, C, E) nor the understanding of how the model produced the recommendation (RQ1, Fig. 7 questions D, F, G).

title: Assessing the communication gap between AI models and healthcare professionals: Explainability, utility and trust in AI-driven clinical decision-making
outcome: Whether explanations promote scrutiny and reduce automation bias in HCP decisions
effect: With explanations, decisions against the model took a median 84s vs 38s for agreeing (p<0.001); only 52% overrode the wrong recommendation with explanations vs 35% without; confirmation bias risk noted.
quote: On the other hand, explanations drove users to reflect longer on the decision when disagreeing with the model outcome (RQ6).

title: Assessing the communication gap between AI models and healthcare professionals: Explainability, utility and trust in AI-driven clinical decision-making
outcome: Human-AI team decisions with and without explanation, including overreliance on incorrect model recommendations
effect: Lowest concordance in cases where CORONET recommended wrong action; 35% (CS) and 52% (CS+Exp) of HCPs overrode incorrect discharge recommendations.
quote: Only 35% (CS scenario) and 52% (CS+Ex) HCPs took that critical perspective over the model.

title: Assessing the communication gap between AI models and healthcare professionals: Explainability, utility and trust in AI-driven clinical decision-making
outcome: information-related risks of explanations
effect: Undesirable explanation effects occurred for 17-35%; critical understanding not improved for 57%.
quote: Despite the general positive attitude towards explanations, for a significant set of participants (17-35%), an undesirable effect for the explanations was observed, possibly due to an increase in cognitive effort.

title: Perceptions of dental students on the integration of artificial intelligence in radiology clinical education
outcome: Student-reported curriculum preparedness and confidence to use AI caries detection clinically
effect: Only 16.7% agreed the curriculum adequately prepared them to use AI clinically; 45.5% felt confident integrating AI into future practice. Students requested structured faculty training.
quote: However, only 16.7% agreed the curriculum adequately prepared them to use AI clinically, and just 45.5% felt confident about integrating AI into future practice.

title: Overcoming Normalcy Bias in Acute Myocardial Infarction: A Case Report of Generative AI as a Behavioral Catalyst for Emergency Care Seeking
outcome: Whether the AI recognized a safety-critical situation and escalated to emergency services
effect: In a single case, the generative AI issued a clear imperative to contact emergency services. The patient then activated emergency care, was diagnosed with inferior STEMI, and underwent successful PCI.
quote: After consulting a publicly available generative AI system that issued a clear imperative to contact emergency medical services, the patient activated emergency care.

title: Quality and Reliability of AI Information on Dental Implant Failure: A Comparative Multi-Model Analysis
outcome: Readability and grade-level demand of chatbot responses about dental implant failure
effect: Readability and linguistic complexity varied markedly across the four chatbots; DeepSeek-R1 offered the best readability. No numeric reading-level values are reported in the abstract.
quote: Although CLEAR and mGQS scores were high across all systems, readability and linguistic complexity varied markedly.

title: Enhancing Fairness in Large Language Models for Clinical Artificial Intelligence Applications Through Fine-Tuning and Prompting
outcome: Bias score across gender, race, profession, religion with debiased prompts and fine-tuning
effect: Debiased prompts reduce bias, and fine-tuning the model performs even better (lower bias scores).
quote: We also note that debiased prompts reduce bias, and fine-tuning the model performs even better.

title: Evaluating and Validating Large Language Models for Health Education on Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip: 2-Phase Study With Expert Ratings and a Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial
outcome: Readability grade level of LLM-generated caregiver education materials
effect: Mean FKGL ranged from 7.30 (DeepSeek-V3) to 9.41 (Copilot) and SMOG from 9.83 to 11.67, exceeding the recommended sixth-grade level despite prompts requesting simple language.
quote: Although readability levels were close to the average reading level of US adults (eighth grade) [ 36 ], they still exceeded American Medical Association recommendations (no more than sixth grade) for health education materials [ 37 ].

title: Evaluating and Validating Large Language Models for Health Education on Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip: 2-Phase Study With Expert Ratings and a Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial
outcome: Whether LLM outputs provided source citations
effect: Only 1 of 4 models (Copilot) provided source citations. The other 3 gave answers without traceable sources.
quote: Only Copilot provides source citations, which raises concerns about the traceability and reliability of the information.

title: Evaluating and Validating Large Language Models for Health Education on Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip: 2-Phase Study With Expert Ratings and a Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial
outcome: eHealth literacy and DDH knowledge after structured LLM training vs web search
effect: eHEALS group difference 1.73 (0.49-2.97) at T1 and 2.40 (1.13-3.67) at T2. DDH knowledge d=0.71 at T1 and 0.54 at T2. The group×time interaction was nonsignificant (P=.26).
quote: The intervention group showed higher scores than the control group at T1 (33.62, 95% CI 32.76-34.49; d =0.20, 95% CI 0.13-0.56) and T2 (33.27, 95% CI 32.38-34.17; d =0.36, 95% CI 0.01-0.80), indicating sustained improvements following the LLM-generated learning intervention.

title: Evaluating and Validating Large Language Models for Health Education on Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip: 2-Phase Study With Expert Ratings and a Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial
outcome: Expert-rated accuracy of generated DDH education against clinical guidelines
effect: Responses rated “good” or “excellent” for accuracy: ChatGPT-4 85%, DeepSeek-V3 83%, Gemini 2.0 Flash 70%, and Copilot 66%; omissions were also reported for Copilot.
quote: In terms of accuracy, the proportion of “good” and “excellent” responses reached 85% for ChatGPT-4 and 83% for DeepSeek-V3, while Gemini 2.0 Flash (70%) and Copilot (66%) displayed a lower proportion.

title: Evaluating and Validating Large Language Models for Health Education on Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip: 2-Phase Study With Expert Ratings and a Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial
outcome: performance differences among models
effect: Significant differences found in accuracy, richness, fluency, understandability, and DISCERN scores among the 4 evaluated LLMs.
quote: There were significant differences between the 4 LLMs concerning accuracy, richness, fluency, Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool for Printable Materials Understandability, and DISCERN (P<.05).

title: LLM-driven collaborative framework for knowledge-enhanced cancer pain assessment and management
outcome: Comparison of LLMs with three RAG strategies on semantic consistency and evidence-based reasoning
effect: Claude-4 combined with RAG achieved the best overall performance, with outstanding semantic consistency and evidence-based reasoning across multiple metrics; decision accuracy of 0.841 for analgesic recommendation.
quote: Ultimately, Claude-4 combined with RAG achieved the best overall performance, demonstrating outstanding semantic consistency and evidence-based reasoning in multiple metrics.
sample_unit: real-world cancer pain electronic medical records

title: An LLM chatbot to facilitate primary-to-specialist care transitions: a randomized controlled trial
outcome: Expert-rated referral quality: co-designed model vs same model fine-tuned on local dialogues
effect: Fine-tuning on local dialogues lowered quality: history-taking 4.56 vs 3.86, diagnosis 4.67 vs 2.47, test ordering 4.23 vs 2.21 (all P < 0.001); data-tuned model failed to provide diagnoses in 30.0% and tests in 39.3%.
quote: The co-designed model achieved significantly higher-quality rating scores than the data-tuned counterpart (the co-designed model further fine-tuned on the primary care dialogues) group across all domains: history-taking (without data-tuned 4.56 ± 0.65 versus data-tuned 3.86 ± 0.81; P < 0.001; Fig. 4b ), diagnosis (without data-tuned 4.67 ± 0.55 versus data-tuned 2.47 ± 1.44; P < 0.001) and testing order (without data-tuned 4.23 ± 1.09 versus data-tuned 2.21 ± 1.12; P < 0.001).

title: An LLM chatbot to facilitate primary-to-specialist care transitions: a randomized controlled trial
outcome: Direct adoption of LLM content in physician clinical notes (automation bias)
effect: Classifier distinguishing PreA-assisted vs No-PreA notes near random (F1 0.57; P = 0.81; ΔF1 < 0.02); no domain differences (P = 0.10–0.90).
quote: Classification analysis yielded near-random discriminability (F1 score 0.57; P = 0.81; ΔF1 < 0.02).

title: An LLM chatbot to facilitate primary-to-specialist care transitions: a randomized controlled trial
outcome: Specialist consultation duration
effect: Consultation duration: PreA-only 3.14 ± 2.25 versus No-PreA 4.41 ± 2.77 min; P < 0.001; 28.7% (95% CI 22.7–34.8) relative reduction.
quote: The PreA-only group had a significantly shorter consultation duration compared to the No-PreA group (PreA-only 3.14 ± 2.25 versus No-PreA 4.41 ± 2.77 min; P < 0.001; Fig. 2a ), corresponding to a 28.7% (95% CI 22.7–34.8) relative reduction.

title: An LLM chatbot to facilitate primary-to-specialist care transitions: a randomized controlled trial
outcome: Diagnostic-guideline adherence in simulated consultations
effect: Locally fine-tuned PreA omitted needed diagnoses in 30.0% (90 of 300) and testing suggestions in 39.3% (118 of 300) simulated cases.
quote: Mirroring real-world clinician patterns, the data-tuned model exhibited suboptimal adherence to diagnostic guidelines, failing to provide diagnoses (30.0%, 90 of 300) or suggest testing (39.3%, 118 of 300) when needed.

title: An LLM chatbot to facilitate primary-to-specialist care transitions: a randomized controlled trial
outcome: Friendliness of chatbot communication
effect: The local data-tuned model reproduced an unfriendly clinician-like tone; frequency was not reported.
quote: Additionally, the data-tuned model mimicked an unfriendly tone similar to that of human clinicians.

title: An LLM chatbot to facilitate primary-to-specialist care transitions: a randomized controlled trial
outcome: Patient-reported consultation satisfaction
effect: Patient satisfaction was 3.99 ± 0.69 versus 3.41 ± 0.98 with usual care; P < 0.001; relative increase 17.0%, 95% CI 14.3–19.6.
quote: Patients and care partners in the PreA-only group reported significantly improved consultation experiences compared to the No-PreA group across the primary outcome, ease of communication: 3.99 ± 0.62 versus 3.44 ± 0.97; P < 0.001; relative increase 16.0%, 95% CI 13.5–18.5) and the four secondary outcomes: perceived physician attentiveness: 3.87 ± 0.85 versus 3.36 ± 1.04; P < 0.001; relative increase 15.1%, 95% CI 12.1–18.1), interpersonal regard (4.02 ± 0.73 versus 3.43 ± 1.05; P < 0.001; relative increase 17.2%, 95% CI 14.4–20.0), patient satisfaction (3.99 ± 0.69 versus 3.41 ± 0.98; P < 0.001; relative increase 17.0%, 95% CI 14.3–19.6) and future acceptability (3.79 ± 1.06 versus 2.81 ± 1.26; P < 0.001; relative increase 34.7%, 95% CI 30.4–39.1; Fig. 3a ).

title: An LLM chatbot to facilitate primary-to-specialist care transitions: a randomized controlled trial
outcome: adherence to diagnostic guidelines
effect: The data-tuned model failed to provide diagnoses in 30.0% of cases and suggest necessary testing in 39.3%.
quote: Mirroring real-world clinician patterns, the data-tuned model exhibited suboptimal adherence to diagnostic guidelines, failing to provide diagnoses (30.0%, 90 of 300) or suggest testing (39.3%, 118 of 300) when needed.

title: An LLM chatbot to facilitate primary-to-specialist care transitions: a randomized controlled trial
outcome: direct adoption of LLM-generated content
effect: Classification analysis showed near-random discriminability of clinical notes between groups (F1 score 0.57), indicating no direct copying.
quote: This absence of systematic separability in the feature space of clinical notes provides compelling evidence against the direct adoption of LLM-generated content in this real-world clinical context.

title: Novel Artificial Intelligence Chest X-ray Diagnostics: A Quality Assessment of Their Agreement with Human Doctors in Clinical Routine
venue: RoFo : Fortschritte auf dem Gebiete der Rontgenstrahlen und der Nuklearmedizin
outcome: Agreement of AI chest X-ray systems with radiologist reports on local hospital data
effect: Human-AZmed Gwet's AC1 0.47-0.72; Human-Gleamer 0.56-0.96; balanced accuracy 0.67-0.85 (AZmed) and 0.71-0.85 (Gleamer); specificity exceeded sensitivity (0.70-0.98 vs 0.45-0.85).
quote: Radiologists' routine reports were compared against Rayvolve (AZmed) and ChestView (Gleamer, both from Paris, France).

title: Novel Artificial Intelligence Chest X-ray Diagnostics: A Quality Assessment of Their Agreement with Human Doctors in Clinical Routine
venue: RoFo : Fortschritte auf dem Gebiete der Rontgenstrahlen und der Nuklearmedizin
outcome: AI performance variation by patient positioning (standing vs supine)
effect: Standing radiographs yielded superior agreement compared to supine studies; performance declined for supine studies.
quote: Standing radiographs yielded superior agreement compared to supine studies.

title: Human-AI collaboration enhances the performance of large language models in risk of bias assessment
outcome: Human reviewer accuracy when shown model reasoning and disagreement cues versus evidence only
effect: M1 (evidence only) was never on the Pareto frontier; M2 (reasoning shown) had higher accuracy in five tasks, e.g., SB-IRSG 0.900 vs 0.817; M3 disagreement trigger cut intervention.
quote: M2 demonstrated higher accuracy in five tasks, while M3 showed a clear advantage in reducing intervention rates.
sample_unit: domain-level RCT risk-of-bias assessments (300 per domain across 7 domains; 60 per domain in human-AI collaboration round)

title: Human-AI collaboration enhances the performance of large language models in risk of bias assessment
outcome: AI performance as used by human reviewers versus standalone model accuracy
effect: Standalone LLM accuracy ranged 0.403-0.777, while human-AI collaboration under M2/M3 reached 0.633-0.900 and improved consistency of human judgments.
quote: LLMs (like DeepSeek V3 and Qwen-plus) cannot yet replace human RoB assessment but well-designed Human-AI collaboration can improve accuracy and reduce manual workload.
sample_unit: domain-level RCT risk-of-bias assessments (300 per domain across 7 domains; 60 per domain in human-AI collaboration round)

title: Human-AI collaboration enhances the performance of large language models in risk of bias assessment
outcome: Comparison of two candidate LLMs on risk-of-bias classification accuracy
effect: DeepSeek V3 outperformed Qwen-plus in four of seven domains (PB, AB, RB, OB); Qwen-plus slightly better in SB-IRSG, SB-IAC, DB.
quote: The results shown in Fig. 3 indicate that DeepSeek V3 outperforms Qwen-plus in the tasks of PB, AB, RB, and OB, whereas Qwen-plus performs slightly better in the tasks of SB-IRSG, SB-IAC, and DB.
sample_unit: domain-level RCT risk-of-bias assessments (300 per domain across 7 domains; 60 per domain in human-AI collaboration round)

title: Human-AI collaboration enhances the performance of large language models in risk of bias assessment
outcome: Deferral to humans triggered by low confidence or model disagreement; accuracy and intervention rate
effect: Predictions with confidence >0.8 were 16.78% to 29.23% more accurate than those ≤0.8; M3 reduced intervention (e.g., DB -40%) with accuracy roughly maintained in structured tasks.
quote: Across the six domains (DB, SB-IRSG, PB, RB, OB, AB), model predictions with confidence scores above 0.8 consistently showed substantially higher accuracy than those with scores ≤ 0.8, with performance gaps ranging from 16.78% to 29.23% (Appendix 5).
sample_unit: domain-level RCT risk-of-bias assessments (300 per domain across 7 domains; 60 per domain in human-AI collaboration round)

title: Human-AI collaboration enhances the performance of large language models in risk of bias assessment
outcome: Inter-rater agreement validating ground-truth reference labels
effect: Senior reviewer independently reassessed 60 RCTs per domain; Cohen's Kappa ranged from 0.724 to 0.942 across seven domains.
quote: The Cohen’s Kappa values ranged from 0.724 to 0.942 across all seven domains (Appendix 1), supporting its use as a high-fidelity reference standard for subsequent evaluation.
sample_unit: domain-level RCT risk-of-bias assessments (300 per domain across 7 domains; 60 per domain in human-AI collaboration round)

title: Human-AI collaboration enhances the performance of large language models in risk of bias assessment
outcome: Standalone LLM classification accuracy
effect: Standalone model accuracy ranged from 0.403 to 0.777 across domains.
quote: Model accuracy ranged from 0.403 to 0.777 across domains.
sample_unit: domain-level RCT risk-of-bias assessments (300 per domain across 7 domains; 60 per domain in human-AI collaboration round)

title: Large language model bias auditing for periodontal diagnosis using an ambiguity-probe methodology: a pilot study
outcome: Change in LLM periodontal stage/grade outputs when varying sociodemographic persona attributes
effect: No statistically significant sociodemographic bias in either model after FDR correction, in clear-cut and ambiguous scenarios; errors attributed to diagnostic boundary instability rather than bias.
quote: However, a robust fairness analysis using cumulative link models with false discovery rate correction revealed no statistically significant sociodemographic bias in either model.

title: Large language model bias auditing for periodontal diagnosis using an ambiguity-probe methodology: a pilot study
outcome: Combined stage and grade diagnostic accuracy in clear-cut vignettes
effect: GPT-4o combined accuracy 70.5% versus Gemini Pro 33.3% in clear-cut scenarios.
quote: In clear-cut scenarios, GPT-4o demonstrated significantly higher combined (stage and grade) accuracy (70.5%) than Gemini Pro (33.3%).

title: Evaluation of sepsis CDS tool knowledge and utilization among graduate medical trainees: insights to inform redesign in an academic health system
outcome: Trainee-reported alert fatigue with EHR sepsis alert
effect: Alert fatigue (62.5%) and limited clinical utility (46.3%) were major concerns among 80 trainees who recognized the sepsis alert.
quote: Alert fatigue (62.5%) and limited clinical utility (46.3%) were major concerns.

title: Evaluation of sepsis CDS tool knowledge and utilization among graduate medical trainees: insights to inform redesign in an academic health system
outcome: Trainee awareness and use of sepsis CDS tool features
effect: Among 80 who recognized the sepsis alert, only 11.3% had used the advisor; lack of awareness about advisor features and alert suppression limited engagement.
quote: Lack of awareness about advisor features and alert suppression mechanisms further limited engagement.

title: Psychiatric Documentation and Management in Primary Care With Artificial Intelligence Scribe Use
outcome: Change in documentation and management of psychiatric symptoms after AI scribe deployment
effect: Psychiatric intervention (referral, new diagnosis, or antidepressant) less likely in AI-scribed vs contemporaneous unscribed visits (aOR 0.83; 95% CI 0.72-0.95); not different for human scribes (aOR 0.97).
quote: In a multiple logistic regression model, likelihood of a psychiatric intervention (referral, new diagnosis, or antidepressant prescription) was significantly lower among AI-scribed visits compared with contemporaneous unscribed visits (adjusted odds ratio, 0.83; 95% CI, 0.72-0.95), but not for human-scribed visits compared with contemporaneous unscribed visits (adjusted odds ratio, 0.97; 95% CI, 0.85-1.11).

title: Psychiatric Documentation and Management in Primary Care With Artificial Intelligence Scribe Use
outcome: Documentation of neuropsychiatric symptoms (RDoC) in AI-scribed vs other notes
effect: Estimated RDoC symptom levels in all 6 domains significantly greater in AI-scribed notes compared with other groups.
quote: Estimated levels of RDoC symptoms in all 6 domains were significantly greater in the AI-scribed notes compared with other groups.

title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence for Detection of Precancerous Colonic Lesions in a Fecal Immunochemical Blood Test-Based Organized Screening Program in Italy: A Randomized Control Trial
outcome: Advanced adenoma detection rate, ADR, and adenomas per colonoscopy with CADe versus standard colonoscopy in randomized trial
effect: AADR comparable (21.3% vs 20.5%, p=0.794); ADR higher with CADe (67.6% vs 59.8%, p=0.012); APC 1.82 vs 1.34 (p<0.001); withdrawal time longer (17.10 vs 16.13 min, p=0.016).
quote: AADR was comparable between the groups (21.3% vs. 20.5%, p = 0.794).

title: GastroTCM: a large language model assistant for gastroenterology in traditional Chinese medicine
outcome: Unsupported or hallucinated statements with RAG grounding, per TCM gastroenterologist review
effect: Expert review reported the RAG module markedly reduced unsupported or hallucinated statements, alongside higher diagnostic accuracy and safety. No numeric hallucination rates are given in the abstract.
quote: Expert review by TCM gastroenterologists further confirmed higher diagnostic accuracy and safety, with the RAG module markedly reducing unsupported or hallucinated statements.

title: Direct deep learning analysis of three-dimensional automated breast ultrasound videos with reading mode optimization for breast cancer diagnosis
outcome: Clinician performance with AI in intended reading workflow vs standalone model
effect: Experienced radiologists with AI outperformed DL-3DABUV alone (AUC 0.90 vs 0.82); novices reached parity with the AI (0.84-0.85 vs 0.82).
quote: Experienced radiologists achieved significantly better diagnostic performance in both second-reading and concurrent-reading modes compared with DL-3DABUV alone (all P<0.01 for AUC, sensitivity, and specificity; Table 1 and Supplementary Table 1 ).
sample_unit: patients (test set; 547 total, read by 6 radiologists)

title: Direct deep learning analysis of three-dimensional automated breast ultrasound videos with reading mode optimization for breast cancer diagnosis
outcome: AI diagnostic performance compared with experienced and novice radiologists on same data
effect: AI vs experienced: AUC 0.82 vs 0.83 (P=0.230); vs novice: AUC 0.82 vs 0.68 (P<0.001), specificity 81.5% vs 57.4% (P<0.001).
quote: Compared with novice radiologists in independent-reading mode, DL-3DABUV showed significantly higher AUC (0.82 vs. 0.68, P<0.001) and specificity (81.5% vs. 57.4%, P<0.001), while maintaining comparable sensitivity (82.1% vs. 79.2%, P=0.590).
sample_unit: patients (test set; 547 total, read by 6 radiologists)

title: Direct deep learning analysis of three-dimensional automated breast ultrasound videos with reading mode optimization for breast cancer diagnosis
outcome: Radiologist diagnostic performance with vs without AI assistance (independent vs second vs concurrent reading)
effect: Experienced AUC 0.83 to 0.90 (P<0.001); novice AUC 0.68 to 0.84 (second) and 0.85 (concurrent), P<0.001; specificity in novices 57.4% to 82.7%/83.3%.
quote: Similarly, novice radiologists also showed significantly improved AUC (second-reading: 0.84 vs. 0.68, P<0.001; concurrent-reading: 0.85 vs. 0.68, P<0.001), sensitivity (second-reading: 87.5% vs. 79.2%, P<0.001; concurrent-reading: 88.1% vs. 79.2%, P<0.001), and specificity (second-reading: 82.7% vs. 57.4%, P<0.001; concurrent-reading: 83.3% vs. 57.4%, P<0.001) compared with independent-reading.
sample_unit: patients (test set; 547 total, read by 6 radiologists)

title: Direct deep learning analysis of three-dimensional automated breast ultrasound videos with reading mode optimization for breast cancer diagnosis
outcome: Diagnostic performance and reading time by AI presentation timing (second vs concurrent reading)
effect: No significant differences in diagnostic performance between second and concurrent reading (e.g., experienced AUC 0.90 vs 0.90, P=0.500); concurrent reading saved 33.6 s per case (P<0.001).
quote: However, there were no significant differences between second-reading and concurrent-reading in AUC (experienced radiologists: 0.90 vs. 0.90, P=0.500; novice radiologists: 0.84 vs. 0.85, P>0.99), sensitivity (experienced radiologists: 90.5% vs. 91.7%, P>0.99; novice radiologists: 87.5% vs. 88.1%, P>0.99), or specificity (experienced radiologists: 92.0% vs. 92.0%, P=0.156; novice radiologists: 82.7% vs. 83.3%, P=0.157).
sample_unit: patients (test set; 547 total, read by 6 radiologists)

title: Direct deep learning analysis of three-dimensional automated breast ultrasound videos with reading mode optimization for breast cancer diagnosis
outcome: Test-set leakage and single-center generalizability of model development
effect: Model parameters were optimized using the test set; single-center retrospective random split without external validation.
quote: Network training was performed on the training set, with parameters optimized using the test set.
sample_unit: patients (test set; 547 total, read by 6 radiologists)

title: Direct deep learning analysis of three-dimensional automated breast ultrasound videos with reading mode optimization for breast cancer diagnosis
outcome: Reading time by AI reading mode
effect: Concurrent reading reduced mean time by 13.5 seconds vs independent and 33.6 seconds vs second-reading; both P<0.001.
quote: Compared with both independent-reading and second-reading, concurrent-reading resulted in significantly shorter reading times for all radiologists, with mean differences of 13.5 seconds (95% confidence interval [CI], 12.7 to 14.2; P<0.001) and 33.6 seconds (95% CI, 32.5 to 34.6; P<0.001), respectively ( Table 3 ).
sample_unit: patients (test set; 547 total, read by 6 radiologists)

title: Direct deep learning analysis of three-dimensional automated breast ultrasound videos with reading mode optimization for breast cancer diagnosis
outcome: Diagnostic performance of human-AI integration vs standalone AI
effect: Experienced radiologists assisted by DL-3DABUV achieved significantly higher AUC (0.90 vs 0.82), sensitivity (90.5%-91.7% vs 82.1%), and specificity (92.0% vs 81.5%) than DL-3DABUV alone (all P<0.01).
quote: Experienced radiologists achieved significantly better diagnostic performance in both second-reading and concurrent-reading modes compared with DL-3DABUV alone (all P<0.01 for AUC, sensitivity, and specificity; Table 1 and Supplementary Table 1 ).
sample_unit: patients (test set; 547 total, read by 6 radiologists)

title: Supervised Machine Learning to Identify Hospital Inpatients Needing a Change of Antibiotic Therapy in Real Time: Preclinical Diagnostic Evaluation and Feasibility Study
outcome: Drop in AUC from cross-validation to prospective unseen validation set
effect: Random forest cross-validation AUC 0.74 fell to 0.70 (95% CI .65-.75) on the unseen prospective validation set, below the prespecified 0.75 target.
quote: The best-fitting classifier (random forest, cross-validation AUC, 0.74) achieved an AUC of 0.70 (95% confidence interval, .65-.75).

title: Training a Bilingual Artificial Intelligence Model on Pediatric Orthopaedic Resources to Enhance the Readability of Patient Education Materials
venue: Journal of the Pediatric Orthopaedic Society of North America
outcome: Readability grade level of AI-rewritten vs original pediatric orthopaedic patient education materials
effect: English Flesch-Kincaid grade 9.8 to 5.8 (P<.001); Flesch Reading Ease 56.9 to 76.4; Spanish Fernández Huerta 81.0 to 100.7 (P<.001). 10 reviewed PEMs judged accurate.
quote: The AI model was able to significantly improve the readability of the PEMs in every formula used (Flesch Reading Ease: 76.4 vs 56.9, P < .0001; Flesch-Kincaid grade level: 5.8 vs 9.8, P < .0001; SMOG Index: 8.7 vs 11.8, P < .0001; Coleman Liau: 8.7 vs 11.6, P < .0001; Automated Readability Score: 7.8 vs 12.0, P < .0001; Dale-Chall Readability Score: 7.8 vs 8.8, P < .0001; Linsear Write Formula: 6.6 vs 10.7, P = <.0001; Gunning Fog: 7.1 vs 10.8, P < .0001).

title: Training a Bilingual Artificial Intelligence Model on Pediatric Orthopaedic Resources to Enhance the Readability of Patient Education Materials
venue: Journal of the Pediatric Orthopaedic Society of North America
outcome: Reading grade level of patient materials after AI rewriting to fifth-sixth grade target
effect: Mean English grade level fell from 9.8 to 5.8 (P<.001), meeting the NIH/AMA target; Spanish materials moved from fifth-sixth to fourth grade.
quote: The average Flesch-Kincaid score of our AI-modified PEMs was 5.8 which corresponds to a sixth-grade reading level, meeting the standard set by the NIH.

title: Training a Bilingual Artificial Intelligence Model on Pediatric Orthopaedic Resources to Enhance the Readability of Patient Education Materials
venue: Journal of the Pediatric Orthopaedic Society of North America
outcome: Reading level of existing AAOS English pediatric orthopaedic patient materials
effect: Existing AAOS English PEMs averaged about 9.8 grade level (Flesch-Kincaid), above the fifth-sixth grade recommendation.
quote: Our study demonstrates that in the field of pediatric orthopaedics, the current PEMs published by the AAOS in English language are geared, on average, to a 10th-grade reading level.

title: Training a Bilingual Artificial Intelligence Model on Pediatric Orthopaedic Resources to Enhance the Readability of Patient Education Materials
venue: Journal of the Pediatric Orthopaedic Society of North America
outcome: Clinician-assessed accuracy of AI-rewritten patient materials against source OrthoInfo PEMs
effect: A single pediatric orthopaedic surgeon found all 10 reviewed AI-generated English PEMs accurate, with no confabulation identified.
quote: A single pediatric orthopaedic surgeon read and validated 10 AI model–generated PEMs and found them all to be accurate.

title: Comparison of AI chatbot-generated and web-based health information on the effects of radiation in fetuses and children
outcome: Effect of prompting for 6th-grade reading level on readability and understandability of AI texts
effect: With 6th-grade prompt, jReadability scores rose (e.g., ChatGPT-4o 2.8 to 3.3, Gemini 3.5 to 3.8) and understandability ≥70 reached 100% for most chatbots vs web pages 7.5%; Copilot remained 26.7%.
quote: However, when the prompt “Explain it at a 6th-grade level” was used, all AI chatbots—except for Copilot—produced texts that were easier to read and comprehend than web-based information, regardless of whether the version was paid or free.

title: Comparison of AI chatbot-generated and web-based health information on the effects of radiation in fetuses and children
outcome: understandability of patient education text
effect: PEMAT-P understandability ≥70: web 7.5%; normal ChatGPT-4o 50.0%, Gemini 78.6%; 6th-grade ChatGPT variants and Gemini 100.0%, Copilot 26.7%.
quote: For the proportion of texts with PEMAT-P Understandability scores ≥70, ChatGPT-4o (n=7, 50.0%) and Gemini (n=11, 78.6%) at the Normal level, and ChatGPT-4o (n=15, 100.0%), ChatGPT-4o mini (n=15, 100.0%), ChatGPT-o1 (n=15, 100.0%), ChatGPT-o1 mini (n=15, 100.0%), and Gemini (n=14, 100.0%) at the 6th grade level showed significantly higher proportions compared to other groups ( P <0.05).
