title: Comparative performance of LLMs and machine learning in predicting complications after percutaneous kyphoplasty for osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures
outcome: LLM predictive performance versus traditional ML models and surgeons on same data
effect: LLMs comparable to TML for BCL (F1 0.857-0.871 vs 0.758-0.867) but worse for NVF zero-shot (F1 0.309 vs RBF-SVM 0.536); LLMs did not outperform TML models.
quote: The LLMs did not outperform the TML models in the domain-specific tasks.
sample_unit: prospective test samples for BCL prediction (116 for NVF)

title: Comparative performance of LLMs and machine learning in predicting complications after percutaneous kyphoplasty for osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures
outcome: Surgeon prediction performance with versus without LLM predictions and explanations
effect: BCL: surgeon F1 rose from 0.675-0.684 to 0.724-0.752; NVF: subtle contrary changes, Surgeon 1 F1 0.310 to 0.370-0.409, Surgeon 2 0.322 to 0.308-0.315.
quote: After consultation of the predictions and interpretations from either LLMs, their performances showed subtle but contrary change that F1 score slightly increased to 0.370–0.409 and MCC to 0.185–0.266 for Surgeon 1 , while the numbers slightly decreased to 0.308–0.315 and 0.061–0.077 for Surgeon 2 .
sample_unit: prospective test samples for BCL prediction (116 for NVF)

title: Comparative performance of LLMs and machine learning in predicting complications after percutaneous kyphoplasty for osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures
outcome: LLM prediction accuracy against ground-truth outcomes
effect: Zero-shot LLMs predicted all samples would develop NVF (100% vs 18% actual); NVF F1 0.309, MCC 0.044; subtype prediction poor.
quote: For example, both LLMs under zero-shot prompting predicted all samples would develop NVF, far more than the actual occurrence rate (100% vs. 18%), for which nearly all LLMs’ explanation highlighted low BMD as the primary determining factor.
sample_unit: prospective test samples for BCL prediction (116 for NVF)

title: Comparative performance of LLMs and machine learning in predicting complications after percutaneous kyphoplasty for osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures
outcome: Clinician performance when assisted by LLM output versus unassisted
effect: LLM assistance improved surgeon BCL prediction (F1 0.739-0.752 vs 0.684 for Surgeon 1) but gave no consistent benefit for NVF.
quote: Whether the decision-support value of output from LLMs demonstrated highly depend on model’s overall accuracy and reliability on the task.
sample_unit: prospective test samples for BCL prediction (116 for NVF)

title: Comparative performance of LLMs and machine learning in predicting complications after percutaneous kyphoplasty for osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures
outcome: Reproducibility of LLM outputs across three repeated runs
effect: Gwet's AC1 0.856-0.994 for zero-shot and 0.730-0.850 for few-shot, indicating perfect to substantial consistency.
quote: ChatGPT and DeepSeek exhibited equally perfect consistency in three-time repeat responses for zero-shot prediction (Gwet’s AC1, 0.856–0.994) and substantial-to-perfect consistency for few-shot prediction (Gwet’s AC1, 0.730–0.850; Supplementary Table 3 ).
sample_unit: prospective test samples for BCL prediction (116 for NVF)

title: Comparative performance of LLMs and machine learning in predicting complications after percutaneous kyphoplasty for osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures
outcome: repeat response consistency
effect: Zero-shot Gwet’s AC1 0.856–0.994; few-shot Gwet’s AC1 0.730–0.850.
quote: ChatGPT and DeepSeek exhibited equally perfect consistency in three-time repeat responses for zero-shot prediction (Gwet’s AC1, 0.856–0.994) and substantial-to-perfect consistency for few-shot prediction (Gwet’s AC1, 0.730–0.850; Supplementary Table 3 ).
sample_unit: prospective test samples for BCL prediction (116 for NVF)

title: Comparative performance of LLMs and machine learning in predicting complications after percutaneous kyphoplasty for osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures
outcome: predictive performance of LLMs compared to traditional machine learning models
effect: LLMs did not outperform TML models; RBF-SVM had highest F1 (0.514) and MCC (0.414) for NVF, while TML models had superior MCCs (0.384–0.416) for BCL
quote: The LLMs did not outperform the TML models in the domain-specific tasks.
sample_unit: prospective test samples for BCL prediction (116 for NVF)

title: Evaluating large language models for simplifying non-English medical consent with clinician involvement
outcome: Content quality (risk, overall) of LLM-simplified consent forms with vs without clinician revision
effect: Clinician revision raised risk score from 3.28 to 3.69 (p=0.016) and overall from 2.86 to 3.64 (p=0.004); LMM risk β=0.42, overall β=0.78; restored to original-level quality.
quote: The risk score increased from 3.28 (SD = 0.55) to 3.69 (SD = 0.66), p = 0.016; the overall score also rose from 2.86 (SD = 0.36) to 3.64 (SD = 0.31), p = 0.004.
sample_unit: informed consent documents (each in 3 versions, rated by 4 surgeons and 4 laypersons)

title: Evaluating large language models for simplifying non-English medical consent with clinician involvement
outcome: Output variability of LLM simplification across temperature settings
effect: Structural simplification consistent across web, 0.1 and 0.9 temperature; lower temperature retained more difficult terms, higher temperature gave more rephrasing and semantic variability.
quote: Lower-temperature outputs tended to retain more technical and difficult terminology, whereas higher-temperature outputs exhibited more extensive rephrasing and greater semantic variability.
sample_unit: informed consent documents (each in 3 versions, rated by 4 surgeons and 4 laypersons)

title: Evaluating large language models for simplifying non-English medical consent with clinician involvement
outcome: layperson comprehension
effect: Average score increased from 2.64 (SD = 0.57) to 3.53 (SD = 0.38), p = 0.008.
quote: In contrast, layperson comprehension improved significantly, with the average score increasing from 2.64 (SD = 0.57) to 3.53 (SD = 0.38), p = 0.008.
sample_unit: informed consent documents (each in 3 versions, rated by 4 surgeons and 4 laypersons)

title: Evaluating large language models for simplifying non-English medical consent with clinician involvement
outcome: content quality after clinician review
effect: Risk score 3.28 to 3.69, p = 0.016; overall 2.86 to 3.64, p = 0.004.
quote: The risk score increased from 3.28 (SD = 0.55) to 3.69 (SD = 0.66), p = 0.016; the overall score also rose from 2.86 (SD = 0.36) to 3.64 (SD = 0.31), p = 0.004.
sample_unit: informed consent documents (each in 3 versions, rated by 4 surgeons and 4 laypersons)

title: Evaluating large language models for simplifying non-English medical consent with clinician involvement
outcome: LLM content completeness
effect: Risk score decreased 3.61 to 3.28, p = 0.016; overall dropped 3.53 to 2.86, p = 0.004.
quote: Specifically, the risk score decreased from 3.61 (SD = 0.71) to 3.28 (SD = 0.55), p = 0.016, while the overall score dropped from 3.53 (SD = 0.29) to 2.86 (SD = 0.36), p = 0.004.
sample_unit: informed consent documents (each in 3 versions, rated by 4 surgeons and 4 laypersons)

title: Benchmarking agreement between large language models and published clinical trial conclusions across four artificial intelligence platforms
outcome: LLM concordance with published clinical trial conclusions on benchmark RCT interpretation
effect: Concordance with published conclusions: ChatGPT 100.0%, Gemini 84%, Grok3 72%, Claude 68%; possible training-data contamination may inflate alignment.
quote: ChatGPT demonstrated the highest concordance with published conclusions at 100.0%, followed by Gemini at 84%, Grok3 at 72%, and Claude at 68%.
sample_unit: landmark RCTs (NEJM) interpreted by each of four LLMs

title: Multidimensional evaluation of large language models in radiology report readability
outcome: Patient subjective and objective comprehension of LLM-simplified vs original reports
effect: Subjective comprehension 3.59±0.74 to 4.68±0.47; objective 1.64±0.84 to 2.78±0.42 (P<0.05); STAI-6 anxiety 16.74 to 10.44 in 800 patients
quote: The results of clinical setting validation showed that, compared with the original radiology reports (subjective comprehension scores: 3.59 ± 0.74；objective comprehension scores: 1.64 ± 0.84), reading the reports simplified by DeepSeek-R1 significantly improved patients’ subjective comprehension scores (4.68 ± 0.47; P < 0.05; r = 0.91；95%CI:0.89–0.92) and objective comprehension scores (2.78 ± 0.42; P < 0.05; r = 0.90；95%CI:0.88–0.91).
sample_unit: radiology reports (plus 800 patients in clinical setting validation)

title: Multidimensional evaluation of large language models in radiology report readability
outcome: Key information point accuracy with unoptimized vs optimized structured prompts
effect: Accurate KIP: ChatGPT-4.0 52.2% to 86.1%; DeepSeek-R1 61.7% to 91.1%; Grok-3 99.4% to 100%
quote: Using the optimized prompt framework, quantitative results showed that the optimized prompts significantly improved the translation accuracy of ChatGPT-4.0 and Deep Seek-R1, as evidenced by higher key information point (KIP) retention rates (Table 5 ).
sample_unit: radiology reports (plus 800 patients in clinical setting validation)

title: Multidimensional evaluation of large language models in radiology report readability
outcome: Output consistency across 10 repeated runs of same report
effect: With unoptimized prompts, accurate KIP rates were 52.2% (ChatGPT-4.0), 61.7% (DeepSeek-R1), 99.4% (Grok-3) across repeated outputs
quote: The variability within the same model’s response to identical inputs highlights the inherent randomness of LLMs, which contributes to output inconsistency.
sample_unit: radiology reports (plus 800 patients in clinical setting validation)

title: Multidimensional evaluation of large language models in radiology report readability
outcome: Radiologist-identified omissions and inaccuracies in LLM-simplified reports
effect: Omissions per report: ChatGPT 0.072, Grok 0.047, DeepSeek 0.093; inaccuracies 0.038, 0.069, 0.05
quote: The findings show that these translations regularly include information omissions and inaccuracies.
sample_unit: radiology reports (plus 800 patients in clinical setting validation)

title: Multidimensional evaluation of large language models in radiology report readability
outcome: Comprehension of LLM-simplified reports by age and education level
effect: Significant age × education interaction on subjective and objective comprehension (P<0.05); lower education associated with lower comprehension
quote: The results of the second-stage 2 × 2 factorial analysis (age × educational level) demonstrated that age and educational level had significant interactive effects on both subjective and objective comprehension scores ( P < 0.05).
sample_unit: radiology reports (plus 800 patients in clinical setting validation)

title: Multidimensional evaluation of large language models in radiology report readability
outcome: Age- and education-related differences in comprehension of AI-simplified reports
effect: Older participants had better comprehension within both educational strata: Cliff’s |Δ| = 0.32 for high education and 0.41 for low education; adjusted P < 0.05.
quote: Results indicated significant differences: younger and older participants differed notably in understanding the reports, with older participants showing better comprehension than younger, both in high-education groups (Group 1 vs. Group 3；effect size Cliff’s |Δ| = 0.32; 95% CI: 0.21, 0.39) and low-education groups (Group 2 vs. Group 4；effect size Cliff’s |Δ| = 0.41; 95% CI: 0.32, 0.53) (adjusted P < 0.05 after Bonferroni correction; Fig. 2c, d ).
sample_unit: radiology reports (plus 800 patients in clinical setting validation)

title: Artificial intelligence assisted colorectal lesion detection in private practices a randomized controlled study
outcome: Adenoma detection rate with AI-assisted vs traditional colonoscopy in randomized trial
effect: ADR 34.5% with computer-aided colonoscopy vs 32.9% with traditional colonoscopy (p = 0.656); no significant difference between groups.
quote: The ADR (CAC:34.5% vs TC:32.9%; p = 0.656) was not significantly different between the groups.

title: Implementing AI innovation in radiology departments in the English NHS: a qualitative study on the experiences of professionals, patient groups and innovators
outcome: Implementation challenges reported by innovators and professionals regarding governance of AI in the NHS
effect: Innovators and healthcare professionals reported fragmented legal and regulatory frameworks and unclear governance within the NHS as key implementation challenges.
quote: Innovators as well healthcare professionals highlighted a number of implementation challenges, particularly around fragmented legal and regulatory frameworks and unclear governance within the NHS.
sample_unit: participants (34 professional interviews, 7 innovator staff interviews, 14 PPIE focus group participants)

title: Large Language Models in Clinical Decision Support: A Comparative Analysis of Chat-GPT and Breast Radiologists on ACR Appropriateness Criteria
outcome: Consistency and reproducibility of ChatGPT ratings across four independent samplings
effect: Current ChatGPT versions lack consistency and reproducibility relative to radiologists; radiologists were often as variable or less variable as a group than the same ChatGPT version.
quote: In summary, radiologists were closer to the ACR AC and were oftentimes as variable or even less variable as a group than the same ChatGPT version at the same time.
sample_unit: imaging decisions rated (10 ACR breast imaging clinical variants)

title: Large Language Models in Clinical Decision Support: A Comparative Analysis of Chat-GPT and Breast Radiologists on ACR Appropriateness Criteria
outcome: Agreement of ChatGPT imaging appropriateness ratings with ACR Appropriateness Criteria
effect: All ChatGPT versions had significant mean bias vs ACR (GPT-4o 2.463; GPT-4 1.7623; GPT-3.5 2.4691; all p<0.001) versus radiologists 0.2438 (p=0.489).
quote: All versions of ChatGPT had larger mean biases that were significant (GPT-4o: 2.463; GPT-4: 1.7623, GPT-3.5: 2.4691, all p<0.001).
sample_unit: imaging decisions rated (10 ACR breast imaging clinical variants)

title: Large Language Models in Clinical Decision Support: A Comparative Analysis of Chat-GPT and Breast Radiologists on ACR Appropriateness Criteria
outcome: ChatGPT versions versus breast radiologists agreement with ACR criteria
effect: Radiologists had lowest mean bias (0.2438, p=0.489) and smallest slope bias; all ChatGPT versions had significant bias (p<0.001).
quote: Radiologists had the lowest overall mean bias (0.2438) relative to the ACR (p = 0.489).
sample_unit: imaging decisions rated (10 ACR breast imaging clinical variants)

title: Precision Risk Model Using Quantitative Assessment of Vascular Severity in Telemedicine-Based Screening
outcome: Discrimination of model with vascular severity versus gestational age alone for 2-week TR-ROP
effect: Adding vascular severity improved AUROC vs GA alone: difference 0.13 (95% CI 0.06-0.19) in i-ROP and 0.08 (95% CI 0.03-0.14) in SUNDROP.
quote: Adding vascular severity improved discrimination vs GA alone (AUROC difference 0.13 [95% CI, 0.06-0.19] in i-ROP; 0.08 [95% CI, 0.03-0.14] in SUNDROP).
sample_unit: infants (559 i-ROP training; 1544 SUNDROP external validation)

title: Precision Risk Model Using Quantitative Assessment of Vascular Severity in Telemedicine-Based Screening
outcome: Model performance on external SUNDROP cohort versus development i-ROP data
effect: The threshold achieved 100% sensitivity with specificity 63% in i-ROP and 73% in SUNDROP; performance held in the external cohort.
quote: A decision threshold achieved 100% sensitivity with moderate specificity (i-ROP 63%; SUNDROP 73%).
sample_unit: infants (559 i-ROP training; 1544 SUNDROP external validation)

title: Physician Gestalt Compared With Artificial Intelligence Model to Predict Intubation in Critically Ill Patients
outcome: Sensitivity and specificity of ML intubation prediction versus intensivist prediction on the same patients
effect: Sensitivity 0.190 (physicians) vs 0.714 (Vent.io); specificity 0.960 vs 0.673. Vent.io was better when intubation was needed (OR 18.68); physicians were better when it was not (OR 24.80).
quote: Vent.io had significantly greater odds of being correct when patients required intubation compared with physicians (OR 18.68; 95% CI, 1.87-186.31; p = 0.013).

title: Exploring the Ethical and Practical Considerations of Artificial Intelligence in Real-World Health Care Settings: Stakeholder Focus Group Study
outcome: Stakeholder perceptions of AI governance for validation, auditing, and use in the clinic
effect: Participants identified insufficient systematic governance on validation, auditing, and use of AI tools in the clinic across the Texas Medical Center.
quote: However, they also identified many challenges, including significant barriers to accessing quality datasets for training, insufficient systematic governance on the validation, auditing, and use of AI tools in the clinic, and limited patient involvement in AI development decisions.
sample_unit: focus group participants (clinicians, developers, administrators, patient advocates)

title: Exploring the Ethical and Practical Considerations of Artificial Intelligence in Real-World Health Care Settings: Stakeholder Focus Group Study
outcome: Stakeholder views on accountability for AI-related patient care errors
effect: Accountability was unresolved; participants were split on whether the provider should take full responsibility for patient care errors resulting from AI.
quote: Accountability also remained an unresolved issue, with participants split on whether the provider should take full responsibility for any patient care errors resulting from AI.
sample_unit: focus group participants (clinicians, developers, administrators, patient advocates)

title: Exploring the Ethical and Practical Considerations of Artificial Intelligence in Real-World Health Care Settings: Stakeholder Focus Group Study
outcome: Patient involvement in AI development decisions as reported by participants
effect: Participants identified limited patient involvement in AI development decisions as a challenge.

sample_unit: focus group participants (clinicians, developers, administrators, patient advocates)

title: Exploring the Ethical and Practical Considerations of Artificial Intelligence in Real-World Health Care Settings: Stakeholder Focus Group Study
outcome: Where AI models are validated relative to where they are deployed
effect: Validation occurring primarily in well-resourced locations like the TMC raised worries about a digital divide, heightened for safety-net and underresourced settings.
quote: Discussion on validation of models occurring primarily in well-resourced locations like the TMC raised worries about a potential digital divide in health care.
sample_unit: focus group participants (clinicians, developers, administrators, patient advocates)

title: Predicting radiology no-shows with machine learning: Methodological pitfalls and practical considerations
outcome: Data leakage risk and temporal inconsistencies in radiology no-show model development and validation
effect: Models trained on 2022-2023 data and tested on 2024 data reached best AUC 0.71; temporal inconsistencies highlighted data leakage risk, and data quality varied across features and sites.
quote: Feature engineering was constrained by predictor granularity, and temporal inconsistencies highlighted the risk of data leakage.

title: An adaptive differential privacy framework for clinical llms with context-aware noise calibration, hierarchical budgeting, and real-time auditing
outcome: Membership inference risk reduction with differential privacy and privacy auditing in clinical LLM
effect: Mitigated membership inference risk by 65.9% versus state-of-the-art privacy-preserving LLMs; utility-privacy trade-off improved 15.8% at ε=0.1, δ=10⁻⁶.
quote: By improving the utility–privacy trade-off by 15.8%, mitigating membership inference risk by 65.9%, and reducing computational overhead by 23.4%, the framework establishes a more secure, efficient, and trustworthy foundation for clinical AI deployment.
sample_unit: documents/records (MIMIC-III 2.1M documents, i2b2 858K records, proprietary hospital dataset 1.5M records)

title: A robust vision language model for molecular status prediction and radiology report generation in adult-type diffuse gliomas
outcome: Performance of IDH prediction and report generation across internal and external sites
effect: IDH AUCs were 0.85-0.95 across internal and external datasets. Report generation fell from BLEU-1 0.50 and ROUGE-L 0.49 internally to 0.32 and 0.36 on the AMC dataset.
quote: In terms of RRG, the BLEU-1 and ROUGE-L scores were 0.50 and 0.49 in the internal validation, respectively, and 0.32 and 0.36 on the AMC dataset, respectively.
sample_unit: patients in the validation and external test sets (100 internal, 75 AMC, 170 TCGA, 477 UCSF)

title: A robust vision language model for molecular status prediction and radiology report generation in adult-type diffuse gliomas
outcome: Neuroradiologist rating of clinical acceptability of generated radiology reports
effect: 37.8% of generated reports were superior or equal to the original reports. 91.0% were clinically acceptable, so about 9% were not acceptable.
quote: Overall, 37.8% of generated reports were considered superior or equal to the original reports, while 91.0% of generated reports were considered clinically acceptable by neuroradiologists.
sample_unit: patients in the validation and external test sets (100 internal, 75 AMC, 170 TCGA, 477 UCSF)

title: Use of natural language processing tools in musculoskeletal disability assessment: generating reports and calculating impairment percentages in Turkish health commission settings
outcome: Correct calculation of disability percentages by LLMs across scenarios
effect: ChatGPT-4o failed to calculate correct disability percentages in 55.6% of scenarios; Data Analyst failed in 88.9%.
quote: However, ChatGPT-4o failed to calculate correct disability percentages in 55.6%, and Data Analyst failed in 88.9% of scenarios.

title: Use of natural language processing tools in musculoskeletal disability assessment: generating reports and calculating impairment percentages in Turkish health commission settings
outcome: Reliability of AI-generated disability reports and percentage calculations requiring expert review
effect: Narrative reports were rated very good (ChatGPT-4o) and good (Data Analyst), but disability percentage calculations were frequently wrong, so expert oversight remains essential.
quote: While NLP tools can assist in generating structured disability reports, they currently lack the precision needed for calculating disability percentages reliably.

title: To be Healed or Hacked? - User-Centered Ethical Design for Embodied AI in Mental Health Care
venue: IEEE transactions on visualization and computer graphics
outcome: Effect of higher data autonomy on self-disclosure to embodied AI therapist
effect: Higher data autonomy led to greater self-disclosure; no effect on perceived trust.
quote: Results indicated that higher data autonomy led to greater self-disclosure, while transparency had no significant effect.

title: To be Healed or Hacked? - User-Centered Ethical Design for Embodied AI in Mental Health Care
venue: IEEE transactions on visualization and computer graphics
outcome: self-disclosure to AI therapist
effect: Transparency had no significant effect on self-disclosure in the VR study (N=90).
quote: Results indicated that higher data autonomy led to greater self-disclosure, while transparency had no significant effect.
sample_unit: participants (in-person VR study); online survey N=152 mental health patients

title: An AI-based mental health guardrail and dataset for identifying psychiatric crises in text-based conversations
outcome: Sensitivity and specificity of a guardrail detecting psychiatric crises in text messages
effect: On the Verily dataset, sensitivity 0.990, specificity 0.992, F1 0.939, category-level sensitivity 0.917-0.992, specificity ≥0.978. On the NVIDIA subset, sensitivity 0.982, accuracy 0.921, specificity 0.859.
quote: The VMHG demonstrated high sensitivity (0.990) and specificity (0.992) on the Verily dataset, with an F1-score of 0.939 and high category-level sensitivity (0.917-0.992) and specificity (≥0.978).

title: An AI-based mental health guardrail and dataset for identifying psychiatric crises in text-based conversations
outcome: Missed and false-positive crisis detection versus comparator guardrails
effect: VMHG had significantly higher sensitivity than NVIDIA and OpenAI guardrails (all p < 0.001), with comparable specificity to OpenAI (p = 0.094) and lower than NVIDIA (p < 0.001).
quote: Compared with NVIDIA and OpenAI guardrails, the VMHG achieved significantly higher sensitivity (all p < 0.001) and comparable specificity (NVIDIA p < 0.001, OpenAI p = 0.094).

title: Comparison of AI-generated radiology impressions: a multi-stakeholder evaluation
outcome: Preference for AI impressions by original vs independent radiologists and oncologists
effect: Original radiologists slightly preferred their own impressions to the custom model (h = 0.18, p = 0.0716), while independent radiologists showed no preference (h = -0.03, p = 0.78). Both groups rated generic model impressions lower.
quote: Original radiologists slightly preferred their own impressions to the custom model (h = 0.18, p = 0.0716), while independent radiologists showed no preference (h = -0.03, p = 0.78).

title: Comparison of AI-generated radiology impressions: a multi-stakeholder evaluation
outcome: Comparison of custom AI, generic LLM and radiologist impressions on completeness, correctness, and utility
effect: Custom model achieved near parity with human impressions; generic LLM impressions were less preferred by radiologists (h 1.04-1.22 original; 0.66-0.69 independent, p < 0.001) and less concise (r = 0.85-0.87).
quote: Custom model impressions achieved near parity with human impressions; original radiologists rated their own impressions slightly more complete (r = 0.22, p = 0.0016).

title: Validation of a prediction model for postpartum hospital use in geographic contexts with greater rural representation
venue: American journal of obstetrics & gynecology MFM
outcome: Calibration and AUC after local intercept recalibration and coefficient re-estimation
effect: Intercept update corrected calibration; re-estimating coefficients raised AUC to 0.69 (SC) and 0.70 (FL), with slight gains in subgroups.
quote: Model updating improved calibration in both states ( Figure ), with substantial improvement after adjusting model intercepts

title: Validation of a prediction model for postpartum hospital use in geographic contexts with greater rural representation
venue: American journal of obstetrics & gynecology MFM
outcome: Model discrimination across racial/ethnic, Medicaid, and rural subgroups
effect: AUC was lower in Black (0.63-0.65), Medicaid (0.64-0.67), and rural (0.65-0.66) groups than overall (0.68-0.69) with the original model.
quote: AUC decreased when models were run separately among Black, Hispanic, Medicaid-insured, and rural residents.

title: Validation of a prediction model for postpartum hospital use in geographic contexts with greater rural representation
venue: American journal of obstetrics & gynecology MFM
outcome: Performance of the model in external, later-period, multi-state data versus development
effect: External validation showed similar AUC but overestimated absolute risk, so calibration was poor.
quote: However, calibration was poor and indicated systematic overprediction of PHU risk.

title: Validation of a prediction model for postpartum hospital use in geographic contexts with greater rural representation
venue: American journal of obstetrics & gynecology MFM
outcome: Calibration of NYC-developed model applied to SC and FL populations
effect: Original NYC coefficients gave overestimated, extreme risk in new states; calibration slope 0.64 in SC and 0.63 in FL, while AUC stayed 0.68-0.69.
quote: Calibration slope was 0.64 in SC and 0.63 in FL, suggesting that predicted risks were more extreme compared to observed risk.

title: Validation of a prediction model for postpartum hospital use in geographic contexts with greater rural representation
venue: American journal of obstetrics & gynecology MFM
outcome: Model performance when extended to new geographic populations, before and after updating
effect: NYC model overestimated risk in SC/FL but modest updating yielded well-calibrated models with AUC 0.69-0.70.
quote: Modest model updating, including recalibration of intercepts and re-estimation of coefficients, yielded well-calibrated models without requiring new predictors.

title: Validation of a prediction model for postpartum hospital use in geographic contexts with greater rural representation
venue: American journal of obstetrics & gynecology MFM
outcome: Performance across sites (states) of prediction model
effect: Discrimination was similar across SC (AUC 0.68) and FL (0.69) versus NYC 0.69, but calibration was poor in both states.
quote: The model achieved an AUC of 0.68 (95% CI 0.67 –0.68) and 0.69 (95% CI 0.68–0.69) in discriminating PHU among SC and FL births, respectively ( Table 3 ).

title: Validation of a prediction model for postpartum hospital use in geographic contexts with greater rural representation
venue: American journal of obstetrics & gynecology MFM
outcome: Local historical validation
effect: Calibration slope was 0.64 in SC and 0.63 in FL, indicating overly extreme predicted risks.
quote: Calibration slope was 0.64 in SC and 0.63 in FL, suggesting that predicted risks were more extreme compared to observed risk.

title: Evaluating the Impact of Artificial Intelligence Scribes on Clinical Workflow and Documentation Quality: A Randomized Controlled Trial
outcome: Medical errors in AI scribe versus conventional documentation, reviewed by the surgeon
effect: 19 medical errors in the AI scribe group vs 9 in the conventional group; no significant difference in spelling or grammatical errors.
quote: There were 19 medical errors in the AI scribe group compared to only nine errors in the conventional group.

title: Evaluating the Impact of Artificial Intelligence Scribes on Clinical Workflow and Documentation Quality: A Randomized Controlled Trial
outcome: Physician and administrative documentation processing time with AI scribe versus conventional methods
effect: Statistically significant reduction in both physician and administrative processing times (P < 0.0001).
quote: Use of AI scribes resulted in a statistically significant reduction in both physician and administrative processing times (P < 0.0001).

title: Evaluating the Impact of Artificial Intelligence Scribes on Clinical Workflow and Documentation Quality: A Randomized Controlled Trial
outcome: Patient perceptions of AI scribe use
effect: Patients were not negatively affected by AI scribe use and the vast majority found it helpful (no numbers given in abstract).
quote: Patients were not negatively affected by using an AI scribe, and the vast majority found it helpful.

title: Assessing the Safety and Clinical Appropriateness of Breast Cancer Advice From Consumer-Grade Large Language Models
venue: Journal of medical imaging and radiation oncology
outcome: Consistency of LLM answers across three repeated runs of the same question
effect: ChatGPT and Perplexity provided consistent answers to all questions; all three models performed well on reliability.
quote: All three models performed well in terms of reliability, with ChatGPT and Perplexity providing consistent answers to all questions.

title: Assessing the Safety and Clinical Appropriateness of Breast Cancer Advice From Consumer-Grade Large Language Models
venue: Journal of medical imaging and radiation oncology
outcome: Clinical appropriateness of LLM answers with WA-specific terminology versus general questions
effect: Appropriate answers: ChatGPT 97%, Perplexity 90%, Gemini 87%. Inappropriate responses were more common with WA-specific terminology, particularly for Perplexity and Gemini.
quote: Inappropriate responses were more common when questions included WA-specific terminology, particularly for Perplexity and Gemini.

title: Hidden failure modes of large language models in healthcare-associated infection surveillance: a structured evaluation using NHSN definitions
outcome: LLM classification accuracy against gold-standard NHSN definitions, including false positives
effect: Overall accuracy 87.6% (184/210) with 25 false positives and 1 false negative; lowest for CDI (81.0%) and CLABSI (80.4%); model overcalled infections.
quote: Consistent with prior work, these findings indicate that LLMs tend to overcall HAIs: they are overly sensitive and insufficiently specific.
sample_unit: case-prompt classifications (70 synthetic vignettes x 3 prompting strategies)

title: Hidden failure modes of large language models in healthcare-associated infection surveillance: a structured evaluation using NHSN definitions
outcome: accuracy by prompt structure
effect: Accuracy improved from 78.6% standard to 88.6% structured and 95.7% constrained; Cochran’s Q(2) = 18.2, P < .001.
quote: The constrained (95.7%) and structured (88.6%) prompts showed higher accuracy than the standard (78.6%) prompt (McNemar P = .00049 and P = .0156, respectively).
sample_unit: case-prompt classifications (70 synthetic vignettes x 3 prompting strategies)

title: Hidden failure modes of large language models in healthcare-associated infection surveillance: a structured evaluation using NHSN definitions
outcome: Incorrect LLM classifications that would require clinician verification
effect: 26 misclassified vignettes; errors in exclusion rules, quantitative thresholds, and hierarchical attribution persisted even under constrained prompting (constrained accuracy 95.7%). Authors conclude human oversight is needed.
quote: Taken together, these findings suggest that LLMs of this kind require human oversight and are not yet ready for fully autonomous deployment in HAI surveillance.
sample_unit: case-prompt classifications (70 synthetic vignettes x 3 prompting strategies)

title: Hidden failure modes of large language models in healthcare-associated infection surveillance: a structured evaluation using NHSN definitions
outcome: Suitability of LLM output as stand-alone surveillance classification
effect: Model overcalled HAIs with false positives 33.3% under standard prompt and 7.1% constrained; authors state it cannot function as an autonomous HAI surveillance tool, only as decision-support with human final decisions.
quote: Currently, GPT-5.1 Thinking cannot function as an autonomous HAI surveillance tool.
sample_unit: case-prompt classifications (70 synthetic vignettes x 3 prompting strategies)

title: Detecting stigmatizing language with large language models: mind the settings
outcome: LLM accuracy detecting stigmatizing language versus human-annotated reference standard
effect: Best configuration (8B, temp 0.25, examples) had 70.2% accuracy, TPR 94.1%, TNR 47.4%; many false positives on neutral clinical descriptions.
quote: The best performance in terms of overall accuracy was the 8B (largest) model with a temperature of 0.25 (smallest) with examples, which achieved an overall accuracy of 70.2%.

title: Detecting stigmatizing language with large language models: mind the settings
outcome: accuracy by few-shot prompting
effect: Six no-example configurations were bottom 6 for overall accuracy, but top 6 for TNR.
quote: Of the 12 overall variations, the 6 models without examples made up the bottom 6, the worst performers in terms of overall accuracy, although they were the top 6 performers in terms of TNR.

title: Performance evaluation of mainstream large language models in autoimmune hepatitis patient education: a comparative study of readability, quality, and reliability
outcome: Readability of LLM-generated AIH patient education text relative to general patient reading level
effect: Relatively high readability levels across models suggest further simplification may be needed for general patient populations; disease mechanism and diagnostic content showed higher linguistic complexity.
quote: Although most models produced moderate-to-good quality information, relatively high readability levels suggest that further simplification may be needed for general patient populations.

title: Performance evaluation of mainstream large language models in autoimmune hepatitis patient education: a comparative study of readability, quality, and reliability
outcome: Plain-language comprehensibility of LLM-generated patient education content
effect: Readability varied significantly across content themes, with disease mechanism and diagnostic texts showing higher linguistic complexity; models differed significantly in readability, quality and suitability (all p < 0.05).
quote: Readability varied significantly across content themes, with texts related to disease mechanisms and diagnostic processes exhibiting higher linguistic complexity.

title: Key aspects of fine-tuning and applying LLM-as-a-judge for clinical data summaries in the radiological workflow
outcome: Consistency of LLM judge scores for the same summary across scale sizes and prompt granularities
effect: The same summary got 3/4, 4/5, 6/7 and 4/10 completeness from Mistral; inconsistency more pronounced at larger scales; often three different scores across three prompt granularity variants.
quote: When reviewing the responses of LLMs-as-a-Judges, periodic inconsistencies in scores assigned to the same summary across different scale granularities became apparent.
sample_unit: LLM-generated summaries of EHRs (30 patients, 6 summarizing LLMs)

title: Key aspects of fine-tuning and applying LLM-as-a-judge for clinical data summaries in the radiological workflow
outcome: clinically significant omissions in AI summaries
effect: Expert Completeness averaged 3.26/5 while Grammar and Terminology averaged 4.4/5.
quote: Therefore, in our experiment, experts rated the summarizations with relatively high scores according to the criterion of Grammar and Terminology (on average 4.4 out of 5) but with substantially lower scores according to the criterion of Completeness (on average 3.26 out of 5).
sample_unit: LLM-generated summaries of EHRs (30 patients, 6 summarizing LLMs)

title: Key aspects of fine-tuning and applying LLM-as-a-judge for clinical data summaries in the radiological workflow
outcome: Agreement of LLM-as-a-Judge with expert reference standard for hallucination detection
effect: Kendall's W for hallucination detection was 0.37–0.55 across judges and prompt configurations; authors conclude LLM judges are not advisable for detecting hallucinations in semantically difficult medical text.
quote: Our results indicate that it is not advisable to use LLM-as-a-Judges to search for hallucinations in texts, especially when analyzing a semantically difficult medical text.
sample_unit: LLM-generated summaries of EHRs (30 patients, 6 summarizing LLMs)

title: Key aspects of fine-tuning and applying LLM-as-a-judge for clinical data summaries in the radiological workflow
outcome: automatic metric validity for medical summaries
effect: ROUGE-1 0.29–0.38, BLEU 0.06–0.12, BERTScore 0.72–0.77; authors judged automated metrics poorly applicable.
quote: The results presented in Table 4 indicate that automated metrics are poorly applicable to our task.
sample_unit: LLM-generated summaries of EHRs (30 patients, 6 summarizing LLMs)

title: Key aspects of fine-tuning and applying LLM-as-a-judge for clinical data summaries in the radiological workflow
outcome: LLM-as-judge hallucination detection
effect: Kendall W for hallucination detection was 0.37–0.55 across models/prompt detail; authors advised against LLM-as-Judges for semantic hallucinations.
quote: In general, all models showed rather low consistency with experts, which indicates the weak ability of LLM to detect semantic hallucinations in medical texts.
sample_unit: LLM-generated summaries of EHRs (30 patients, 6 summarizing LLMs)

title: Accuracy and readability of LLM-generated responses for gout management: a benchmark study based on ACR guidelines
outcome: Readability of LLM gout responses (FKGL, ARI) for patient education
effect: GPT-5 produced the most complex responses (FKGL: 12.89 ± 2.22, ARI: 14.87 ± 2.40), with the lowest readability; DeepSeek-R1 generated the longest outputs.
quote: In terms of readability, GPT-5 produced the most complex responses (FKGL: 12.89 ± 2.22, ARI: 14.87 ± 2.40), while DeepSeek-R1 generated the longest outputs.

title: Accuracy and readability of LLM-generated responses for gout management: a benchmark study based on ACR guidelines
outcome: Reading grade level of LLM gout patient-education responses
effect: GPT-5 responses averaged FKGL 12.89 and ARI 14.87, well above typical patient reading levels; GPT-5 had the lowest readability.
quote: In terms of readability, GPT-5 produced the most complex responses (FKGL: 12.89 ± 2.22, ARI: 14.87 ± 2.40), while DeepSeek-R1 generated the longest outputs.

title: Optimizing ChatGPT Applying prompt engineering to frequently asked questions in urologic oncology
venue: Canadian Urological Association journal = Journal de l'Association des urologues du Canada
outcome: Readability, understandability and actionability of ChatGPT patient education responses before vs after prompt engineering
effect: Grade reading level 10.5 to 5.3 (p<0.0001); reading ease 42 to 71.7 (p<0.0001); PEMAT-P understandability 88.4-95.5%; actionability 25.6-84.2%; DISCERN 3.42-4.47.
quote: Using prompt engineering, DISCERN (3.42-4.47, p<0.0001), PEMAT-P understandability (88.4-95.5%, p<0.0001), actionability (25.6-84.2%, p<0.0001), grade reading level (10.5-5.3, p<0.0001), and reading level (42 [college level] to 71.7 [7th grade], p<0.0001), all significantly improved.

title: Optimizing ChatGPT Applying prompt engineering to frequently asked questions in urologic oncology
venue: Canadian Urological Association journal = Journal de l'Association des urologues du Canada
outcome: Reading grade level of ChatGPT patient materials with and without prompt engineering for sixth-grade target
effect: Grade reading level fell from 10.5 to 5.3 (p<0.0001); reading level from college (42) to 7th grade (71.7).
quote: PEMs are recommended to be written at or below a sixth-grade reading level but are regularly written at a college reading level.

title: Optimizing ChatGPT Applying prompt engineering to frequently asked questions in urologic oncology
venue: Canadian Urological Association journal = Journal de l'Association des urologues du Canada
outcome: reading level of AI-generated patient education materials
effect: Baseline ChatGPT answers had a grade reading level of 10.5 and reading level of 42 (college level), exceeding recommended patient education levels.
quote: ChatGPT answers are highly accurate but at too advanced a reading level and lacked explanations of benefits, risks, visual aids, actionability, and citations.

title: Immersive, Interactive, Intelligent Patient Educational System for Venous Thromboembolism (ChatVTE): Development and Validation Study
outcome: Expert Likert ratings of accuracy, completeness, consistency, and safety: retrieval-augmented ChatVTE vs ChatGPT
effect: ChatVTE outperformed ChatGPT on accuracy, completeness, consistency (all P<.001, r>0.5) and safety (P=.01, r=0.327). The comparison is confounded, since the two systems differ in model as well as retrieval.
quote: Expert evaluation demonstrated that ChatVTE significantly outperformed ChatGPT in accuracy, completeness, consistency (all P<.001, r>0.5), and safety (P=.01, r=0.327).

title: FedKGC: Federated Knowledge-Grounded Calibration Framework for Hallucination Mitigation in Medical LLMs
venue: IEEE journal of biomedical and health informatics
outcome: Hallucination rate of medical LLM with knowledge-grounded calibration versus standard federated baselines
effect: FedKGC achieved a 28% reduction in hallucination rates compared with standard federated baselines on non-IID MIMIC-IV partition and MedHallu benchmark, under differential privacy.
quote: Evaluation on a non-IID partition of the MIMIC-IV dataset and the MedHallu benchmark demonstrates that FedKGC achieves a 28% reduction in hallucination rates compared to standard federated baselines while strictly adhering to $(\epsilon, \delta)$-Differential Privacy guarantees.

title: A comparative analysis of AI scribes versus human documentation in simulated general practice consultations
outcome: Hallucination and documentation quality of AI scribe vs human notes (modified PDQI-9)
effect: Significant differences in accuracy (P=0.022), thoroughness (P<0.001), succinctness (P<0.001) and freedom from hallucination (P=0.025); overall PDQI-9 difference not significant (P=0.071). Both AI and human notes contained hallucinations.
quote: The finding that both AI and human documentation contain 'hallucinations' challenges the assumption that human‑generated documentation represents the gold standard of clinical documentation quality.

title: Machine learning to predict ureteral access sheath placement failure in flexible ureteroscopy: development and prospective validation
outcome: Model AUC versus senior urologists' prediction of UAS placement failure in prospective cohort
effect: Simplified RF model achieved an AUC of 0.872 in prospective validation, significantly surpassing the predictive accuracy of senior urologists.
quote: During prospective validation, the simplified RF model achieved an AUC of 0.872, significantly surpassing the predictive accuracy of senior urologists.

title: Comparative Analysis of Large Language Models for Pediatric Kidney Stone Patient Education: A Multi-dimensional Assessment of Readability, Quality and Reliability
outcome: Readability of chatbot responses on pediatric kidney stones (ARLC, ARI, SMOG grade levels)
effect: Google Gemini had the highest reading levels (ARLC 14.93, ARI 16.2, SMOG 13.32); readability differed significantly among chatbots (p < 0.001, eta2 = 0.195-0.512).
quote: Google Gemini demonstrated the highest reading levels across all metrics (ARLC: 14.93, ARI: 16.2, and SMOG: 13.32), whereas ChatGPT, Claude, and DeepSEEK produced less complex test (p < 0.001; large effect sizes, η2 = 0.195-0.512).

title: Comparative Analysis of Large Language Models for Pediatric Kidney Stone Patient Education: A Multi-dimensional Assessment of Readability, Quality and Reliability
outcome: Reading level of LLM-generated patient education material relative to patient needs
effect: Google Gemini responses were consistently more complex and less accessible; its reading levels were ARLC 14.93, ARI 16.2, SMOG 13.32, with significant differences across chatbots.
quote: Although ChatGPT and Google Gemini provided more reliable information, Google Gemini's responses were consistently more complex and less accessible.

title: Chatbots and Diabetes: Is There Gender Bias?
outcome: Flesch-Kincaid reading grade level of LLM responses versus sixth-grade health literacy guideline
effect: All platforms generated content at high school to college grade reading levels, exceeding recommended sixth-grade health literacy guidelines.
quote: All platforms generated content at high school to college grade reading levels, exceeding recommended sixth-grade health literacy guidelines.

title: Chatbots and Diabetes: Is There Gender Bias?
outcome: Readability of LLM diabetes advice for patients
effect: All four LLMs produced high school to college level text, above the recommended sixth-grade level; DeepSeek used more specialized clinical terminology.
quote: All platforms generated content at high school to college grade reading levels, exceeding recommended sixth-grade health literacy guidelines.

title: Chatbots and Diabetes: Is There Gender Bias?
outcome: Differences in LLM responses when patient gender was varied in the prompt
effect: DeepSeek exhibited greater gender discrepancy than the other 3 LLMs; the others showed less discrepancy.
quote: DeepSeek incorporated more specialized clinical terminology and referenced specific diabetes guidelines not mentioned by ChatGPT, and exhibited greater gender discrepancy than the other 3 LLMs.

title: Bias Patterns in the Application of LLMs for Clinical Decision Support: A Comprehensive Study
outcome: Output disparities when patient demographic attributes varied in clinical vignette prompts across eight LLMs
effect: Counterfactual demographic red-teaming revealed various disparities across protected groups; larger models were not necessarily less biased and medical fine-tuning did not consistently outperform general-purpose models.
quote: Our experiments reveal various disparities across protected groups.

title: Bias Patterns in the Application of LLMs for Clinical Decision Support: A Comprehensive Study
outcome: Fairness of LLM outputs across protected patient subgroups in clinical decision support
effect: LLMs demonstrated significant social biases in clinical scenarios, influenced by model architecture and prompt engineering.
quote: LLMs demonstrate significant social biases in clinical scenarios that are influenced by model architecture and prompt engineering.

title: ChatGPT and patient education in benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, in French and in English
venue: European annals of otorhinolaryngology, head and neck diseases
outcome: Alignment of ChatGPT BPPV answers with AAO-HNSF guidelines, graded 1-4 by two otolaryngologists
effect: 12 of 14 responses fully guideline-aligned (grade 4/4); 2 accurate but lacking detail on fall risk in older persons (grade 3/4); English and French responses uniform.
quote: The 2 other responses, although accurate, lacked detail on the risk of falls in older persons with BPPV (grade 3/4).

title: Evaluation of the applicability of AI chatbots in addressing health management issues for living kidney donors
outcome: Expert-rated accuracy and integrity of chatbot answers to living kidney donor FAQs
effect: Copilot lowest: accuracy 3.35 (3.18, 3.52), integrity 3.40 (3.09, 3.71); ChatGPT-4.0 highest: accuracy 4.05 (3.89, 4.21), integrity 4.00 (3.82, 4.18).
quote: In contrast, ChatGPT-4.0 achieved the highest median accuracy [4.05 (3.89, 4.21)] and integrity [4.00 (3.82, 4.18)], closely followed by ChatGPT-3.5[4.01 (3.88, 4.16)], [3.98 (3.85, 4.11)].

title: Performance of a Sepsis Prediction Model Across Different Sepsis Definitions
outcome: Positive predictive value and lead time at model score thresholds (alert burden from false positives)
effect: At the Sepsis-3 Youden threshold (score 9), PPV was 11.4% with median lead time 3.4 h; PPV was 6.8% for SEP-1 and 5.9% for ASE. AUPRC was 0.11-0.24.
quote: Although the model provided some advance warning before sepsis onset, a high false-positive rate may limit its clinical utility without careful threshold selection and tailored implementation.

title: Initial Insights Into an Institutional Secure Large Language Model for Magnetic Resonance Imaging Examination Requests: Retrospective Study
outcome: Protocol accuracy of sLLM versus board-certified radiologists against consensus reference standard
effect: Overall protocol accuracy 93.1% (566/608) for sLLM vs 91.4% for Rad 3 (P=.23) and 92.1% for Rad 4 (P=.40); contrast accuracy 94.4% vs 92.1% for Rad 3 (P=.027).
quote: Overall protocol accuracy was 93.1% (566/608; 95% CI 89.6-96.6) for the sLLM, 91.4% (556/608; 95% CI 87.6-95.3) for Rad 3, and 92.1% (560/608; 95% CI 88.4-95.8) for Rad 4 (sLLM vs Rad 3 P=.23 vs Rad 4 P=.40).

title: Initial Insights Into an Institutional Secure Large Language Model for Magnetic Resonance Imaging Examination Requests: Retrospective Study
outcome: Manual review of discordant sLLM outputs for hallucinations against real patient EMR inputs
effect: No clinically significant hallucinations were identified in a manual review of discordant cases.
quote: No clinically significant hallucinations were identified in a manual review of discordant cases.

title: Real-world text-only inference of PI-RADS v2.1 from prostate MRI reports using large language models: a lesion-level, zone-aware study
outcome: Reproducibility, temporal stability, and invalid outputs across model versions
effect: GPT-5.2 outperformed ChatGPT-4o in paired analyses but produced invalid outputs in a minority of cases; intra-model reproducibility and temporal stability were also evaluated.
quote: GPT-5.2 outperformed ChatGPT-4o in paired analyses but produced invalid outputs in a minority of cases.
sample_unit: lesion-level entries from prostate MRI reports (1,118 patients)

title: The next best teacher: Using large language models to provide technical advice to trainees in regional Anaesthesia
outcome: Existence of references supplied by LLMs in regional anaesthesia advice
effect: All references from Bing and Gemini were real; only 25% of ChatGPT's references existed.
quote: All the references supplied by Bing and Gemini were real, whereas only 25% of the references supplied by ChatGPT existed.
sample_unit: anaesthetist raters (each rating LLM advice on seven regional nerve blocks)

title: Publicly available multimodal large language models for ocular surface infections: benchmarking against corneal specialists in triage, diagnosis and treatment
outcome: LLM diagnostic accuracy on real clinical cases by input modality versus corneal specialists
effect: Image-only accuracy was lowest (best GPT-5, 61.4%; κ=0.38); text-only GPT-5 83.3% vs specialists 87-90%; treatment accuracy 81-85% vs 90-98%.
quote: Treatment accuracy remained lower (81-85% vs 90-98%), while urgency triage matched experts in multimodal input.
sample_unit: microbiologically confirmed infectious keratitis and conjunctivitis cases

title: Publicly available multimodal large language models for ocular surface infections: benchmarking against corneal specialists in triage, diagnosis and treatment
outcome: Multimodal LLM diagnosis, treatment and triage compared with corneal specialists on same cases
effect: Image+text near-human accuracy (Perplexity 96.7%; GPT-5 91.7%) without consistently surpassing specialists; text-only and image-only were below specialists; treatment accuracy lower.
quote: Combined image+text achieved near-human accuracy without consistently surpassing corneal specialists (Perplexity 96.7%; κ=0.95; GPT-5 91.7%; κ=0.87).
sample_unit: microbiologically confirmed infectious keratitis and conjunctivitis cases

title: Publicly available multimodal large language models for ocular surface infections: benchmarking against corneal specialists in triage, diagnosis and treatment
outcome: Performance variation across input conditions (image-only, text-only, image+text) and hallucinations
effect: Performance depended strongly on input modality; image-only was worst with frequent fungal and Acanthamoeba misclassification and hallucinations confined to the image-only setting.
quote: Image-only accuracy was lowest (best GPT-5, 61.4%; κ=0.38) with frequent misclassification of fungal and Acanthamoeba keratitis and hallucinations confined to this setting.
sample_unit: microbiologically confirmed infectious keratitis and conjunctivitis cases

title: Diagnostic accuracy of multimodal large language models in differentiating epileptic from functional seizures in smartphone recorded videos
outcome: Alignment of model confidence scores with correctness of seizure classification
effect: All models reported high confidence scores (median 8.0–9.0) that were poorly aligned and did not correlate with correctness.
quote: All models reported high confidence scores (median 8.0–9.0) that were poorly aligned and did not correlate with correctness.

title: Increasing Large Language Model Accuracy for Care-Seeking Advice Using Prompts Reflecting Human Reasoning Strategies in the Real World: Validation Study
outcome: Intertrial output variability of LLM triage advice across 10 repeated runs per prompt
effect: Median Fleiss kappa 0.766 (default), 0.717 (recognition-primed), 0.751 (data-frame); most frequent recommendation consistency 76.9%, 66.9%, 71.1%; variability similar across prompts.
quote: Intertrial reliability—that is, the frequency with which a vignette received the same advice from the same model across multiple trials—was comparable across all prompts, with median Fleiss κ values of 0.766 (IQR 0.706‐0.884) for the default prompt, 0.717 (IQR 0.681‐0.743) for the recognition-primed prompt, and 0.751 (IQR 0.725‐0.773) for the data-frame prompt ( Table 3 ).
sample_unit: individual model assessments (45 vignettes x 10 models x 3 prompts x 10 repetitions)

title: Increasing Large Language Model Accuracy for Care-Seeking Advice Using Prompts Reflecting Human Reasoning Strategies in the Real World: Validation Study
outcome: triage over- and under-escalation errors
effect: Higher-than-necessary urgency accounted for 88% of errors (95% CI 87%‐88.9%); lower-than-necessary urgency 12% (11.1%‐13%).
quote: Across all 3 prompts, the models tended to recommend higher-than-necessary urgency (accounting for 88% of all errors, 95% CI 87%‐88.9%) rather than lower-than-necessary urgency (12% of all errors, 95% CI 11.1%‐13%).
sample_unit: individual model assessments (45 vignettes x 10 models x 3 prompts x 10 repetitions)

title: Increasing Large Language Model Accuracy for Care-Seeking Advice Using Prompts Reflecting Human Reasoning Strategies in the Real World: Validation Study
outcome: LLM care-seeking advice accuracy against physician-panel gold standard
effect: Overall accuracy with default prompt was 63.3% (95% CI 61.9%-64.7%); self-care accuracy only 13.4% with default prompt.
quote: The average accuracy across all models, vignettes, and trials was 63.3% (95% CI 61.9%‐64.7%) for the default prompt, 67.6% (95% CI 66.3%‐69%) for the recognition-primed prompt, and 66.7% (95% CI 65.3%‐68%) for the data-frame prompt.
sample_unit: individual model assessments (45 vignettes x 10 models x 3 prompts x 10 repetitions)

title: Predicting Momentary Suicidal Ideation From Smartphone Screenshots Using Vision-Language Models: Prospective Machine Learning Study
outcome: Discrimination of momentary suicidal ideation for personalized (temporal holdout) versus new-individual (subject holdout) models
effect: Temporal holdout (personalized) AUC=0.83, AUPRC=0.77; subject holdout near chance (AUC≈0.50). Authors propose personalized VLM monitoring after a calibration period.
quote: Screen content predicts short-term SI with clinically meaningful accuracy when models are personalized but does not generalize across individuals.

title: Predicting Momentary Suicidal Ideation From Smartphone Screenshots Using Vision-Language Models: Prospective Machine Learning Study
outcome: Generalization of performance to unseen individuals
effect: Subject holdout AUC≈0.50 (near chance); a simple lexical screening method retained modest discrimination (AUC=0.62).
quote: Subject holdout generalization was near chance (AUC≈0.50), though a simple lexical screening method retained modest discrimination (AUC=0.62).

title: Toward Automating the Summarization of Cancer Pathology Reports Using Large Language Models to Improve Clinical Usability
outcome: LLM summary vs physician summary completeness and correctness against original pathology reports
effect: LLM summaries scored higher on all objective metrics (P<.0001) vs physician summaries; DeepSeek, Mistral, Llama 3.1, 3.2 rated more complete (P=.017, <.0001) with comparable correctness (P=1.000).
quote: Using the original pathology reports as the ground truth, the LLM-generated summaries achieved higher scores across all objective evaluation metrics compared with physician pathology summaries (P < .0001).

title: Precision Grounding: augmenting large language models with evidence-based databases for trustworthy genetic variant summarization
outcome: Accuracy and completeness of variant summaries with curated-database grounding versus web-search grounding
effect: Precision Grounding outperformed web-search grounding, with significantly higher accuracy (4.76, +0.74) and completeness (4.94, +0.84) on 5-point Likert scale; fewer clinically significant hallucinations.
quote: Precision Grounding outperformed web-search grounding, achieving significantly higher accuracy and completeness scores, which were based on a 5-point Likert-Scale of 4.76 (+0.74) and 4.94 (+0.84), respectively.

title: irAE-GPT: leveraging large language models to identify immune-related adverse events in electronic health records and clinical trial datasets
outcome: Generalisability of GPT irAE detection across two EHR systems and seven clinical trials
effect: GPT models demonstrated generalisable abilities in identifying irAEs across EHRs and clinical trial reports; high sensitivity and specificity but only moderate PPV, suggesting overprediction.
quote: The GPT models demonstrated generalisable abilities in identifying irAEs across EHRs and clinical trial reports.

title: Validation of the safety, empathy and utility of a large language model conversation agent for parents of autistic and neurodivergent children
outcome: LLM identification and flagging of safeguarding issues in parent/carer questions
effect: The LLM correctly flagged the safeguarding issue in 100% of the presented questions.
quote: The LLM identified and correctly flagged the safeguarding issue in 100% of the presented questions.

title: Validation of the safety, empathy and utility of a large language model conversation agent for parents of autistic and neurodivergent children
outcome: Blind-rated comparison of LLM and clinician responses to 50 parent/carer questions
effect: Ratings for LLM and clinician responses were highly correlated. The evaluator identified response provenance 74% of the time.
quote: The ratings for LLM and clinician’s responses were highly correlated and the evaluator was able to distinguish which the provenance of the responses (74%).

title: Impact of an AI prognostic tool on clinician performance in colorectal liver metastases
outcome: Reader AUC for 3-year mortality with versus without AI tool assistance
effect: Model assistance significantly improved AUC for 3-year mortality prediction (mean difference 0.091; 95% CI 0.001-0.181; P = 0.048); decision time 2.53 vs 3.04 minutes.
quote: Model assistance significantly improved the AUC for 3-year mortality prediction (mean difference 0.091; 95% CI 0.001-0.181; P = 0.048) and consistently improved accuracy across secondary prognostic endpoints.

title: Benchmarking of large language models to determine candidacy for spine surgery and comparison with conventional machine learning
outcome: LLM versus conventional random forest accuracy for spine surgery recommendation on same vignettes
effect: Zero-shot ChatGPT3.5 RMSE 0.37, AUROC 0.79; random forest RMSE 0.12, AUROC 0.96; fine-tuned LLMs AUROC 0.81-0.90, all below random forest.
quote: The random forest model, trained on the structured data, achieved superior performance (RMSE = 0.12, AUROC = 0.96).

title: ChatGPT as a Tool for Perioperative Safety: Evaluating Drug Interaction Detection in Anesthetic Regimens
outcome: Accuracy of LLM detection of clinically significant drug-drug interactions in anesthetic regimens versus Lexicomp
effect: ChatGPT accurately identified 76 of 80 clinically significant DDIs (sensitivity 95%); four responses incorrect, omitting additional relevant interactions or comprehensive management recommendations.
quote: Across both trials, ChatGPT accurately identified 76 of 80 clinically significant DDIs (sensitivity 95%) with four responses classified as Incorrect.

title: The Impact of Specific Prompt Engineering Techniques on the Readability of LLM-Generated Patient Materials in Gastroenterology and Hepatology
outcome: Readability (SMOG, FKGL) of LLM patient explanations by prompt technique versus 6th grade target
effect: No prompt technique or model consistently produced outputs at or below 6th grade level by SMOG (p<0.001); more constrained prompts yielded significantly more readable outputs (p<0.001).
quote: No prompt technique or model consistently produced outputs at or below a 6th grade reading level when assessed by the SMOG index, the preferred metric when assessing healthcare materials (p < 0.001).

title: The Impact of Specific Prompt Engineering Techniques on the Readability of LLM-Generated Patient Materials in Gastroenterology and Hepatology
outcome: Reading level of LLM-generated patient materials relative to recommended 6th grade level
effect: No prompt technique or model consistently produced output at or below 6th grade SMOG level; less constrained prompts produced less readable outputs across 2655 outputs.
quote: No prompt technique or model consistently produced outputs at or below a 6th grade reading level when assessed by the SMOG index, the preferred metric when assessing healthcare materials (p < 0.001).

title: Invasive haemodynamic validation of an artificial intelligence echocardiographic tool for detecting heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
outcome: Negative predictive value and sensitivity of AI HFpEF detection versus invasive haemodynamics
effect: Sensitivity 30%, specificity 88%, PPV 86%, NPV 33% (exercise RHC, n=28); with PCWP/CO slope, sensitivity 27%, NPV 16%. Negative AI results cannot exclude HFpEF.
quote: Due to limited sensitivity, the tool is best utilized to enrich identification of patients with clearly abnormal haemodynamics rather than to exclude HFpEF, particularly in early or borderline cases.

title: Evaluating the Performance of Large Language Models for Generating Emergency Department Discharge Instructions
outcome: Physician-rated accuracy, clarity, completeness, understandability of GPT-4 discharge instructions
effect: Ratings generally exceeded 4/5; >50% rated 5/5 in each domain; about 25% scored ≤3/5 for completeness or understandability; IRR fair (κ=0.40).
quote: However, approximately 25% of instructions scored ≤ 3/5 for completeness or understandability.
sample_unit: ED diagnoses (discharge instruction sets per model)

title: ChatTogoVar: a TogoVar-based retrieval-augmented generation system for precise genomic variant interpretation
outcome: Accuracy of variant interpretation answers with vs without database-retrieval grounding, versus comparators
effect: ChatTogoVar (RAG grounded in TogoVar) achieved the highest score for 135/150 questions, outperforming a general-purpose LLM and a specialized system; LLM scoring of all 1500 questions confirmed the trend.
quote: ChatTogoVar achieved the highest score for 135/150 questions, outperforming both a general-purpose LLM and an existing specialized system.

title: Multicenter validation and updating of the ELDER-ICU model for severity assessment in elderly critical illness
