quote: Paid-access platforms outperformed free-access platforms in DISCERN (median 42, IQR 36-45 vs 33, IQR 23.8-41.3; P<.001), PEMAT-P (median 52.6, IQR 46-54 vs 46, IQR 26.3-47.4; P=.002), and WRR (median 26.8, IQR 23.2-26.8 vs 10.7, IQR 3.57-19.6; P<.001).
sample_unit: chatbot platform responses to a single standardized query, rated by 7 neurologists

title: Errors in AI-Transformed Patient-Centered Mental Health Documentation Written by Psychiatrists: Qualitative Pre-Post Study
outcome: Errors introduced by LLM when converting psychiatric notes into patient-facing text
effect: Five categories of clinically relevant errors identified (clinical misinterpretation, attribution, content distortion, abbreviation/terminology, structural/syntax) despite improved readability; errors described as prevalent.
quote: However, critical errors remain prevalent and can impair clinical judgment, understanding of patient circumstances, clarity of medication regimens, and interpretation of clinical observations.

title: Errors in AI-Transformed Patient-Centered Mental Health Documentation Written by Psychiatrists: Qualitative Pre-Post Study
outcome: Errors in AI-transformed clinical notes that would reach patients without clinician review
effect: Five categories of clinically relevant errors found in LLM-revised notes, including misrepresentation of suicidality assessments; authors conclude clinician oversight is essential.
quote: To safely integrate artificial intelligence-generated documentation into psychiatric care, clinician oversight and targeted model refinement are essential.

title: Assessing the clinical reasoning of large language models on complex rheumatology cases: A multidimensional evaluation of four artificial intelligence
outcome: Correlation between LLM reasoning quality and expressed certainty (calibration)
effect: Weak, non-significant associations between reasoning quality and expressed certainty across all models (rho range -0.156 to 0.215, all p>0.05), indicating miscalibration.
quote: However, Spearman correlation analysis revealed uniformly weak and non-significant associations between reasoning quality and expressed certainty across all models (ρ range: -0.156 to 0.215, all p>0.05), indicating fundamental miscalibration.
sample_unit: complex rheumatologic case vignettes (each evaluated at 3 time points per model)

title: Assessing the clinical reasoning of large language models on complex rheumatology cases: A multidimensional evaluation of four artificial intelligence
outcome: Temporal stability/reproducibility of LLM outputs across repeated runs at Days 1, 5, 10
effect: Temporal stability was excellent for ChatGPT (ICC=0.84) and good for DeepSeek (ICC=0.79).
quote: Temporal stability was excellent for ChatGPT (ICC=0.84) and good for DeepSeek (ICC=0.79).
sample_unit: complex rheumatologic case vignettes (each evaluated at 3 time points per model)

title: Assessing the clinical reasoning of large language models on complex rheumatology cases: A multidimensional evaluation of four artificial intelligence
outcome: Hallucination frequency of LLMs on rheumatology cases
effect: ChatGPT lowest hallucination rate (7.4%); Gemini highest (18.5%).
quote: ChatGPT demonstrated the highest reasoning score (3.89±0.23) and lowest hallucination rate (7.4%), while Gemini showed the highest hallucination frequency (18.5%).
sample_unit: complex rheumatologic case vignettes (each evaluated at 3 time points per model)

title: Evaluating Large Language Models in Crisis Detection: A Real-World Benchmark from Psychological Support Hotlines
venue: IEEE journal of biomedical and health informatics
outcome: LLM performance versus trained human operators on crisis assessment tasks
effect: LLMs comparable or superior on suicide plan identification and risk assessment; humans retained advantages on mood status recognition and suicidal ideation detection.
quote: Compared to trained human operators, LLMs achieved comparable or superior performance on suicide plan identification and risk assessment, while humans retained advantages on mood status recognition and suicidal ideation detection.

title: Evaluating Large Language Models in Crisis Detection: A Real-World Benchmark from Psychological Support Hotlines
venue: IEEE journal of biomedical and health informatics
outcome: LLM performance on real-world crisis transcripts across four tasks
effect: F1 0.880 suicidal ideation, 0.779 suicide plan, 0.907 risk assessment; mood recognition max F1 0.709.
quote: LLMs showed strong results in suicidal ideation detection (F1 = 0.880), suicide plan identification (F1 = 0.779), and risk assessment (F1 = 0.907), with notable gains from few shot prompting and fine-tuning.

title: Research on the generalization of a blood donor recruitment framework based on machine learning
venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
outcome: Recall at new sites after fine-tuning with 10% local data
effect: Fine-tuning with 10% local data raised Suzhou RF recall from 0.67 to 0.77 and Yangzhou MLP recall from 0.58 to 0.68.
quote: Subsequent fine-tuning with 10% local data further enhanced performance on top of direct generalization (Suzhou RF recall increased to 0.77, Yangzhou MLP to 0.68), rather than compensating for any shortcomings of generalization.
sample_unit: prospective SMS recruitment rounds (model development used 11,616 Nanjing SMS records)

title: Research on the generalization of a blood donor recruitment framework based on machine learning
venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
outcome: Cross-site recall of Nanjing-trained models in Suzhou and Yangzhou
effect: Transferred RF recall was 0.67 in Suzhou vs 0.77 locally, and 0.63 in Yangzhou vs 0.64 locally. MLP recall was 0.63 and 0.58.
quote: Specifically, the RF model achieved a recall of 0.67 in Suzhou (compared to 0.77 with local optimization) and 0.63 in Yangzhou (versus 0.64 locally), while the MLP model attained recall scores of 0.63 and 0.58, respectively.
sample_unit: prospective SMS recruitment rounds (model development used 11,616 Nanjing SMS records)

title: Research on the generalization of a blood donor recruitment framework based on machine learning
venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
outcome: Recruitment success compared with conventional donor selection
effect: High-willingness donor recruitment success was 408.28%, 25.19%, and 47.31% higher than conventional methods in Nanjing, Suzhou, and Yangzhou, respectively.
quote: On average, the recruitment success rate for high-willingness donors was 408.28%, 25.19%, and 47.31% higher than that of conventional methods in Nanjing (χ 2 = 35.471, p = 0.000), Suzhou (χ 2 = 9.384, p = 0.009), and Yangzhou (χ 2 = 96.701, p = 0.000), respectively, as shown in Table 1 .
sample_unit: prospective SMS recruitment rounds (model development used 11,616 Nanjing SMS records)

title: Research on the generalization of a blood donor recruitment framework based on machine learning
venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
outcome: recall rates across separate sites
effect: models achieved recall rates of 0.63 and 0.67 in Suzhou, and 0.58 and 0.63 in Yangzhou
quote: The fine-tuned models demonstrated good generalizability, achieving recall rates of 0.63 and 0.67 in Suzhou, and 0.58 and 0.63 in Yangzhou, respectively.
sample_unit: prospective SMS recruitment rounds (model development used 11,616 Nanjing SMS records)

title: Research on the generalization of a blood donor recruitment framework based on machine learning
venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
outcome: recruitment success rate in prospective validation
effect: increased the recruitment success rate for high-willingness donors by an average of 151.57%
quote: It increased the recruitment success rate for high-willingness donors by an average of 151.57% (up to 408.28% in Nanjing) while recruitment efficiency increased by an average of 96.52% (up to 138.75% in Yangzhou).
sample_unit: prospective SMS recruitment rounds (model development used 11,616 Nanjing SMS records)

title: ArcMAP - ML assisted medical concept mapping to accelerate NHS data standardization
outcome: Top-1 accuracy for lab test mapping before vs after fine-tuning on local data
effect: BioLORD top-1 accuracy rose from 37.0% (baseline) to 91.6% after fine-tuning on local hospital data; all models reached 89.0-93.0% top-1 with full training data.
quote: Our results demonstrate the importance of domain-specific fine-tuning, with top-1 accuracy for laboratory test names increasing from 37.0% to 91.6%.
sample_unit: source concepts (6,179 medication names and 2,261 laboratory test names)

title: ArcMAP - ML assisted medical concept mapping to accelerate NHS data standardization
outcome: Real-world lab test mapping accuracy vs published benchmark performance
effect: Models reporting 80%-90% top-1 on standard benchmarks achieved baseline top-1 below 40% on real NHS laboratory test names (BioLORD 37.0%).
quote: Consequently, baseline top-1 accuracies remain below 40%, underscoring that pre-training on biomedical literature and ontology definitions alone is insufficient to capture the extreme variability and abbreviation patterns encountered in laboratory test naming.
sample_unit: source concepts (6,179 medication names and 2,261 laboratory test names)

title: ArcMAP - ML assisted medical concept mapping to accelerate NHS data standardization
outcome: Cosine similarity confidence for correct vs incorrect predictions
effect: Mean cosine similarity 0.97 ± 0.06 for correct (n=457) vs 0.81 ± 0.14 for incorrect (n=64) predictions; Welch t=8.8, p<0.01.
quote: Results indicate a significant difference in mean similarity score under Welch's t -test (t-statistic: 8.8 p -value <0.01), highlighting the model's ability to quantify uncertainty in its predictions.
sample_unit: source concepts (6,179 medication names and 2,261 laboratory test names)

title: ArcMAP - ML assisted medical concept mapping to accelerate NHS data standardization
outcome: Mapping accuracy when generalizing to an unseen hospital
effect: BioLORD top-1 accuracy decreased from 91.6% in the fully fine-tuned setting to 73.5% when evaluated on hospitals excluded from training.
quote: Evaluating the onboarding of a new hospital (Exp1-S3) revealed a reduction in mean performance, with BioLORD's top-1 accuracy decreasing from 91.6% in the fully fine-tuned setting to 73.5%.
sample_unit: source concepts (6,179 medication names and 2,261 laboratory test names)

title: ArcMAP - ML assisted medical concept mapping to accelerate NHS data standardization
outcome: Mapping accuracy on a held-out new hospital and variation across hospitals
effect: Weighted top-1 accuracy on an unseen hospital was 73.5% vs 91.6% fully fine-tuned; per-hospital finetuned top-1 ranged 25.0% to 96.3%; baseline std across hospitals 7.9% for lab tests.
quote: However, when simulating the onboarding of a new hospital, the system achieves a weighted average top-1 accuracy of only 73.5%, indicating substantial variability across NHS hospital systems.
sample_unit: source concepts (6,179 medication names and 2,261 laboratory test names)

title: ArcMAP - ML assisted medical concept mapping to accelerate NHS data standardization
outcome: mapping efficiency
effect: estimated >2-fold increase in efficiency when using ArcMAP compared to manual sessions
quote: In contrast, during the manual mapping sessions without ArcMAP, only 31.7 ± 0.9 ( Supplementary Table 2 ) concepts were mapped on average, resulting in an estimated >2-fold increase in efficiency when using ArcMAP.
sample_unit: source concepts (6,179 medication names and 2,261 laboratory test names)

title: Development, validation, and pilot implementation of a prognostic model to predict future foot complications among people with diabetes recently discharged from hospital
outcome: Variation in discrimination and calibration across held-out hospitals
effect: Pooled AUROC 0.71 (95% CI 0.70-0.73) and 0.72 (0.70-0.73), but discrimination and calibration varied substantially across hospitals.
quote: However, discrimination and calibration varied substantially across hospitals.

title: Development, validation, and pilot implementation of a prognostic model to predict future foot complications among people with diabetes recently discharged from hospital
outcome: Performance in held-out sites using internal-external cross-validation
effect: Good pooled discrimination in held-out hospitals (AUROC 0.71, 0.72), but substantial variation in discrimination and calibration across hospitals.
quote: However, discrimination and calibration varied substantially across hospitals.

title: Open-Source Large Language Models Distilled DeepSeek-R1 Pose Challenges for On-Premises Clinical Deployment in Medical Diagnosis: A Comparative Study of Performance
outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of reasoning models versus their base models on the same cases
effect: R1-671B beat DeepSeek-V3 (95.45% vs 88.18%; p=0.008); R1-8B underperformed Llama3.1-8B (47.27% vs 64.54%; p=0.003); no significant differences for mid-sized models.
quote: The study concludes that the DeepSeek-R1-671B shows potential for medical diagnosis, but distilled models do not exceed their base models.

title: Open-Source Large Language Models Distilled DeepSeek-R1 Pose Challenges for On-Premises Clinical Deployment in Medical Diagnosis: A Comparative Study of Performance
outcome: Error modes in chain-of-thought for incorrect diagnostic cases, including diagnostic priority inversion
effect: Three error modes prevalent across distilled models: reasoning drift, red-flag recognition failure, and diagnostic priority inversion (qualitative; no counts reported).
quote: Qualitative analysis of the chain-of-thought outputs in incorrect cases revealed three universally prevalent error modes across distilled models: Reasoning drift, Red-Flag recognition failure, and diagnostic priority inversion.

title: Open-Source Large Language Models Distilled DeepSeek-R1 Pose Challenges for On-Premises Clinical Deployment in Medical Diagnosis: A Comparative Study of Performance
outcome: Recognition of red-flag (serious) findings in incorrect diagnostic cases
effect: Red-flag recognition failure was one of three universally prevalent error modes in distilled models' incorrect cases (qualitative; no counts reported).
quote: Qualitative analysis of the chain-of-thought outputs in incorrect cases revealed three universally prevalent error modes across distilled models: Reasoning drift, Red-Flag recognition failure, and diagnostic priority inversion.

title: Fluoroscopic image-driven deep learning model for predicting intussusception irreducibility during air enema in children
outcome: Radiologist diagnostic performance with versus without AI assistance
effect: Assistive use significantly improved radiologists' performance (all P < 0.01): AUC improvements of 0.095-0.072, balanced accuracy gains of 8.6-11.7%, specificity increases of 18.7-22.6%.
quote: When used as an assistive tool, the model significantly improved radiologists' diagnostic performance (all P < 0.01), with AUC improvements of 0.095-0.072, balanced accuracy gains of 8.6-11.7%, and specificity increases of 18.7-22.6%.
sample_unit: cases (real-world test set: 46 irreducible and 802 reducible)

title: Fluoroscopic image-driven deep learning model for predicting intussusception irreducibility during air enema in children
outcome: AI model AUC compared with radiologists and other methods on same data
effect: Model AUC 0.89 vs intermediate radiologist 0.804 (P < 0.001) and senior radiologist 0.842 (P = 0.108); outperformed comparative methods (AUC ranges 0.823-0.877 and 0.634-0.826).
quote: The model demonstrated superior performance compared with that of the intermediate radiologist (AUC: 0.89 vs. 0.804; P < 0.001) and comparable performance to that of a senior radiologist (AUC: 0.89 vs. 0.842; P = 0.108).
sample_unit: cases (real-world test set: 46 irreducible and 802 reducible)

title: Evaluating large language models for orthodontic consultation in patients with periodontitis: a study of reliability, quality, and readability
outcome: Readability (FRE, FKGL) of LLM responses to periodontitis orthodontic patient questions
effect: All models produced university-level readability; DeepSeek-V3 most readable (FRE 33.61, FKGL 10.10); Claude-Sonnet-4 least readable (FRE 4.73, FKGL 13.72).
quote: All models produced responses with university-level readability.

title: Evaluating large language models for orthodontic consultation in patients with periodontitis: a study of reliability, quality, and readability
outcome: Reading level of LLM patient-education responses versus recommended thresholds
effect: All models exceeded recommended readability thresholds for patient education; FKGL ranged from 10.10 (DeepSeek-V3) to 13.72 (Claude-Sonnet-4).
quote: All models exceed recommended readability thresholds for patient education.

title: Measuring the gap: correlating synthetic-to-real drift with PHI de-identification performance
outcome: Correlation of train-to-eval lexical/semantic drift with out-of-distribution PHI tagger F1
effect: Drift measures moderately correlated with out-of-distribution F1; models trained on broad clinical sources transferred better than those trained on legal or narrowly synthetic data.
quote: We found that compact distributional and embedding-based drift measures moderately correlate with out-of-distribution F1 score, a practically important result because drift estimation can improve synthetic-data quality control and alignment.

title: Independent validation of the Mosamatic deep learning automated skeletal muscle and adipose tissue segmentation tool in an external Chinese cancer patient cohort
outcome: Agreement of automated vs manual CT segmentation on local historical data against reference standard
effect: Median Dice 0.973 muscle, 0.980 VAT, 0.967 SAT; Lin's CCC 0.983-1.000; excellent generalizability without recalibration in Chinese cohort
quote: The Mosamatic tool displays excellent generalizability to analyse body compositions in Chinese gastric cancer patients and can facilitate cachexia research.

title: Independent validation of the Mosamatic deep learning automated skeletal muscle and adipose tissue segmentation tool in an external Chinese cancer patient cohort
outcome: Performance of European-trained model in Chinese external population
effect: Excellent generalizability without recalibration; low BMI (<18.5) and ascites impaired agreement between methods
quote: The Mosamatic tool displayed excellent generalizability without recalibration to analyse body composition on the 3rd lumbar vertebral CT images in Chinese gastric cancer patients.

title: The Role of Explanations in AI-Generated Alerts: Qualitative Study of Clinical Views on Explainable AI in Predictive Tools
outcome: Clinician reaction to discrepant explanations from different XAI methods (disagreement problem)
effect: Discrepancies between explanations from different XAI methods were not a major concern to clinicians as long as the predictive alerts were accurate.
quote: Discrepancies in explanations generated by different XAI methods were not a major concern, provided that the AI-generated predictive alerts were accurate.

title: The Role of Explanations in AI-Generated Alerts: Qualitative Study of Clinical Views on Explainable AI in Predictive Tools
outcome: Clinician perceived value of explanations for AI predictive alerts
effect: Clinicians valued explainability, especially in complex or unfamiliar situations, when explanations were clear, plausible and actionable; its importance diminished with familiarity and expertise.
quote: Clinicians valued explainability, particularly in complex or unfamiliar situations, when explanations were clear, plausible, and actionable.

title: Artificial Intelligence for histopathological diagnosis and grading of breast cancer in Ethiopia
outcome: DeepGrade grading performance on local retrospective slides against pathologist reference
effect: 100% specificity for low-grade tumours, 82.05% sensitivity for high-grade, AUC 0.914, agreement 86.79%, Kappa 0.71 (95% CI 0.51-0.90)
quote: The DeepGrade model reached a 100% specificity for low-grade tumours and an 82.05% sensitivity for high-grade tumours, with an AUC of 0.914 and an agreement level of 86.79%.

title: ChatGPT in Public Cardiovascular Healthcare: Accuracy, Limitations, and Implications
venue: Journal of evaluation in clinical practice
outcome: Correctness of ChatGPT diagnostic hypotheses, recommended exams and lab tests versus physician records
effect: ChatGPT correct in 43% of diagnostic hypotheses, 5% of recommended supplementary exams, and 10% of laboratory tests; responses often partially accurate and unnecessarily detailed.
quote: When compared to physicians' records, ChatGPT provided correct responses in 43% of diagnostic hypotheses, 5% of recommended supplementary exams, and 10% of laboratory tests.

title: Reliability and readability of five AI chatbots for concussion health advice across retrieval augmented and pretrained models
outcome: Reading grade level of chatbot concussion advice versus 6th-grade benchmark
effect: No chatbot met the 6th-grade level on all measures; most exceeded 10th grade; Perplexity lowest FKGL 7.46; Copilot FKGL 12.55, Gemini 12.97; FRES 27.7–54.2 vs 80–90 target.
quote: The overall result was the noncompliance of all five AI platforms: none of them achieved the recommended 6th grade reading level (AMA/CDC standard) in all measures.

title: Reliability and readability of five AI chatbots for concussion health advice across retrieval augmented and pretrained models
outcome: Information quality (DISCERN, EQIP) of retrieval-augmented vs pretrained chatbots
effect: Perplexity Pro DISCERN 47.36 vs ChatGPT 36.18 and EQIP 65.00 vs 52.73; RAG systems higher than ChatGPT/Gemini (r=0.545–0.638); GQS did not differ (p=0.373).
quote: Dunn post hoc testing (Table 2 ) showed that Perplexity Pro scored significantly higher than ChatGPT and Gemini on both DISCERN and EQIP ( r = 0.545–0.638), indicating large effect sizes for these comparisons.

title: Reliability and readability of five AI chatbots for concussion health advice across retrieval augmented and pretrained models
outcome: Transparency and attribution of chatbot responses via JAMA benchmarks
effect: JAMA transparency uniformly low: ChatGPT 0.00, DeepSeek 0.00, Gemini 0.00, Copilot 0.64, Perplexity 1.00 out of 4 (H=40.35, p<0.001).
quote: JAMA-based transparency remained uniformly low (p < 0.001).

title: Reliability and readability of five AI chatbots for concussion health advice across retrieval augmented and pretrained models
outcome: Output quality against Amsterdam Consensus reference standards via DISCERN, EQIP, GQS
effect: Quality varied by model: DISCERN 36.18–47.36, EQIP 52.73–65.00; GQS moderate to good (2.91–3.36) without significant differences (p=0.373).
quote: Kruskal–Wallis testing identified significant between-model differences for DISCERN ( H = 20.161, p = 0.0005, η 2 = 0.323), EQIP ( H = 20.432, p = 0.0004, η 2 = 0.329), and JAMA ( H = 40.350, p < 0.001, η 2 = 0.727).

title: Reliability and readability of five AI chatbots for concussion health advice across retrieval augmented and pretrained models
outcome: Plain-language comprehensibility of AI-generated patient education outputs
effect: All five chatbots exceeded 6th-grade level; FKGL and GFI stayed above 10th grade for most; FRES far below the 80–90 plain-English range.
quote: Both FKGL and GFI indices maintained the content at both high-school to collegiate reading level (> 10th grade).

title: Performance Modeling of Lightweight Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models for Low-Resource Plastic Surgery Settings
outcome: Semantic similarity to reference answers across RAG configurations, including database size and embedding model
effect: Larger database sizes significantly improved semantic similarity (size 5: +0.043, p = 0.001); bge-large-en-v1.5 improved performance (p = 0.0016); Bio_ClinicalBERT reduced it (p < 0.001). Mean similarity up to 0.786.
quote: Larger database sizes significantly improved semantic similarity, with the largest gain at intermediate sizes (e.g., size 5: +0.043, p = 0.001).

title: Unlikely Storyteller: Leveraging Narrative-Based Communication in LLM-Generated Medical Advice
outcome: Terminology explanation frequency per reply across clinician, unprompted AI, and prompted AI
effect: Terminology explanations per reply: clinician 0.301, unprompted AI 1.337, prompted AI 1.981; replies with no explanation fell from 81.1% (clinician) to 38.3% (unprompted) to 15.3% (prompted).
quote: With the narrative prompt, explanation density increased further to 1.981 (95% CI [1.901, 2.061]), while the share of replies offering no explanation fell to 15.3% (Wilson 95% CI [0.132, 0.177]).

title: Unlikely Storyteller: Leveraging Narrative-Based Communication in LLM-Generated Medical Advice
outcome: Coded empathy (verbal support, emotion-symptom linkage) in clinician vs zero-shot vs narrative-prompted LLM replies
effect: Verbal empathy per reply: 0.092 clinician, 0.434 unprompted, 1.99 prompted. Emotion-symptom linkage: 2.6%, 14.4%, 99.1%.
quote: Under narrative prompting, however, the probability becomes near-universal (99.1%; 95% CI 98.3–99.5%).

title: More AI, Less Care-Seeking? A National Survey Experiment on the Impact of AI Intensity on Patient Care-Seeking Intention in Chinese Family Doctor Services
outcome: Patient care-seeking intention (7-point) by AI integration intensity versus human-only vignette
effect: Versus human-only, low (β=-0.682), medium (β=-1.053), high (β=-1.267) AI intensity lowered care-seeking intention (all p<0.001); sharpest drop when the doctor deferred completely to AI.
quote: Relative to the human-only baseline, low (β = −0.682, p < 0.001), medium (β = −1.053, p < 0.001), and high (β = −1.267, p < 0.001) AI intensity were each associated with significantly lower care-seeking intention, demonstrating a graded negative effect.

title: Assessing the Accuracy and Readability of Generative Artificial Intelligence Responses for Esophageal and Gastric Cancer Patients
outcome: Reading grade level of GenAI responses to patient questions (Flesch-Kincaid Reading Ease, Grade Level, SMOG)
effect: All four models (Kimi, DeepSeek, ChatGPT, Gemini) produced responses requiring 11th-grade to college reading level.
quote: The responses produced by all models required a reading capacity from 11th-grade to college level.

title: Assessment of Stage Two Hypertension Treatment Plans Written by Generative AI
outcome: Whether LLM hypertension treatment plans provided sources
effect: LLMs often did not provide sources; composite scores varied widely (Perplexity 8.17/9 to Dyna AI 3.75/9).
quote: LLMs tended to adhere to clinical guidelines and provide detailed responses but often did not provide sources or instruct users to see a healthcare professional.
sample_unit: LLM-generated treatment plans (one per model), each scored by six blinded reviewers

title: Assessment of Stage Two Hypertension Treatment Plans Written by Generative AI
outcome: Whether LLM treatment plans instructed users to see a healthcare professional
effect: LLMs often did not instruct users to see a healthcare professional.
quote: LLMs tended to adhere to clinical guidelines and provide detailed responses but often did not provide sources or instruct users to see a healthcare professional.
sample_unit: LLM-generated treatment plans (one per model), each scored by six blinded reviewers

title: Predictive Utility of the Vedolizumab Clinical Decision Support Tool in a Real-World IBD Cohort: Differential Performance in Crohn's Disease and Ulcerative Colitis
outcome: Predictive value of CDST risk groups for clinical, endoscopic outcomes and persistence in local real-world cohort
effect: CDST failed to predict PRO-2 clinical remission; in CD it associated with week-52 CSFR (p=0.04), endoscopic outcomes (p<0.001), persistence (p=0.004); no predictive association in UC.
quote: In UC, no predictive association was observed for either clinical or endoscopic outcomes nor treatment persistence; however, we observed relatively high remission rates despite CDST-based stratification.

title: PKGPT: Expert-Orchestrated Recursive LLM Agent for Automated NONMEM PopPK Modeling with Human Benchmarking
outcome: Run-to-run reproducibility of LLM-generated NONMEM models across repeated runs
effect: Run-to-run reproducibility was variable; PKGPT also missed clinically established covariates in all datasets.
quote: Across datasets, PKGPT did not identify clinically established covariates, and run-to-run reproducibility was variable.

title: Artificial intelligence adoption in French cardiovascular care: a multiprofessional survey of barriers and facilitators
outcome: Self-reported confidence in AI diagnostic outputs with versus without explanations, among cardiologists
effect: High confidence in therapeutic contexts rose from 64% without explanations to 84% with explanations (stated confidence in a survey, not measured decision quality).
quote: Explainability increased confidence (among cardiologists, high confidence 64% in therapeutic contexts vs. 84% with explanations).

title: A Cross-Sectional Study Evaluating the Quality of AI-Generated Patient Education Guides on Diet and Exercise for Diabetes, Hypertension, and Obesity Using ChatGPT-4o, Google Gemini 1.5, Claude Sonnet 4, Perplexity, and Grok
outcome: Readability (Flesch-Kincaid grade level) of LLM-generated patient education brochures
effect: ChatGPT lowest grade level (5.2 ± 0.8), Flesch Reading Ease 70.0 ± 5.1; Gemini and Claude at about 9th grade reading level.
quote: Gemini and Claude produced longer, more elaborate brochures that received higher reliability ratings (3.0 ± 0.0 and 3.0 ± 1.0, respectively) but were at higher reading levels (≈ 9th grade).

title: Evaluating the Accuracy, Readability, and Consistency of Artificial Intelligence Models in Patient Education for Rheumatoid Arthritis, Osteoarthritis, and Psoriatic Arthritis
outcome: Readability grade level of LLM patient education responses versus AMA/NIH recommended sixth-to-eighth grade
effect: No model consistently met sixth-to-eighth grade levels; OpenEvidence was at or above 17th grade, while ChatGPT and Gemini averaged 11.9-12.0 grade.
quote: No model consistently met the American Medical Association (AMA)/National Institutes of Health (NIH)-recommended reading levels for sixth through eighth grade.

title: Evaluating the Accuracy, Readability, and Consistency of Artificial Intelligence Models in Patient Education for Rheumatoid Arthritis, Osteoarthritis, and Psoriatic Arthritis
outcome: Reading level of AI-generated patient education material relative to recommended level
effect: All three LLMs produced content above recommended reading levels; OpenEvidence was at or above 17th grade (postbaccalaureate), ChatGPT and Gemini about 12th grade.
quote: No model consistently met the American Medical Association (AMA)/National Institutes of Health (NIH)-recommended reading levels for sixth through eighth grade.

title: Evaluating the Accuracy, Readability, and Consistency of Artificial Intelligence Models in Patient Education for Rheumatoid Arthritis, Osteoarthritis, and Psoriatic Arthritis
outcome: Day-to-day consistency (Jaccard similarity) of LLM responses to identical questions
effect: ChatGPT was most stable (range <0.07), Gemini moderately variable, OpenEvidence had the widest range (0.24) and highest average similarity (0.383).
quote: ChatGPT showed the highest day-to-day stability (range: <0.07), Gemini moderate variability, and OpenEvidence both the widest range (0.24) and the highest average similarity (0.383).

title: Deriving the OTA/AO fracture classification from routinely collected radiology reports using a large language model
venue: OTA international : the open access journal of orthopaedic trauma
outcome: Agreement with expert OTA/AO labels with retrieval-augmented generation versus zero-shot and chain-of-thought prompting
effect: On radiology reports the 3 strategies performed similarly (RAG did not improve). On ideal descriptions RAG was better: full-label accuracy 0.38 with RAG vs 0.08 without.
quote: On the other hand, RAG did not improve performance on classification labels produced from radiology reports, which could be due to the imprecise nature of the descriptions contained within the reports, rendering the extra data less useful and providing an opportunity for future training.

title: Deriving the OTA/AO fracture classification from routinely collected radiology reports using a large language model
venue: OTA international : the open access journal of orthopaedic trauma
outcome: LLM classification performance given imprecise real-world radiology report descriptions versus ideal descriptions
effect: Agreement fell from almost perfect at bone/location level to slight at subgroup level (accuracy 0.09 zero-shot) on radiology reports; ideal descriptions performed better.
quote: The consequence was that the LLM classifications could only be as precise as the descriptions they were generated from.

title: Deriving the OTA/AO fracture classification from routinely collected radiology reports using a large language model
venue: OTA international : the open access journal of orthopaedic trauma
outcome: explanation fidelity

title: A TyG-UHR-based machine learning model for screening lean MAFLD: development and external validation
outcome: Calibration/probability accuracy on external NHANES hold-out before vs after local recalibration
effect: Brier score fell from 0.286 to 0.109 and log loss from 1.253 to 0.388 after recalibration; AUC 0.826 vs 0.810; calibration intercept 0.103, slope 0.684.
quote: Probability accuracy improved significantly: the Brier score decreased from 0.286 to 0.109, and the log loss from 1.253 to 0.388.

title: A TyG-UHR-based machine learning model for screening lean MAFLD: development and external validation
outcome: Performance on external population versus internal test set
effect: Internal test AUC 0.995 versus external NHANES hold-out AUC 0.826 before recalibration and 0.810 after; miscalibration before recalibration.
quote: On the hold-out validation subset, discrimination was good before recalibration (AUC = 0.826) (Fig. 5 A) and remained similar after applying the fixed calibrator (AUC = 0.810).

title: A TyG-UHR-based machine learning model for screening lean MAFLD: development and external validation
outcome: candidate algorithm comparison
effect: XGBoost best: AUC 0.995, F1 0.955, accuracy 0.992, precision/specificity 1.000, sensitivity 0.914; RF second AUC 0.990.
quote: XGBoost demonstrated the best discrimination (AUC 0.995) and, at the F1-max threshold, the strongest overall classification performance with an F1 score (F1) of 0.955, accuracy (ACC) of 0.992, precision (PRE) of 1.000, specificity (SPE) of 1.000, and sensitivity (SEN) of 0.914.

title: Clinical-ShiftEval: a framework for simulating and evaluating model adaptation in dynamic clinical NLP tasks
venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
outcome: Performance degradation of static clinical NLP models under distributional and task-definition drift
effect: Conventional supervised models showed severe degradation, up to 82% F1 drop in LSI and 43% in TDE.
quote: Conventional supervised models showed severe degradation under these shifts (up to a drop of 82% F1 in LSI and 43% in TDE).

title: Clinical-ShiftEval: a framework for simulating and evaluating model adaptation in dynamic clinical NLP tasks
venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
outcome: Recovery of performance and error rates after retraining on new-period data
effect: After retraining on period B, FNR and FPR decreased markedly toward baseline; the confusion-matrix diagonal was largely restored in LSI.
quote: After retraining on period B data, both FNR and FPR decreased markedly, approaching baseline levels.

title: Clinical-ShiftEval: a framework for simulating and evaluating model adaptation in dynamic clinical NLP tasks
venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
outcome: Model performance when applied to a new label set or task definition (new context)
effect: Legacy models trained on period A had severe F1 drops on period B; both FNR and FPR increased substantially in TDE.
quote: When the model trained on period A was directly evaluated on period B without retraining, both error rates increased substantially relative to the baseline evaluation on period A.

title: Clinical-ShiftEval: a framework for simulating and evaluating model adaptation in dynamic clinical NLP tasks
venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
outcome: F1 drop on shifted period B data
effect: Conventional supervised models dropped up to 82% F1 in LSI and 43% in TDE.
quote: Conventional supervised models showed severe degradation under these shifts (up to a drop of 82% F1 in LSI and 43% in TDE).

title: Wheeze detection in real-world pediatric care: AI applied to smartphone lung auscultation
outcome: Wheeze detection accuracy and F1-score across pediatric age subgroups
effect: Overall accuracy 87% (95% CI 86-89), F1 61% (56-66); best accuracy in adolescents (92%), best F1 in pre-school children (64%), so performance varied by age group.
quote: The best accuracy was found in adolescents (92%, 95% CI 90-94) and the best global F1-score in pre-school children recordings (64%, 95% CI 58-71).

title: Sociodemographic bias in large language model clinical trial screening
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
outcome: LLM trial eligibility and related-domain judgments across counterfactual sociodemographic label variants versus control
effect: Across 58 protocols and 5.3 million evaluations, eligibility judgments were largely stable across identities. Race and ethnicity had minimal effects after accounting for socioeconomic status. Homelessness produced the largest negative eligibility shift and pronounced effects in adherence, resources, and trust.
quote: Homelessness produced the largest negative eligibility shift and pronounced effects in adherence, resources, and trust.
sample_unit: LLM evaluations (58 protocols, control plus 33 identity variants, nine LLMs)

title: What do clinicians edit in ambient AI-drafted clinical documentation? A qualitative content analysis
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
outcome: Frequency of clinician edits to ambient AI note content (facts, orders, symptoms, medications, diagnoses)
effect: Most edited content was clinical facts: orders 40.0%, symptoms 30.3%, medication prescriptions 27.3%, diagnosis descriptions 25.9%; terminology edits 11.6%, language style 7.2%.
quote: The most frequently edited content pertained to clinical facts including orders (eg, procedures, lab tests) (40.0%), symptoms (30.3%), medication prescriptions (27.3%), and diagnosis descriptions (25.9%).

title: What do clinicians edit in ambient AI-drafted clinical documentation? A qualitative content analysis
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
outcome: Need for specialty-specific detail edits in ambient AI drafts
effect: Thematic analysis found clinicians edited drafts to add medical specialty-specific details, one of 5 main edit types, indicating generic drafts fit specialties poorly.
quote: The results of our thematic analysis show that most edits can be categorized into one of the following 5 types: to revise factual discrepancies, to add medical specialty-specific details, to express diagnostic certainties, to convert patient expressions into objective assessments recorded in medical terms, and to reorganize or condense content.

title: Awareness, attitudes, and perceived barriers to artificial intelligence adoption in Turkish clinical biochemistry laboratories: An exploratory cross-sectional survey
outcome: Proportion of laboratory staff who had received AI-related training
effect: 57.6% had never received AI-related training; 83.5% cited absence of trained personnel as a barrier; greatest knowledge deficits in image processing (49.4% no knowledge) and predictive analytics (35.9%).
quote: More than half (57.6%) had never received AI-related training, and current use of AI tools in routine practice was minimal.

title: Diagnostic accuracy and citation integrity of four large language models on otolaryngology vignettes
venue: European archives of oto-rhino-laryngology : official journal of the European Federation of Oto-Rhino-Laryngological Societies (EUFOS) : affiliated with the German Society for Oto-Rhino-Laryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
outcome: Citation hallucination rate in LLM diagnostic responses
effect: ChatGPT-4 produced the fewest citations and had the highest hallucination rate (23.0%); OpenEvidence provided more consistent and verifiable references.
quote: OpenEvidence and Perplexity generated the most citations per response, while ChatGPT-4 produced the fewest and had the highest hallucination rate (23.0%).

title: Benchmarking large language models in breast cancer care: agreement with radiology-led multidisciplinary tumor board decisions
venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
outcome: LLM treatment recommendation concordance with multidisciplinary tumor board decisions as comparator
effect: ChatGPT-4o 83.2%, Claude 3.7 Sonnet 79.7%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 79.4% overall concordance; Luminal A ~66%; mastectomy F1 <58; axillary dissection F1 ≤23.5.
quote: ChatGPT-4o demonstrated the highest overall concordance with MDTB decisions (83.2%), followed by Claude 3.7 Sonnet (79.7%) and Gemini 2.5 Pro (79.4%).

title: Patient and Public Perceptions of Artificial Intelligence in Breast Imaging and Clinical Decision-Making: An Exploratory Cross-Sectional Survey Study
outcome: Patient awareness of and trust in AI use in breast clinics
effect: 80% reported no knowledge of AI use in breast clinics; only 37% would trust AI findings. Knowledge gap identified as a barrier to acceptance.
quote: Eighty percent reported no knowledge of AI use in breast clinics, and only 37% would trust AI findings.

title: A Comparison of a Customized Peripheral Artery Disease (PAD)-Specific Generative AI Chatbot and General-Purpose AI Chatbots for PAD Patient Education
outcome: Readability grade level of chatbot patient-education responses, plain-language customized vs general chatbots
effect: VERA (5th-grade system prompt) median FK grade 6.6 vs 7.5 ChatGPT, 9.0 Gemini, 8.0 Claude; Flesch Reading Ease 72 vs 52.5-57 (p<0.001 vs each). Comprehensiveness lower.
quote: VERA produced responses at a median grade level of 6.6 [4.7, 7.0] compared with 7.5 [6.2, 9.7] for ChatGPT, 9.0 [7.4, 10.2] for Gemini, and 8.0 [6.7, 9.0] for Claude.

title: A Comparison of a Customized Peripheral Artery Disease (PAD)-Specific Generative AI Chatbot and General-Purpose AI Chatbots for PAD Patient Education
outcome: Expert-rated accuracy of knowledge-base-grounded chatbot vs ungrounded general chatbots
effect: Accuracy high across all chatbots; pooled overall difference p=0.02 but no pairwise differences after Holm correction; grounded VERA was less comprehensive (p<0.001 vs each).
quote: When accuracy scores were pooled across all prompts, there was a statistically significant overall difference among chatbots ( p = 0.02; Kruskal-Wallis); however, no pairwise comparisons remained statistically significant after Holm correction ( Table 4 ).

title: A Comparison of a Customized Peripheral Artery Disease (PAD)-Specific Generative AI Chatbot and General-Purpose AI Chatbots for PAD Patient Education
outcome: Flesch-Kincaid grade level of PAD education responses
quote: VERA produced responses at a median grade level of 6.6 [4.7, 7.0] compared with 7.5 [6.2, 9.7] for ChatGPT, 9.0 [7.4, 10.2] for Gemini, and 8.0 [6.7, 9.0] for Claude.

title: Quality of Autism Information Generated by Artificial Intelligence Tools: Implications for Paediatric Care
venue: Journal of paediatrics and child health
outcome: Reading level of AI-generated autism responses versus recommended paediatric 6th-8th grade level
effect: Readability levels consistently exceeded recommended guidelines for paediatric health materials (6th-8th grade reading level) across platforms.
quote: Several tools produced generally accurate explanations of ASD; however, readability levels consistently exceeded recommended guidelines for paediatric health materials (i.e., the 6th-8th grade reading level).

title: Quality of Autism Information Generated by Artificial Intelligence Tools: Implications for Paediatric Care
venue: Journal of paediatrics and child health
outcome: Plain-language comprehensibility (readability) of AI-generated autism information
effect: Readability consistently exceeded recommended 6th-8th grade level for paediatric health materials.
quote: Several tools produced generally accurate explanations of ASD; however, readability levels consistently exceeded recommended guidelines for paediatric health materials (i.e., the 6th-8th grade reading level).

title: Exploring LLM-based chatbot effectiveness in answering questions related to the risks and benefits of orthognathic treatment: a cross-sectional study
outcome: Flesch Reading Ease of chatbot responses to patient questions on orthognathic treatment
effect: Readability differed significantly across chatbots; Gemini and ChatGPT responses were more accessible than Copilot's. No numeric scores or comparison with patient literacy level appear in the abstract.
quote: Readability varied significantly with Gemini and ChatGPT producing more accessible responses than Copilot.

title: Impact of an Ambient AI Scribe on Medical Student Objective Structured Clinical Examination Notes: Nonrandomized Clinical Trial
outcome: Omissions in ambient AI scribe notes (symptom duration, important details)
effect: Symptom duration appeared in the chief complaint of 17% (8/47) of AI notes; 55.3% (26/47) of students agreed the AI note left out important details.
quote: Post hoc analysis of AI notes revealed that symptom duration, an explicit criterion required for full QNOTE credit in the chief complaint element, was mentioned in the chief complaint section in 17% (8/47) of the AI notes.

title: Impact of an Ambient AI Scribe on Medical Student Objective Structured Clinical Examination Notes: Nonrandomized Clinical Trial
outcome: Note quality change after incorporating AI note (overreliance on flawed output)
effect: Chief complaint scores declined (P=.05), with fully acceptable 34% vs 44.7% and unacceptable 14.9% vs 6.4%; other 9 elements similar; 10.6% (5/47) declined ≥20 points.
quote: In paired analysis of QNOTE elements between human-only and hybrid notes among AI scribe participants, the largest element-level change was a decline in chief complaint scores ( P =.05) driven by fewer “fully acceptable” (16/47, 34% vs 21/47, 44.7%) and more “unacceptable” (7/47, 14.9% vs 3/47, 6.4%) hybrid notes as compared to human-only notes, respectively.

title: Impact of an Ambient AI Scribe on Medical Student Objective Structured Clinical Examination Notes: Nonrandomized Clinical Trial
outcome: chief complaint scores
effect: Chief complaint scores declined because AI notes often omitted symptom duration, a locally required criterion for full credit.
quote: The difference in chief complaint scores was likely due to conciseness in AI notes that often omitted symptom duration, an explicit criterion for full credit on QNOTE.

title: Impact of an Ambient AI Scribe on Medical Student Objective Structured Clinical Examination Notes: Nonrandomized Clinical Trial
outcome: incorporation of omissions into final note
effect: In paired analysis, hybrid notes had significantly lower chief complaint scores (P=.05) with fewer fully acceptable notes than human-only notes due to automation bias.
quote: In paired analysis of QNOTE elements between human-only and hybrid notes among AI scribe participants, the largest element-level change was a decline in chief complaint scores ( P =.05) driven by fewer “fully acceptable” (16/47, 34% vs 21/47, 44.7%) and more “unacceptable” (7/47, 14.9% vs 3/47, 6.4%) hybrid notes as compared to human-only notes, respectively.

title: Clinical Implementation of AI for Pulmonary Embolism Detection in over 30 000 CT Pulmonary Angiography Examinations
outcome: Real-time expert adjudication of radiologist-AI discordances against concordance and unique diagnoses
effect: Overall concordance 97.79%; adjudication favored radiologist in 88.73% of discordances; unique diagnoses by radiologist 14.97% vs AI alone 0.81%.
quote: Expert adjudication favored the radiologist in 88.73% of discordances.

title: Clinical Implementation of AI for Pulmonary Embolism Detection in over 30 000 CT Pulmonary Angiography Examinations
outcome: Radiologist interpretation of all cases alongside AI; unique PE diagnoses by radiologist vs AI alone
effect: Unique diagnosis by radiologist 483 of 3226 (14.97%), about 19 times AI alone (26 of 3226, 0.81%).
quote: The rate of unique diagnosis by the interpreting radiologist (483 of 3226 [14.97%]) was approximately 19 times that of the AI tool alone (26 of 3226 [0.81%]).

title: Automatic Speech Recognition and Large Language Models for Multilingual Pathology Report Generation: Proof-of-Concept Study
outcome: Comparison of three candidate LLMs on the same transcripts via automated metrics and pathologist ranking
effect: Qwen2:72b outperformed Llama3.1:70b and Gemma2:27b across all 5 automated metrics (all P<.001) and had the lowest error rate, showing large differences between candidates.
quote: Pairwise Wilcoxon tests showed that Qwen2:72b outperformed Llama3.1:70b and Gemma2:27b across all 5 automated metrics (all P <.001).
sample_unit: simulated mixed Chinese-English pathology dictation audio recordings

title: Automatic Speech Recognition and Large Language Models for Multilingual Pathology Report Generation: Proof-of-Concept Study
outcome: Pathologist-coded report-level errors
effect: Total error rates were 16.8% (21/125), 45.6% (57/125), and 92.8% (116/125) for Qwen2, Llama3.1, and Gemma2.
sample_unit: simulated mixed Chinese-English pathology dictation audio recordings

title: Automatic Speech Recognition and Large Language Models for Multilingual Pathology Report Generation: Proof-of-Concept Study
outcome: Pathologist-coded report-level errors (irrelevant text, Chinese output, factual errors) in LLM-generated reports
effect: Total error rates were 16.8% (21/125) for Qwen2:72b, 45.6% (57/125) for Llama3.1:70b, and 92.8% (116/125) for Gemma2:27b.
sample_unit: simulated mixed Chinese-English pathology dictation audio recordings

title: Safety and diagnostic accuracy of large-language model application of PECARN head injury algorithm
outcome: LLM NPV and accuracy versus ED clinicians on PECARN head injury risk classification
effect: Optimized Features Model NPV 0.98, accuracy 0.89 versus ED clinicians NPV 0.99, accuracy 0.92; all models had high NPV comparable to PEM physicians.
quote: The GPT model with the highest combination of NPV and accuracy was the prompt-engineered "Optimized Features Model" (NPV = 0.98, accuracy = 0.89), which performed similarly to that of the ED clinicians in both NPV (0.99) and accuracy (0.92).

title: Dataset effects outweigh algorithmic effects in determining fairness of healthcare machine learning
outcome: Sex-group accuracy gap (Gender Accuracy Gap) across datasets and classifiers
effect: Gender accuracy gaps varied markedly across datasets; the same algorithm showed negligible bias in one dataset and substantial bias in another. Dataset identity explained 63.4% of |GAG| variance.
quote: Mixed-effects interaction modelling showed that the same algorithm could display negligible bias in one dataset and substantial bias in another.
sample_unit: datasets (3 datasets x 10 classifiers x 3 sex-ratio sampling scenarios)

title: Dataset effects outweigh algorithmic effects in determining fairness of healthcare machine learning
outcome: Effect of balanced sex-ratio sampling (50/50 vs 90/10, 10/90) on sex accuracy gap
effect: Balanced sampling reduced disparities but did not eliminate them; sampling scenario contributed 0.2% of |GAG| variance.
quote: Balanced sampling reduced disparities but did not eliminate them, consistent with residual sex-associated signal/feature structure beyond representation imbalance.
sample_unit: datasets (3 datasets x 10 classifiers x 3 sex-ratio sampling scenarios)

title: Clinically-applicable prediction of hospital stay and patient similarity retrieval in paediatric cardiology using machine learning
outcome: Prospective performance of length-of-stay model in silent mode on live NHS admissions
effect: Random Forest mean precision 0.77 ± 0.03 and sensitivity 0.76 ± 0.04 during silent deployment (1,052 admissions), versus 0.88 ± 0.02 accuracy in retrospective benchmarking.
quote: The Random Forest model shows mean precision and sensitivity of 0.77  ± 0.03 and 0.76  ± 0.04 during NHS silent deployment (1,052 admissions).

title: Clinically-applicable prediction of hospital stay and patient similarity retrieval in paediatric cardiology using machine learning
outcome: Model length-of-stay prediction performance compared against clinician predictions
effect: Random Forest achieved the best length-of-stay prediction accuracy (0.88 ± 0.02), outperforming clinicians.
quote: Our models surpass clinician performance in length of stay prediction and show promise for case retrieval, supporting data-driven decision-making in paediatric cardiology and beyond.

title: Global physician perspectives on artificial intelligence in healthcare across 50 countries and territories
outcome: Proportion of physicians with formal AI training; association of training with AI use
effect: 17.7% had received formal training; 27.8% had used AI in practice. Trained physicians were >3 times as likely to use AI (adjusted OR 3.40; 95% CI 2.31-5.01).
quote: However, only 27.8% had used AI in practice, and 17.7% had received formal training.

title: The Best of Both Worlds: How Combining a Large Language Model and a Rule-Based Algorithm Makes Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infection Surveillance More Efficient
venue: Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America
outcome: LLM sensitivity and specificity for CAUTI classification on local historical cases versus infection preventionist gold standard
effect: Combined rule-based logic plus CLEAR-LLM achieved sensitivity 90.0% and specificity 93.5% on 919 local flagged cases; after adjudication 93.6% and 98.6%.
quote: Combining rule-based logic with Clinical Entity Augmented Retrieval (CLEAR) input into an LLM achieved the highest sensitivity (90.0%) and specificity (93.5%).

title: A large comprehensive comparison of large language models on ophthalmology board exams
venue: Graefe's archive for clinical and experimental ophthalmology = Albrecht von Graefes Archiv fur klinische und experimentelle Ophthalmologie
outcome: Calibration of LLM self-assessed confidence against correctness
effect: Confidence calibration varied widely across models; ChatGPT-5 showed superior discrimination (AUC = 0.827); majority of LLMs showed poor calibration of self-assessed confidence.
quote: However, the majority of LLMs exhibit significant error rates and poor calibration of self-assessed confidence.

title: Randomized trial of electronic health record implemented AI risk prediction in kidney transplant care
outcome: Patient-reported graft-loss treatment conversations and SDM outcomes versus usual care
effect: Despite AUC-ROC 0.923, conversations did not differ: intervention 14/36 (39%) vs control 16/40 (40%), p = 1.00; no differences in secondary clinical, SDM, relationship, or distress outcomes.
quote: Passive EHR availability of AI risk estimates did not improve communication or SDM-related outcomes.

title: Randomized trial of electronic health record implemented AI risk prediction in kidney transplant care
outcome: Clinician tool utilization and barriers to use
effect: Mean reported utilization 29% (SD 37%); one physician 100%, others 0–30%. Barriers included separate EHR tab without direct workflow integration and no alerts for high-risk scores.
quote: Users described the following reasons as main barriers to use the system: lack of immediate clinical consequence or no perceived need for risk stratification, lack of time during the visit, no direct integration into workflow since the integration was provided in another tab of the EHR, no alerts in case of high-risk scores.

title: Randomized trial of electronic health record implemented AI risk prediction in kidney transplant care
outcome: Clinician-reported tool utilization and workflow barriers
effect: Utilization averaged 29%, SD 37%; one physician reported 100%, remaining physicians 0–30%. Reported barriers included time constraints, a separate EHR tab, absent high-risk alerts, and no perceived clinical consequence.
quote: The reported utilization differed highly between physicians (one physician reported 100% utilization, while all remaining physicians reported 0–30%; mean 29%, SD 37%), precluding meaningful stratified analysis by clinician-level uptake.

title: Randomized trial of electronic health record implemented AI risk prediction in kidney transplant care
outcome: conversation frequency about treatment options
effect: Conversation frequency did not differ between the intervention and control groups (39% vs 40%).
quote: Conversation frequency did not differ between groups (intervention 14/36 [39%] vs control 16/40 [40%]; chi-square p = 1.00).

title: Randomized trial of electronic health record implemented AI risk prediction in kidney transplant care
outcome: barriers to system use
effect: Clinicians reported a lack of immediate clinical consequence for the risk stratification as a main barrier to using the system.
quote: Users described the following reasons as main barriers to use the system: lack of immediate clinical consequence or no perceived need for risk stratification, lack of time during the visit, no direct integration into workflow since the integration was provided in another tab of the EHR, no alerts in case of high-risk scores.

title: Comparative accuracy of a predictive algorithm versus cardiologist assessment for 90-day readmission in decompensated chronic heart failure
outcome: 90-day readmission prediction: algorithm versus three cardiologists on same patients
effect: PRED'IC AUC 0.81, sensitivity 81.8%, specificity 69.7%; cardiologists sensitivity 90.9%, specificity 35.8%. Algorithm flagged 35% high risk versus 67% by cardiologists.
quote: Cardiologists demonstrated higher sensitivity (90.9%) but lower specificity (35.8%).

title: Comparative accuracy of a predictive algorithm versus cardiologist assessment for 90-day readmission in decompensated chronic heart failure
outcome: Algorithm performance across age and sex subgroups (exploratory)
effect: Consistent algorithmic performance across sex and age categories, with slightly higher specificity among older men.
quote: Subgroup analyses showed consistent algorithmic performance across sex and age categories, with slightly higher specificity among older men.

title: AI-WAR: a novel warfarin management software with a bidirectional LSTM dosing model improves time in therapeutic range
outcome: Anticoagulation quality (TTR, time in target INR) and adverse events, AI-WAR vs conventional management
effect: Median TTR 48.7% vs 81.3% (P<0.001); time in target INR 36.3% vs 61.9% (P<0.001); elevated INR 12.0% vs 16.8%; adverse events 9.6% vs 19.7% (P<0.001).
quote: Compared with conventional management, AI-WAR significantly improved median TTR (48.7% vs. 81.3%, P < 0.001), increased time in target INR (36.3% vs. 61.9%, P < 0.001), and reduced both elevated INR percentage (12.0% vs. 16.8%) and overall adverse event rate (9.6% vs. 19.7%, P < 0.001).

title: Assessing large language model responses to pediatric depression FAQs: a cross-sectional study on readability, accuracy, and sentiment
outcome: Readability of LLM responses on pediatric depression (Flesch Reading Ease, Flesch-Kincaid grade level)
effect: DeepSeek FRE 54-55, grade ~9.5; ChatGPT-5 FRE 49-50, grade ~10.5; Copilot FRE 43-44, grade ~10.8. All above plain-language level.
quote: Copilot-5 had the lowest Reading Ease score of 43 to 44 and the highest grade level near 10.8.
sample_unit: questions (FAQs about pediatric depression, each submitted to 3 LLMs)

title: CRITIC-RAG: Knowledge-Augmented Large Language Models With Verified Retrieval for Improved Medical Reasoning
venue: IEEE journal of biomedical and health informatics
outcome: Medical QA accuracy and answer similarity with verified retrieval versus baseline LLM
effect: Accuracy improved from 41.3% to 48.8% on MedQA; BERTScore rose from 68.1% to 74.4% on MedicationQA using LLaMA-3.
quote: For instance, CRITIC-RAG improves accuracy from 41.3% to 48.8% on MedQA and boosts BERTScore from 68.1% to 74.4% on MedicationQA using LLaMA-3.

title: Automated tooth numbering on panoramic radiographs versus cone-beam computed tomographs: a diagnostic accuracy study of a commercial artificial intelligence system
outcome: Proportion of examinations with completely error-free automated tooth numbering
effect: 148/171 (86.5%) panoramic and 155/171 (90.6%) CBCT examinations were error-free, so about 1 in 10 to 1 in 7 needed at least one manual correction, despite 99.29% per-tooth accuracy.
quote: At the case level, 148/171 (86.5%) panoramic radiographs and 155/171 (90.6%) cone-beam computed tomography examinations were error-free.
sample_unit: paired panoramic radiograph and CBCT examinations (patients)

title: Clinical Performance of Computer-Aided Detection System for Gastric Neoplasms: A Non-Randomized Confirmatory Trial (G-CADe Trial) (With Video)
venue: Digestive endoscopy : official journal of the Japan Gastroenterological Endoscopy Society
outcome: CAD sensitivity across four sites, lesion subgroups, and imaging modes
effect: Sensitivity 92.0% (WLI) and 96.5% (LCI). WLI-CAD EYE was lower for lesions <10 mm (88.9%) and anterior wall (79.4%); LCI-CAD EYE was ≥90% in all subgroups.
quote: WLI-CAD EYE showed relatively low sensitivity for lesions < 10 mm (88.9%) and those located on the anterior wall (79.4%), whereas LCI-CAD EYE achieved ≥ 90% sensitivity in all subgroups.

title: Accuracy and hallucination behaviors of artificial intelligence-based large language models for dental implant identification on radiographs
outcome: LLM accuracy identifying implant level, connection, brand, manufacturer on radiographs versus reference
effect: Structural characteristics identified with accuracies of 51.67% to 82.5%; brand and manufacturer recognition 4.17%-32.78%.
quote: Structural characteristics (implant level and connection type) were identified with accuracies ranging from 51.67% to 82.5%, whereas brand and manufacturer recognition remained consistently poor (4.17%-32.78%).
sample_unit: radiographic images (each queried six times per model)

title: Accuracy and hallucination behaviors of artificial intelligence-based large language models for dental implant identification on radiographs
outcome: Abstention/deferral versus hallucination rates across LLMs on implant identification
effect: Hallucinations were >87% of errors in all models; ChatGPT-5 showed higher abstention and lower hallucination frequency.
quote: Hallucinations represented the predominant error type (>87% of errors in all models), while ChatGPT-5 showed a comparatively higher rate of abstention and lower hallucination frequency.
sample_unit: radiographic images (each queried six times per model)

title: Accuracy and hallucination behaviors of artificial intelligence-based large language models for dental implant identification on radiographs
outcome: Overconfident definitive incorrect responses (hallucinations) among errors
effect: Hallucinations (definitive incorrect answers) exceeded 87% of errors in all four models; newer model abstained more often.
quote: Hallucinations represented the predominant error type (>87% of errors in all models), while ChatGPT-5 showed a comparatively higher rate of abstention and lower hallucination frequency.
sample_unit: radiographic images (each queried six times per model)

title: Vision-weighted diagnostic gain (VWDG) in the diagnosis of oral malignant and potentially malignant lesions: A multimodal comparative analysis
venue: Journal of stomatology, oral and maxillofacial surgery
outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of multimodal LLMs compared with board-certified oral medicine experts on same lesions
effect: Experts had highest Top-1 accuracy (65.3%); ChatGPT-5 multimodal (Top-1 50.0%) approached expert-level performance at Top-3 and Top-5; Gemini showed limited benefit from images.
quote: Experts achieved the highest Top-1 accuracy (65.3%), but ChatGPT-5 multimodal outputs approached expert-level performance at Top-3 and Top-5.

title: Automated Analysis of Radiation Oncology Incident Reports Using Large Language Models: A Multi-Institutional Technical Validation Study
venue: International journal of radiation oncology, biology, physics
outcome: LLM performance differences across two institutions' incident reports
effect: Institution 1 summary scores 3.34→4.20 (d=0.78) vs institution 2 3.61→4.02 (d=0.34, P=.055); Round 2 summaries ≥4: 80.0% vs 68.9%.
quote: Performance improvements establish technical feasibility for further development, while institutional variation suggests that site-specific factors may influence system effectiveness, which warrants further investigation.

title: A bilingual evaluation of chatbot performance in bruxism-related information: accuracy and readability across two models
outcome: Readability of chatbot bruxism responses in English and Turkish for patient comprehension
effect: No significant readability difference between chatbots (Turkish p=0.646; English p=0.745). Authors conclude high readability levels limit patient accessibility and simplification is necessary.
quote: However, high readability levels limit patient accessibility, and no association was found between accuracy and readability, indicating that simplification is necessary for effective patient education.

title: A workflow utilizing general-purpose large language models for efficient structuring and data mining of bone scintigraphy narratives
outcome: Global quality score of LLM extraction across three hospital centers
effect: DeepSeek-R1 (P=.277) and GPT-o3 (P=.072) stable across centers; DeepSeek-V3 and Gemini 2.5 Pro differed significantly across centers (P<.001), e.g., V3 4.53 at ZS vs 4.93 at FJ.
quote: In contrast, DeepSeek-V3 and Gemini 2.5 Pro showed unstable performance when confronted with heterogeneous content from different centers, with statistically significant differences in global quality scores across the three centers ( P <.001 for both).

title: A workflow utilizing general-purpose large language models for efficient structuring and data mining of bone scintigraphy narratives

quote: All LLMs better predicted CPT codes (91.5% correct) than ICD-10 codes (23.9% correct).

title: Assessing Large Language Models for Clinical Coding in Hand Surgery: Effect of Note Authorship, Prompt Design, and Diagnosis/Procedure Type
venue: The Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
outcome: LLM coding performance across note authors and prompt designs

quote: No differences in LLM coding performance were observed between note authors ( P = 0.09 ICD-10, P = 0.48 CPT) or prompt types ( P = 0.27 ICD-10, P = 0.62 CPT).

title: Assessing Large Language Models for Clinical Coding in Hand Surgery: Effect of Note Authorship, Prompt Design, and Diagnosis/Procedure Type
venue: The Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
outcome: LLM coding performance across note authors and prompt types

title: External Evaluation Reveals Reduced Performance of the PathFX Survival Model in 1018 Patients With Extremity Metastases
outcome: Discrimination and calibration of PathFX survival predictions in external local cohort
effect: Best model (18-month) AUC 0.63, Brier 0.22, calibration slope 0.58, intercept 0.21; other AUCs did not exceed 0.68; survival systematically underestimated.
quote: In general, the accuracy and other performance parameters we observed for PathFX were inadequate for clinical use.

title: External Evaluation Reveals Reduced Performance of the PathFX Survival Model in 1018 Patients With Extremity Metastases
outcome: PathFX performance differences across sex, race and treatment-period subgroups
effect: Better discrimination in females and poorer performance with flatter calibration slopes in patients who were not White; no clear differences by treatment period.
quote: The subgroup analyses suggested heterogeneity; that is, the model exhibited a better discrimination in females and poorer performance in patients who were not White with flatter calibration slopes.

title: External Evaluation Reveals Reduced Performance of the PathFX Survival Model in 1018 Patients With Extremity Metastases
outcome: Calibration of PathFX in local population indicating need for recalibration
effect: Intercepts positive at all time points (survival underestimated); slopes <1 (overconfident probabilities); recalibration or redevelopment recommended.
quote: Intercepts were positive for all time points, which means that the model systematically underestimated survival in this patient population.

title: AI assisted detection of large vessel occlusion on non-contrast CT: multinational validation and reader study
outcome: Clinician diagnostic performance with versus without AI assistance, including automation bias
effect: AI assistance increased pooled AUC from 0.718 to 0.852, sensitivity from 46.6% to 63.7%, and specificity from 91.9% to 94.9% (all P<0.001); automation bias reliance-level BHR 9.25.
quote: AI assistance significantly increased pooled AUC values from 0.718 to 0.852, sensitivity from 46.6% to 63.7%, and specificity from 91.9% to 94.9% (all P<0.001).

title: AI assisted detection of large vessel occlusion on non-contrast CT: multinational validation and reader study
outcome: Standalone AI performance on independent external multinational cohorts
effect: AUC 0.963 (95% CI 0.946 to 0.975) in Korean cohort and 0.899 (95% CI 0.858 to 0.939) in US cohort.
quote: Standalone AI achieved AUC values of 0.963 (95% CI 0.946 to 0.975) in the Korean cohort and 0.899 (95% CI 0.858 to 0.939) in the US cohort.
sample_unit: patients (NCCT scans) in external validation cohorts; 8 physician readers in reader study

title: An evaluation of artificial intelligence assisted prostate biopsy reporting in the Articulate Pro study
outcome: Pathologist diagnosis, turnaround time, and IHC use with vs without AI assistance
effect: Second-read AI changed diagnosis or Grade Group in 21/386 (5.4%), 5 (1.3%) potentially affecting management; concurrent-read reduced mean turnaround by 30.1 h at one site; IHC reduced at all sites (ORs 0.50, 0.43, 0.33).
quote: AI-assisted workflows showed significantly reduced mean turnaround time with concurrent-read compared to unassisted-read by 30.1 h (p < 0.0001) at one site with significant reductions in cases requiring immunohistochemistry in all sites (Odds Ratios 0.50,0.43,0.33, p < 0.0001, p = 0.01, p = 0.001).

title: An evaluation of artificial intelligence assisted prostate biopsy reporting in the Articulate Pro study
outcome: Reporting turnaround time and cases requiring immunohistochemistry
effect: Concurrent-read reduced mean turnaround time by 30.1 h (p < 0.0001) at one site; immunohistochemistry decreased across all sites (Odds Ratios 0.50,0.43,0.33, p < 0.0001, p = 0.01, p = 0.001).
quote: AI-assisted workflows showed significantly reduced mean turnaround time with concurrent-read compared to unassisted-read by 30.1 h (p < 0.0001) at one site with significant reductions in cases requiring immunohistochemistry in all sites (Odds Ratios 0.50,0.43,0.33, p < 0.0001, p = 0.01, p = 0.001).

title: An evaluation of artificial intelligence assisted prostate biopsy reporting in the Articulate Pro study
outcome: workflow and performance outcomes
effect: Prospective evaluation in clinical deployment found AI assistance significantly reduced turnaround times and unnecessary testing.
quote: AI-assisted workflows showed significantly reduced mean turnaround time with concurrent-read compared to unassisted-read by 30.1 h (p < 0.0001) at one site with significant reductions in cases requiring immunohistochemistry in all sites (Odds Ratios 0.50,0.43,0.33, p < 0.0001, p = 0.01, p = 0.001).

title: Evaluating large language models for diagnostic reasoning from unstructured clinical narratives in epilepsy
outcome: Accuracy of sources and citations in LLM reasoning outputs, verified by two raters
effect: Citation accuracy was 76% for GPT-4 versus 19% for Mixtral-8x7B; correct predictions could rest on hallucinated knowledge and inaccurate citation.
quote: Additionally, Fig. 3 (d) demonstrates GPT-4’s superior citation accuracy (76% for GPT-4 vs. 19% for Mixtral), indicating GPT-4’s enhanced ability to provide evidence-based sources for its decision.

title: Evaluating large language models for diagnostic reasoning from unstructured clinical narratives in epilepsy
outcome: Performance sensitivity to input variation: narrative length, persona prompt, and language
effect: Performance varied with description length (U-shaped, up to 32%), persona (GPT-4 +13.68%), and language (Mixtral -8% in same-language non-English setting; GPT-4 -1.4%, n.s.).
quote: However, in the same-language setting (non-English symptoms and prompt), Mixtral’s performance declines substantially by 8%, while GPT-4 remains stable (-1.4%, n.s.).

title: Evaluating large language models for diagnostic reasoning from unstructured clinical narratives in epilepsy
outcome: Calibration and confidence of LLM likelihood outputs versus correctness
effect: Confidence and Brier calibration improved with prompt engineering (FS-CoT, SC best); GPT-4 best calibrated even zero-shot, but high confidence does not guarantee correctness.
quote: Notably, GPT-4 shows the best calibration, even in the zero-shot condition.

title: Evaluating large language models for diagnostic reasoning from unstructured clinical narratives in epilepsy
outcome: LLM F1 for seizure onset zone localization compared with clinicians and naive baseline
effect: Zero-shot F1 of GPT-4 52.27% and Mixtral 51.66% versus clinicians 48.77% and 46.75%; naive classifier 38.21%.
quote: Exceptions are Mixtral-8 × 7B and GPT-4, which achieved substantially higher F1 scores than all other models of 51.66% and 52.27%, respectively (95% CI: [51.43, 51.90], [52.04, 52.50]), comparable to the clinician’s performance: Clinician 1 - 48.77% (95% CI: [48.53, 49.02]) and Clinician 2 - 46.75% (95% CI: [46.51, 46.99]).

title: Evaluating large language models for diagnostic reasoning from unstructured clinical narratives in epilepsy
outcome: expert-rated reasoning correctness and completeness
effect: In 81 CoT responses, GPT-4 correctness/completeness 56.79%/65.00% vs Mixtral 29.63%/34.57%, p<0.05.
quote: As shown in Fig. 3 (b) GPT-4 significantly outperformed Mixtral in both correctness (56.79% vs. 29.63%; z-test for proportions, p <0.05) and completeness (65.00% vs. 34.57%; z-test for proportions, p <0.05).

title: Evaluating large language models for diagnostic reasoning from unstructured clinical narratives in epilepsy
outcome: hallucinated reasoning and inaccurate citations
effect: Clinical experts found correct predictions could rely on hallucinated knowledge and inaccurate source citation.
quote: However, reasoning analysis by clinical experts reveal that correct prediction can be based on hallucinated knowledge and inaccurate source citation, underscoring the need to improve interpretability of LLMs in clinical use.

title: Evaluating large language models for diagnostic reasoning from unstructured clinical narratives in epilepsy
outcome: F1 across prompt strategies
effect: Median F1 improvement vs zero-shot: Few-Shot 6.49%, CoT 9.62%, FS-CoT 9.49%, SC 10.02%.
quote: Importantly, we observed a substantial performance increase when introducing prompt-engineering across all models: Median F1 improvement relative to ZS was 6.49% for Few-Shot prompting, 9.62% for CoT, 9.49% in FS-CoT, and 10.02% increase for SC.

title: Machine learning outperforms serum creatinine for early risk stratification of hepatorenal syndrome: a prospective single-center validation
outcome: Model AUC versus serum creatinine standard for HRS diagnosis in prospective cohort
effect: ML model AUC 0.994 (95% CI 0.985-0.998) versus serum creatinine AUC 0.803; p < 0.001
quote: This represented a substantial and statistically significant improvement over serum creatinine-based diagnosis (AUC = 0.803; p < 0.001).
sample_unit: patients (prospective validation cohort with decompensated cirrhosis)

title: Accuracy, readability, and content coverage of AI-generated responses to questions on functional appliances
outcome: Reading level of AI-generated patient education responses versus recommended patient literacy thresholds
effect: AI responses were generally accurate and comprehensive but difficult to read, requiring college-level literacy; ChatGPT-5 had the most difficult-to-read responses (P < .001).
quote: AI-generated information on functional appliances was generally accurate and comprehensive but often exceeded recommended patient literacy thresholds.
sample_unit: questions (each answered by four AI models)

title: Accuracy, readability, and content coverage of AI-generated responses to questions on functional appliances
outcome: Readability of AI-generated patient education responses in plain language

quote: AI-generated responses were generally accurate and comprehensive but difficult to read, requiring college-level literacy.
sample_unit: questions (each answered by four AI models)

title: Algorithmic bias in clinical resource allocation by a large language model: a cross-sectional in-silico evaluation of 13,608 decisions
outcome: Change in LLM resource allocation choices when patient sociodemographic attributes were varied
effect: Age 25 vs 50 raised odds of selection (OR 3.31; 95% CI 2.96-3.71); income over $5M cut odds by 75% (OR 0.25); model favored racial minorities, women and non-binary individuals over White men.
quote: Being 25 years old increased the odds of selection more than threefold compared to a 50-year-old (OR 3.31; 95% CI, 2.96-3.71; p < 0.001), while earning over $5 million annually reduced the odds by 75% (OR 0.25; 95% CI, 0.22-0.28; p < 0.001).

title: Robustness of Healthcare ML Under Data Quality Degradation: A Dimension-Wise Analysis on MIMIC-IV
venue: Studies in health technology and informatics
outcome: Model performance under controlled missing, incoherent, invalid, imprecise and duplicate data at inference time
effect: Performance declined with increasing degradation, with largest losses when degradations occurred at inference time. Completeness, coherence and validity were the most detrimental dimensions.
quote: Model performance declined with increasing degradation, with the largest losses observed when degradations occurred at inference time.

title: Robustness of Healthcare ML Under Data Quality Degradation: A Dimension-Wise Analysis on MIMIC-IV
venue: Studies in health technology and informatics
outcome: Model robustness to perturbed or missing input data across five data quality dimensions
