outcome: Reading grade level of LLM education materials after instruction to target lower reading level, and accuracy
effect: Models reduced reading levels by 4.8 (ChatGPT), 6.9 (Gemini), 3.8 (Copilot) grade levels (P<.001) without compromising accuracy; seventh-grade target only reached by Gemini (7.9), others ~10-11.
quote: When instructed to revise patient education materials to improve understandability, all 3 large language models reduced reading levels by 4.8 grade levels (ChatGPT), 6.9 grade levels (Gemini), and 3.8 grade levels (Microsoft Copilot) ( P < .001) without compromising accuracy.
sample_unit: frequently asked questions (plus 10 conditions of patient education materials)

title: Ability of Large Language Models to Answer Patients' Questions and Generate Educational Materials for Uncommon Retinal Conditions
outcome: Expert-rated accuracy and completeness of LLM answers to patient FAQs
effect: Mean accuracy 4.02, 4.16, 3.81 and completeness 4.07, 4.25, 3.62 (Likert 1-5); Copilot significantly less accurate and complete than ChatGPT and Gemini; experts noted some inaccuracies.
quote: Post hoc Dunn testing showed that responses generated by both ChatGPT and Google Gemini were significantly more accurate than those generated by Microsoft Copilot.
sample_unit: frequently asked questions (plus 10 conditions of patient education materials)

title: Ability of Large Language Models to Answer Patients' Questions and Generate Educational Materials for Uncommon Retinal Conditions
outcome: Reading grade level of LLM responses to patient FAQs and default education materials
effect: FAQ responses averaged grade 15.3 (ChatGPT), 15.7 (Gemini), 14.6 (Copilot); default education materials 15.1, 14.8, 14.6 grade level, far above the recommended seventh grade.
quote: However, the default reading level of these responses was substantially higher than what is recommended by the American Medical Association for the seventh-grade reading level, potentially limiting patient comprehension.
sample_unit: frequently asked questions (plus 10 conditions of patient education materials)

title: Ability of Large Language Models to Answer Patients' Questions and Generate Educational Materials for Uncommon Retinal Conditions
outcome: Accuracy and completeness of LLM materials generated for lower health literacy (seventh-grade) target
effect: Accuracy at seventh-grade level 4.60, 4.55, 4.20 vs unspecified 4.70, 4.85, 4.30; no significant differences in accuracy or completeness between reading level conditions.
quote: There were no significant differences in accuracy or completeness among the 3 large language models when comparing patient education materials generated at an unspecified reading level with those generated at the seventh-grade reading level.
sample_unit: frequently asked questions (plus 10 conditions of patient education materials)

title: Ability of Large Language Models to Answer Patients' Questions and Generate Educational Materials for Uncommon Retinal Conditions
outcome: composite readability grade level of LLM FAQ responses
effect: ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot generated FAQ responses at mean grade levels of 15.3 ± 1.4, 15.7 ± 1.9, and 14.6 ± 1.3, respectively (P = .002)
quote: Responses to patients’ frequently asked questions generated by ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot were written at mean grade levels of 15.3 ± 1.4, 15.7 ± 1.9, and 14.6 ± 1.3, respectively ( F = 6.67, P = .002).
sample_unit: frequently asked questions (plus 10 conditions of patient education materials)

title: Same child, different risk: demographic bias in childhood obesity attribution by large language models
outcome: Change in obesity risk attribution when child demographic attributes varied in prompts
effect: Socioeconomic status produced low-income attribution in 40/42 decisions (decision change rate 19.0%); urban-rural decision change rate 52.4%; most models attributed higher risk to Black and Hispanic/Latino children.
quote: Socioeconomic status produced the most consistent attribution pattern (low-income attribution in 40/42 decisions; decision change rate 19.0%).

title: Same child, different risk: demographic bias in childhood obesity attribution by large language models
outcome: Neutral-prompt scores for stigmatizing language, representation and cultural fit across seven LLMs
effect: All models had a 100% Stigmatizing/Harmful Language pass rate, but representation and cultural fit were universally weak; Claude mean 3.00 ± 0.91 vs GLM 1.44 ± 0.51.
quote: All models achieved a 100% Stigmatizing/Harmful Language pass rate, yet representation and cultural fit were universally weak.

title: Same child, different risk: demographic bias in childhood obesity attribution by large language models
outcome: Differences in LLM obesity risk attribution across demographic subgroups and between models
effect: Between-model differences significant (Kruskal-Wallis H = 46.21, p < 0.001); urban-rural attribution directionally inconsistent across models, with Western models favoring rural and Chinese-origin models urban attribution.
quote: Urban-rural attribution showed the greatest cross-model directional inconsistency (decision change rate 52.4%), with Western-origin models favoring rural attribution and Chinese-origin models favoring urban attribution.

title: Validation of an Artificial Intelligence-Derived ECG Algorithm for Detecting Cardiac Amyloidosis in Patients With Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction: Clinical Application and Prognostic Implications
venue: Journal of the American Heart Association
outcome: AI ECG algorithm discrimination in internal versus external cohort from a different center
effect: Internal AUC 0.87 (sensitivity 83%, specificity 91%); external AUC 0.84 (sensitivity 89%, specificity 79%). Specificity was lower in the external cohort.
quote: In the external cohort, the area under the curve was 0.84 (95% CI, 0.76-0.92), with sensitivity 89% (95% CI, 78%-94%) and specificity 79% (95% CI, 63%-90%).
sample_unit: patients (internal validation cohort with preserved EF and analyzable ECGs)

title: AI Clinical Decision Making Compared with Fellowship-Trained Hand Surgeons: A Case-Based Study
outcome: Concordance of commercial LLM platforms with surgeon plurality on hand surgery vignettes, by case complexity
effect: All four platforms 100% concordant on easy cases; on complex cases Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3/5 (60%), ChatGPT-4 and Open Evidence 1/5 (20%). Overall 78% for Claude/Gemini, 56% for ChatGPT-4/Open Evidence.
quote: Performance diverged on complex cases: Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini each achieved concordance on 3 of 5 complex cases (60%), whereas ChatGPT-4 and Open Evidence each achieved concordance on 1 of 5 (20%).
sample_unit: clinical vignettes (answered by 15 hand surgeons and 4 AI platforms)

title: Discordance Between Textual Reasoning and Visual Interpretation in Large Language Models for Low Back Pain: Cross-Sectional Quantitative Evaluation and Exploratory Multimodal Stress Test
outcome: Readability of LLM low back pain advice (FRE, SMOG) and understandability (PEMAT)
effect: Textual advice remained difficult to read, although understandability scores were robust.
quote: However, textual advice remained difficult to read, although understandability scores were robust.
sample_unit: individual recommendations extracted from LLM responses to 25 low back pain questions (plus 5 multimodal stress-test cases)

title: Discordance Between Textual Reasoning and Visual Interpretation in Large Language Models for Low Back Pain: Cross-Sectional Quantitative Evaluation and Exploratory Multimodal Stress Test
outcome: Multimodal LLM image interpretation performance versus textual accuracy on low back pain cases
effect: Text accuracy 88.4% (1605/1816), but in pure imaging tasks the average diagnostic score was poor, with models failing to identify core pathologies.
quote: In pure imaging tasks featuring complex but clinically representative pathologies, the average diagnostic score was poor, with models failing to identify core pathologies.
sample_unit: individual recommendations extracted from LLM responses to 25 low back pain questions (plus 5 multimodal stress-test cases)

title: Discordance Between Textual Reasoning and Visual Interpretation in Large Language Models for Low Back Pain: Cross-Sectional Quantitative Evaluation and Exploratory Multimodal Stress Test
outcome: Cross-modal alignment under adversarial clinical-radiological mismatch cases
effect: Models exhibited "textual masking," aligning visual findings with text cues rather than imaging evidence in Q29-Q30.
quote: In comprehensive diagnostic analysis tasks (Q29-Q30), models exhibited "textual masking," aligning visual findings with text cues rather than imaging evidence.
sample_unit: individual recommendations extracted from LLM responses to 25 low back pain questions (plus 5 multimodal stress-test cases)

title: Discordance Between Textual Reasoning and Visual Interpretation in Large Language Models for Low Back Pain: Cross-Sectional Quantitative Evaluation and Exploratory Multimodal Stress Test
outcome: Safety disclaimer coverage in textual versus multimodal interactions
effect: Disclaimer coverage dropped from 82.8% (207/250) in textual tasks to 28% (14/50) in multimodal interactions.
quote: Crucially, safety disclaimer coverage dropped precipitously from 82.8% (207/250) in textual tasks to 28% (14/50) in multimodal interactions.
sample_unit: individual recommendations extracted from LLM responses to 25 low back pain questions (plus 5 multimodal stress-test cases)

title: Readability of AI-Generated Patient Visit Summaries in Orthopedic Surgery: Retrospective Analysis
outcome: Proportion of AI-generated visit summaries meeting sixth- and eighth-grade readability benchmarks
effect: Mean FKGL 9.3; only 0.4% (4/982) met sixth-grade and 14.2% (139/982) met eighth-grade threshold.
quote: Only 0.4% (4/982) of PVS met the sixth-grade benchmark and 14.2% (139/982) met the eighth-grade threshold.

title: Readability of AI-Generated Patient Visit Summaries in Orthopedic Surgery: Retrospective Analysis
outcome: Reading grade level of AI-generated patient-facing summaries relative to recommended sixth-grade level
effect: Mean FKGL 9.3 (SD 1.2), FRES 57.6 (fairly difficult); GFI 12.4, CLI 11.0, SMOG 12.4.
quote: Among 982 analyzed PVS, the mean FKGL was 9.3 (SD 1.2, 95% CI 9.2-9.4) and the mean FRES was 57.6 (SD 7.9, 95% CI 57.1-58.1), corresponding to "fairly difficult."

title: A stacking model for AI-assisted diagnosis of suspected pituitary microadenomas on non-contrast T1COR MRI: a multicenter reader study on bridging the experience gap
outcome: Radiologist diagnostic accuracy unaided versus with AI assistance across experience levels
effect: AI assistance significantly improved accuracy across all experience levels; with combined model, seniors reached 75.4-79.0% in internal validation and up to 85.4% in hardest external cohort, ~30% absolute gain over unaided.
quote: In the reader study with 315 lesions and five radiologists, AI assistance significantly improved diagnostic accuracy across all experience levels.

title: A stacking model for AI-assisted diagnosis of suspected pituitary microadenomas on non-contrast T1COR MRI: a multicenter reader study on bridging the experience gap
outcome: Model performance across multiple sites/external cohorts
effect: Combined model achieved AUCs of 0.818 (EVC1) and 0.899 (EVC2) in the external validation cohorts, outperforming single-modality approaches.
quote: The combined model outperformed all single-modality approaches across validation cohorts, achieving AUCs of 0.818 (EVC1) and 0.899 (EVC2) with balanced sensitivity and specificity (EVC2: 0.929 and 0.833, respectively).

title: Improving Pelvic Floor Disorder Education: A Second Pilot of a Retrieval-Augmented AI Chatbot Model
outcome: Expert-rated response quality (QAMAI) and usability (SUS) of a chatbot grounded in AUGS materials
effect: Median QAMAI score 28 (IQR 24-29.8); mean SUS 81.8 ± 11.2; no comparator arm in this pilot; citation consistency and clinical depth noted as needing improvement.
quote: A retrieval-augmented ChatGPT model trained on AUGS materials generated high-quality responses with excellent usability.

title: An Electronic Health Record-Integrated, Large Language Model-Powered Tool to Triage Surgical Patients
outcome: Sensitivity and specificity of LLM surgical comanagement triage tool in prospective deployment, with physician review as reference
effect: Sensitivity 0.94 (95% CI 0.91-0.96), specificity 0.74 (95% CI 0.71-0.77); LLM misclassification accounted for 2 of 19 false-negative cases (11%).
quote: Using treating physicians' determinations as the reference standard, the tool had high sensitivity (0.94; 95% CI, 0.91-0.96) and moderate specificity (0.74; 95% CI, 0.71-0.77) for identifying patients appropriate for SCM.

title: Threshold and Predictive Alerts of Continuous Glucose Monitoring and Glycemic Control in Hospitalized Adults With Diabetes: A Randomized Clinical Trial
outcome: Time in range with predictive plus threshold alerts vs threshold alone or no alerts
effect: Predictive plus threshold alerts showed no TIR difference vs no alerts (3.1% [95% CI −0.8% to 6.9%]; P = .11) or vs threshold only (−0.8% [95% CI −4.7% to 3.0%]; P = .61), despite more alerts (7012 vs 5163).
quote: The addition of predictive alerts did not confer further glycemic benefit beyond threshold alerts alone.

title: Threshold and Predictive Alerts of Continuous Glucose Monitoring and Glycemic Control in Hospitalized Adults With Diabetes: A Randomized Clinical Trial
outcome: Time in target glucose range with threshold and predictive alerts enabled versus disabled
effect: Threshold alerts versus alerts off: adjusted TIR difference 3.9% [95% CI, 0.1%-7.8%]; Holm-adjusted P = .04. Adding predictive alerts: −0.8% [95% CI −4.7% to 3.0%]; Holm-adjusted P = .61.
quote: In this randomized clinical trial of hospitalized adults with diabetes, CGM threshold alerts modestly improved glycemic control compared with CGM use without alerts, whereas the addition of predictive alerts did not confer further glycemic benefit beyond threshold alerts alone.

title: Perceptions, knowledge and adoption of artificial intelligence in rheumatology: results from a British Society for Rheumatology survey
outcome: Self-rated AI knowledge and digital confidence among rheumatology staff
effect: Only 6% self-rated their AI knowledge as excellent; one in four reported excellent confidence in digital technology; 64-66% wanted education on safe LLM use and ethical/safe AI use.
quote: One in four reported excellent confidence in using digital technology, with only 6% self-rating their AI knowledge as excellent.
sample_unit: survey respondents (rheumatology healthcare professionals and researchers)

title: Augmenting Head and Neck Multidisciplinary Tumor Board Recommendations With Locally Run Large Language Models: Prospective Evaluation of Real-World Implementation
outcome: LLM recommendation concordance with MDT reference decisions and expert-rated medical adequacy
effect: Curative/palliative concordance 94% (16/17) gemma-3-12b vs 59% (10/17) gpt-oss-20b; same first-line regimen 35% (6/17) and 41% (7/17); median adequacy 5 (IQR 2-5) and 4 (IQR 3-5).
quote: Concordance regarding the curative or palliative therapy regimen reached 94% (16/17, 95% CI 71%-100%); for gemma-3-12b and 59% (10/17, 95% CI 33%-82%) for gpt-oss-20b.

title: Augmenting Head and Neck Multidisciplinary Tumor Board Recommendations With Locally Run Large Language Models: Prospective Evaluation of Real-World Implementation
outcome: LLM recommendations compared with multidisciplinary tumor board decisions on the same cases
effect: LLMs substantially improved the MDT recommendation in 1/17 cases (6%); first-line regimen matched MDT in 35% (gemma) and 41% (gpt-oss); LLMs cannot replace MDTs.
quote: In one case, 6% (1/17, 95% CI 0%-29%), the LLM was able to substantially improve the MDT recommendation by underscoring a follow-up examination that had not yet been performed.

title: Augmenting Head and Neck Multidisciplinary Tumor Board Recommendations With Locally Run Large Language Models: Prospective Evaluation of Real-World Implementation
outcome: Rate of potentially hazardous information in LLM outputs rated by MDT members
effect: Potentially hazardous information in 27% (25/93) of ratings for gemma-3-12b and 17% (14/83) of ratings for gpt-oss-20b.
quote: MDT members stated potentially hazardous information in 27% (25/93, 95% CI 18%-37%) of ratings for gemma-3-12b and 17% (14/83, 95% CI 9%-26%) of ratings for gpt-oss-20b.

title: Large Language Models for Oncology Guideline Maintenance: Prospective Case Study
outcome: Accuracy of LLM evidence synthesis and overstated evidence in predicted guideline updates
effect: Models captured 36.7% to 40% of substantive updates, frequently overstating evidence; extraction accuracy up to 99.2% for single studies but declined in multisource synthesis.
quote: In the predictive task, models captured 36.7% to 40% of substantive updates, often identifying landmark approvals, but frequently overstating evidence.

title: Large Language Models for Oncology Guideline Maintenance: Prospective Case Study
outcome: Position-dependent accuracy decline in long-form LLM-generated guideline drafts
effect: GPT's endpoint accuracy dropped from 84.6% in the first half of the drafted guideline to 38.5% in the second half.
quote: We observed a position-dependent performance drop in long-form generation, with GPT's endpoint accuracy dropping from 84.6% in the first half of the drafted guideline to 38.5% in the second half.

title: Large language models for MoCA-defined cognitive risk screening in obstructive sleep apnea using polysomnography and brain MRI reports: A retrospective single-center pilot study
outcome: Discrimination (AUC) of LLMs versus AHI rule and structured/TF-IDF baselines for MoCA<26
effect: AHI rule AUC 0.456; age-and-education model 0.759; GPT-5.2 0.698 (98.6% sensitivity, 47.4% specificity); Gemini 3 Pro 0.884, exceeding baselines after Holm correction.
quote: Gemini 3 Pro achieved the highest discrimination (AUC 0.884, 95% CI 0.822-0.934), exceeding the age-and-education model, the full structured model, the gradient-boosted structured model, and the input-matched TF-IDF model after Holm correction within their respective comparison families.

title: Comparative evaluation of large language models in answering patient questions following periodontal and peri-implant examination: an expert-based study
venue: Journal of stomatology, oral and maxillofacial surgery
outcome: Readability of LLM patient-education responses (Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level) across models
effect: Claude had the lowest Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level (7.54 ± 1.27) and the most favorable readability profile. Grade levels for the other models are not given in the abstract.
quote: Conversely, Claude performed significantly better regarding response completeness (4.77 ± 0.22) and demonstrated the most favorable overall readability profile, yielding the lowest Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level (7.54 ± 1.27).
sample_unit: LLM responses (40 patient-style queries x 3 models)

title: Acceptability of AI-Assisted Psychotherapy to Prospective Patients and Their Intent to Continue Treatment: A Vignette Study
outcome: Acceptability and continuation intent under transparent vs covert therapist AI use
effect: Covert AI use produced the strongest declines in acceptability and continuation intent; transparency reduced but did not eliminate negative reactions (all p<0.001 vs control).
quote: Transparency reduced, but did not eliminate, negative reactions.

title: Acceptability of AI-Assisted Psychotherapy to Prospective Patients and Their Intent to Continue Treatment: A Vignette Study
outcome: acceptability and continuation intent
effect: Therapist AI use reduced acceptability and continuation intent versus control; all p<0.001; covert use produced strongest declines.
quote: Across all models, therapist use of AI substantially reduced perceived acceptability and continuation intent compared with the control scenario (all p<0.001).

title: Evaluation and comparison of large language model responses to common discharge questions from patients with acute coronary syndrome after percutaneous coronary intervention: An expert-rated comparative study
outcome: Expert-rated accuracy and guideline concordance of LLM post-PCI discharge answers
effect: ChatGPT scored higher than DeepSeek in accuracy, guideline concordance, completeness, total quality (adjusted P=0.015, 0.015, 0.019, 0.005). Five-domain satisfactory rates 100.0% vs 90.7% (P=0.125).
quote: After pairing and Holm adjustment, ChatGPT scored higher in accuracy, guideline concordance, completeness, and total quality (adjusted P=0.015, 0.015, 0.019, and 0.005).
sample_unit: LLM responses (25 questions x 2 models x 3 responses)

title: Evaluation and comparison of large language model responses to common discharge questions from patients with acute coronary syndrome after percutaneous coronary intervention: An expert-rated comparative study
outcome: Expert-adjudicated safety flags (major error or potentially harmful recommendation) in LLM responses
effect: 149/150 responses (99.3%) met primary safety criterion: ChatGPT 75/75, DeepSeek 74/75 (98.7%); one DeepSeek response had major error and harmful recommendation.
quote: Overall, 149/150 responses (99.3%; 95% CI, 96.3%-100.0%) met the primary safety criterion: 75/75 for ChatGPT (100.0%; 95% CI, 95.2%-100.0%) and 74/75 for DeepSeek (98.7%; 95% CI, 92.8%-100.0%).
sample_unit: LLM responses (25 questions x 2 models x 3 responses)

title: Do bots provide correct and adequate guidance regarding acidity: A blinded comparison rated by patients and physicians
outcome: Readability of LLM answers to acidity questions, plus patient-rated comprehensibility
effect: ChatGPT-5 was most readable, about high-school level; Gemini-2.5 and Claude-4 were more linguistically complex. Patients rated comprehensibility uniformly high across all models.
quote: Readability analysis showed that ChatGPT-5 produced the most accessible responses, corresponding approximately to a high-school reading level, whereas Gemini-2.5 and Claude-4 generated more linguistically complex content.

title: Development of an LLM pipeline exceeding physician-documented cardiovascular risk scores under routine clinical conditions
outcome: Agreement and deviation of AI pipeline scores vs treating physicians and other LLM configurations against expert ground truth
effect: Pipeline mean Krippendorff's α 0.78 vs 0.32 standalone LLMs, 0.39 RAG, 0.31 treating physicians; mean RMSE 0.89 vs 5.81, 1.85, 1.34.
quote: Pipeline-generated scores showed substantially higher agreement with expert adjudication than standalone LLMs, LLMs with RAG, and treating physicians (mean Krippendorff's α: 0.78 vs. 0.32 vs. 0.39 vs. 0.31) and lower deviation from ground truth (mean RMSE: 0.89 vs. 5.81 vs. 1.85 vs. 1.34).

title: Perception and accuracy of an AI-based contactless wellness screening system in dental setting; a cross-sectional study
outcome: Agreement of AI contactless vitals with automated and manual reference measurements in local patients
effect: No significant differences for respiratory rate and oxygen saturation (p>0.05); significant differences for heart rate, SBP, DBP vs automated device (p<0.05); BP limits of agreement ±30 mmHg SBP, ±20 mmHg DBP.
quote: There were no significant differences between the contactless AI-based device system and automated or manual measurements for respiratory rate and oxygen saturation (p > 0.05).

title: Error Detection and Correction in Chinese Radiology Reports Using Large Language Models: Real-World Clinical Validation Study
outcome: LLM error detection performance compared with human readers of varying expertise
effect: DeepSeek-R1 detection 83% vs junior radiologists 80% (P=.39) and senior radiologists 78% (P=.19); better than nonradiologists 66% and nonphysicians 38% (P<.001). Standalone LLM only; no human-with-AI arm.
quote: DeepSeek-R1 showed performance comparable to radiologists (83%, 95% CI 76%-89% vs 80%, 95% CI 72%-86% for junior radiologists and 78%, 95% CI 70%-85% for senior radiologists; P=.39 and P=.19, respectively) and significantly better performance than that of nonradiologists and nonphysicians (83%, 95% CI 76%-89% vs 66%, 95% CI 57%-74% and 38%, 95% CI 30%-47%; P<.001, respectively).

title: Error Detection and Correction in Chinese Radiology Reports Using Large Language Models: Real-World Clinical Validation Study
outcome: Comparison of eight LLMs and eight human readers on identical error-detection reports
effect: DeepSeek-R1 had the highest test-set detection rate at 89% (P=.001-.007 vs other 7 models) and matched radiologists (83% vs 80% and 78%).
quote: On the test set, DeepSeek-R1 achieved the highest overall detection rate at 89% (95% CI 87%-90%), significantly better than the other 7 models (P=.001-.007).

title: Error Detection and Correction in Chinese Radiology Reports Using Large Language Models: Real-World Clinical Validation Study
outcome: LLM error detection performance across Chinese and English reports
effect: DeepSeek-R1 and Claude-3.5-Sonnet detected 94% and 93% of errors in external English MIMIC-III reports; internal Chinese validation 83% and 80%.
quote: On the external validation set, DeepSeek-R1 and Claude-3.5-Sonnet achieved detection rates of 94% (95% CI 89%-97%) and 93% (95% CI 88%-97%), respectively.

title: Evaluation of Prompt Design and Internal Reasoning in Chatbot-Based Medical History Taking: Simulation Study
outcome: Checklist history coverage
effect: Prompt detail was significant: F1,65=56.74; P<.001; η²G=0.085; DT mean coverage 72.3% vs MN 54.0%.
quote: This analysis showed significant main effects of prompt detail ( F 1, 65 =56.74; P <.001; η² G =0.085) and internal reasoning ( F 1, 65 =47.45; P <.001; η² G =0.096).

title: Evaluation of Prompt Design and Internal Reasoning in Chatbot-Based Medical History Taking: Simulation Study
outcome: History coverage of LLM chatbot configurations versus rule-based baseline on same cases
effect: DT coverage 72.3% vs choice baseline 51.1% (Hedge g 1.53, P<.001); MN did not differ significantly from choice (P>.99).
quote: Post hoc pairwise t tests with Bonferroni correction ( Table 2 ) showed that the DT mode significantly outperformed all other configurations.

title: Evaluation of Prompt Design and Internal Reasoning in Chatbot-Based Medical History Taking: Simulation Study
outcome: Coverage versus rule-based baseline
effect: DT outperformed Choice (t65=9.71; P<.001; g=1.53), but MN and Choice did not differ (t65=1.48; P>.99).
quote: The MN and choice modes did not differ significantly ( P >.99).

title: A large language models-assisted and expert-corrected workflow for preoperative anesthesia assessment drafts: A single-centre exploratory feasibility study
outcome: Clinically relevant errors in LLM-generated anesthesia assessment drafts reviewed by anesthesiologists
effect: Thirty-two error instances were identified across the 15 cases, including errors related to proposed plans, ASA physical status classification, and abnormal test interpretation.
quote: The LLM-generated drafts were structurally complete but contained clinically relevant errors, mainly in risk assessment and anesthetic plan formulation.

title: A large language models-assisted and expert-corrected workflow for preoperative anesthesia assessment drafts: A single-centre exploratory feasibility study
outcome: Whether expert review of LLM drafts identifies errors requiring correction before resident-facing use
effect: Expert review found 32 error instances across 15 cases; authors conclude expert correction was essential before resident-facing use.
quote: In this single-centre exploratory study, an LLM-assisted workflow was feasible for producing preliminary preoperative anesthesia assessment drafts, but expert correction was essential before resident-facing use.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Chest Radiography: A Prospective Crossover Multi-Reader Study on Diagnostic Performance and Workflow Efficiency
outcome: Reader diagnostic accuracy with versus without AI assistance in intended deployment mode
effect: AI assistance did not improve diagnostic accuracy; for pleural effusions and pulmonary nodules accuracy decreased in several reader-tool pairings due to increased false positives.
quote: AI assistance did not improve diagnostic accuracy.
sample_unit: patients (1861 radiographs) read by five readers

title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Chest Radiography: A Prospective Crossover Multi-Reader Study on Diagnostic Performance and Workflow Efficiency
outcome: Clinician performance with AI in the intended workflow versus without AI
effect: No improvement in diagnostic accuracy with AI; accuracy decreased in several reader-tool pairings for effusions and nodules through increased false positives.
quote: For pleural effusions and pulmonary nodules, accuracy decreased in several reader-tool pairings due to increased false positives.
sample_unit: patients (1861 radiographs) read by five readers

title: Multidisciplinary dental treatment planning by artificial intelligence: A comparative evaluation
venue: Journal of prosthodontics : official journal of the American College of Prosthodontists
outcome: Clinical knowledge accuracy and diagnostic completeness of AI dental treatment plans versus specialist reference
effect: Mean scores: OpenEvidence 7.7, ChatGPT-5 7.6, Gemini 5.1, Copilot 4.7 out of 10; clinically significant diagnostic errors observed across all evaluated systems.
quote: OpenEvidence and ChatGPT-5 demonstrated greater agreement with the expert reference standard, although clinically significant diagnostic errors were observed across all evaluated systems.
sample_unit: clinical cases (intraoral photo plus periapical radiograph)

title: Multidisciplinary dental treatment planning by artificial intelligence: A comparative evaluation
venue: Journal of prosthodontics : official journal of the American College of Prosthodontists
outcome: Comparison of candidate AI tools on identical cases against expert reference standard
effect: Four AI tools compared on the same 10 cases; scores varied meaningfully: OpenEvidence 7.7±1.4, ChatGPT-5 7.6±1.1, Gemini 5.1±1.2, Copilot 4.7±3.1.
quote: Mean total scores were highest for OpenEvidence (7.7 ± 1.4) and ChatGPT-5 (7.6 ± 1.1), followed by Google Gemini (5.1 ± 1.2) and Microsoft Copilot (4.7 ± 3.1).
sample_unit: clinical cases (intraoral photo plus periapical radiograph)

title: Barriers to Understanding: Readability of Online Laryngomalacia Resources for Parents
outcome: Readability of laryngomalacia parent education materials, including AI chatbot outputs, versus recommended sixth-to-eighth-grade level
effect: Only 1 of 19 resources (5.3%) met recommended reading levels; mean FKGL 10.61 (SD 2.24); AI chatbots and Australian hospital websites were particularly inaccessible.
quote: 94.7% of laryngomalacia parental education materials exceeded recommended readability levels.
sample_unit: unique online resources (Google results, hospital pages, and AI chatbot outputs)

title: Barriers to Understanding: Readability of Online Laryngomalacia Resources for Parents
outcome: Reading level of parent education materials versus guideline-recommended sixth-to-eighth-grade level
effect: Mean FKGL was 10.61 (SD=2.24), exceeding guidelines; Australian hospitals mean FKGL 13.80; UK hospitals 9.45, still above recommendations.
quote: Mean FKGL was 10.61 (SD=2.24) across all resources, significantly exceeding guidelines.
sample_unit: unique online resources (Google results, hospital pages, and AI chatbot outputs)

title: Readability and Quality of Large Language Model Patient Education for Trigeminal Neuralgia: A Cross-Sectional Study
outcome: Readability indices, PEMAT understandability/actionability, and GQS of LLM patient education responses
effect: Readability differed significantly across models. GPT-5 was the most linguistically complex but scored highest on PEMAT and GQS. Wenxin Yiyan was the most readable but generally scored lower on PEMAT and GQS. Prevention/rehabilitation and etiology topics were harder to read.
quote: GPT-5 generated the most linguistically complex responses but achieved the highest ratings for educational suitability and information quality.

title: AI-assisted radiographic fracture detection and length of stay in the adult ambulatory orthopedic emergency department: a before-after cohort study with a disease-specific internal control
outcome: ED length of stay and revisit rates before vs after AI fracture detection deployment, with internal control
effect: Mean F-E LOS fell 135.6 to 127.5 min (Δ -8.13; 95% CI -11.52 to -4.70); F-C control unchanged (Δ +0.37 min); interaction -7.99 min (p=0.004); early revisits did not increase.
quote: Mean F-E LOS decreased from 135.6 to 127.5 min (Δ -8.13 min; 95% CI -11.52 to -4.70; p < 0.001) and median LOS from 114.0 to 109.8 min (p < 0.001); the F-C control was unchanged (Δ + 0.37 min; 95% CI -3.95 to +4.74; p = 0.87); the cohort-by-period interaction was -7.99 min (95% CI -13.36 to -2.62; p = 0.004).

title: Testing Knowledge Boundaries: Adversarial Evaluation of LLMs for Antimicrobial Stewardship
venue: Clinical microbiology and infection : the official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
outcome: dangerous AMS recommendations
effect: Danger flags ranged from 6.7% to 16.7% across models.

effect: Public model fine-tuned on MIMIC-IV-ECG gave AF precision 0.359 and F1 0.523, SR F1 0.677 on ICU expert data, showing dataset shift.
quote: Off-the-shelf model showed limited transferability (F1 = 0.68 for sinus rhythm (SR), 0.52 for atrial fibrillation (AF)).
sample_unit: ECG segments (10-second ICU segments from 226 patients, expert-annotated test set)

title: Leveraging ECG foundation models in critical care for sinus rhythm and atrial fibrillation classification
outcome: Model performance stratified by sex and age subgroups
effect: Minimal differences between sexes and greater variability across age groups for AF than SR, attributed to small uneven subgroup sizes rather than genuine bias.
quote: Demographic analyses showed minimal differences between sexes and greater variability across age groups for AF than for SR, again likely reflecting uneven and small subgroup sizes rather than genuine model bias (Figure 5 ) [ 35 ].
sample_unit: ECG segments (10-second ICU segments from 226 patients, expert-annotated test set)

title: Leveraging ECG foundation models in critical care for sinus rhythm and atrial fibrillation classification
outcome: Robustness to varying lead configurations, noisy segments and temporal windows
effect: Performance stable across 5-10s windows and broadly consistent across lead combinations; lower performance on noisy-but-interpretable segments than clean ones.
quote: Performance was stable across temporal windows, with slightly greater–but still modest–variability across lead configurations, likely influenced by the imbalance between the 1–4 and 5–8 lead groups (Appendix Tables 13 – 14 ).
sample_unit: ECG segments (10-second ICU segments from 226 patients, expert-annotated test set)

title: Leveraging ECG foundation models in critical care for sinus rhythm and atrial fibrillation classification
outcome: Label consistency and performance variation across public datasets/sites
effect: Within-dataset F1 varied by source: SR F1 0.989 Chapman-Shaoxing, 0.971 PTB-XL, 0.799 Georgia, 0.651 CPSC; AF F1 0.756 Georgia vs 0.944 Chapman-Shaoxing.
quote: In contrast, Georgia and CPSC showed weaker and more variable performance, particularly for SR (Table 1 ), suggesting annotation inconsistencies or distribution shifts.
sample_unit: ECG segments (10-second ICU segments from 226 patients, expert-annotated test set)

title: Leveraging ECG foundation models in critical care for sinus rhythm and atrial fibrillation classification
outcome: Dataset documentation completeness and its relation to label consistency
effect: Georgia dataset lacked formal procedural documentation and showed weaker label consistency; well-documented PTB-XL and Chapman-Shaoxing showed stronger consistency.
quote: In contrast, the Georgia dataset lacks formal procedural documentation entirely, providing only its geographical origin.
sample_unit: ECG segments (10-second ICU segments from 226 patients, expert-annotated test set)

title: Leveraging ECG foundation models in critical care for sinus rhythm and atrial fibrillation classification
outcome: reference-label annotator agreement
effect: Pairwise kappa median was 0.60 for SR and 0.49 for AF.
quote: Pairwise kappa among annotators had a median of 0.60 for SR and 0.49 for AF.
sample_unit: ECG segments (10-second ICU segments from 226 patients, expert-annotated test set)

title: Leveraging ECG foundation models in critical care for sinus rhythm and atrial fibrillation classification
outcome: robustness to temporal windows and lead variation
effect: Second-half F1 changes vs first-half: Pub AF –0.015, SR –0.006; Pub+weak AF –0.000, SR –0.004.
quote: Performance was stable across temporal windows, with slightly greater–but still modest–variability across lead configurations, likely influenced by the imbalance between the 1–4 and 5–8 lead groups (Appendix Tables 13 – 14 ).
sample_unit: ECG segments (10-second ICU segments from 226 patients, expert-annotated test set)

title: Organ Segmentation with Machine Learning Models
outcome: Whether per-organ Dice, HD95 and surface Dice reveal model differences hidden by aggregate Dice
effect: Rankings reshuffle by 10-13% on small, complex organs; boundary fidelity separates models into tiers that the Dice ranking hides; aggregate Dice alone judged unsafe for selection.
quote: Selecting a model on aggregate Dice alone is therefore unsafe for organ-specific clinical tasks: per-organ overlap and boundary metrics should be the primary acceptance criteria for selecting a model before clinical deployment.
sample_unit: CT scans (AMOS training/evaluation; TotalSegmentator external set)

title: Organ Segmentation with Machine Learning Models
outcome: Whether model performance ordering generalizes to an independent external dataset
effect: Model ordering largely held on the external TotalSegmentator set (Spearman ρ=0.84), with reshuffling on small organs.
quote: This ordering largely holds on the external set (Spearman ρ=0.84).
sample_unit: CT scans (AMOS training/evaluation; TotalSegmentator external set)

title: Automating the Management of Extraspinal Findings in Magnetic Resonance Imaging Spine Studies Using a Privacy-Preserving Large Language Model: Retrospective Validation Study
outcome: PP-LLM accuracy on local historical MRI reports versus clinician reference standard
effect: Detected 99.8% (400/401) of ESFs; Gwet kappa 0.959 versus reference standard, comparable to two human readers (0.943, 0.934); 8 downgraded and 4 upgraded C-RADS classifications.
quote: The PP-LLM demonstrated almost perfect agreement with the reference standard (Gwet κ=0.959, 95% CI 0.937-0.981), comparable to two human readers (reader 1: κ=0.943; reader 2: κ=0.934), with no statistically significant difference in C-RADS classification accuracy.

title: Large Language Models as a New Tool for Therapists in Internet-Based Cognitive Behavioral Therapy: Blinded Clinician Rating Pilot Experiment
outcome: Clinician-rated quality of LLM vs human therapist responses across five quality dimensions
effect: Ratings were similar on a 1-5 scale, e.g. overall quality LLM 4.00 vs human 3.96 (d=0.06); empathy LLM 4.31 vs human 4.08 (d=0.42); helpfulness LLM 3.85 vs human 3.93.
quote: LLM-generated responses were judged to be of comparable quality to those written by human therapists, though qualitative feedback indicated they were at times generic and insufficiently challenging.

title: Large Language Models as a New Tool for Therapists in Internet-Based Cognitive Behavioral Therapy: Blinded Clinician Rating Pilot Experiment
outcome: Clinician perception of tone, empathy and appropriateness of LLM-generated therapeutic responses
effect: LLM responses had higher empathy ratings (4.31 vs 4.08, d=0.42), but qualitative feedback described them as generic and at times excessively empathetic. Raters identified the LLM source correctly 63% of the time.
quote: Qualitative analysis indicated that LLM-generated responses were perceived as polished but also generic and at times excessively empathetic.

title: The Performance of Large Language Models in Extracting Intestinal Symptoms From Electronic Health Records: Retrospective Observational Study
outcome: Comparison of 12 candidate open-source LLMs on same annotated data to select configuration
effect: Qwen3-8b no-role macro F1 0.89 vs Llama3.1-8b 0.35-0.40 and Llama2-Chinese-7b 0.00-0.11; model choice greatly affected performance.
quote: Among all configurations, Qwen3-8b with no-role prompting achieved a macro F 1 -score of 0.89 and balanced accuracy of 0.95±0.06, with an inference time of 3.64 seconds per record, whereas Qwen3-1.7b under zero-shot prompting achieved a macro F 1 -score of 0.85 with a faster inference time of 1.61 seconds.

title: The Performance of Large Language Models in Extracting Intestinal Symptoms From Electronic Health Records: Retrospective Observational Study
outcome: Inter-rater agreement of independent annotators establishing the reference standard
effect: Two independent trained raters; symptom-specific Cohen kappa 0.87 to 1.00, overall mean 0.92 (SD 0.02); discrepancies resolved by consensus adjudication.
quote: Symptom-specific Cohen κ ranged from 0.87 to 1.00.

title: Transient Ischemic Attack Diagnosis using Explicit Criteria Outperforms Artificial Intelligence: a Prospective Cohort Study
outcome: Diagnostic sensitivity and specificity of AI versus explicit diagnostic criteria for TIA, against neurologist reference standard
effect: AI sensitivity 98.5%, specificity 11.7%; EDCT v1-3 sensitivities 95.5%, 91.0%, 91.0% with specificities 23.3%, 43.3%, 46.7%. AI labelled 119/127 patients as TIA.
quote: Structured clinical criteria (EDCT) outperformed an advanced AI model in distinguishing TIA from mimics in an emergency setting.

title: Artificial intelligence responses to toilet training questions: A reliability and readability analysis of ChatGPT and gemini applications
outcome: Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level of chatbot responses to toilet training questions
effect: Gemini produced a higher (more complex) Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level than ChatGPT, particularly for Questions 3 and 7. No numeric grade levels are given in the abstract.
quote: Regarding readability, Gemini produced responses with a higher Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level (i.e., more complex reading level), particularly for Questions 3 and 7.

title: Improvement of Clinical Practice Guideline Appraisal by Human Experts and AI Agents by Using Structured Guidance: Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Validation Study
outcome: AI agent-human agreement on AGREE II with vs without workbook grounding via retrieval

quote: Using the arithmetic mean across expert 1 and expert 2 consistently for both models, the modified ICC for DeepSeek-R1 rose from 0.613 to 0.709, while o1-mini increased from 0.629 to 0.687.

title: Improvement of Clinical Practice Guideline Appraisal by Human Experts and AI Agents by Using Structured Guidance: Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Validation Study
outcome: Unsupported statements, incorrect references, and overconfident interpretations in AI appraisals
effect: Even with workbook support, AI agents occasionally generated unsupported section references and overinterpreted ambiguous text, so human verification is needed.
quote: Despite these improvements, AI agents occasionally generated unsupported statements, including incorrect section references and overly confident interpretations of ambiguous text [ 55 , 56 ].

title: Improvement of Clinical Practice Guideline Appraisal by Human Experts and AI Agents by Using Structured Guidance: Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Validation Study
outcome: AI agent appraisal compared against human experts on the same guidelines (agreement and time)
effect: DeepSeek-R1 ICC 0.711 vs reference, close to expert 1 (0.734) and above expert 2 (0.651); 5.44 min per guideline vs 14.97 and 7.39 min for experts.
quote: In contrast, DeepSeek-R1 completed appraisals in a mean of 5.44 (SD 0.16) minutes per guideline while maintaining reliability comparable to the more time-intensive human approach.

title: Improvement of Clinical Practice Guideline Appraisal by Human Experts and AI Agents by Using Structured Guidance: Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Validation Study
outcome: Human expert AGREE II agreement
effect: Mean ICCs increased from -0.09–0.66 before the workbook to 0.84-0.92 across AGREE II domains after it.
quote: After introducing a structured guideline appraisal workbook, agreement among human experts improved markedly-mean intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) increased from -0.09 to 0.66 to 0.84-0.92 across AGREE II domains.

title: LLM-Assisted Interpretation of Kinematic Gait Data in Children with Cerebral Palsy: A Pilot Study on Gait Deviation Detection and Surgical Group Recommendations
outcome: LLM output self-consistency across three repeated runs

quote: The LLM showed high self-consistency (>90% across runs).

outcome: Temporal drift in discrimination and calibration of frozen model across BRFSS cycles

title: Algorithmovigilance in AI-Based Oral-Health Surveillance: Temporal Drift, Cross-Survey Differences, and Predictor-Level Structural Stability in Population-Level Severe Tooth Loss Prediction
outcome: Calibration instability missed by discrimination alone
effect: Observed/expected ratio declined 1.0061 to 0.7893; CITL shifted 0.0097 to −0.3645; ECE increased 0.0069 to 0.0352.

title: Evaluation of a large language model for clinician-facing preoperative cost-communication preparation in total knee arthroplasty
outcome: Reproducibility of covered checklist items and safety classification across three repeated LLM runs

quote: Of 180 CL-MNCIs, 126 (70.0%) were covered in all three runs, and case-level agreement in safety classification ranged from 87.5 to 95.8%.

title: Evaluation of a large language model for clinician-facing preoperative cost-communication preparation in total knee arthroplasty
