effect: Fine-tuning raised Qwen3-8B hit1 from 68.41% to 79.84%, highest among evaluated models; physician-adjudicated Hit1 91.6% versus 93.5% for GPT-5.6 Sol (1000 cases).
quote: Fine-tuning increased Qwen3-8B's hit1 from 68.41% to 79.84%, the highest among the evaluated models on the internal test set.

title: Image-Based Diagnosis of Oral Lesions: Performance of a Vision-Language Model versus Human Clinicians
venue: Otolaryngology--head and neck surgery : official journal of American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery
outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of AI versus clinicians of varying expertise against histopathology
effect: Three-class diagnostic accuracy 94.2% for AI-Gemini vs 67.0% to 86.5% for nonsurgeon clinicians; head and neck surgeon highest for precise diagnosis (97.7% vs AI 88.0%).
quote: Three-class diagnostic accuracy was 94.2% for AI-Gemini and 67.0% to 86.5% for nonsurgeon clinicians.

title: The Alignment Paradox of Medical Large Language Models in Infertility Care: Decoupling Algorithmic Improvement From Clinical Decision-Making Quality
outcome: Whether automatic field-level metrics predict expert-rated clinical quality of LLM infertility decision support
effect: GRPO had highest automatic performance (e.g., infertility type accuracy 92.57%), yet blinded experts rated SFT directionally higher on reasoning and feasibility; SFT chosen best in 51.2% vs GRPO 26.2%.
quote: Outcome-based metrics alone are insufficient proxies for clinical utility in ART decision support.

title: The Alignment Paradox of Medical Large Language Models in Infertility Care: Decoupling Algorithmic Improvement From Clinical Decision-Making Quality
outcome: Hallucination rate in LLM outputs on expert review of 100 paired cases
effect: Hallucination rates were 15% (GRPO) and 18.5% (SFT); expert review found clinically unsupported content despite higher automatic performance.
quote: Hallucination rates were 15% (GRPO) and 18.5% (SFT), indicating that higher automatic performance did not eliminate clinically unsupported content and that neither model is ready for clinical deployment.

title: Comparative cost analysis of community-based tuberculosis screening: Computer-Aided Detection (CAD) alone versus CAD with point-of-care C-reactive protein testing in South Africa and Lesotho
outcome: CAD4TBv7 score distribution and threshold validity across sites and X-ray equipment
effect: Pre-specified site thresholds had to be re-determined during the initial trial phase because CAD score distributions depended heavily on each site's radiological equipment.
quote: Site-specific CAD4TBv7 thresholds were pre-specified based on target sensitivity levels but required re-determination during the initial trial phase, as CAD score distributions were found to be highly dependent on the radiological equipment used at each site.

title: Comparative cost analysis of community-based tuberculosis screening: Computer-Aided Detection (CAD) alone versus CAD with point-of-care C-reactive protein testing in South Africa and Lesotho
outcome: Modelled cost per TB case detected at higher prevalence
effect: At modelled 1% TB prevalence with participant numbers and total costs held constant, cost per case decreased from USD 5,454 to USD 2,887 (CAD4TBv7) and USD 7,486 to USD 3,975 (CAD4TBv7-CRP).
quote: However, the average cost per TB case detected decreased substantially to USD 2,887 (95% UI: USD 2,272–3,587) for the CAD4TBv7 approach and USD 3,975 (95% UI: USD 3,157-4,907) for the CAD4TBv7-CRP approach ( Table 2 ) when compared with the primary analysis.

title: Multicenter External Validation of the PIPRA Model for Postoperative Delirium in Older Adults
outcome: External validation discrimination of PIPRA versus development dataset
effect: AUC 0.73 (95% CI 0.69-0.77) vs 0.80 (0.77-0.82) in development; imperfect calibration at higher risks limits use of absolute risk estimates.
quote: PIPRA discriminated with an AUC of 0.73 (95% CI: 0.69-0.77), compared to the AUC of the original development dataset (0.80 (95% CI: 0.77-0.82)).

title: Multicenter External Validation of the PIPRA Model for Postoperative Delirium in Older Adults
outcome: Need for local recalibration given imperfect calibration in external validation
effect: Imperfect calibration, particularly at higher risks, limits direct use of absolute risk estimates; local recalibration required before implementation.
quote: Local recalibration and dedicated implementation studies are required before considering its general implementation to guide targeted delirium prevention.

title: Large-Scale Large Language Model (LLM)-Assisted Report Mining for Elbow Tendon Co-occurrence Epidemiology: Prevalence, Association, and Validation
outcome: LLM extraction accuracy versus blinded human review of 400 sampled reports
effect: Accuracy 84.2% (kappa 0.685) for distal biceps and 85.2% (kappa 0.705) for common extensor; common extensor systematically over-classified (sensitivity 96.1%, specificity 78.5%, McNemar p<0.001).
quote: Human validation of 400 reports demonstrated substantial agreement for both variables (distal biceps: accuracy 84.2%, κ = 0.685; common extensor: accuracy 85.2%, κ = 0.705).

title: Improving Reliability and Explainability of Medical Question Answering Through Atomic Fact-Checking in Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models: Creation and Validation Study
outcome: Answer quality on AMEGA benchmark with atomic fact-checking versus RAG alone
effect: Significant improvement for all LLMs tested (P<.001 for 13/16 models, P<.01 for 2/16, P<.05 for 1/16); human-rated overall answer improvement up to 50% on tumor board cases.
quote: The AMEGA auto-evaluation analysis revealed a significant improvement in answer quality by applying our fact-checking algorithm in contrast to RAG only for all LLMs tested ( P <.001 for 13/16 models, P <.01 for 2/16 models, and P <.05 for 1/16 models; Figure 3 ; see Table S6 in Multimedia Appendix 1 ).

title: Improving Reliability and Explainability of Medical Question Answering Through Atomic Fact-Checking in Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models: Creation and Validation Study
outcome: Accuracy of tracing each atomic fact to supporting guideline chunk
effect: Simple chain-of-thought prompt identified the correct chunk in 75% of cases as first choice and 91.9% among the top 3 chunks.
quote: A simple chain-of-thought prompt using GPT-4o identified the correct chunk in 75% of cases as the first choice and in 91.9% of cases among the top 3 chunks, outperforming a complex chain-of-thought prompt (instructing the LLM to assign scores and then rank) and cosine similarity with a text-embedding model (see Figure S4 in Multimedia Appendix 1 and Table S3 in Multimedia Appendix 1 for prompts).

title: Improving Reliability and Explainability of Medical Question Answering Through Atomic Fact-Checking in Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models: Creation and Validation Study
outcome: Whether post-hoc verification against guideline evidence improves factuality beyond RAG grounding
effect: Atomic fact-checking added to RAG improved answer quality; answers improved in 20%, 10%, 50% and 7.7% of cases versus worsened in 8%, 0%, 7.5% and 3%.
quote: However, since the proportion of answers that improved (20%, 10%, 50%, and 7.7%) was substantially higher, the overall effect of fact-checking clearly enhanced the answer quality.

title: RadCoT: a Radiological Chain-of-Thought framework for enhanced error detection in radiology reports
outcome: LLM error-detection F1 under standard prompting versus structured RadCoT prompting across seven models
effect: Mean micro-averaged F1 rose from 0.77 ± 0.06 (standard) to 0.85 ± 0.06 (RadCoT; p = 0.003); interpretation errors improved from 0.57 to 0.75.
quote: RadCoT significantly improved the mean micro-averaged F1 across all models from 0.77 ± 0.06 (standard) to 0.85 ± 0.06 (RadCoT; p = 0.003).

title: External validation of the VOID predictive model for sacral neuromodulation in non-obstructive urinary retention and/or slow urinary stream
outcome: External discrimination and calibration of VOID model for predicting permanent SNM implantation
effect: AUC 0.627 (fair discrimination), Brier score 0.221 (poor overall accuracy), imperfect calibration; only female sex remained independently associated (OR 2.08, 95% CI 1.14-3.79).
quote: The VOID model demonstrated only fair discrimination and suboptimal calibration, precluding immediate clinical use without prior recalibration.

title: Guideline-Based Evaluation of Large Language Models in Psoriasis Treatment
outcome: Critical safety errors in guideline-based psoriasis treatment recommendations, LLMs versus dermatologists
effect: Experts made 1 critical error; LLMs made 5-9 each (Q = 17.10, P = 0.004). Experts made no critical errors in high-risk scenarios; all LLMs made at least one.
quote: Experts made no critical errors in high-risk scenarios, whereas all LLMs made at least one.

title: Real-Time Artificial Intelligence Diagnostic Copilot in Simulated Primary Care Consultations: Randomized Simulation Study
outcome: Physician Top-3 diagnostic accuracy with versus without AI assistance
effect: Adjusted Top-3 accuracy 62.3% unassisted vs 74.6% AI-assisted (AOR 2.68, 95% CI 1.24 to 6.12; P=.01); Top-1 inconclusive (AOR 1.83, P=.08).
quote: Adjusted Top-3 diagnostic accuracy was 62.3% (95% CI 49.1% to 75.7%) in the unassisted condition and 74.6% (95% CI 63.7% to 85.4%) in the AI-assisted condition (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] 2.68, 95% CI 1.24 to 6.12; χ21=6.4, P=.01).

title: Real-Time Artificial Intelligence Diagnostic Copilot in Simulated Primary Care Consultations: Randomized Simulation Study
outcome: Concordance with incorrect AI suggestions as a measure of overreliance
effect: With an incorrect operative AI suggestion, concordance was 38.8% unassisted vs 55.8% AI-assisted; not statistically significant (AOR 2.08, 95% CI 0.89 to 5.19; P=.09).
quote: In risk scenarios with an incorrect operative AI suggestion, adjusted concordance was 38.8% in the unassisted condition and 55.8% in the AI-assisted condition, but the between-condition comparison was not statistically significant (AOR 2.08, 95% CI 0.89 to 5.19; χ21=2.9, P=.09).

title: Validation of a machine learning model to non-invasively exclude spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
outcome: NPV of previously developed SBP model in temporally later national VA cohort
effect: Cohort of 4192 patients, 15.0% with SBP; NPV 93.6%, 92.0%, 90.9% at <5%, <10%, <15% thresholds. In 107-patient chart-review subgroup NPV was 100%, 97.5%, 95.4%.
quote: At the <5%, <10%, and <15% thresholds for probability of SBP-negativity predicted by the ML model, negative predictive values (NPVs) were 93.6%, 92.0%, and 90.9%, respectively.

title: Safety-Oriented Benchmarking of Large Language Models in Risk-Based Management of Abnormal Cervical Screening Results: Scenario-Based Benchmark Study
outcome: Guideline concordance and unsafe major errors in ASCCP management, by scenario complexity
effect: Error rates rose from 3.1% in low-complexity to 29% in high-complexity scenarios; DeepSeek V3.2 unsafe major error-free rate was 75% under guideline-directed prompt.
quote: Error rates increased substantially with scenario complexity, rising from 3.1% in low-complexity to 29% in high-complexity scenarios.
sample_unit: model responses (60 synthetic scenarios x 3 models x 2 prompt arms x 3 repetitions)

title: Safety-Oriented Benchmarking of Large Language Models in Risk-Based Management of Abnormal Cervical Screening Results: Scenario-Based Benchmark Study
outcome: Effect of guideline-directed prompt package versus baseline prompt on safety and concordance
effect: Guideline-directed prompt package associated with higher odds of unsafe major error-free performance (OR 3.76, 95% CI 2.45-5.77) and exact concordance (OR 8.27, 95% CI 4.14-16.52).
quote: In the main-effects model, the guideline-directed prompt package was associated with higher odds of both unsafe major error-free performance (odds ratio [OR] 3.76, 95% CI 2.45-5.77; P<.001) and exact concordance (OR 8.27, 95% CI 4.14-16.52; P<.001).
sample_unit: model responses (60 synthetic scenarios x 3 models x 2 prompt arms x 3 repetitions)

title: Safety-Oriented Benchmarking of Large Language Models in Risk-Based Management of Abnormal Cervical Screening Results: Scenario-Based Benchmark Study
outcome: Safety and concordance with guideline-directed prompt package versus baseline prompt
effect: Guideline-directed prompting improved unsafe major error-free performance (OR 3.76) and exact concordance (OR 8.27).
quote: The guideline-directed prompt package was associated with improvement in both safety and guideline concordance, but even the best-performing model remained vulnerable in complex, history-dependent scenarios.
sample_unit: model responses (60 synthetic scenarios x 3 models x 2 prompt arms x 3 repetitions)

title: Large-scale esophageal cancer screening through noncontrast computed tomography and artificial intelligence
outcome: False positives after calibration on real-world local cohort data
effect: Calibration in real-world cohort (three centers, n = 35,402) reduced false positives by 72.7% while preserving sensitivity; prospective PPV 42.2%, low-dose screening specificity 99.94%.
quote: Calibration in a real-world cohort (three centers, n = 35,402) reduced false positives by 72.7% while preserving sensitivity; prospective hospital validation (n = 17,446) achieved a 42.2% PPV, and real-world low-dose screening (n = 10,959) reached 99.94% specificity.

title: AI-assisted vs. textbook-based vs. blended learning for acute abdomen diagnosis: a retrospective cohort study of emergency interns
outcome: Diagnostic accuracy using AI combined with traditional resources vs primarily AI
effect: Accuracy 87.1% blended vs 82.4% AI-assisted; difference not significant (OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.41–1.16, p=0.209). Missed diagnoses 6.7% blended vs 14.3% AI-assisted; misdiagnosis 6.2% vs 3.3%.
quote: The difference between AI-assisted and blended learning was not statistically significant (OR = 0.69, 95% CI: 0.41–1.16, p = 0.209).

title: AI-assisted vs. textbook-based vs. blended learning for acute abdomen diagnosis: a retrospective cohort study of emergency interns
outcome: Diagnostic accuracy with blended versus AI-assisted learning
effect: Accuracy was 87.1% (blended) versus 82.4% (AI-assisted); AI-assisted versus blended OR = 0.69, 95% CI: 0.41–1.16, p = 0.209. Unaided skill retention was not assessed.
quote: The difference between AI-assisted and blended learning was not statistically significant (OR = 0.69, 95% CI: 0.41–1.16, p = 0.209).

title: Guideline Concordance of ChatGPT-Generated Responses on Antibiotic Prophylaxis in Endodontics
outcome: Concordance of ChatGPT-5 antibiotic prophylaxis answers with AHA/AAE/ADA guidelines, rated by one endodontist
effect: Full agreement in 10/17 (58.8%), partial in 4 (23.5%) due to unnecessary expansion of indications, disagreement in 3 (17.6%), mainly immunocompromised cases; no response deemed clinically unsafe.
quote: ChatGPT demonstrated full agreement with expert, guideline-based recommendations in 10 of 17 scenarios (58.8%), particularly in classical teaching domains such as infective endocarditis prophylaxis, antibiotic selection, dosage, and timing.

title: Comparative evaluation of ambient digital scribe systems in clinical documentation
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
outcome: Side-by-side comparison of 3 ambient scribe vendors on identical recordings, Likert ratings and error audit
effect: Vendor A had highest Likert ratings (Friedman χ²(2)=15.529, P<.001 short visit); audit found fewest errors in Vendor B (n=3), then A (n=8), C (n=9). Vendor rankings differed by method.
quote: In this exploratory sample, Vendor A received the highest mean Likert ratings across all 4 domains (Friedman χ²(2) = 15.529, P < .001 short visit; χ²(2) = 10.753, P = .005 long visit).

title: Comparative evaluation of ambient digital scribe systems in clinical documentation
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
outcome: Audit-identified hallucinations, omissions, and inaccuracies in ambient scribe notes
effect: Audit identified errors in all three vendors' notes: Vendor B n=3, Vendor A n=8, Vendor C n=9. Clinician preference did not track audit error counts.
quote: The audit identified fewest errors in Vendor B's notes (n = 3), followed by Vendor A (n = 8) and Vendor C (n = 9).

title: Comparative evaluation of ambient digital scribe systems in clinical documentation
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
outcome: Whether clinician Likert ratings of scribe quality align with transcript-level error audit
effect: Clinician ratings did not track audit error counts; physicians flagged hallucinations more often than the audit confirmed ('pseudo-hallucinations'). After Bonferroni correction only Vendor A vs B on short visit remained significant (P=.0098).
quote: In this sample, clinician preference did not track audit-identified error counts, raising the hypothesis that note-style features influence ratings alongside documentation correctness; larger samples are required.

title: Evaluation of the accuracy and reproducibility of large language models (ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Gemini) in responding to patient-centered lipedema questions
outcome: Reproducibility of LLM answers across repeated sessions
effect: Each model was queried twice; DeepSeek most consistent across sessions, while ChatGPT and Gemini showed more variability, particularly in treatment and quality-of-life questions.
quote: Reproducibility analysis revealed that DeepSeek produced the most consistent responses across sessions, while ChatGPT and Gemini showed more variability, particularly in treatment and quality-of-life questions.

title: Evaluation of the accuracy and reproducibility of large language models (ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Gemini) in responding to patient-centered lipedema questions
outcome: Expert-rated accuracy of LLM answers to patient lipedema questions
effect: Comprehensive and correct responses: DeepSeek 72%, Gemini 64%, ChatGPT 56%; accuracy limited in treatment, follow-up, and maintenance questions.
quote: DeepSeek achieved the highest proportion of comprehensive and correct responses (72%), followed by Gemini (64%) and ChatGPT (56%).

title: A Hybrid Rule-Based and Machine Learning-Based Clinical Decision Support System to Support Prescription Review: Development and External Validation Study
outcome: Alert rates and pharmacist-intervention yield at two external validation hospitals
effect: External alert rates 22.6% (7/31) to 32.1% (310/966); 18.8% (22/117) to 57.1% (4/7) of alerts needed pharmacist intervention; AUC 0.871-0.963; no false negatives identified.
quote: In external validation across 2 hospitals, alert rates ranged from 22.6% (7/31) to 32.1% (310/966), with 18.8% (22/117) to 57.1% (4/7) of alerts requiring pharmacist intervention.

title: Implicit Bias in Large Language Model Diagnosis of Eating Disorders: Experimental Vignette Study
outcome: Change in LLM diagnosis when patient demographics varied in matched-pair vignettes
effect: Black patients OR 6.09 (95% CI 5.13-7.24) and Latine patients OR 9.57 (8.00-11.45) for MDD vs White; Asian patients OR 2.88 for AN; female patients OR 0.43 for AN vs males.
quote: Mixed-effects logistic regression with LLM as a random intercept revealed significant demographic biases: Black patients were over 6 times more likely to receive a major depressive disorder (MDD) diagnosis than White patients with identical presentations (odds ratio [OR] 6.09, 95% CI 5.13-7.24), Latine patients were over 9 times more likely (OR 9.57, 95% CI 8.00-11.45), and Asian patients were nearly 3 times more likely to receive an AN diagnosis (OR 2.88, 95% CI 2.44-3.42).

title: Implicit Bias in Large Language Model Diagnosis of Eating Disorders: Experimental Vignette Study
outcome: LLM diagnostic differences across demographic subgroups with identical clinical content
effect: Significant demographic biases in psychiatric diagnosis; Black OR 6.09 and Latine OR 9.57 for MDD, female OR 0.43 for AN; intermodel Fleiss kappa 0.410 for ambiguous vignettes.
quote: These findings demonstrate that LLMs exhibit systematic demographic biases in psychiatric diagnosis even when clinical content is held constant, revealing measurable patterns that can inform improvements to training data, model architecture, and clinical deployment frameworks.

title: AI-based delineation based on clinical data in MR-guided brachytherapy for cervical cancer reduces delineation time - A prospective paired trial
venue: Physica medica : PM : an international journal devoted to the applications of physics to medicine and biology : official journal of the Italian Association of Biomedical Physics (AIFB)
outcome: Delineation time with versus without AI assistance in intended deployment mode
effect: AI-assisted delineation reduced time by 10.1 min (95% CI 7.4-12), a 31% decrease compared with oncologist delineating from scratch.
quote: AI-based delineations resulted in a time reduction of 10.1 min (95% CI: [7.4, 12] minutes), corresponding to a 31% decrease in delineation time.

title: AI-based delineation based on clinical data in MR-guided brachytherapy for cervical cancer reduces delineation time - A prospective paired trial
venue: Physica medica : PM : an international journal devoted to the applications of physics to medicine and biology : official journal of the Italian Association of Biomedical Physics (AIFB)
outcome: Prospective clinical use of AI on live data with oncologist correction
effect: AI outputs were shown to and corrected by oncologists in live care, not hidden; median mean surface distance between AI and clinical delineations was below 2.1 mm.
quote: When using AI support, the median of the mean surface distance between the AI and clinically used delineation for all OARs and targets was below 2.1 mm.

title: A clinical prediction model to support risk-adapted fibrinogen monitoring during tigecycline therapy: multicenter development and validation
outcome: Calibration drift in prospective temporal validation of the prediction model
effect: Discrimination attenuated in full prospective cohort (AUC 0.693, N=319); calibration drift supported local recalibration before implementation; decision-curve analysis favored model-guided monitoring after recalibration.
quote: In the full prospective eligible cohort (N=319), discrimination attenuated (AUC 0.693) and calibration drift supported local recalibration before implementation.

title: A clinical prediction model to support risk-adapted fibrinogen monitoring during tigecycline therapy: multicenter development and validation
outcome: Model performance on external and temporal prospective validation versus development
effect: Optimism-corrected development, external validation, and prospective validation AUCs were 0.755, 0.731, and 0.714, showing modest attenuation on external and later data.
quote: Optimism-corrected development, external validation, and prospective validation AUCs were 0.755, 0.731, and 0.714, respectively.

title: A clinical prediction model to support risk-adapted fibrinogen monitoring during tigecycline therapy: multicenter development and validation
outcome: decision-analytic utility after recalibration
effect: decision-curve analysis favored model-guided monitoring at prespecified threshold probabilities
quote: After recalibration, decision-curve analysis favored model-guided monitoring at prespecified threshold probabilities.

title: Clinical evaluation and regression test of a commercial deep-learning auto-segmentation model
venue: Journal of applied clinical medical physics
outcome: Geometric and dosimetric performance change after software upgrade of DLS model versus prior version
effect: Head and neck, thorax and male pelvis showed overall consistent performance after 2024A upgrade; version differences limited to selected structures (p<0.05), plus one true spinal canal segmentation failure found only on case-level review.
quote: However, in one patient, the 2024A model failed to correctly segment the spinal canal and instead generated a contour along the chest wall.

title: Clinical evaluation and regression test of a commercial deep-learning auto-segmentation model
venue: Journal of applied clinical medical physics
outcome: Local performance of DLS versus clinical reference contours, with decision on commissioning by site
effect: Abdomen commissioned (DSC 0.95 ± 0.014); breast model not recommended for clinical use (DSC 0.66 ± 0.15, HD95 22.2 ± 9.6 mm) against local reference.
quote: Breast segmentation results showed low performance (DSC 0.66 ± 0.15, MSD 4.8 ± 1.93 mm, and HD95 22.2 ± 9.6 mm) compared to clinical reference, so the breast structure models are not recommended for clinical use.

title: Clinical evaluation and regression test of a commercial deep-learning auto-segmentation model
venue: Journal of applied clinical medical physics
outcome: Unsafe or inaccurate DLS outputs at case level reaching users
effect: Isolated failures found: spinal canal contour along chest wall in one thorax patient, shoulder segmented as breast in one case; esophagus truncated with dose errors up to ~46%.
quote: In one right‐sided breast case, the model incorrectly segmented a shoulder as Breast_R target volume, showing the low robustness performance of the DLS model.

title: Clinical evaluation and regression test of a commercial deep-learning auto-segmentation model
venue: Journal of applied clinical medical physics
outcome: Generalization of vendor DLS model to institutional contouring conventions and anatomy
effect: Breast model discrepancy attributed to differences in contouring guidelines and styles between training data and institutional data; prostate spacers degraded accuracy; unusual anatomy not evaluated.
quote: The breast DLS model was evaluated in version 11B but was not commissioned for clinical use at that time because of the large discrepancy between DLS and the clinical segmentations, likely due to differences in contouring guidelines and styles between the model training data and the institutional contour data.

title: Clinical evaluation and regression test of a commercial deep-learning auto-segmentation model
venue: Journal of applied clinical medical physics
outcome: Revalidation of model after software update to detect performance changes
effect: Regression testing after 2024A upgrade found selective version differences (e.g., mandible, lungs, esophagus, prostate improved; spinal cord DSC decreased significantly p<0.001 due to one failure case).
quote: Version‐related differences were selective rather than consistent across sites.

title: Clinical evaluation and regression test of a commercial deep-learning auto-segmentation model
venue: Journal of applied clinical medical physics
outcome: Pre-release testing of updated model for errors using prior commissioning datasets
effect: Regression testing of upgraded model detected a true spinal canal segmentation failure and a breast segmentation of the shoulder, plus significant changes for several structures.
quote: This represented a true segmentation failure and highlights the importance of case‐level review following model updates.

title: Clinical evaluation and regression test of a commercial deep-learning auto-segmentation model
venue: Journal of applied clinical medical physics
outcome: Post-upgrade segmentation performance
effect: After upgrade, head/neck, thorax, male pelvis had mean DSC 0.81±0.09, 0.84±0.13, 0.89±0.06; selected paired differences p<0.05.
quote: Regression testing showed that, in comparison with the previously commissioned data, mean [± standard deviation (SD)] DSC values were 0.81 ± 0.09 for the head and neck, 0.84 ± 0.13 for the thorax, and 0.89 ± 0.06 for male pelvis.

title: Clinical evaluation and regression test of a commercial deep-learning auto-segmentation model
venue: Journal of applied clinical medical physics
outcome: Local contouring-practice shift
effect: Breast DLS was not commissioned because of large DLS-clinical discrepancies attributed to training versus institutional contouring guideline/style differences.
quote: The breast DLS model was evaluated in version 11B but was not commissioned for clinical use at that time because of the large discrepancy between DLS and the clinical segmentations, likely due to differences in contouring guidelines and styles between the model training data and the institutional contour data.

title: Clinical evaluation and regression test of a commercial deep-learning auto-segmentation model
venue: Journal of applied clinical medical physics
outcome: Unrepresented prostate spacer anatomy
effect: Prostate spacer cases (SpaceOAR, Barrigel) had accuracy suffering because altered anatomy was not represented in training data; no spacer-specific metrics reported.
quote: Version 2024A improved somewhat over 11B, but accuracy still suffered with prostate spacing agents (SpaceOAR, Barrigel), since these alter local anatomy in ways not represented in the DLS training data.

title: Clinical evaluation and regression test of a commercial deep-learning auto-segmentation model
venue: Journal of applied clinical medical physics
outcome: Auto-segmentation geometric performance across software versions
effect: Lung_R DSC improved significantly (p = 0.04), whereas Lung_L DSC decreased significantly (p = 0.03) and MSD worsened (p = 0.02), while most other structures were consistent across versions.
quote: In the thorax cohort, significant improvement was observed for Lung_R DSC ( p = 0.04), whereas Lung_L showed a significant decrease in DSC ( p = 0.03) and worse MSD ( p = 0.02).

title: Performance of Cloud-Hosted Large Vision-Language Models on the Japanese National Examination for Clinical Laboratory Technicians: Comparative Benchmarking Study
outcome: Accuracy on post-knowledge-cutoff exam questions versus historical questions, to check contamination
effect: On 200 post-cutoff 2025 questions, accuracy matched historical averages (GPT-5 91.5%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 90.7%, GPT-4o 82.0%), so no material degradation on unseen questions.
quote: On 200 postknowledge cutoff questions from the 71st examination (2025), model accuracies were comparable to historical averages (eg, GPT-5 91.5%, 95% CI 86.8%-94.6%; Gemini 2.5 Pro 90.7%, 95% CI 85.8%-94.0%; GPT-4o 82.0%, 95% CI 76.1%-86.7%), indicating no material performance degradation on unseen questions.

title: Artificial intelligence as a source of psychotherapy-related psychoeducation: a cross-sectional content analysis of information on eye movement desensitization and reprocessing
outcome: Readability of LLM EMDR psychoeducation responses versus recommended patient education levels
effect: All evaluated models produced responses exceeding commonly recommended readability levels for patient education materials; DeepSeek was most readable.
quote: All the evaluated models produced responses that exceeded the commonly recommended readability levels for patient education materials.

title: Me, my doctor and AI: a qualitative interview study on patients' requirements for trustworthy use of AI-CDSS in ophthalmology
outcome: Patient expectations of being informed when AI-CDSS contributes to their care
effect: Almost all participants expected to be informed when AI-CDSS were used; preferences on the amount and format of information varied.
quote: Almost all participants expected to be informed when AI-CDSS were used, although preferences regarding the amount and format of information varied.

title: Social Status and Clinical Resource Allocation by a Large Language Model: An Evaluation of 30,618 Decisions
outcome: Change in LLM allocation choices when non-clinical patient attributes varied counterfactually with clinical need held constant
effect: Indigenous OR 16.48 and Black OR 8.07 vs White; high-status occupation OR 0.064; friend of leadership OR 0.121; major donor OR 0.092; choice-score concordance 95.1%.
quote: Indigenous and Black race were associated with substantially higher odds of selection relative to White race (Indigenous: OR 16.48, 95% CI 14.85-18.28; Black: OR 8.07, 95% CI 7.32-8.90), corresponding to position-balanced absolute increases in selection probability of 30.7 and 16.3 percentage points, respectively.

title: Social Status and Clinical Resource Allocation by a Large Language Model: An Evaluation of 30,618 Decisions
outcome: LLM allocation decisions varying by demographic and social attributes despite identical clinical need
effect: Large position-averaged associations between non-clinical attributes and allocation; position-balanced selection probability increases of 30.7 (Indigenous) and 16.3 (Black) percentage points versus White.
quote: In this controlled audit, the LLM's allocation decisions varied substantially according to demographic and social characteristics despite identical stated clinical need, prognosis, and expected benefit.

title: Development and Effects of a Metaverse-Based Generative AI Nursing Informatics Competency Education Program for Clinical Nurses
outcome: Self-reported nursing informatics competency and ethical awareness of AI use
effect: The six-week generative AI education program improved nursing informatics competency more than control (p < 0.01), sustained at 4 weeks. Ethical awareness of AI use, self-efficacy, and EBP also improved (all p < 0.01), but these were unadjusted for multiplicity.
quote: Compared with the control group, the intervention group demonstrated a significantly greater improvement in nursing informatics competency, the pre-specified primary outcome (p < 0.01), sustained at the four-week follow-up.

title: Development and Effects of a Metaverse-Based Generative AI Nursing Informatics Competency Education Program for Clinical Nurses
outcome: ethical awareness of AI use
effect: The intervention group demonstrated greater improvements for ethical awareness of AI use (p < 0.01).
quote: Greater improvements were also observed for the secondary outcomes-general self-efficacy, ethical awareness of AI use, and evidence-based practice (all p < 0.01)-though these findings should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating given the absence of multiplicity adjustment.

title: Artificial intelligence-based diagnostic decision support for primary care of older adults using collective intelligence and imitation learning
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
outcome: Clinician disagreement with model recommendations versus observed practice in randomized blinded equivalence study

quote: In clinician-validation, diagnostic disagreements were statistically equivalent between model recommendations and observed practice while order disagreements were not.

title: Local adaptation of a chest radiograph AI model for pulmonary tuberculosis triage in Uzbekistan: Pooled and site-stratified internal validation and exploratory workstation integration
outcome: Discrimination of locally adapted vs public baseline TB classifier on held-out set
effect: Adapted held-out ROC AUC 0.9902; paired AUC difference from public baseline 0.0054 (95% CI -0.0077 to 0.0230; p = 0.4864), no statistical superiority.
quote: The paired AUC difference from the public baseline was 0.0054 (95 % CI -0.0077 to 0.0230; p = 0.4864), showing no statistical superiority.

title: Local adaptation of a chest radiograph AI model for pulmonary tuberculosis triage in Uzbekistan: Pooled and site-stratified internal validation and exploratory workstation integration
outcome: Site-stratified AUC performance of adapted model at two sites

quote: Adapted held-out AUCs were 0.9844 (0.9375-1.0000) at the District Hospital and 0.9973 (0.9841-1.0000) at the TB Dispensary; these were site-stratified internal estimates, not institution-held-out validation.

title: Local adaptation of a chest radiograph AI model for pulmonary tuberculosis triage in Uzbekistan: Pooled and site-stratified internal validation and exploratory workstation integration
outcome: Adapted model versus public baseline AUC
effect: AUC difference from public baseline was 0.0054 (95% CI -0.0077 to 0.0230; p = 0.4864), showing no statistical superiority.
quote: The paired AUC difference from the public baseline was 0.0054 (95 % CI -0.0077 to 0.0230; p = 0.4864), showing no statistical superiority.

title: ProMem-agent: Procedural memory-augmented large language model agents for clinical trajectory reasoning
outcome: External dataset performance and calibration versus internal MIMIC-IV test performance
effect: Without recalibration, AUC/AUPRC were 0.823/0.402 on eICU, 0.831/0.429 on MIMIC-III, and 0.803/0.361 on HiRID versus 0.836/0.481 internally; calibration slopes 0.88, 0.91, 0.85 versus 0.97 internally.
quote: Without memory reconstruction or external recalibration, AUC/AUPRC values were 0.823/0.402 on eICU, 0.831/0.429 on MIMIC-III, and 0.803/0.361 on HiRID.

title: Generative AI responses to exercise-related questions asked by patients with multiple sclerosis: An evaluation of quality, accuracy, and readability
outcome: Flesch Reading Ease of chatbot responses to MS exercise questions
effect: Mean FRE scores were 41.70 (ChatGPT) and 38.21 (Gemini); both classified as 'difficult' readability; no significant difference between models (p > 0.05).
quote: The mean FRE scores for ChatGPT and Gemini were 41.70 and 38.21, respectively, with responses from both models classified at a "difficult" readability level.

title: Generative AI responses to exercise-related questions asked by patients with multiple sclerosis: An evaluation of quality, accuracy, and readability
outcome: Readability of AI-generated patient education responses
effect: Both models' responses were at a 'difficult' readability level (mean FRE 41.70 and 38.21), limiting patient accessibility.
quote: Nonetheless, patient accessibility could be limited by the poor readability metrics observed in both tools.

title: Evaluating large language models for myocardial infarction public health education: a comparative study on information quality, transparency and readability
outcome: Readability of LLM-generated MI patient education text versus sixth-grade benchmark
effect: All three models failed to meet the recommended sixth-grade reading benchmark, indicating high reading difficulty; Claude was relatively more comprehensible than the others.
quote: Regarding readability, although Claude generated relatively more comprehensible text, all models failed to meet the recommended sixth-grade reading benchmark, indicating high reading difficulty.

title: Impact of AI assistance on pharmacist and pharmacy trainee accuracy and automation bias during medication order verification: A randomized simulation trial
venue: American journal of health-system pharmacy : AJHP : official journal of the American Society of Health-System Pharmacists
outcome: User accuracy with vs without AI assistance in medication order verification; overreliance assessed
effect: AI assistance raised overall accuracy (adjusted OR 1.58; 95% CI 1.16-2.15). Correct AI recommendations raised accuracy to 80.2%, incorrect AI recommendations lowered it to 26.1%.
quote: AI assistance was associated with significantly higher overall accuracy (adjusted odds ratio, 1.58; 95% confidence interval, 1.16-2.15).

title: Impact of AI assistance on pharmacist and pharmacy trainee accuracy and automation bias during medication order verification: A randomized simulation trial
venue: American journal of health-system pharmacy : AJHP : official journal of the American Society of Health-System Pharmacists
outcome: Automation bias: acceptance of incorrect AI recommendations and accuracy when disagreeing with AI
effect: Participants accepted 80.2% of correct and 73.9% of incorrect recommendations; accuracy dropped to 21.7% when users disagreed with the AI.
quote: Participants demonstrated high concordance with AI suggestions, accepting 80.2% of correct recommendations and 73.9% of incorrect recommendations.

title: Impact of AI assistance on pharmacist and pharmacy trainee accuracy and automation bias during medication order verification: A randomized simulation trial
venue: American journal of health-system pharmacy : AJHP : official journal of the American Society of Health-System Pharmacists
outcome: Clinician accuracy as used with AI in workflow versus unassisted, by experience level
effect: AI-assisted accuracy was higher (aOR 1.58); benefit greatest among students, least among PGY2 residents; accuracy depended on AI correctness.
quote: Subgroup analysis showed the greatest benefit among students and the least benefit among PGY2 residents.

title: The readability and quality paradox: Comparing ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity outputs on pediatric chest pain queries
outcome: Readability of chatbot responses on pediatric chest pain versus sixth-grade reading level threshold
effect: Median readability scores for all three chatbots were significantly above the sixth-grade threshold (p < 0.001); Perplexity was significantly more difficult than ChatGPT and Gemini (p < 0.0167).
quote: The median readability scores computed across all three AI models were found to be statistically and significantly above the targeted sixth-grade comprehension threshold, indicating a high level of difficulty (p < 0.001).

title: Augmenting patient safety surveillance in radiation oncology with large language model-based root cause analysis: A proof-of-concept study
outcome: Hallucination rate in LLM-generated root cause analyses of radiation oncology incidents
effect: All four models exhibited some degree of hallucination, ranging from 11% to 61%; models differed significantly in hallucination rate (p < 0.05).
quote: All models exhibited some degree of hallucination, ranging from 11% to 61%.

title: Real-Time Precision Psychiatry for Schizophrenia: A Microfluidic Genotyping and Super-Learner Platform for Treatment Response Prediction
outcome: Model error on internal cross-validation versus temporally later external validation cohort
effect: Cross-validated RMSE 7.08 (R2 = 0.89) versus external validation RMSE 9.02 (R2 = 0.76), so performance was lower on external data.
quote: The Super Learner model achieved a cross-validated RMSE of 7.08 (R2 = 0.89) and an external validation RMSE of 9.02 (R2 = 0.76).
sample_unit: patients (model development cohort; external validation N=90)

title: Evaluating the Reliability, Accuracy, and Readability of ChatGPT-3.5 and GPT-4 in Providing Patient Education Related to Glenohumeral Joint Osteoarthritis
outcome: Flesch-Kincaid reading level of chatbot responses to patient questions
effect: GPT-3.5 Flesch-Kincaid score 18.3 versus GPT-4 15.4 (significantly higher for GPT-3.5), indicating difficult reading level in both.
quote: On the Flesch- Kincaid scale, GPT-3.5 responses had a significantly higher score of 18.3 compared to GPT-4's 15.4, indicating a more difficult reading level in GPT-3.5's responses.

title: Evaluating the Reliability, Accuracy, and Readability of ChatGPT-3.5 and GPT-4 in Providing Patient Education Related to Glenohumeral Joint Osteoarthritis
outcome: Evidence-based support rating of chatbot responses by surgeons
effect: Both ChatGPT-3.5 and GPT-4 scored lowest on the evidence-based criterion; overall averages 19.7/25 (GPT-3.5) and 18.7/25 (GPT-4).
quote: Both models scored lowest on "Evidence-based" prompts.

title: Transporting a pediatric surgical site infection prediction model to the electronic health record: external validation, harmonization, and recalibration
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
outcome: Discrimination and calibration of registry-derived model on local EHR data
effect: Direct application to institutional EHR cohort: c-statistic 0.60, Brier 0.07, calibration slope 0.15, O/E 0.25, versus registry c-statistic 0.75 and slope 1.00.
quote: Direct application to the institutional EHR cohort produced inflated predicted risk and poor performance, with c-statistic 0.60, Brier score 0.07, calibration slope 0.15, and O/E ratio 0.25.

title: Transporting a pediatric surgical site infection prediction model to the electronic health record: external validation, harmonization, and recalibration
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
outcome: Calibration after logistic recalibration in local EHR cohort
effect: Logistic recalibration restored calibration slope and O/E ratio to 1.00 after predictor harmonization (slope 0.81, O/E 1.35 beforehand).
quote: Logistic recalibration restored calibration slope and O/E ratio to 1.00.

title: Transporting a pediatric surgical site infection prediction model to the electronic health record: external validation, harmonization, and recalibration
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
outcome: Compatibility of model predictor definitions with EHR data
effect: Diagnosis-code predictor misalignment between registry and EHR degraded performance; omitting open-ended diagnosis-code indicators improved c-statistic to 0.70, Brier 0.03, slope 0.81, O/E 1.35.
quote: After omitting open-ended diagnosis-code indicators, performance improved, with c-statistic 0.70, Brier score 0.03, calibration slope 0.81, and O/E ratio 1.35.

title: Transporting a pediatric surgical site infection prediction model to the electronic health record: external validation, harmonization, and recalibration
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
outcome: EHR validation performance
effect: Direct EHR application: c-statistic 0.60, Brier score 0.07, calibration slope 0.15, O/E ratio 0.25.
quote: Direct application to the institutional EHR cohort produced inflated predicted risk and poor performance, with c-statistic 0.60, Brier score 0.07, calibration slope 0.15, and O/E ratio 0.25.

title: Transporting a pediatric surgical site infection prediction model to the electronic health record: external validation, harmonization, and recalibration
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
outcome: registry-to-EHR transportability
effect: Models performing well under internal or registry validation were not directly transportable to real-world EHR environments.
quote: These findings highlight a key challenge for clinical translation: models that perform well under internal or registry-based validation may not be directly transportable to real-world EHR environments.

title: Improving access to rare-disease knowledge: A retrieval-augmented question answering framework for Wilson's disease
outcome: Accuracy and clinical relevance of LLM answers with versus without retrieval grounding
effect: Retrieval grounding substantially improved biological accuracy and clinical relevance; ~7B models performed competitively when paired with the retrieval pipeline (no numbers in abstract).
quote: Our results demonstrate that retrieval grounding substantially improves biological accuracy and clinical relevance, and that smaller, deployable language models (on the order of 7B parameters) can perform competitively when paired with a well-designed retrieval pipeline.

title: A clinical decision support framework for automated M-protein isotype classification from capillary zone electrophoresis immunotyping signals
venue: Clinica chimica acta; international journal of clinical chemistry
outcome: Accuracy of confidence-based triage separating high-confidence samples from those routed to expert review
effect: 62.2% of samples assigned to the high-confidence zone at 96.2% accuracy; external high-zone accuracy was 98.8%; lower-confidence cases routed to expert review.
quote: The confidence triaging system assigned 62.2% of samples to a high-confidence zone at 96.2% accuracy.

title: A clinical decision support framework for automated M-protein isotype classification from capillary zone electrophoresis immunotyping signals
venue: Clinica chimica acta; international journal of clinical chemistry
outcome: Calibration and conformal prediction coverage of model uncertainty estimates
effect: Conformal prediction achieved 95.9% empirical coverage; probability calibration used with confidence-based triaging.
quote: Conformal prediction achieved 95.9% empirical coverage.

title: A clinical decision support framework for automated M-protein isotype classification from capillary zone electrophoresis immunotyping signals
venue: Clinica chimica acta; international journal of clinical chemistry
outcome: Performance drop on independent external samples with frozen weights versus internal performance
effect: External validation accuracy was 0.871 versus internal 0.872; tuning-free cascade out-of-fold accuracy 0.866, indicating negligible hyperparameter overfitting.
quote: External validation accuracy was 0.871.

title: Improving patient communication and understanding of medical reports through text simplification with ChatGPT: a comparative study
outcome: Lay participants' comprehension accuracy and ratings of simplified versus original medical reports
effect: Simplified reports rated higher for clarity, structure, and usefulness (p<0.001); comprehension improved (e.g., MRI 80.3% vs 53.7%; p<0.001); FRE 48.4 vs 22.9.
quote: Across all document types, patients rated simplified texts significantly higher in clarity, structure, and usefulness (p < 0.001), with significantly improved comprehension accuracy (e.g., MRI 80.3% vs. 53.7%; p < 0.001).

title: Burn Extent and Fitzpatrick Skin Tone Assessment from Clinical Photographs: Systematic and Random Error in Multimodal Large Language Models
outcome: Within-image variability across five repeated queries of the same photograph
effect: Median within-image range was 5.0-25.0 pp across repeated queries; averaging the five answers reduced error by only 0.24-2.22 pp.
quote: Across repeated queries, the median within-image range was 5.0-25.0 pp; averaging the five answers reduced error by only 0.24-2.22 pp.

title: Comparison of Multimodal Large Language Models and Oral and Maxillofacial Radiologists in the Detection of Incidental Findings on Panoramic Radiographs: A CBCT-Referenced Diagnostic Accuracy Study
outcome: Diagnostic performance of multimodal LLMs versus expert radiologists on same radiographs against CBCT reference
effect: Expert sensitivity 89.5-91.6%, specificity 92.0-93.0%, accuracy 91.8-92.9% versus LLMs 75.1-83.1%, 88.0-90.0%, 86.8-89.0%; reader effect significant (p<0.001).
quote: Under the consumer-interface conditions and access period tested, the LLMs performed below the experts, particularly for high-risk findings, and should not be used independently to evaluate panoramic radiographs.
sample_unit: panoramic radiographs (4500 finding-level decisions per reader)

title: Comparison of Multimodal Large Language Models and Oral and Maxillofacial Radiologists in the Detection of Incidental Findings on Panoramic Radiographs: A CBCT-Referenced Diagnostic Accuracy Study
outcome: Sensitivity of LLMs for high-risk findings on enriched single-center data
effect: In the exploratory high-risk group, expert sensitivity was 90.9-93.2% versus 62.9-78.0% for the LLMs; the dataset was finding-enriched and single-center, so estimates cannot be transferred to routine populations.
quote: In the exploratory high-risk group, expert sensitivity ranged from 90.9 to 93.2% versus 62.9-78.0% for the LLMs.
sample_unit: panoramic radiographs (4500 finding-level decisions per reader)

title: Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Video Monitoring for Inpatient Fall Prevention: A Retrospective Matched Cohort Study
outcome: Inpatient fall incidence and fall-related injuries before vs after AI video monitoring implementation
effect: Fall rate 1.017 vs 1.286 per 1000 patient-days (exposed vs non-exposed), but no statistically significant effect in Firth logistic or Cox regression.
quote: However, penalized likelihood logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards regression revealed no statistically significant effect of artificial intelligence-assisted video monitoring on fall reduction.

title: Development and Preliminary Evaluation of an AI-Assisted Clinical Decision Support System for Personalized Musculo-Skeletal Pain Management in Integrative Nursing Practice
outcome: Clinically meaningful pain improvement and VAS reduction, AI-assisted vs standard care in non-randomized pilot
effect: Improvement in 85.7% (18/21) vs 71.4% (15/21) (p = 0.449); mean VAS reductions 3.9 ± 1.2 vs 3.2 ± 1.4 (p = 0.092); not statistically significant.
quote: During a preliminary prospective feasibility implementation, clinically favorable numerical trends were observed in the AI-assisted group compared with standard care, including clinically meaningful improvement in 85.7% (18/21) versus 71.4% (15/21) of patients (p = 0.449) and mean VAS reductions of 3.9 ± 1.2 versus 3.2 ± 1.4 (p = 0.092).
sample_unit: patients (retrospective cohort for model development); 42 patients in prospective pilot

title: Quality and Readability of Four AI Chatbots Answering Search-Derived Patient Questions About Primary Aldosteronism: A Cross-Sectional Comparative Study
outcome: Readability of chatbot responses against sixth-grade patient-education benchmark
effect: No readability measure met the sixth-grade benchmark; language was overly complex.
quote: No readability measure met the sixth-grade benchmark.

title: Laboratory Medicine Decision Support-Beyond Exam Passing: A Blinded 100-Case Text-Based Benchmark of Diagnostic Accuracy, Management Quality, and Safety for ChatGPT, Gemini, and DeepSeek-LLM Decision Support in Laboratory Medicine
outcome: Unsafe or guideline-discordant recommendations and primary diagnostic concordance in laboratory medicine vignettes
effect: Unsafe or guideline-discordant recommendations in 2% (ChatGPT-5.2), 4% (Gemini), 5% (DeepSeek); fully concordant primary diagnoses in 88%, 84%, 82% of cases.
quote: Unsafe or guideline-discordant recommendations were uncommon but present (2%, 4%, 5%).

title: Comparative Expert Evaluation of Multimodal Large Language Models for Pediatric Rash Diagnosis: Clinical Utility, Safety, Information Quality, and Readability
outcome: Diagnostic correctness of multimodal LLM responses to pediatric rash vignettes versus reference diagnosis
effect: At least one platform missed the reference diagnosis in 9/15 vignettes; all three missed porphyria. 82.2% of CUS ratings were in categories 4-5.
quote: In the single-query diagnostic assessment, at least one platform missed the reference diagnosis in 9/15 vignettes, and all three missed porphyria.

title: Comparative Evaluation of a New Autonomous AI Agent Versus Frontier LLMs for AI-Generated Patient Information Sheets on Pediatric Pathologies
outcome: Readability (FKGL) and understandability (PEMAT-U) of AI-generated patient information sheets across platforms
effect: Eli5a v2.0 had highest understandability (PEMAT-U 95.05 ± 1.23) and lowest reading grade (FKGL 5.45 ± 0.51); other platforms scored lower on readability and understandability, with platform differences significant (p<0.001).
quote: Eli5a v2.0 obtained the best results for patient-centered communication, with the highest understandability (PEMAT-U 95.05 ± 1.23) and readability (FKGL 5.45 ± 0.51) and an actionability score among the highest of the five platforms (PEMAT-A 89.00 ± 2.62, not significantly different from Perplexity or Doximity).
sample_unit: pediatric oral pathology conditions (patient information sheets per platform)

title: Comparative Evaluation of a New Autonomous AI Agent Versus Frontier LLMs for AI-Generated Patient Information Sheets on Pediatric Pathologies
outcome: Reading grade level of AI-generated patient materials
effect: Eli5a v2.0 FKGL 5.45 ± 0.51 (most appropriate reading grade level); other platforms had higher grade levels, with trade-off between quality/reliability and lay accessibility.
quote: Claude Sonnet 4.6 led in overall quality whereas Eli5a v2.0 achieved the highest understandability and the most appropriatereading grade level.
sample_unit: pediatric oral pathology conditions (patient information sheets per platform)

title: Comparative Evaluation of a New Autonomous AI Agent Versus Frontier LLMs for AI-Generated Patient Information Sheets on Pediatric Pathologies
outcome: Reliability and quality variability of AI-generated patient materials requiring clinician review
effect: DISCERN reliability ranged from 54.50 ± 4.26 (Eli5a) to 70.50 ± 3.20 (Doximity); GQS best for Claude at 4.25 ± 0.39; authors conclude all materials need clinician review.
quote: Platform selection should therefore be matched to the communication task, and all AI-generated patient materials require clinician review before use.
sample_unit: pediatric oral pathology conditions (patient information sheets per platform)

title: Deep Learning for Schatzker Classification on Anteroposterior Radiographs: A Controlled Benchmark and a Transferable Control Protocol
outcome: Whether archive-assembly artifacts (accompanying CT section) leak label information and inflate benchmark performance
effect: Fracture vs no classifiable fracture: network 0.833 vs 0.814 for a no-pixel model (p=0.264); coronal CT section accompanied 126/128 fracture patients but 24/58 others (p=2.9e-19).
quote: a coronal computed tomography section accompanied 126 of 128 fracture patients but 24 of 58 others (p = 2.9 × 10-19)
sample_unit: patients (421 AP knee radiographs; 128 fracture patients in the main six-class analysis)

title: Integrating Clinical Priorities into the Technical Validation of Machine Learning Classifiers: A Generalizable Framework Demonstrated on Opioid Misuse Screening
outcome: Whether clinically weighted metrics, CIs, and threshold choice change model ranking versus raw accuracy
effect: Raw accuracy ranked CSBT-Untuned highest (0.867) but it detected only 38.5% of misuse cases; balanced accuracy/CDPS ranked CSBT-Tuned highest (0.696). Bootstrap CIs showed CSBT-Tuned and RUSBoost overlap.
quote: WEAS reversed this ordering, ranking CSBT-Tuned highest (0.696), followed by RUSBoost (0.690) and CSBT-Untuned (0.658).
sample_unit: survey respondents in the held-out test set (NSDUH 2015-2019)

title: Integrating Clinical Priorities into the Technical Validation of Machine Learning Classifiers: A Generalizable Framework Demonstrated on Opioid Misuse Screening
outcome: Effect of decision threshold choice on sensitivity, false positives, and net benefit
effect: Lowering threshold to 0.33 raised sensitivity from 38.5% to 51.3% and false positives from 119 to 207, reducing PPV from 42.2% to 35.9%; model preference shifted with cost ratio (crossover c_FN≈3.03).
quote: The threshold reduction that increased CSBT-Tuned sensitivity from 38.5% to 51.3% simultaneously increased false positives from 119 to 207, reducing PPV from 42.2% to 35.9%.
sample_unit: survey respondents in the held-out test set (NSDUH 2015-2019)

title: Integrating Clinical Priorities into the Technical Validation of Machine Learning Classifiers: A Generalizable Framework Demonstrated on Opioid Misuse Screening
outcome: Leakage-free preprocessing and strict holdout test evaluation
effect: Preprocessing fit on training only, target-leakage variables excluded, and test set used once; validation performance consistent with test. However, only internal random split of one survey dataset, no external validation.
quote: Across all three models, validation set performance was consistent with test set results.
sample_unit: survey respondents in the held-out test set (NSDUH 2015-2019)

title: Integrating Clinical Priorities into the Technical Validation of Machine Learning Classifiers: A Generalizable Framework Demonstrated on Opioid Misuse Screening
outcome: high raw accuracy concealing poor positive class detection
effect: CSBT-Untuned achieved 86.7% raw accuracy but missed 61.5% of positive cases (sensitivity 38.5%, 139 false negatives)
quote: The results demonstrate that while CSBT-Untuned achieved the highest raw accuracy of 86.7%, it missed 61.5% of positive cases.
sample_unit: survey respondents in the held-out test set (NSDUH 2015-2019)

title: Flatfoot and artificial intelligence: Can language models be trusted for patient education?
outcome: Readability (Flesch-Kincaid grade level, reading ease) of chatbot responses to flatfoot questions
effect: Gemini FK grade 9.2 ± 1.1 vs ChatGPT 11.8 ± 1.4 (P<.001); reading ease 59.4 ± 6.2 vs 42.5 ± 5.3 (P<.001). Both above typical patient-level reading grade.
quote: Gemini also generated longer responses (165 ± 20 vs 120 ± 15 words, P < .001) and showed better readability, with lower Flesch-Kincaid grade level (9.2 ± 1.1 vs 11.8 ± 1.4, P < .001) and higher Flesch reading ease score (59.4 ± 6.2 vs 42.5 ± 5.3, P < .001).

title: Physician readiness for artificial intelligence integration in clinical screening and diagnosis: Multicenter cross-sectional study in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia
outcome: Physician-reported barrier of insufficient AI training and knowledge of AI concepts
effect: Insufficient training was the most frequently reported barrier (58.9%); only 50.3% demonstrated good knowledge of AI concepts and applications.
quote: The most frequently reported barriers were insufficient training (58.9%) and lack of trust in AI systems (53.8%).

title: Large language models for late-life depression: a blinded benchmark of clinical safety, geriatric appropriateness, and triage.
outcome: Under-triage rate among high-risk late-life depression questions
effect: Under-triage occurred in 16.7%, 26.7%, and 36.7% of high-risk responses for ChatGPT, Gemini, and Doubao respectively; high-risk acceptable rates 63.3%, 50.0%, 36.7%.
quote: Among high-risk questions, clinically acceptable response rates were 63.3%, 50.0%, and 36.7%, while under-triage occurred in 16.7%, 26.7%, and 36.7% of responses, respectively.

title: Large language models for late-life depression: a blinded benchmark of clinical safety, geriatric appropriateness, and triage.
outcome: Test-retest clinical consistency of responses across repeated conversations
effect: Test-retest clinical consistency was 90.0% for ChatGPT, 83.3% for Gemini, and 73.3% for Doubao on 30 resubmitted questions.
quote: Test-retest clinical consistency was highest for ChatGPT (90.0%), followed by Gemini (83.3%) and Doubao (73.3%).

title: Large language models for late-life depression: a blinded benchmark of clinical safety, geriatric appropriateness, and triage.
outcome: Major safety errors and clinically acceptable responses for late-life depression questions
effect: Major safety errors in 5.6% (ChatGPT), 10.0% (Gemini), 16.7% (Doubao); clinically acceptable 78.9%, 72.2%, 60.0%.
quote: Major safety errors occurred in 5.6% of ChatGPT responses, 10.0% of Gemini responses, and 16.7% of Doubao responses (raw P = 0.015; FDR-adjusted q=0.023).

title: Diagnostic performance of large language models for discrepancy detection in non-English resident-authored abdominal CT and MRI reports: a Turkish-language evaluation.
outcome: LLM discrepancy detection sensitivity on non-English (Turkish) radiology reports by model

title: Large language model-based triage to identify antiretroviral therapy adherence barriers and risk levels in patient messages.
outcome: Robustness of model classifications to demographic descriptors in inputs, by model
effect: Flan-T5 models were more robust to demographic descriptors than other LLMs; GPT-4.1 and Gemma3 often misclassified inputs as "None." No numbers given in the abstract.
quote: On external datasets, Flan-T5 models outperformed other LLMs (P < .001), and were more robust to demographic descriptors, while GPT-4.1 and Gemma3 often misclassified inputs as "None."

title: Large language model-based triage to identify antiretroviral therapy adherence barriers and risk levels in patient messages.

effect: Barrier detection Macro-F1 fell from 0.83 (test) to 0.71 (external); risk stratification fell from 0.79 to 0.57.
quote: Flan-T5-xl achieved the best barrier detection (Macro-F1 = 0.83 test/0.71 external), and Flan-T5-large excelled in risk stratification (0.79/0.57).

title: Three Large Language Models (LLMs), One Heart: A Comparative Evaluation of ChatGPT, Claude, and DeepSeek in Cardiac Imaging Patient Education.
outcome: Readability of LLM-generated cardiac imaging patient leaflets versus recommended health-literacy standards

title: Three Large Language Models (LLMs), One Heart: A Comparative Evaluation of ChatGPT, Claude, and DeepSeek in Cardiac Imaging Patient Education.
outcome: Reading level of AI-generated patient materials relative to recommended levels
effect: All three models produced content above recommended health-literacy standards; ChatGPT least readable (FRE 50.70), DeepSeek most readable (FRE 70.73).
quote: However, all three models produced content above recommended patient health-literacy standards.

title: Locally deployed large language model for real-world lecanemab eligibility pre-screening.
outcome: Eligibility classification accuracy of LLM pipeline versus rule-based extractor comparator on hold-out set
effect: LLM-based pipeline achieved 94% accuracy and Cohen's kappa 0.90, significantly surpassing the rule-based comparator (80% accuracy).
quote: The LLM-based pipeline achieved 94% accuracy and a Cohen's kappa of 0.90 on the hold-out set, significantly surpassing the rule-based comparator (80% accuracy) and demonstrating performance comparable to human experts.

title: Locally deployed large language model for real-world lecanemab eligibility pre-screening.
outcome: Accuracy against expert consensus on independent hold-out set of local memory clinic reports
effect: Optimized on development set (n = 97) and evaluated on independent hold-out set (n = 99); 94% accuracy, kappa 0.90 against expert consensus.
quote: In a two-stage design, LLM-based extraction prompts, a deterministic rule-based extractor, and a shared downstream rule-based classifier were optimized on a development set (n = 97) and evaluated on an independent hold-out set (n = 99), with expert consensus as ground truth.

title: Cloud-Based and Locally Deployed Language Models in Nursing and Health Care: An AI Act-Aligned Framework
outcome: Resistance to explicit harmful prompts and progressive jailbreak attempts across LLMs
effect: DeepSeek-R1, Perplexity Sonar, Mistral Large 2, and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct failed to resist even explicit harmful prompts; Claude 3 Opus resisted both explicit harmful prompts and all jailbreak attempts.
quote: DeepSeek-R1, Perplexity Sonar, Mistral Large 2, and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct failed to resist even explicit harmful prompts; Claude 3 Opus resisted both explicit harmful prompts and all jailbreak attempts, while demonstrating null sycophancy.

title: Cloud-Based and Locally Deployed Language Models in Nursing and Health Care: An AI Act-Aligned Framework
outcome: Accuracy and focus of references generated by LLMs
effect: Claude 3.7 Sonnet (extended thinking) produced 75.9% of accurate, focused references.
quote: For instance, Claude 3.7 Sonnet (extended thinking) produced 75.9% of accurate, focused references, and achieved high average scores both in clinical safety and data security (mean 6.73, SD 0.23 and mean 6.83, SD 0.41, respectively).

title: Development of a ChatGPT-based assistant in multidisciplinary team discussions in oncological urology: the UroMDT Advisor study
outcome: Expert urologist rating of GPT-generated MDT report accuracy, completeness, clarity
effect: Final reports rated accurate in 90%, fairly accurate 8%, inaccurate 2%; completeness high in 95%; clarity high in 95%.
quote: After resolution of discordant ratings, the GPT-generated final reports were rated as accurate in 90% of cases, fairly accurate in 8%, and inaccurate in 2%.

title: Development of a ChatGPT-based assistant in multidisciplinary team discussions in oncological urology: the UroMDT Advisor study
outcome: Agreement of GPT recommendations with urologists, oncologists, radiation oncologists, and final MDT decision
effect: Exact agreement 61.7%, 66.7%, 63.3%, 66.7%; Cohen's kappa 0.401, 0.489, 0.441, 0.482 (moderate agreement).
quote: Exact agreement between UroMDT Advisor and urologists, oncologists, radiation oncologists, and final MDT decisions was 61.7%, 66.7%, 63.3%, and 66.7%, respectively; the corresponding unweighted Cohen's kappa values were 0.401, 0.489, 0.441, and 0.482.

title: Making medical AI benchmarks clinically interpretable: the case of mental health
outcome: Difference between mental health domain and overall HealthBench benchmark scores
effect: Mental health point estimates differed from overall estimates by -0.034 to +0.047 across deployments; domain composition uneven (postpartum depression 26.8%, suicidal crisis 4.5%, psychosis 0.9%, eating disorders 1.5%).

title: Evaluating reasoning-tuned large language models for clinical decision-making in spine surgery
outcome: Standalone LLM output ratings by surgeons; confounding of presentation clarity with clinical ratings

title: When Treatment Gets More Complicated: AI Readability Declines in Breast Cancer Patient Education
outcome: Readability grade level (FKGL) of LLM breast cancer patient education answers vs 6th-grade threshold

title: When Treatment Gets More Complicated: AI Readability Declines in Breast Cancer Patient Education

outcome: Cross-iteration stability of LLM responses to identical questions (ICC)

title: AI-generated guidance for non-specialist physicians managing inflammatory bowel disease: expert evaluation and case-based testing of GPT-4 and DeepSeek
outcome: Non-specialist physician vignette test scores before vs after reviewing AI outputs
effect: Median per-round score (0-10) rose from 5.5 to 8.0 for GPT-4 (Δ=3.0, p<0.001) and from 6.0 to 8.0 for DeepSeek (Δ=2.5, p<0.001); between-model difference p=0.781.

title: AI-generated guidance for non-specialist physicians managing inflammatory bowel disease: expert evaluation and case-based testing of GPT-4 and DeepSeek
outcome: Presence of red-flag/referral triggers and safety omissions in LLM IBD guidance
effect: Both models showed inconsistent red-flag/referral triggers and safety omissions; no harmful recommendations were identified.
quote: Across both models, common limitations included limited patient‑level individualization, inconsistent red‑flag/referral triggers, and lack of verifiable, time‑stamped references; no harmful recommendations were identified, but safety omissions were present in both models.

title: AI-generated guidance for non-specialist physicians managing inflammatory bowel disease: expert evaluation and case-based testing of GPT-4 and DeepSeek

title: A Multi-Model, Pixel-Native Framework for Automated Computed Tomography Series Labeling and Characterization: Proof-of-Concept Study
outcome: Framework classification F1 on internal versus external TCIA CT cohorts
effect: Internal weighted F1 0.920-1.000, macro-F1 0.879-1.000; external weighted F1 0.946-1.000, macro-F1 0.777-0.929, so the external macro-F1 lower bound was lower.

title: A tri-modal, offline, and explainable framework for 12-lead electrocardiogram interpretation: fusing deterministic rules, a local residual network, and an agentic vision-language model
outcome: Macro-AUROC on external cohort without retraining versus internal test fold

quote: Applied without retraining to an independent cohort (Chapman-Shaoxing, n = 1599) the model retains a macro-AUROC of 0.898.

title: A tri-modal, offline, and explainable framework for 12-lead electrocardiogram interpretation: fusing deterministic rules, a local residual network, and an agentic vision-language model
outcome: AUROC under added noise with signal-quality gate

title: Tomosynthesis and Synthesized-2D Breast AI Outputs in a Biopsy-Referred Cohort: A Diagnostic Study of Agreement and Incremental Decision-Support Value
venue: Journal of imaging informatics in medicine
outcome: Cancers receiving a negative (low) AI score at the cohort-derived threshold
effect: 30 cancers were negative by the tomosynthesis output; 25 had no mammographic correlate on re-review, and breast density did not fully explain this. Authors advise against using a low AI score alone to downgrade a suspicious finding.
quote: Of 30 cancers negative by the tomosynthesis output, 25 had no mammographic correlate on re-review, and breast density did not fully explain this pattern.

title: Evaluating the impact of social determinants of health on model performance and fairness in artificial intelligence for glaucoma progression prediction
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
outcome: Fairness (GEO) and AUROC of SDoH-aware vs SDoH-unaware glaucoma progression models
effect: SDoH-aware model lowered GEO in internal set (0.098 vs 0.216) and mixed-population site (0.172 vs 0.378) with negligible AUROC change; no improvement at rural high-DCI site (0.241 vs 0.228).
quote: Incorporating SDoH features can improve algorithmic fairness regarding socioeconomic disparities without sacrificing predictive accuracy; however, these benefits do not universally transfer to external sites with demographically dissimilar cohorts.

title: Evaluating the impact of social determinants of health on model performance and fairness in artificial intelligence for glaucoma progression prediction
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
outcome: Model fairness metrics across socioeconomic subgroups and external sites
effect: Fairness (GEO) varied by site: improved internally (0.098 vs 0.216) and at mixed-population site (0.172 vs 0.378), marginal at urban site (0.491 vs 0.504), none at rural site (0.241 vs 0.228).
quote: AI models require rigorous external validation across diverse populations to ensure equity prior to clinical implementation.

title: Evaluating the impact of social determinants of health on model performance and fairness in artificial intelligence for glaucoma progression prediction
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
outcome: Fairness benefit transfer to external sites with demographically dissimilar cohorts
effect: Fairness gains did not generalize to a highly urbanized low-DCI site (0.491 vs 0.504) or a rural high-DCI site (0.241 vs 0.228).
quote: However, fairness benefits did not universally generalize to demographically dissimilar external cohorts.
